This has quickly become one of my favourite albums of this year and represents a major change in direction from the last two albums. There is more a groove to this album than even "Innerspeaker" and the guitars have either been removed or treated so much that one of Kevin's trademarks has all but disappeared. If you have been following Kevin over the last year, this really isn't much of a surprise. Consider his "Like a Version" cover of Andre 3000's "Prototype" and his work with Mark Ronson and they are very much in line with "Currents". "Cause I'm a Man" (a real highlight on the album) has been cut from the same cloth as "Prototype" and "Daffodils".

Another huge change is he did not use Dave Friedman on this album. Gone is the distortion and Lo-Fi sound, replaced by a much more cleaner sound. Some of the songs may appear to be simple in structure, but closer listening reveals a lot of detail and flourishes. This album is a real pleasure to listen to on headphones.

Some have mentioned Todd Rundgren's name as an influence and it is still here, but instead of copying Todd, Kevin has synthesized his influence into something new. Kevin openly admitted that "A Wizard a True Star" was a major influence on "Lonerism". "Currents" shows similarities to "Hermit of Mink Hollow". Both albums are about break ups and the aftermath (Melody Prochet, Bebe Beaull respectively), both albums were composed, written and performed by a single individual. There are large pop and blue eyed soul components in each album. Todd can only wish he could write a "Reality In Motion" or "Love / Paranoia" song now though his influence on these songs is evident.

For those that were disappointed in this album, especially for the lack of guitars, I can understand your view. Tame Impala's changes have been revolutionary instead of just evolutionary whichalways alienates some old fans. I personally find this to be a great album.

product_title: Sleep at the Edge of the Earth
review_headline: Wilderun's Sophomore Album Is the Stuff of Legends
review_body:
For their second album, Boston-based folk metal band Wilderun decided to pull out all of the stops. This can be a dangerous thing for some bands - add in a few eclectic instruments here, an orchestra, a choir, and they can end up sounding aimless and disjointed and/or just plain corny.

Wilderun avoided all of the pitfalls and reaped all of the gains, producing one of the best folk metal albums I've heard this decade. There is a definite progressive and power metal feel throughout, yet the band seems unconstrained by any single metal subgenre, weaving seamlessly in and out of passages that evoke the progressive death metal of Opeth, with moments of thrash and even black metal elements making an appearance. All of this is anchored by a definite Celtic/medieval feel, with orchestration often subtly embedded to reinforce the general movie-soundtrack epic-ness of the entire perfectly produced work.

The 11-minute masterpiece "The Means to Preserve" contains every one of the elements that blend to make this album an eye-opener, from beautiful tenor vocals, to soaring choruses with rich orchestration, to heavy death metal riffs with growls that would make Mikael Akerfeldt proud.

After dozens of listens, Sleep at the Edge of the Earth stands alongside my favorite folk metal albums, which include Ensiferum's self-titled, Moonsorrow's Kivenkantaja, and Falkenbach's Asa.

product_title: Anne Murray The Best Of...So Far - 20 Greatest Hits
review_body:
Greatest hits collections have a way of growing and evolving over the course of time, which is the case with this collection. We originally had a 10 song Anne Murray "Greatest Hits" album (and I can't even find that one on Amazon, which surprised me), and later we "moved up" to this one.

What happens with some greatest hits collections is that they don't QUITE have enough hits to fill the media, so they add in a few other good songs that really didn't chart. For example, "Nobody Loves Me Like You Do" didn't chart at all. "Now and Forever" peaked at #94. Those aren't really greatest hits, but they are enjoyable songs that you get as a bonus along with all the music that DID make the Top 50 on the US charts.

On various charts, Anne hit #1 with Snowbird, Danny's Song, A Love Song, You Won't See Me, You Needed Me, I Just Fall in Love Again, Shadows in the Moonlight, Broken Hearted Me, and Daydream Believer ... most from her immense popularity in the late 70s. She had several other Top 10 hits, and they are all here.

Highly recommended.

I heard about Mike Thompson from a friend of mine that's a big fan. He kept telling me to get Thompson's full length that just came out. I was like, "eh, ok, sure man". And for the bonus points, he's got Collin Raye trading lead vocals on Thunder Island! Awesome! Plus, Collin Raye isn't the only hot shot on this album. He has Mark Slaughter, from the band Slaughter, playing a bunch of guitar solos that will blow you away. I had no clue he was a guitar player, but he's on 5 or 6 songs, and he's awesome on each one. review_headline: A step down again, but not without its moments
review_body:
P.O.D. has had a pretty up and down career. After their triple platinum hit in Satellite, the guitarist Marcos Curiel left and the album that followed was pretty bad. Testify was a pretty good bounce-back album, while When Angels & Serpents Dance took another step down despite still being listenable. Murdered Love was the big bounce-back album that meshed Satellite and Testify together very well. But now there's a new album, and considering the pattern we've seen lately, perhaps it was inevitable that this would be another step down to a degree.

For this album, P.O.D. decided to try and do a concept album, complete with moments of dialogue in between songs. Unfortunately, the thing pretty much falls flat in their faces as the story itself is somewhat unclear. What they're trying to do is more obvious (show a guy finding redemption in life), but the path there is muddled. During several tracks, it seems as if the \\"character\\" has issues with varying degrees of paranoia (although it almost seems legit in the story) and apparent drug use. Okay, fine--but then there are a couple tracks that almost seem to have no place in the story at all (more on that later). And then the closing title track has an opening dialogue sequence that has seemingly no connection with the rest of the story. Ultimately, I found it easier to just screw the concept story and just focus on the songs themselves.

Let's start off by noting that \\"This Goes Out to You\\" is not a very good song and a horrible lead single. It's basically a dedication track with a generic riff and a cheesy chorus (\\"Hey! You! This goes out to you! For all the things that you do!\\"). Also of note is that it has no place in the story at all, thus making one wonder why it was on the final track list in the first place and not a stand-alone single or a deluxe edition track. Fortunately, this is mostly as bad as it gets--save for \\"Want It All,\\" which tries to experiment around with some odd horns and almostChristmas-y sounds and ends up being one of their worst songs in a while.

As for the rest of the songs, there's a few standouts as well as a few middle-ground songs. The album opener \\"Am I Awake\\" is definitely somewhere in the middle, as it has a good guitar riff but a mediocre chorus. The best part of it, oddly, is the opening myriad of sound bytes during the first 75 seconds. There's two more songs that have plenty of meat on the guitar front in \\"Somebody's Trying to Kill Me\\" and \\"Get Down\\" (which I also struggle to see where it fits in the \\"story\\") but it seems as if that's all they focused on for those two songs was the guitar, and forgot to include overall catchiness or great rhythm. They're decent songs and have better choruses than \\"Am I Awake,\\" but they're not highlights.

Two of the three better hard rock songs that are actually heavy punk songs--\\"Speed Demon\\" and \\"Revolucion.\\" They are both quite enjoyable, but the latter is probably the better of the two due in part to guest vocals from Lou Koller of Sick Of It All and a nice reggae interlude which helps shake things up a little bit. \\"Rise of NWO\\" is also a big highlight due to its strong chorus vocals and it actually being quite catchy.

The highlight of the album, by far, is \\"Criminal Conversations.\\" Nothing else on the album even comes close (except *maybe* \\"Rise of NWO\\"). Featuring Maria Brink from In This Moment, this song takes a slower pace with an ethereal feel. Sandoval's and Brink's vocals are combined to near perfection, and the song picks up in pace near the end for a big finish. If you do nothing else, at least buy this song by itself.

P.O.D., once again, tries to do something a little different. Give them credit for trying to branch out some more, and this album definitely has its moments, but overall it could've been a lot better. In the future, they should probably try to avoid concept albums, because it didn't work for them here. With that said, The Awakening is a decent album as a whole, but there are a couple massive missteps and it really doesn't live up to its name.

review_headline: A Score That Humanizes Addiction, A Wonderful Character Examination
review_body:
Film is a way for us to explore every aspect of our own humanity, and not everything is fairy tales and rainbows. I once asked someone if they watched True Detective when season 1 was airing. They said no, reasoning that there is enough rape and murder in reality so why would anyone want to watch that on TV. I understand it, I don’t agree with it. Exploring the darker sides of humanity is important and I feel the more you explore then the more you understand and form your own understandings. Such is the case with Animals, which explores a couple in love who slowly descend into a life of drug addiction. I found the score by Ian Hultquist to be something special here in that it really does a great job at humanizing people that most people see as scum and degenerates.

The score for Animals is so simple yet hits the characters with precision. Now even if the film had a large budget and wasn’t a small independent feature, I still think this approach would be perfect. The acoustic guitar is used for the music that accompanies the true Bobbie and Jude (our protagonists). This acoustic guitar is an analog instrument, it’s alive, it’s true and it’s not being masked or diffused. Once our characters slip into darkness we are introduced to an electronic trancelike transition point. This perfectly represent the euphoria of drug use, that escape that people seek. This of course then transitions into a darker more dreary electronic soundscape. At this point our characters are in the hell they created for themselves, and musically it's built around them as we travel through their journey to get back to their true selves. We finish back with guitars and euphoria at the end signaling a transformation. Now you may knock a score that only totals 16-minutes, but rest assured that it feels complete. Songs populate the rest of the soundtrack and are used within the film to weave with the score, but the fact that the score is a complete narrative makes it very effective.

The gentle strumming of an acoustic guitar introduces us to our loving couple before an electronic wash of despair and hopelessness consumes them in this story of addiction. While addiction is something we as a society seem to associate with inferior beings, Animals attempts to humanize and understand people in this situation. Ian Hultquist’s simple yet effective score achieves this through a gentle and nuanced approach.e.

Make no mistake, there is a lot of trance in this album but it has evolved, as all things should after over a decade. And like all previous years, the "on the beach" mix is a lot more relaxing trance than the "in the club" mix. And they both have different energies. Chances are, if you've enjoyed Armin's year albums in the past, you are going to enjoy this one, no doubt about it. There are some tracks on here which are absolutely stellar. review_headline: DON'T LET IT GO TO WASTE, FIND A WAY TO BUY THIS ALBUM!!!
review_body:
Never have I heard a band mature so much after just one album. While Living Creatures, the bands' first full length, was a somewhat loose concept album, Allomaternal takes Stolas to the next level of musicianship and lyrical writing. The story of a group of girls leaving home and finding their way in a savage world is told hauntingly with catchy vocals harshly screamed and beautifully sung by vocalist/guitarist Jason Weiche and drummer Carlo Marquez. When Carlo isn't busy singing his heart out he's playing the hell out of some drums. He goes from understated to in your face at the drop of a dime and it's nothing short of awe inspiring. Bassist RJ Reynolds sets a nice groove when he's not busy thinking of all the crazy ideas that make up this brutal story. Then there's guitarist Sergio Medina.... an absolute BEAST of a man when it comes to writing amazing guitar work. From blindingly fast and frantic on tracks "Fair Chase" and "Allokinetic" to sleepy and dreamy on tracks "Hiraeth" and "Somatic". The depth showcased from all four members is mightily impressive.

Overall this album is an incredible follow up from a young band that will hopefully be around for years to come. With an opening that lulls you into a false sense of calm, to an end that leaves you gasping and your jaw on the floor, it's hard to come away feeling less than a little curious about where this band is heading next. SO STOP READING AND BUY THIS THING ALREADY!

review_headline: An Amazing,Masterful Compilation of Four Full Albums!!! Radioactive Rocks!!!
review_body: This is an incredible four album compilation of Tommy Denander's project, RADIOACTIVE, first four albums dating back to 1991. This album is definitely some excellent rock 'n' roll and for the price it's a must have album!!! This is just some phenomenal writing, performing and production. You just won't get tired of listening to this great hard rockin' AOR album.Tommy Denander's guitar sears throughout the album! The vocals, the drumming and bass playing are all exceptional. Radioactive has a style all of it's own, it's own niche in the world of AOR greats. If I had to put Radioactive into a comparison I have to combine Toto (on steroids) with Mr. Mister, Survivor, throw in some Robin Trower & Procol Harum and maybe a little of the UK'S band FM and you'd be gettin' close. There is some amazing funk rock on this album as well that will take you back to the late '70's /early '80's with horns and jazz-rock interludes included (just listen to "Celebration of Innocence"track 7)! However, despite the age of some of these tunes in this LEGACY, the album sounds as if it is a brand new work. If you are an AOR fan or just want to hear a great deal of excellently written, performed and produced rock'n'roll...and a whole lot more for a low price, you owe it to yourself to download this work! You will not be disappointed! I have listened through the album numerous times and still come back to it and listen again even as I am writing this review. Just listen to "Waitin' For A Miracle" and you'll be hooked! What an absolute musical feast!

product_title: The World We Used to Know
review_headline: Funky, groovy, catchy, and very danceable
review_body:
How do I convince you to check this group out? I don't know exactly how to describe their sound. I've seen "djent" and "groove metal" used to describe them, but what if -- like me -- you're not familiar with those terms?

So, here's my attempt to describe them:
They're metal, but they're not brutal or super heavy. They're progressive, but they don't go off an extended musical tangents (except for one song). They stick to very familiar song-oriented structures, but the instrumentation is just so . . . out there. As with any progressive rock band worthy of the name, the musicianship is mindboggling. The guitar riffs and bass runs are just phenomenal, and often so in sync it's hard (for me) to tell which is which. The drums are at times off-kilter, but always drive the song forward without going off the rails. The music and the vocals are very melodic. Similar to Voyager Australia, they sound almost like a New Wave or techno band playing metal on real instruments instead of synthesizers. Funky, groovy, catchy, and very danceable. It's almost impossible to listen to them and not move at least a little bit.

All I can say, is if you like upbeat music, whether it's pop, techno, New Wave, rock, or metal, I think you'll like this.

Lorne Balfe has proven to be a masterful documentary composer with many of them under his belt so far. He brings a human and emotional touch to his doc scores that never make them feel like doc scores. This continues with Manny, and his score stands out here because the score is so focused from the POV of Manny Pacquiao that it instantly becomes an emotional portrait of a rags to riches story with all the varying complexities that come with that kind of success.

Manny’s journey from growing up poor in the Philippines to becoming one of the most successful boxers in the history of the sport is a story the whole world connects to. It also helps that he’s likable, never cocky and always caring towards others. Lorne helps us go on Manny’s journey from his impoverished childhood to having the whole world watch him in the ring. The score becomes very personal, and I think that happens through the instrumentation here. It doesn’t feel like generic filler or generic sounding. In fact it’s quite emotional and very touching. We literally start from the ground and work up. From the gentle plucking of a guitar to a more jazzy scene filled with ethnic percussion, the score carries its unique voice that is shaped around Manny as a person. Lorne does a fantastic job of shaping the bustling and growing aspects of Manny’s life beyond boxing as well. Pacquiao literally becomes a spokesman and role model for his home country and people, and it places this newfound responsibility on his shoulders. The music shows us how he accepts all this, it places an emotional stamp on moments in his life. When the score needs to build for that fighting spirit, it never feels hokey or forced. We get a surmounting rush and feel the energy, but we never lose the intimate nature of the music. I think the genuine nature of Manny Pacquiao as a human being lent itself to allow Lorne to craft one of his more emotionally rooted scores here. This isn’t some boxing documentary with that “fighting spirit”. I was very surprised to find gorgeous music that I really connected with. This is a real life human journey that we take through this music. It’s a simple and effective portrait of man who is excelling in what he does best, and being the best person he can be.

Manny is not a boxing score full of bravado and triumph. It’s a gorgeously executed portrait of rising from nothing and building character through extraordinary circumstances. Lorne has painted a wonderful journey of Pacquiao’s path from poverty to greatness, and all the complexities and responsibilities that he needed to shoulder as his success grew. Instead of making him seem like Superman, Lorne lets us into the fragility and emotionality of Manny as a human being. As a portrait of a human journey we can all relate to, it’s an emotionally resonant story that deserves your attention. It also proves how Balfe as a composer can craft a score that opens a window into a person instead of a life that most of us probably wouldn’t be able to relate to. Whether or not the documentary itself can be seen as a glorified PR piece or not doesn't negate how effective the score is within it.at “fighting spirit”. review_headline: To much a copy of early 80s influences.
review_body: I really loved Lust for Youth's "Growing Seeds" album. With the following album, "Perfect View" it was easy to see he was smoothing out his edges and heading in a more pop oriented direction. Yet both those albums still had many of the same attributes I enjoy - A mimicing of early eighties analog minimal wave, a smattering of grimy and dissonant electronics that added the sounds of early industrial acts into the mix, and a slight dour, ominous vibe of gothiness for good measure. I can recognize that this is a well produced, reasonably good group of synth pop songs.  But this album really didn't catch on for me. This album sounds EXACTLY like early Depeche Mode, Heaven 17 and especially New Order. Except it's not nearly as catchy. The leap from the previous albums dark tones and driving synth beats have given way to a more polished, BRIGHTER and less danceable record. It seems like both a transitional album and a less interesting commercial stab at the same time. Being an older listener like myself can have its disadvantages sometime when it comes to records that sound LESS than their influences. Because unless you are completely recontextualizing something for me - I need a better reason to play the music other than that it is a good facsimile of records I've known for 25 years! Terribe album art, too.

"You want something really different? An unanticipated whirlwind of delirium that defies pigeonholing in nine parts. Featuring 9 tracks of varying depth and purpose, our sorcery promises nothing to the dinner whores yet delivers the essential for those who have awakened." Our Newest Working and by Far the Re/Defining Artistic Element Of 1000 Young Revealed; "In Flagrante Delicto". Take your senses off the ordinary and the mind will follow.......

In a decisive step away from the comfortably familiar sonic bombast and cryptic vernacular exhibited by previous Works; “Agape e Katsika” (1992), “Blaspheme Often”(1992), “House of Saturn House of Mars” (1993), founders Khopesh Hahn and Otto Thoennes chose to reduce 1000 Young to its naturally occurring core dynamics. They began to experiment with the latent resonance and often subtle radiance of acoustic instrumentation and a redefined approach to the textural labyrinths of the duos signature vocal tapestry. In addition to these somewhat slight yet noticeable shifts in their conjoined musical expression, Thoennes and Hahn also made deliberate adjustments to the lyrical themes at play during the writing process of their latest Work “In Flagrante Delicto”, artfully describing the various permutations and incarnations experienced by the two men during their respective timelines as standalone Artists in league, subjectively and para-cosmically.

Among the nine pieces contained within their current Method, 1000 Young explore a desire for the particular brand of self-refinement attained through unflinching examinations of Intent, the beneficial disciplines of consensual isolation and the illuminations encountered therein, the Indulgent danger and ice cold sensuality of whip-thin winter Love and the ever appealing rendezvous by firelight in forests green with new arrivals and basement tenements alike, scorched beautifully black by centuries of elusive gypsy laughter.

Although only a Tool, “In Flagrante Delicto” entices and beckons the listener to venture within and without, deeper than they have ever Knowingly been before, on a journey towards An Awakening that, once Recognized and honestly pursued, Becomes the personal responsibility of All who are Capable of nurturing and maintaining the One Promise that True Sentience delivers.

product_title: The Many Faces Of Dorothy Donegan
review_headline: Two sets of Donegan live fourteen years apart
review_body:
This is a live album featuring Donegan's performances set fourteen years apart. I am not going to attempt to describe the music because there are sound samples on the MP3 version of the album's product page at [[ASIN:B0013SF404 The Many Faces Of Dorothy Donegan]]. If you are already a fan you know that the samples are only a hint of the music because Donegan is notorious for going off on tangents (musically).

I will say that if you are only now exploring Donegan's body of work this is a collection of songs that truly portray some of her many faces. I love the mix that spans ragtime to covering a Stevie Wonder hit. And everything in between.

The first nine tracks are from a performance in Antibes, France on July 22, 1975. Donegan is backed by Arvell Shaw on bass and Panama Francis on drums. All of the remaining tracks were recorded at Chicago's London House circa 1961.

Tracks 10 through 13 were recorded on April 14, 1961, and the dates of the remaining tracks are lost to time. Note that track 14 is misnamed at the time of this review. It's Misty and not the misspelled Mistry in the listing. Also lost to time are the names of her bassists and drummers from the London House dates. Unfortunately, that is too typical of Donegan's work, which is sadly under documented. But, on the positive side, she did leave behind a large body of recorded work and this album showcases her talents perfectly.

Can only image being 25 instead of 5 and being on the Minneapolis music scene in the mid 1980's. Almost out of nowhere over the course of a few short years? A functionally electronic funk sound,where synthesizers had taken over for the horn lines and the rhythm section ruled the day,was coming out of the city in massive doses. You had Prince and his proteges. But some of them wanted to express their own voice outside the talented purple puppet master. The Time's Jesse Johnson was the second,following the bands Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis a year or so earlier. And this first album showcased something that many may miss about that place and time.

"Be Your Man" and "Just Too Much" are right on time twin city grooves-full of phat bass and the flamboyant new wave synthesizer squiggles. "Let's Have Some Fun" adds some percussive high up on the neck rhythm guitar as yet more glue for an extension of the basic sound. "I Want My Girl" is a breezier pop ballad while "Special Love" is a slower song that's defined by a harder edged drum machine and electronic orchestration. "She Won't Let Go" is a lean,mean slice of Minneapolis funk that's right out of the sound of Jesse's former group. And my favorite on the album. "Can You Help Me" and "She's A Doll" add more of Jesse's Henrix style rock leadto the occasion along with that rhythm guitar flavor.

The more I hear this album? The more I love it. It's a very uptempo album. Full of that classic Minneapolis sound all the way. Listening to it though? There are strong indications that Jesse is not merely impersonating Prince at all. Years of digging deeper into the early 80's Twin City funk scene points to it being a thoroughly collaborative effort. And this album,which does include some members of the revamped latter edition of The Time as part of the revue,showcases how much Jesse probably contributed as an all in one guitarist/singer/songwriter/producer along with the scenes more famous musical son of the time. Anyone who doubts the talent of Mr. Jesse Johnson would be advised to seek out this high energy Minneapolis funk classic from the mid 80's!the scenes more famous musical son of the time. product_title: Mad Max: Fury Road - Original Motion Picture Soundtrack (Deluxe Version)
review_headline: The Ecstasy of Film Scoring Awaits Inside!
review_body: There isn't one thing I can say negatively about this score.  Not. One. Thing!  This is a film score you have to listen to in its entirety to appreciate fully and I'll admit that I didn't do that the first time around, so mesmerized was I by some of the tracks.  I had the opportunity to listen to a friend's copy of the score shortly before I watched the film in 3D and I was held captive by a handful of the tracks on the score.  Then, I bought my own copy and listened to it all the way through.  My reason for 5 stars is in no small part due to the fact that the score has been presented in its entirety.  There's not one piece of music I remember hearing in the film that isn't on this expanded soundtrack and THAT is always a plus!  I am truly amazed by Holkenborg's range in this score; from bombastic, percussive action to emotive pieces of tragic loss, there's not a track to be missed here.  Some of my favorite tracks are, "Storm Is Coming (Extended Version)", "Brothers In Arms (Extended Version)", "Many Mothers (Extended Version)", "Chapter Doof", "Let Them Up" and "Mary Jo Bassa (Bonus Track)".  These are hard choices, though, because all of the tracks blend together for a musical experience that is as exhilarating as the film is spectacular.  Holkenborg's work on Fury Road gets my highest praise and it's a score that I will cherish for years to come, an instant classic.

product_title: The Definitive Coasters (A Sides & B Sides)
review_headline: This is without doubt the definitive package.
review_body:
Definitive is the right word, both for this compilation and the group themselves. The Coasters were the most important, not to mention the best, vocal group of the rock'n'roll era, and this wonderful collection is at least as essential for lovers of rock'n'roll/r&b as the 50s recordings of Elvis, Jerry Lee Lewis, Chuck Berry and Little Richard.
What we have here are all 30 of the singles cut by The Coasters between the mid 50s and early 60s, almost all of them written by the peerless Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, along with the flip sides. Clever, funny, slangy, sometimes risque (for the time) lyrics and terrific tunes given their definitive renditions by a marvellous group of musicians and - of course - The Coasters themselves. And there's a fascinating alternative version of "I'm a hog for you" included wherein a snorting sax takes over the guitar role

Excellent soundtrack. You've got funky dance grooves like "the Power Plant," and more traditional Bionic Commando stuff in the theme (which is itself a loving tribute to the original soundtrack). In the first 20 seconds or so of the first track, you get a lot of this- the groove deepens and broadens as the melody begins to build itself off, and suddenly I'm parachuting into the game again.

I heard a snippet of this song once on the Netflix commercial in 2014 and instantly wanted to hear the whole song if it existed, and buy it if I could. I searched and searched but finally gave up. I even emailed the composer; no answer. I'm delighted to find it here on Amazon now  It's funny how a certain song and arrangement can immediately tickle your music bone and you're instantly humming it, even the lyrics heard once are memorized almost indelibly.  I experienced this with: Donovan's Wear Your Love Like Heaven; Pachelbel's Canon in D; The Exodus Theme; Al Stewart's Roads to Moscow; Patti Griffin's Cold As It Gets; Mike Oldfield's Tubular Bells (the main theme); The Beatles, You Never Give Me Your Money and With a Little Help From My Friends.  In the middle of the night I heard on a radio in the other room in 1979, just faintly, music that seared into my unconscious, which I heard the DJ back announce as John Renbourn's work on the album Black Balloon. It was decades before I ever found it. The track: Medley: The Mist Covered Mountains of Home / The Orphan / Tarboulton.  This tune, Real Magic, is perfect for a playlist on an MP3 player for personal listening, an easy going party, or in the car. It lifts your spirits, dare I say, magically? Congrats to the songwriter, the producer and the musicians for a work well done. Wish it were much better known!

05-04-2015  Here is the 1972 recordings of the Brahms Symphonies, plus fillers, the "Tragic Overture," and the "Haydn variations.  Kurt Sanderling leads the Dresden Staatskapelle in the famous venue, the Lukaskirche of Berlin.  They have survived on the "Eurodisc" label as taped in January and March of 1972, and, as I clearly recall, they were the very first CDs I bought right after my first player, a single play Denon, which lasted me some 10-13 years, starting in 1990, my first year as a radiology technologist fresh out of Indiana University.  Over a span of 3 discs, we get all four of these masterpieces, plus a nice booklet and, of course, the velvety sound of the Dresdeners.  The total elapsed timing is 3 hours, 17 minutes and 55 seconds, every moment filled with sublime sound and a nice sturdy plastic box with stiff outer case.  I di believe they ran me about $12 to $13.    ARTISTIC IMPRESSIONS   At thet time, upon first listening to the 2nd Symphony, I was swept away by the rapturous cello treatment of the main theme, as it has never sounded better to these old ears.  Over the ensuing 25 years, I have amassed cycles by the following, Wand, Solti/CSO, Barenboim/CSO, Levine/CSO, Szell/Cleveland, Haitink/Concertgebouw, Mackerras/Scottish, Haitink/LSO, Klemperer/Philharmonia, Boult, Bohm, etc.  Plus, a smattering of individual treatments from the likes of Walter, von Dohnanyi, some Giulini, Previn, Zinman and so on.  I am undecided regarding Alsop and Tennstedt, but may add them as well.   I  hovered about Brahms as to whether or not he was a GREAT composer, or not, since there was a familiarity to him that almost seduced me into regarding his work as "routine" and not possessing the high distinction of Beethoven.  All that was swept under the rug, after I began learning his chamber music, notably his Violin Sonatas, his solo piano pieces, generally from about Op. 116 onward.  The concerti soon became a hot topic with me, but the ViolinConcerto took a ong time to begin glowing.  Now, it has shone like a radiant star for well over 20-25 years, exemplified by Pearlman and Kennedy, and the "German Requiem," well, that's simply off the charts! !   Currently selling for under $4.00, this 3 CD set is a bargain at any price, so, I implore you to not delay and get yourself a copy today.  Even at Sanderling's slow tempi, this music sings like little else, and I find more long-term satisfaction with his music than even with Bruckner or Mahler.  the real treasure of this presentation is the sound of the rich, full and absolutely stunning tone and articulation of the Dresden Staatskapelle, perhaps the fifth greatest orchestra, maybe even replacing my beloved Chicagoans.   Regardless, it makes no point to argue but to simply embrace the overall effect of this set of compositions, and , with that, I really can say no more than this--------Brahms IS one of the GREAT composers, along side Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Haydn, and a "hybrid "of Bach/Mendelssohn/and perhaps Mahler (?).  Don't fret, Enjoy and just let this man speak to you.    As ever, best wishes for years of happy listening and a hearty God bless you, all, Tony.    A.  M.  D.  G.

"Love Notes" is a two-disc solo piano collection of original commissioned love songs by Danny Wright. With more than forty albums to his credit, Wright has touched and healed a lot of hearts along the way, so it is no surprise that people turn to him to create very special and personal gifts for loved ones. This collection presents some of the very best of those works. To complete each commission, Wright requests a photo of the subject and a paragraph that describes the person, and then he creates a one-of-a kind piece of music inspired by what he has seen and heard. Each piece is a gem unto itself, and with the common themes of love and passion, the set exudes warmth, tenderness, and, most importantly, love. The two CDs are comprised of a total of twenty tracks, all solo piano. With a combined total of 104 minutes of music, the discs would make wonderful background music for a romantic dinner, reading, driving, daydreaming, and any other activity that would be enhanced by warm, melodic piano music. It is also very satisfying and relaxing for listening with full attention (does anyone do that anymore?).

Danny Wright is one of the most popular and best-loved contemporary pianists in the world, and his Love Notes gives a very good indication of why. He is also an internationally-registered Steinway Artist and appears regularly in concert in Las Vegas. Classically-trained from an early age and into college, Wright is known for his arrangements of Broadway show tunes and movie themes, which are often flashy and demonstrate Wright’s virtuosity. His original music tends to be much more subdued and flowing and, I think, even more beautiful, as it comes from a spiritual place deep within. If you are new to Wright’s original compositions, this is a great place to start!

A treat for the ears, "Love Notes" is recommended!

review_headline: Review excerpt from Music and Media Focus
review_body:
This desire to help others through his music runs deep in Adam Andrew's motivation. In his words, \\"I planned out song themes ahead of time, wanting each song to be about emotional experiences that bring healing and inspiration to people.\\" The album is presented in a trilogy format, with three sections of four songs each, and captures the experience of a 24-hour retreat into nature for reflection and renewal.

The album opens with the title track, and like it's name, \\"A Thousand Springs,\\" right from the beginning, the music surges in a fast-moving current that evoked images of a powerful stream coursing along with foam and spray splashing in the sunlight. Adam's command of the keyboard is impressive, providing a number of \\"wow\\" moments for me throughout the album. There were a few musical surprises in the second track as Adam accents his neo-classical ambience with some unexpected bluesy phrasing that caught my attention right away.

Interestingly, the second section of the trilogy reflects a different facet of Adam's musical spectrum. The moods are more introspective and sometimes wistful as they embody ideas of forgiveness, letting go, grieving, and emptiness. As Adam shares: \\"I compose from places of both joy and sadness.\\" One of the things that stands out to me in Adam's playing and composing is his ability to move seamlessly through various emotional states, not only from song to song, but often within the boundaries of a particular composition. The last two tracks, \\"Believe\\" and \\"Foundation Trails,\\" are among my favorites for their wonderfully optimistic air, which leaves the listener feeling refreshed and renewed by the end of the album.

A Thousand Springs is an excellent showcase for this up and coming composer/pianist. Adam's well-developed sense of melody, and his impressive keyboard technique that is both sophisticated and sensitive, make for an evocative listening experience. It has been said that fans of solo piano artists such as Jim Brickman and David Lanz, would find a lot to like in Adam's music, and I can see that. With such a strong start as his first two albums indicate, Adam Andrews will be an artist to keep an eye on in the future as well as in the present.such as Jim Brickman and David Lanz, would find a lot to like in Adam's music, and I can see that. review_headline: Cinemascope: Music to Rediscover Music Appreciation With
review_body:
This disc had my full attention immediately. It wasn't solely because of Bill King's playing, the compositions, recording quality or any one thing that could be pointed to; it was everything about what came through the speakers. A look at the title, 'That's The Way of the World', brought a smile, a moment of reflection and the thought that "I could see that". The musical content of the second piece 'Audrey in Silk' immediately brought the notation about "history remembering her as pretty" to mind. This of course is despite her spending her teen years doing ballet to raise money for the Dutch Resistance against the Nazis" to mind. Like Audrey the beauty in Bill's music is radiant but it has depth that extends far beyond the obvious perceptions.

Bill's musical world is one where everything has its story and where the layers in those narratives peel themselves back to continually reveal new ones. It's a spectrum where images flow freely from the music regardless of whether the listener is familiar with the narrative or title. The sense of everything having a story is that strong. Reading a title however will direct the mind to specific corners of the imagination. With the title in mind the deliriously haunting melody of the beautiful 'Newsreel' evokes images of being in an old theatre watching a silent footage of events from that era. 'Strayhorn' conjures up pictures of musicians playing in dimly lit clubs with shadows almost closing in around them.

Those are just a few examples. The images drawn by the music are anything but set in stone though and without the titles the images shift. Being in a different mood when listening changes perceptions. Not referencing the titles and giving the imagination fee reign allows a myriad of impressions to form. Thoughts can be distinct or just blurs of vividly impressionistic swashes cascading past with profoundly focused emotional content. That's an illusion too though because, only after listening, does one realize their journey ran a gamut of emotional responses. Ultimately the only constant is that the music will draw varied and strong emotional reactions along with vivid impressions of strong visuals.

It would be wrong to describe this music as "easy listening" because there's so much to it but it's not only very easy to listen to, it also draws the listener back with an attraction that's magnetic. No matter how many times it's heard there's always a sense of having new facets, new beauty, or just the joy of revisiting an old and cherished friend. King's playing is a joy to listen to with the best elements of expression and spontaneity permeating each note. The recording, done at Inception Sound Studios by Engineer Mike Haas, has a translucently clarity that realizes the personal nature of King's playing fully.

The music is excellent from start to finish. Everything has a freedom of flow that exists within a framework that reveals its strength by keeping the listener securely focused. 'The Last Piano Lesson, 'Clear Mountain Moon', 'Desert Orchid', 'Just Us' and 'Cheyenne Autumn' to name some, are indescribably beautiful in ways that deepens their lustre with each hearing. It's a joy of constant discovery through music and one that's only receives its due when given the listener's undivided attention.

This is an incredible recording, and it's on my desert island list along with Dave Holland's Extensions, Miles' Kind of Blue, Coltrane's A Love Supreme, Joe Diorio's 20th Century Impressions and Steps' Smokin' in the Pit, Chick Corea's Three Quartets, and Keith Jarrett's Still Live, and Chick Corea's Light as a Feather.

There are several different types of tunes on this disc. Starting with my favorite, Lopsy Lu, this shuffle jazz-rock tune is all about the drums. Tony Williams, a desert island drummer of mine, along with Steve Gadd, Jack DeJohnette, Philly Joe and Vinnie Colaiuta, completely drives the show. I frequently play this tune for non-jazz people and they're always transfixed on the drumming. It's not that Tony overpowers anything, his drumming is just so magnetic on this tune, that it draws you in. For example, he really unfolds his playful side by accentuating the second triplet again and again. At one point, he throws the band, but graciously recoups with them, adding to the charm of the song. Jan Hammer's synth solo is one of my favorite air-synth pieces to perform.

"Power" is a simple, biting, driving jazz-rock tune. It starts with Tony playing a solo like the ones he used to warm up his clinics with. Very simple techniques: just singles and doubles in an unbroken stream, with superb dynamics and orchestration.

"Spanish Phases" is a string piece with solo bass. Stanley plays upright here, and shows his mastery.

"Life Suite Part 2" is a fast latin inspired tune with Tony again at the center. His style is playful, authoritative and dramatic at the same time. He plays a beautiful solo over the band with snares off, creating a timbale sound. With the amount of notes he plays, he maintains a light and loose sound, which is incredibly cool.

"Life Siute Part 4" is again a medium rocker. It starts very light and simple. Tony really holds back at the beginning but notice howhe adds incredible tension by leaving out a beat here and there. Then comes the buildup and Tony leads the ensemble into a truly majestic cooking sequence. A true joy to listen to.

Tommy's vocals have all of the emotional strength here that made Roy such a powerful front man before him, and the orchestration is simply sublime.

product_title: The Very Best Of Frankie Valli & The 4 Seasons
review_body: I can remember sitting on the kitchen counter (unless mom or dad were in the room) and a new song came over the radio behind me. WLS AM played the Silver Dollar Survey during the week day afternoons for "kids" after school. A new group introduced a fresh harmonious sound - "Sherry." My older sisters sat enthralled, listening to the sound. Up till now, young crooners tried to replace older ones or groups played fast licks on rhythm guitars. No one brought a "group" sound that didn't mimic Barber Shop (like the Four Lads and others). The Four Seasons were new, fresh and dominated the charts for the next two years before the Beach Boys knocked them out of first place. This CD/album represents the best of their sound. They pointed the way for groups like the Mamas and the Papas who emulated their style five years later.

One of the greatest albums I've heard the past year. Melodysheep is the artist behind the 'Symphony of Science' series, real name John Boswell. Behind this funny and intriguing remix of people like Carl Sagan, Bill Nye and Carolyn Porco were intelligent and catchy tunes that were kind of lost in the bizarreness of hearing scientists sing.

But on this album, Melodysheep shows what he's worth. It's a fantastically melodious album, at some points danceable and uplifting, and ambient and beautiful at others. It is a shame he hasn't received more attention than he has, because your speakers deserve this album on your next boat trip, beach sunset, rooftop barbecue or romantic candlelight dinner with a twist.

The only downside of this album is that it is such a showcase of the artist's abilities, that the jumps from genre to genre can easily catch the listener by surprise. Sweet piano tunes can quickly be followed by quite intense synths, not always to the best effect. But especially individually, these tracks can easily fit as the soundtrack of your best moments.

review_headline: 'The spirit of contemporary improvised music in it purest, most urgent state.'
review_body:
Born in Perth, West Australia, saxophonist and composer Troy Roberts has received numerous awards including 3 consecutive DownBeat Jazz Soloist Awards and 2 consecutive West Australian Music Industry Awards, a Grammy Nomination medal for his performance on Sammy Figueroa's \\"The Magician\\", and was the only Australian semi-finalist in the 2008 Thelonious Monk International Jazz Saxophone Competition. Graduating with a Bachelor of Music at the young age of 19, he has performed around Europe and the US extensively, and completed his Masters at the University of Miami.

Troy's 6th release reveals the secret riddles and musical rhymes of four wonderfully creative minds. This much-awaited acoustic quartet record is features one of the most innovative of forces and legendary jazz drummer Jeff `Tain' Watts, Venezuelan born pianist Silvano Monasterios, and the ever-swinging Chris Smith on bass.   Troy Roberts' \\"Secret Rhymes\\" is confirmation that redefinition of familiarity is entirely possible, and this will long be considered a new standard for years to come. This project embodies the spirit of contemporary improvised music in its purest and most urgent state, while maintaining the characteristics of nurturing and delicacy that give it balance and scope.  Troy has a unique voice, a sound that is unmistakably his.

The ensemble is Troy Roberts - tenor sax & compositions, Silvano Monasteros - piano, Jeff 'Tain' Watts - drum set, and Chris Smith - upright bass.

The tracks are as follows:
Stella by Starlight
Piano Concerto No. 2
Trick or Treat
Up Jumped Spring
The Little Things
Eyes Pie
Trip
Secret Rhymes

Tight interaction among these fine instrumentalists simply sets off the incredibly fine sound of Troy Roberts - the peerless on! Grady Harp, April 15

I first saw this song on the album Halloween Howls which I had purchased for a fun Halloween get together. When reading the back of the album, I saw track number 8 was called Spooky Scary Skeletons. I took the disk out of the case, shoved it in my player, went to the song, and pressed play. I heard the bones rattling, and spun around, just to find I was alone, and the spookiness that I had heard was coming from the speakers from my CD player. I reached to pause the song, but then a scary voice started singing, and I jerked back away from the counter. I was shivering from head to toe as I stepped backwards slowly. I began to envision spooky scary skeletons ganging around me. I scrambled for the door, and pedaled as fast as I could away from the house on my Westport Adult Folding Tricycle. I rode all through the night.  After traveling thirty two miles, I was starving, and longing for something to eat. The only available food source was the banana stand I saw down the road. I felt as if I could eat every banana that the little stand had, so I spent $1743.35 and purchased the stand. I peeled the first banana, then realized something horrible. I had left my Hutzler 571 Banana Slicer lying next to my CD player, so my large purchase was all for nothing. I continued on. After three days, my body could function, but I was dead on the inside. I knew I couldn't return to my former home, because nothing but spookiness lied there for me, but I also had no chance surviving on the streets. So I sold my tricycle and booked a room in a Motel 8. I am using their computer to warn everyone, this song is more powerful than you can imagine. It stripped me of everything I loved: my house, and my tricycle. So take this in mind when attempting to purchase this song, the consequences can be far worse that you would think. The army should use this song to spook their enemies, and ruin their lives too. Thank you.

product_title: Beethoven: Sonatas For Piano And Violin Nos. 5, 7 & 9
review_headline: Really superb performances from Emmy Verhey (with some help in sorting through the maze of listings on Amazon)
review_body:
I recently happened to learn about the Dutch violinist Emmy Verhey. Her performances of the Tchaikovsky and Mendelssohn violin concertos were included in a budget download I picked up here on Amazon ([[ASIN:B00TC2AC00 The History of Violin (100 Famous Songs)]], and they are excellent. It led me to look further into her repertoire to see what else I could find, and other classical fans familiar with her also had some recommendations, in particular her performances of the Beethoven violin sonatas with the Dutch pianist Carlos Moerdijk, the subject of this review and which I am now enjoying. Also recommended were her recordings of Bach's violin concertos, which I picked up as well ([[ASIN:B001U1MVAA Bach: The Complete Violin Concertos]]).

Some additional background concerning Emmy Verhey, a violinist who I think deserves greater recognition here. In 1966, at the age of 17, she was the youngest prize winning finalist at the International Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow. The wiki article on her reports that a week later, when she graduated from the Amsterdam Conservatory, \\"the public interest for her examination was so huge that it had to take place in the Great Hall (Grote Zaal) of the Concertgebouw.\\" To this day she remains the youngest ever prize winner at the Tchaikovsky competition. She went on to teach violin at Utrecht's Conservatory, from 1983 to 2002, and has performed and recorded worldwide. For much of her career she performed using the 1723 `Earl Spencer' Stradivarius that is now on loan to Scottish violinist Nicola Benedetti. Just last year she announced her retirement effective at the end of the 2014/2015 concert season.

Now, her performances are available on a variety of recordings and collections, but they are not always easy to find. Many are buried within budget compilations such as the \\"History of Violin\\" collection I mentioned above. Others are included in various box sets from Brilliant Classics. Searching through those various listings, here on Amazon and elsewhere, I was able to locate this recording of her Beethoven violin sonatas and purchased it (I obtained my copy from iTunes). I've been listening to it and it's as good as any I'm personally familiar with (my previous reference has been [[ASIN:B0000041UF Violin Sonatas]] performed by Itzhak Perlman and Vladimir Ashkenazy.

In fact I have to say that I personally prefer Verhey's violin performances to Perlman's. I find that she has a warmer tone, smoother and less aggressive, and particularly fine in the quiet delicate passages. She is a very fine violinist, that is something I am coming to appreciate.

These recordings also have a very good balance between the violin and piano, very nicely done job by the technicians in producing the recording.

The recordings are from live recital performances - all of the sonatas were recorded on one day in July, 1990, at three concerts given at the 'Beurs van Berlage' in Amsterdam. I have not noticed any discernable audience noise yet in my listening. The applause is substantial at the end of each sonata.

I give this 5 stars without hesitation, especially given the extremely reasonable pricing here on Amazon for the set of complete violin sonatas.

review_body: Europe is a group of very talented musicians. Out front is Joey Tempest, one of the finest voices in rock. When they debuted in the 1980's we heard a hard edge progressive band. Seven Doors Hotel is still one of my favorite songs. The late 80's brought The Final Countdown. This release cemented Europe as melodic pop metal masters! Heavy keyboards permeated their sound. Out of this World followed the same basic format, and was pure 80"s rock bliss. Prisoners In Paradise strayed away from the formula a little, but not much. Some harder edge sounds returned in some songs to mix with the keyboard heavy sound. Prisoners is still my favourite Europe release. After a hiatus Europe returned. We are now at studio album no. 5 of Europe's return. War of Kings is a blues rock masterpiece. At times you would get the feeling this was a Deep Purple album if Joey wasn't singing. John Norum plays beautifully. Some great guitars are on this release. You hear the keys, but Mic is  channeling his inner Jon Lord. product_title: The Music of Joe Henderson and Original Compositions Live: Sfjazz Center October 23 Through 26, 2014
review_headline: Octet as Jazz Orchestra: Live Sessions
review_body:
The 2014 membership of the SFJAZZ Collective dedicated their 2-CD album to the works of tenor saxophonist Joe Henderson (1937-2001), including 8 familiar and lesser known works among the 18 tracks. The octet consists of saxophonists Miguez Zenón and David Sánchez; Avishai Cohen, trumpet; Warren Wolf, vibraphone; Robin Eubanks on trombone; Edward Simon at the piano; and rhythm men Matt Pensman, bass, and Obed Calvaire, drums. Each musician contributed a composition to the album. [Disc 1] This international ensemble commences their live sessions with Henderson's Recorda-Me (arranged by Zenón), and immediately we hear a well-conceived rendition developed against an Afrobeat, featuring muted trumpet at the outset and a fade after all the other instruments make their entrances. The melodic A Shade of Jade (arranged by Simon) begins with rising and lowering piano arpeggios, as a series of rapid waves, with the vibraphone taking up the driving, energetic beat and horns adding emphasis; mid way, after a fanfare, the music turns hard bop with alto sax at the lead. Penman's Big Tent, Little Tent is a commentary on inclusiveness and exclusiveness within the social politic and within ourselves; of moderate tempo, bright solos and dense harmonic combinations alternate. Eubanks' noisy introduction gels into sonority of horns and a 5/4 bounce; the trombone makes its statement, followed by saxophone and then piano improvisations with Afro-Cuban flavors. Henderson's Inner Urge (Cohen, arranger) is crafted with complex classical approaches, and Cohen admits to immersion in Rachmaninoff. Wolf's Four Stars from Heaven are his children and the title of his sweet and joyous composition; his vibraphone of course is featured. The works ends metaphorically with descending notes. Samuel Beckett wrote Waiting for Godot and David Sánchez wrote Eternal Wait; with similar themes, the jazz piece is comparatively quiet and soft and with beauty, including the bass solo, but the flow never reaches a climax or fruition and instead fades. Drummer Calvaire arranged Henderson's Fire with a good measure of funk and fizz. Chordal horns and swirling percussive keys and mallets lead to solos: saxophone, trombone, and drums in Latin descarga with piano.

[Disc 2] Y Todavia La Quiero (arranged by Sánchez) has a fine, intricate rhythmic base. It launches a soaring alto, followed by vibraphone elaborations and horns marking the rhythmic patterns. The piece is wonderful in its joyous complexity. Next is Afro-Centric (Penman arranged). It begins as a lone bass and soon a noir cast is reflected as the other instruments join in the mystery. Zenón's Synthesis of A Band has 3 parts full of abstraction and opportunity for improvisational explorations, some bright and lyrical, some busy and edgy. And then we come to Black Narcissus: Eubanks arranged it with different harmonies and rendered it slower, hence a bit more solemn although the warmth still is felt. Simon's Locura is a road trip (from Florida to California to be exact) and is episodic, dark, and adventurous. As an artist develops, the created art evolves; Cohen's Evolution is commentary of how some tunes seem to evolve over time. It is a slow work. Beginning with sketchy notes, it grows and expands as the piece proceeds, and at the bridge mid way it is set free and lives with each soloist. Calvaire's Absolvents seeks forgiveness. The music pleads, cries, and is tender. The final track of the album is Henderson's Jinrikisha (Wolf is arranger). It is a good way to say good-bye. The interplay following the introductory riff is filled with an elaborate architecture of structures, expressive improvisations, and at times wild abandon.

Package notes give brief biosketches of each musician, of Joe Henderson, and some information of SFJAZZ (the festivals and new dedicated venue in Civic Center) and the history of the SFJAZZ Collective. To say that this is a tight ensemble of highly talented jazz pros who mesh well is an understatement. They embody contemporary mainstream jazz with an international background.o mesh well is an understatement. They embody contemporary mainstream jazz with an international background.

product_title: Hermann Reutter : Die Brücke Von San Luis Ray (Wien 1955)
review_headline: Dry and colorless, but probably worth hearing for those with a special interest in this kind of thing
review_body: I have often encountered the name of Hermann Reutter (1900-1985), but his extensive musical output (including a series of operas) has been poorly served on disc, except, perhaps, for his songs. Hearing this recording of Die Brücke von San Luis Rey, Scenes from the Novel The Bridge of San Luis Rey by Thornton Wilder, from 1954 may perhaps give a clue as to why. Now, I hasten to add that I have little idea of precisely how representative this opera is of Reutter’s output, but this is written in a sort of dry, acerbic style – somewhere between Weill and Egk – that I don’t think has aged particularly well (though I wouldn't say that of Weill and Egk). There is lots of narration to make all the action and character presentation fit within the relatively short time-frame of the opera, and the musical numbers are pretty inconsequential; simple, austere and based on short, breathless thematic figures that Reutter adamantly refuses to develop. To say that the music is written in service of the text would be an understatement – it rather seems superfluous. It is the kind of style that would intuitively perhaps have made sense for an acerbic political commentary, but Wilder’s story is rather an existential one that Reutter delivers deadpan and matter-of-factly. That said, if you imagine that this could be your kind of thing, then I suppose it is worth hearing once – I did, I admit, find if mildly clever and enjoyable on my first hearing, less so on the follow-ups. I have no complaints about the performance – it’s not like they are given much to work with anyways, and the sound, although dry mono, surely doesn’t miss anything in music like this. Don’t expect much from the booklet, but if you understand German you really don’t need a libretto for a work like this. A curiosity, mainly for the specialist, though I am, I suppose, in the end glad to have heard it.

This is a brave move! Emika (nee Ema Jolly; English-born/Berlin-based electronic composer) has already
turned in two fine albums : her eponymous 2011 debut and 2013's 'DVA', are both splendidly idiosyncratic
examples of the kind of music it is possible to create with technology and a well-honed imagination.

That her third release, 'Klavirni', finds her alone with her piano is a nice surprise. I believe that these compositions
came about, in-part, following a visit back to her home town Milton Keynes (Berlin! Berlin! Now I Understand!)
in the Winter of 2013/2014 where her childhood piano still sits quietly awaiting her return. That she has also
spoken of her admiration for the work of Czech composer Leos Janacek is occasionally evident in these thirteen
solo pieces ( I have long loved his piano cycle 'On The Overgrown Path' myself) and there is something which
feels entirely right about stripping back her muse to the bleached bare bones to see what might be revealed.

Allowing us to hear the lid of her instrument open with a little bang on the second piece 'Dilo 5'
(the compositions are numbered 4 - 16 but we are given no clue as to what might have happened to
numbers 1 - 3!) is a pertinent reminder of the visceral connection between the piano and the player.

Sometimes the inventions are performed "cold" and in one take (e.g. 'Dilo 4') and in others undergo
some additional sonic manipulation with the application of echo and reverb ( 'Dilo 5' and 'Dilo 8')
which make the notes hang in the air like writhing apparitions. This is especially evident on the
strangely haunting 'Dilo 9' where the melody from 'The Daring Young Man On The Flying Trapeze'
makes an appearance in quasi-nightmarish form. I was particularly drawn to the lovely 'Dilo 7' with
its evocative folksong-like tune and the beautifully fragile 'Dilo 15' which sounds as though it might
have beenrecorded under water. All-in-all there is truly nothing not to love in this absorbing project.

I heartily applaud Ms Jolly both for her rich musical acuity and her nerve!

Riverside just keep impressing. Let me start by saying that I love progressive rock and progressive metal, and rank Riverside's Second Life Syndrome among the very best of the genre.

This album keeps the dark, progressive atmosphere of its predecessors, but takes a bit of a different musical approach. The wistful vocals, the catchy melodies, the solid musicianship and the superb songwriting are still present in spades, though it took me a number of listens until they became readily apparent. The album sounds more raw, and incorporates more straightforward rock elements in some of its songs. As a previous reviewer mentioned, at times it sounds like Deep Purple, and I think that's spot on. So basically it's a combination of dark progressive rock with an older, classic rock sound and feel.

If you don't like it at first, if it seems to be a bit too straightforward, give it a few listens. It will grow on you. It's not Second Life Syndrome, but it is one heck of a solid progressive rock album, and is a real pleasure to listen to. Keep up the good work, guys.

Appreciating the music of Stars of the Lid, I followed former Star Adam Wiltzie all the way to his most excellent project called A Winged Victory for the Sullen.  Then I decided to track down the other Star, Brian McBride.  He is now teaming up with Kenneth James Gibson, recording as Bell Gardens, and their 2nd full-length album is *Slow Dawns for Lost Conclusions*.  Their sound is more structured and tune-oriented than Stars' was, but they still have a gauzy, atmospheric quality to the songs.  That comes from the relatively slow tempos and lush, layered vocals.  The Bell Gardens' vocals remind me somewhat The Czars' harmonies or The Engineers "ghost choir" effect; Brian and Ken sing in unison and in harmony without a single voice carrying the melody.  The songs resonate in one's mind during and after listening to them.

review_headline: Intense sonic assault, if only 24+ minutes!
review_body:
This band's name conjures up freak folk, or gently plucked melodies in spring meadows. Recorded and engineered by this York, England, trio in abandoned sheds in a Georgian garden just outside that city, this album to the uninitiated may suggest ballads and its title comfort.

Instead, From Safer Place, the band's first full-length album, unleashes an assault of hardcore and post-punk, as if rather from New York (or at least Brooklyn these trendy days).

"New Sense" roars straight at you, opening this short, intense album (less than 25 minutes), with anthemic back-and-forth vocals barked by songwriter Jonathan Meager. Joined on guitars and vocals by Oliver Grabowski, the pair capture the early-'80s delivery of sharp, tuneful power.

The pace sustains itself into "I'm Not a Man". The band's recording and engineering allows some space into the production. This allows the closing echo of Paddy Carley's drums to resound a moment. Such touches demonstrate how the trio has listened to their forebears, and learned lessons.

Hammering away like a Rites of Spring single from thirty years ago, "A Certain Pleasure" shifts between a loud punch and a catchy jangle. Textural shifts enrich the effect of what could have been a monolithic tribute to aggression. Meager has credited Guy Debord and the French Situationists as influences for his lyrics, but I admit their content, at least on MP3 files sent for preview, eluded me.

Given the band covered Joy Division's "Twenty-Four Hours" on an earlier single, "Black Water" recalls the apocalyptic doom of that seminal group, before it lurches into hardcore, and then back and forth. Vocals remind me of Dischord Records' acts from the 80s onward, and again, these keep the listener alert. The breakneck pace of such movements keeps the tracks fresher, and less predictable.

As if a lost track from New Day Rising, "Natural Vision" churns a guitar riff into tight drum slams, crunching down the howling into the two singers joining to shout down whatever darkness endures.

The title track lightens the severe sonic mood a bit, although the voices keep harsh. Shuffled guitars above the nimble percussion enable the listener to appreciate this subtly textured arrangement. Like many tracks on this, it ends suddenly, and the density of this recording works best in such bursts.

Repeated listening brings out contrasts that audiences of this genre may appreciate. "Remains" chooses a telegraphic pattern for its main structure, but it opens up moments of calm within the hurricane rush of massed vocals and guitars, quite a knack for only three musicians to create.

I wondered if an Orwellian homage might account for the title of "In Front of the Chestnut Tree". Winston Smith's haunting betrayal as memorialized in another song about such a tree may or may not be appropriate. After all, this song remains an instrumental, as Mission of Burma might have penned.

The gentler strains opening "Recurring Face" don't last long. Another race against time, as Fawn Spots crams in a penultimate blast. "Basque Knife" wraps it up with great slabs of sound trundling back and forth, as the guitars chime over the pounding but adroit percussion. Finally, a voice enters.

This call and response, the delay and the satisfaction, comprises the appeal of this genre. It will please those who welcome the frenzy of loud music conveyed with attention to instrumentation and layers of vocals not quite buried in the thick mix. Fawn Spots' debut promises not only an homage to past masters of this intelligent music, but indicates a worthy heir to those passionate 80s punk bands.a guitar riff into tight drum slams, crunching down the howling into the two singers joining to shout down whatever darkness endures.

review_headline: Middle of the Road album - not bad for a debut.  3 great songs, only 1 pretty bad one.  Recommend at the right price.
review_body:
For a debut album, this is pretty good, really. There are 3 great songs, a couple of pretty good songs and the rest are album fillers, really. Currently, it's at $9.99 for the record. I would wait until the price comes down to $5 before you buy it. If all else fails, buy the 3 great songs, or hit up the Greatest Hits album released in 2002, which has the 3 best songs from this album on it. Or - once they re-stock it - you can pick up What Mattered Most and Living In A Moment sold together for $15. Below is my review of the individual songs. Hope it helps :)

The best song on the album is, in fact, the title track - What Mattered Most. The author of the song laments the fact that, though he paid attention to the love of his life, and THOUGHT he knew everything that he should know about her, somehow he missed to big picture because he paid too much attention to the smallest details. As the song says, "I missed the forest for the trees". The tone of the song isn't one that makes you cry through it. It's kind of an upbeat sad song, if that makes sense. He realizes too late the things he knows about his love, aren't the actual important things. He paid attention to details, rather than to her. Great song.

The next best song - I Want My Goodbye Back. This is a rollicking little number that will get your foot tapping and your head bobbing while you sing out loud. All about a man who decided to say goodbye to his love, and comes to find out that he was an idiot and needs to figure out what he has to do to get her back. "momentary, temporary lack of self control". Great song for driving down the road or sitting in rush-hour traffic to take your mind off your troubles.

The third great song is a duet with Stephanie Bentley (whose career never took off, but she has a good voice, especially in combination with Ty's - although my favorite duet partner for him is Jamie O'Neal - they really sound great together). Thesong is a very, very sad song called "Heart Half Empty". It's a beautiful, sweet ballad that bounces between two lovers who have come to the end of their road together and aren't really sure how they should be feeling about it - melancholy for the loss, or hopeful for a future happiness. "should I laugh / or should I cry / love you, hate you, live or die". More of a maudlin song than a cry-in-your-beer tune.

The rest of the songs on the record are typical country fillers. "Pretty Good Thing" will get your toes tapping as he talks about a woman who basically ran roughshod over him during their relationship and he realizes it could have been much worse. "Summer Was A Bummer" is probably my least favorite song. It's so boring, honestly. I listened to it 3 times while re-listening to the record for this review, and I couldn't tell you what it was about, in any detail. Fair to say - his summer wasn't much fun :) "You Don't Mess Around With Jim" is the typical country record that talks about a Southern Born man who is meant to be a bad ass kind of dude. Not bad, but nothing you're not going to hunt down the CD so you can hear that song by itself. "You Just Get One" is actually a sweet little song. As you probably guessed from the title, he is talking that kind of relates dating different people to songs (sometimes they make you laugh, sometimes they make you cry, etc), but you only get one true/real love. "In Your Face" is this record's attempt to have an up-tempo song, but kind of fails. Tragically fails. Basically he is trying to tell the girl that everything she feels is showing on her face, so he can read her pretty well. Again, this is one of those that when I hear it, I skip on to the next one.

The last two songs on the record are actually on the upper echelon of songs on the record. "Love At 90 Miles An Hour" is they typical (though for once typical isn't a bad word) teenagers-in-love-hitting-the-backroads-driving song. It's a good one to bop your head to while you're in the car. And the last song - Hat Full Of Rain - is a very upbeat song that jumps off the record - just kidding. As you can guess from the name of the song, it's a sad song. A very slow, very sad song. It's really not a bad song. It's just one of those that if you're already depressed and you WANT to cry and get more depressed - dust this song off and listen to it. But if you're in a good mood and you want to stay that way? Bypass that one.

So here it is in black and white - my ratings for each song. Make your own decisions, of course, but I hope my notes have helped. If you're a huge Ty Herndon fan, buy the record (but wait for a good deal!), but if you have a passing fancy and just heard a couple songs and you like his voice - buy the 3 great songs and let the album go. In order of best to worse songs

5 stars - "What Mattered Most" (Track 1) [up-tempo]

4 stars - "Heart Half Empty" (Track 5) [medium tempo]; "I Want My Goodbye Back" (Track 6) [up-tempo]

3 1/2 stars - "Love At 90 Miles An Hour" (Track 9) [up-tempo]

3 stars - "Pretty Good Thing" (Track 2) [up-tempo]; "You Just Get One" (Track 7) [slow tempo]

2 1/2 stars - "Hat Full Of Rain" (Track 10) [slow tempo]

2 stars - "You Don't Mess Around With Jim" (Track 4) [up-tempo]; "In Your Face" (Track 8) [up-tempo]

1/2 star - "Summer Was A Bummer" (Track 3) [slow tempo]

If you're over the age of 25 (which most of you aren't), then you might want to YouTube Lee Hazlewood & Nancy Sinatra's classic duets over 3 collaborative albums and a sound that still haunts after 50 years, especially since they had the use of one of the greatest guitarists EVER - the immortal Duane Eddy.

Well, this band, "The Handsome Family," have decided to re-create their sound, their lazy lyrical goodness, the echoes of both acoustic and bass guitars wailing in the background, and gave it just a little more energy then their original predecessors.

Their result is still pretty amazing, and just a touch haunting, and I commend them for their attempt to copy Hazlewood and Sinatra... but the originals sounded better and had a much more clearer delivered message of hopelessness, depression and sadness.

Sorry guys... there's nothing like the real thing.

review_headline: Haunting and harsh, but powerful modern rock number
review_body:
I'll admit, when I saw this song was part of the soundtrack of the movie \\"The Host,\\" I very nearly gave it a pass. I had liked the song when I first heard it, and somehow Weird Al's parody of it, [[ASIN:B00L6GKKOI Inactive]], just made me want to own a copy of the original song even more. (Singers and songwriters take note -- Weird Al is great publicity for your music.) But when I searched for the song on Amazon I saw that there were a few versions available... including the soundtrack version. The fact that it's connected to a Stephanie Meyer movie made me balk at first -- amazing how one inconsequential factor can still taint our enjoyment of something -- but in the end I decided to download it anyhow.

Despite coming from a lackluster movie, Imagine Dragons' \\"Radioactive\\" is a powerful and eerie rock anthem, painting a bleak picture with its lyrics and musical accompaniment.

As one might imagine from a song with such a provocative title, \\"Radioactive\\" portrays a world in ruins, with the survivors \\"sweating rust\\" and \\"breathing chemicals\\" as they speak about the apocalypse and the \\"new age.\\" The eerie, almost harsh electronic sounds accompanying the guitars and drums helps add to the feeling of a world rendered alien and hostile. The lead singer's voice is nothing spectacular, but it does its job, and in the end it's the instrumentals that help carry this song, giving it a harsh but somehow hopeful tone throughout.

If you like modern rock music, give this a shot. It's a powerful and haunting number that quite deserves its popularity.

HINDU LOVE GODS: For the handful of music fetishists who have pondered what WARREN ZEVON would sound like if he rocked out for a whole platter or how R.E.M. would fare minus front man MICHAEL STIPE, here's the short, unvarnished answer. There are certainly worse ways to digest roots of rock legends ROBERT JOHNSON, WOODY GUTHRIE and GEORGE JONES than via HINDU LOVE GODS' ragged but righteous after hours jam session. ZEVON's leathery roadhouse-ready yowl, PETER BUCK's brawny axe attack, BILL BERRY's thrumming bass lines and MIKE MILLS' relentless drum kit bashing stir up a sh!tstorm of sawdust, sweat and suds. Surprisingly effective rave ups of PRINCE's RASPBERRY BERET and GEORGIA SATELLITES' BATTESHIP CHAINS are the only concessions to modern times; everything else is strictly Chitlin' Circuit nirvana, from ALBERT KING's CROSSCUT SAW to that hoariest of blooze staples, MUDDY WATERS' MANNISH BOY. Sandwiched somewhere between THE FLINTSTONES and THE ROLLING STONES, HINDU LOVE GODS was THE stupor-group of 1990...they took no prisoners and made no apologies for it.

review_body:
Us Gen-X'ers have had more than our fair share of childhood favorites ruined by Millennials. Oh Cecilia by the Vamps is a stand-out exception.

Now I love (capital \\"L\\"...heck, capital all the letters... LOVE) Simon & Garfunkel, so rearranging their iconic songwriting is risky business for even the most tenured music vets. Sometimes a good cover comes along, but rarely a good re-work. The Vamps were able to pull apart the melody of the song, swap the folk influence for a reggae sound, trade the strumming six-string for a deliberate picking, and meld the whole thing back together in a way that keeps the soul of [[ASIN:B00136LTT6 Cecilia]], but makes it musically relevant today.

I never thought I would say I prefer another version over a Paul Simon original, but I kinda do. What The Vamps (or their label, at least) has done borders on brilliant. I will confess to never having heard of your band, or Shawn Mendes, before, but well done, boys!
