The first CD Moore has released in three years proves worth the wait, we can really hear how he has continually honed his craft, returning to what works, adding strengthening elements and maintaing the freshness. I have often wondered if Moore had been more aggressively promoted, would he be a household name today. Yet, what I hear in this CD is a true poet and songwriter who has also fully lived a "real life" and it informs his songs. I'm always delighted with how Moore seamlessly switches between language that qualifies as literary poetry and much more "everyday" language, even the rare (but perfectly timed) everyday expression. Other times he seems to invent "everyday expressions" we've never actually heard before.

Moore's sound has co-evolved with his word. I don't want to say the sound "defies genre" because that would imply some kind of rebellious effort where this is honest music. Like the best of the late Johnny Cash recordings, it's truly American, blending elements of folk, blues, rock and punk without sounding like fusion. Moore's voice is beautiful, authentic and vulnerable but flawless. He knows how to work what he has. One disadvantage of the MP3 is I'm not sure who the personnel is on this recording but it sounds like at least some of the players are musicians who have been collaborating with him for years. Some of the past recordings have been "catchier" but these tracks are compelling and poignant and blending of words and sound is at an all new high.

review_headline: Squelchy Eluchqy nods easily around a dubby bassline and by the fourth track ...
review_body:
STYLE
December 2014
Deep downtempo electronica.
Spatialize delivers Radial in conjunction with On The Edge Of Forever as the somewhat darker, more dance-oriented half of a twin release. Radial opens with a sinewy, tenebrous, driving energy about it that is retained until close to the final wind down; the tempo rises and falls, dipping into some bobbing dub grooves in places, but the velvet darkness and prowling dynamism is a near-constant feature. The melodic patterns are tastefully understated, picked out by a range of liquid-clear synths, electric guitar and bright chimes. Arpeggios ripple and burble around the beats, evolving and shapeshifting frequently, peripheral fx tightly embellishing the soundscape. A range of human touches haunt the shadows: spoken phrases; wistful words almost lost under heavy processing; hints of exotic players; tablas and hand drum samples.

IN DEPTH
Nommo opens Radial with shimmering harmonics and twisting metallics layered into a rich ambient texture - some strongly effected German speech introduces the first of multiple arps before a rubbery bass and languid drum beat roll in. Unhurried, gradually unfurling, this gutsy nocturne slinks and grooves its way neatly into the similarly paced Koog and Zalem where some echoing, deftly gated female vocalisations join the party. Squelchy Eluchqy nods easily around a dubby bassline and by the fourth track Floating World, the pace drops into a ponderous swaying rhythm. Eastern instruments away far into the mix lead into a slow tribal beat with lush, lush depth - hits reverberating in space and clean guitar lines playing among the sequence cycles. A dense buoyant bass line forms the mid-tempo backbone to the lustrous Eden, bombing and bouncing in near percussive manner, whilst twinkling synths and summer evening pianos add to the colour. Elusive Symmetry is a collaborative composition with Matt Hillier, samples and synths credited to man behind Ishq. The final two tracks drop the tempo - One Priceless Moment and Altamira both demonstrating the evident mastery over the rhythm section that characterises so much of Spatialize's output - down here in the lower bpms the work put into blending programmed and real drum sounds alongside basses that throb right down in the stomach really stands out. Meandering piano, hypnotic pads, musing voices, tinkling chimes, soporific fade out...

ARTWORK
Cover art for this digital release comes in the form of a bright wheel of radial lights. Spokes, discs, hub and radiance are all created by revolving light patterns of varying degrees of distortion. Full of intricate depth, this image seems fractal in complexity. Straw-hued beams stretch and criss-cross into circular shapes, a warm yellow-orange softness seemingly glowing in the spaces between.

OVERALL
West-Country based UK musician/producer Neil Butler releases Radial (along with On The Edge Of Forever) as a digital package that can be downloaded in all the relevant formats. It has been some time since the previous Spatialize album In The Midst Of Myriads came out back in 2006 - so a double release is most welcome. This collection is comprised of nine mid-length arrangements hovering around the five, six or seven minute mark - just right for the crepuscular dance floor but equally engrossing for attentive listening. You can explore Radial via the project's Bandcamp page or CD Baby if you prefer.

This disc showcases his way with jazz standards, which is typically iconoclastic and uniquely Holdsworth.

I'm only deducting one star for one specific reason - the keyboard player on this release apparently insisted on using a digital piano for this recording (well documented in some of Allan's interviews), and I find 1) his tone is jarring, bright and lacks depth and subtlety, and 2) while his linear soloing can be impressive, his tendency to over-comp with his LH detracts mightily from the overall presentation. And yes, I'm a professional jazz pianist and that's why these things detract from my listening enjoyment.

No one knows exactly what happened to Tom Waits between 1980 and 1983, but whatever occurred had explosively mystical staying power. It changed everything. Some said Waits simply met his wife, Kathleen Brennan, who pushed him to the limits of his yet unfulfilled potential. Others say he stumbled upon, or Brennan introduced him to, the wildly angular and indescribably arcane music of Don Van Vliet, better known as Captain Beefheart. Hints of this shocking second wind metamorphosis pepper Waits' 1980 \\"Heartattack and Vine,\\" but that album and its follow up three years later, the jaw-droppingly inventive \\"Swordfishtrombones,\\" almost sound as though they emerged from anti-matter opposites. Were it not for the immensely distinctive voice, one could conjecture that Waits had either become possessed \\"Being John Malkovich\\" style or some evil impresario had just retired the old Waits and fashioned a new one from a cauldron bubbling with wood planks, ball peen hammers and accordions breathing in reverse. Rarely do artists reinvent themselves to the extent that they become nearly unrecognizable. Something frightening, chilling, glorious or ineffable happened. Ever since Waits has left his diner stool and sweaty unshaved piano behind and spewed one beautifully beguiling masterpiece after another.

The thumping ensemble of descending staccato horn and guitar blats undergirded by construction hammer drums that begins \\"Underground\\" instantly declares Waits' independence from his former self. This sonic surprise reverberates through every remaining song. It also opens weighty creaky doors into a subterranean, murky, creepy yet fully alive world \\"beyond the gopher holes.\\" Waits' horked and hacked vocals hold such conviction that listeners' throats may billow with sympathetic streptococcus. In \\"Shore Leave,\\" zit full of unrequited longing and delicious marimba, Waits' final aspirated falsetto vocals conjures up heaps of dead sailors' souls straining towards unattained dreams and desires. They can't grasp with their hands of vapor. Nothing. \\"Johnsburg, Illinois\\" owes its heritage to \\"Sail Away\\" era Randy Newman. The closest this album comes to Waits' now discarded ex-persona, this delicate ballad drifts along like a full moon gazed at from a wandering oarless rowboat. A similar mood pervades the forlorn \\"Town With No Cheer\\" and the gorgeously melancholic \\"Soldier's Things.\\" Stomping tromping boots and the hammers of Alberich's slaves power \\"16 Shells from a 30.6.\\" It sounds like a Rube Goldberg gone wrong. A fearful wonderful racket. A threat like no other refrains over this din: \\"I'm gonna whittle you into kindlin'.\\" The album's only single, the anthemic \\"In the Neighborhood,\\" evokes a urine soaked Sesame Street, replete with Waits' gift for stark imagery and characterizations. Here \\"the eggs chase the bacon\\" and \\"the kids can't get ice cream 'cause the market burned down.\\"

A single phrase adequately encapsulates \\"Frank's Wild Years\\": \\"never could stand that dog.\\" A demented movie theater keyboard supports the dry unaffected spoken vocals. \\"The obituary mambo,\\" one of the album's most indelible phrases, blesses the title track and its sordid rags to rags tale of a typical Waitsian epic of life gone sour and moldy. Any old time revival could jive and jig to the effervescent \\"Down, Down, Down\\" played with clanking chains. Yet another good 'ol song about Hell. Only one direction to plummet. George Thorogood and Neil Young collaborating on heroin could probably produce \\"Gin Soaked Boy,\\" but Waits didn't need their help. The grit in your teeth guitar sounds like someone filtered it through an abused tuba. \\"Trouble's Braids\\" includes fierce percussion, maybe wooden planks rapped on Formica, and frenetic bass chasing or evading something. The song's fugitive narrator definitely seems troubled and running. For many of the shaggy denizens in this collection of down, out and gone yarns, life just didn't turn out all that good. Thesesongs and stories depict the squalid underside of the cheery lobotomized reality of most mainstream entertainment. It filters that other omnipresent world through broken glass.

Three instrumentals of various moods punctuate the vocal songs. \\"Dave the Butcher\\" enhances the creepiness with its choppy organ skeleton dance rhythms. \\"Just Another Sucker On the Vine\\" enhances the drunkenness with horns and organ that sound powered by fat bulging bellows. Everything ends with the wispily serene and relatively straightforward piano solo \\"Rainbirds.\\" Given the musical chaos that reigned before, this gentle song almost shocks by its mere normalcy. It provides a tentative and unresolved ending. No big explosion. No life-affirming musical number with singing animals and spinning midgets. Just a quiet introspective musical question mark.

Something happened. Something had to have happened. \\"Swordfishtrombones\\" sets the trajectory for Waits' career ever after. Whatever did happen, if Waits ever quits hopefully he can give it to someone else. Powerfully stirring ineffable tones. Impossible throaty sandblasted vocals. An era began here that hopefully won't end. But, as with many of Waits' scraggily downtrodden road rats and bar wenches, things don't always turn out as planned. Unless, of course, they do.

I got into The Chameleons a couple years ago and immediately loved their post-punk sound. "Script of the Bridge" is one of my favorite albums to listen to from start to finish (it's great to listen to on cloudy fall or winter days) and "What Does Anything Mean? Basically" was a great second album. Last year saw the release of "Dreams in Celluloid," which was a compilation album of alternate takes of their songs. But, like a lot of UK bands from this era, they also had the album that was seemingly unreachable, like Big Country's "Restless Natives and Rarities" (which I also recently bought and reviewed). This was that album. It was hard to find and was expensive when you did.

That's not a problem any more, though, as the band recently released the album as a more affordable CD release and an even more affordable MP3 download. All of the tracks on here are great, even if you have already listened to the album versions many times like I have. In some cases, the Peel session tracks are better then their counterparts on the studio albums. For example, I think I actually prefer this version of "Perfume Garden."

I would say that both old and new fans of The Chameleons will get a lot of enjoyment from this album. Even if you already have the studio albums, the Peel session recordings are great. For new fans, I don't think this would be a bad album to purchase first. Although it's usually better to start at the beginning, this album can more or less act as a "best of" to introduce you to the band. Whatever the case, it's definitely a nice addition.

review_headline: Project 86 has done it yet again. Another genuine masterpiece.
review_body:
After eight incredible albums, P86 returns with quite possibly their finest album yet. \\"Knives to the Future\\" tells the story of a soldier who awakens in the middle of a battle with no memory of who he is or from where he came. From the table-setting \\"Intro\\" all the way through the killer finale \\"Oculus,\\" we're taken on a cinematic journey as we climb an icy mountain amidst a solar eclipse.

And, boy, is it a journey well worth taking. Frontman and lyricist Andrew Schwab has long been one of the finest songwriters of his era and he delivers another set of honest, clever, and thought-provoking lyrics. The musicianship is top-notch, and Schwab's signature vocals compliment the instruments perfectly. The band's sound varies beautifully from track to track, yet all the while retaining the high level of intensity members of \\"Team Black\\" (Project 86 fans) have come to love. Check it out! Just press \\"play\\" on track 1 and let the whole album run. You won't want to skip a song!

ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS ON THE SPECIAL EDITION:
The four bonus acoustic songs found only on the \\"Special Edition\\" are definitely worth your time and money. They serve as a nice standalone EP and companion piece to the album proper. They are completely original recordings (not just acoustic covers of songs on the album). They are each beautiful tracks and a nice change of pace from the 12 tracks on the standard album.

review_headline: What we have here from Marion Avenue is a good solid album compiled of songs that have a perspective ...
review_body:
Psychedelic music can be interpreted in so many ways. Approaching it with a modern folky twist can add an interesting element to it. What we have here from Marion Avenue is a good solid album compiled of songs that have a perspective involving true sentimentality and good technique.

Highlights include the song Charon offering shoe-gazing elements mixed with ethereal soundscapes. To just label it as some type of darkwave track would be an injustice as it offers more than that. The Caveman gives you vocal stylizations in the vein of Jeff Buckley without demeaning the artist himself. The music stands as a well developed rock alternative track that sounds current and concise. The same goes for Plastic light.
One Suitcase offers the album a fresh breath of air offering perhaps a more intimate confessional expression of a particular journey in life that can be easily associated with others in this world if you're paying close attention.

All in all, this album is worth checking out and comes highly recommended. To all those who can respect and appreciate true artistry, this is it.

Some of Jackson's best material.  You could say its a new Jackson sound but if you really listen it just a polished mature Jackson doing what he does best.  The remix of The Birds of St. Mark is just fantastic.  Here, Yeah Yeah and Standing in the Breach all have a taste of that new sound but are in reality true Jackson.  One could argue that the other songs on the album as all of them have a country western flavor which I suspect was introduced by Jackson's new band members.  Nevertheless, Jackson makes it work with his lyrics and his forever Jackson voice that touch one's emotions and makes the listener pause and think about what's important in life.  At 66 years, Jackson has not lost anything.  We can only hope we are fortunate enough to experience at least one more album from him.  In any event, buy this one and enjoy!

product_title: All That You Can't Leave Behind
review_body: I've seen that a lot of people don't much care for U2's 2000 music, but I find that puzzling. Following the mess that us Pop (imo, their worst album), All That You Can't Leave Behind represents a come back in the same fashion as Achting Baby following the semi-mess that was Rattle and Hum. This album starts strong, falters a bit, comes back, and then ends on a couple of duds. Here is a track by track review:    1. Beautiful Day - The first single from the album is a doozy. The chorus is an explosion of the entire band at their best. Great lyrics make this a real feel good song. The subdued bridge before the final act of the song cap off this winner of a track. 8.5/10  2. Stuck in a Moment You Can't Get Out Of - A long title, but this song is good. Hard to follow up such a stellar track like \\"Beautiful Day,\\" but this song holds its own. The ending with the horns and harmonies is really good. 7/10  3. Elevation - My personal favorite on the record. It gets a lot of flack for the lyrics, but it's a really fun rock song. The lyrics are certainly not the worst, and I quite like the sing-along nature of them. The quiet buildup in the middle to the chorus explosion is awesome. A fantastic U2 song. 9.5/10  4. Walk On - I actually didn't care much for this song on first listen, but after giving it a fair chance, it's one of my favorites on the record. The ending is phenomenal, especially the name check the album gets. The song is a grower. 8.5/10  5. Kite - A by-the-numbers U2 song, but a great one, nonetheless. The chorus has a nice progression to it, but I have a version in my head that sounds slightly better, but I still love the actual version. The strings don't sound out of place either. A nice track. 8.5/10  6. In a Little While - The guitar riff sounds very RHCP-esque to me, but that's fine. This song doesn't really have chorus, more of a \\"oooohh\\" from Bono, but it's not terrible. I like the sound of this song a good bit. 7/10  7. Wild Honey - A lot of people say thisis where the record falls off, but I disagree. This song is a nice change of pace from the rocking nature of the first 6. A nice acoustic guitar focused song, with some nice plugged in instruments to compliment it. Definitely not a throwaway. 8.5/10  8. Peace on Earth - This is where the record starts to lose it's way. The last bit of this record would be skippable if it weren't for the next track. 5/10  9. When I Look at the World - An oftentimes missed track because of the perceived dropoff, but this track shouldn't be missed. This song is really as good as anything on the first half of the record. A nice song by Bono to his wife. The Edge does some great things on this song as well. 9/10  10. New York - Ok, now the album is avoidable. I don't know, I'm sure they worked hard on these two songs, so I feel bad saying they are throwaway, but from the first lyrics of this track, I immediately want to go back to another song from the album. The song picks up a bit, but the lyrics just aren't there, and it feels like they're trying too hard. 6/10  11. Grace - Another dud. U2's closers are never show-stoppers, but they are usually at the very least listenable, and oftentimes great tracks. Grace isn't that, however. This song goes absolutely nowhere. 5/10

review_headline: Not train songs, but a great album
review_body:
Ride this train (released on LP in 1960) is not a collection of train songs but an imaginary tour to various locations around America. At each location, Johnny sings a song about something that happened there. As such, this is a very varied collection of songs that don't have anything in common except that they explore America's history. This is fair enough as it was Johnny's first such album. As we've seen, Johnny subsequently went on to record albums exploring specific aspects of American history.

My favorite song is Dorraine of Ponchartrain. The sadness of this song is heightened by its length - around five minutes. It remains one of my all-time favorite Johnny Cash songs but you probably won't find it on any of his many compilations. It's not that kind of song. The original LP contained just eight songs, perhaps because the length of some of them, together with the narration between tracks, meant that there wasn't room for any more.

Some versions contain two extra tracks, one of which (Come and ride this train) was maybe intended to be the title track of the original album. The other extra track (The shifting whispering sands) is a duet with Lorne Greene. Johnny later re-recorded this song for another album (Ballads of the true west). These two tracks are not included here.

This is one of Johnny's best albums, and is recognized as such by a lot of people.

All of them are great, but I particularly enjoyed \\"System Recovery,\\" which turned out to be wonderfully addictive.    I replayed that song so much I had trouble moving on to the others. In addition to the music itself, which for me evoked space imagery, there was a wonderful sense of a story unfolding, enhanced by frantic auditory distortions and voices. All of it created a dramatic sense of struggling to solve a problem amid chaos.    \\"Sleep Without Sugar\\" is another favorite. Beautifully quirky and mellow, with an overall lullaby tone, it incorporates repetitive spoken phrases and rhymes for an effect that is hard to describe but memorable.    I was glad, too, to hear some of my favorite songs from his other albums, including \\"Forever Ago\\" and \\"Undergound.\\" I have already raved over them in previous reviews of his other albums \\"Hierocliffics\\" and \\"Hypothetical Jar,\\" which are definitely worth checking out.    Like other Cliff Hays albums this one was easy for me to get into and captures moods that range from playful to melancholy, delivering an overall effect that is beautifully mesmerizing, which is why I will no doubt be returning to this album again and again.

Unless you know who Randy Edelman is, his music is as close to you as the planet Mars. Edelman really is a very accomplished musician,- do the research on him, I did. Although he is best known for his film scores today, he did have it in him to write and perform some reasonably well contribed pop/rock tunes, mostly appearing on the musical scene during the 70's. He did not deliver a #1 tune to speak of- but, his music in my estimation, does require some attention. This song imparticular, "Autumn Days With You" can only be discribed as a romantic and hauntingly pop song filled with regreat and lose,- "What's new," right? Well let's not be to picky gang, after-all it was the seventies and that's what sold records. Edelman had a way with words and music, how else could he win over Hollywood doing movie scores. In any case, check out his albums and if you like 70's pop, then your sure to find a Randy Edelman song that you can enjoy, I highly recommend this one. R.I. reproductions.

Only four stars for what is for many the definitive portrayal of the Don might outrage some devotees of Ezio Pinza but I do this not to denigrate the performance but to alert the potential buyer that despite Naxos's expert clean-up of the original 78's, the sound is still fuzzy and congested. Individual voices emerge best from the orchestral soup and we can hear the allure of Pinza's suave and saturnine seducer. Walter is big-scale conductor who pushes hard without much subtlety but he certainly generates tension and drama. For example, the sestet \\"Mille orbidi pensieri\\" is thrilling in its headlong pace.

Mention has been elsewhere of the surprising success of casting Kipnis as Leporello despite his Slavic Italian and he keeps up with Pinza in their quick - very quick - fire exchanges. I like Rose Bampton's large, powerful and highly expressive Dona Anna who is completely on top of the fearsome demands of \\"Or sai che l'onore\\". Charles Kuhlmann is fine if nothing special as Ottavio and his tenor is more virile than it was to become in the 50's but he only just hangs on to the line in the trickier parts of \\"Il mio tesoro\\". Sayao is a delightful, pert, pure-voiced Zerlina, the best on record, I think. Novotna is a faintly tremulous but impassioned and fiery Elvira, slightly lacking in her lower register. Mack Harrell makes more of Masetto than some of his successors and he has more than enough voice for a part which is too often under-cast. Norman Cordon is not the biggest, blackest Commendatore but, again, is more than adequate and has enough volume and steady intensity to chill the listener.

Pinza himself, of course, had the smoothest, darkest and most flexible of basses, easily able to encompass the vocal demands of the role while always suggesting the wit and charm without which the Don is a detestable thug. Tito Gobbi's beautifully vocalised Giovanni comes, for some, perilously close to being a hard, snarling villain whereas the lilt and twinkle in Pinza's manner is always beguiling, suggestive of his humour and animal magnetism. He was, by all accounts, as enthusiastic a seducer in real life as the character he plays here.

Above all, this performance gels as an ensemble piece which successfully captures the febrile pace and momentum of this opera as primarily a piece of drama rather than just a display of accomplished singing. I can well understand why, despite its sonic limitations, for many it continues to put subsequent recordings in the shade.anner is always beguiling, suggestive of his humour and animal magnetism. A true winner.  This is quality music.

product_title: You Are (from the motion picture Someone Like You)
review_headline: YOU ARE...Reminding Me To Count My Blessings
review_body:
"YOU ARE" is such a beautiful love song, written by Gordon Kennedy, Wayne Kirkpatrick and Wynonna Judd. This composition is infused with such genuine appreciation of all the best aspects of human emotion. That cynical aphorism, about learning to fake sincerity, simply cannot exist in the wonderful world that is "YOU ARE." At its best, music can be unquestionably truthful ,,,and the minute one comprehends this is revelatory: "Yes, as the listener/beholder I know the composer(s) lived these sentiments!" All of us should be so lucky as to experience love from and for such a giving human being, as was the author(s) of these lyrics! The exemplary do live among us, reminding us, when we bother to pay attention, and believe it, that we, too, can live our lives with altruism as one of our ultimate goals. This song humbles me, and reminds me that I, too, have been so blessed.

For me, the melody is every bit the equal of its poetic lyrics; so gently, lovingly expressed. Wynonna's phrasing is pure genius. As a former studio owner, I know that in lesser hands, this song's complexity would have prevented it from ever leaving the studio archives,,,yet Wynonna and company make it seem so incredibly effortless. I've always been in child-like awe of my recording sisters and brothers when they conjure up something as magical as "You Are." ...would have loved being "the proverbial fly on the wall" during this composition's process. (Gee, Mark, do think anyone gets the fact that this song mesmerizes/rhapsodizes you?)

And lastly, if Wynonna's sister, Ashley Judd, the star of the movie, "Someone Like You" in which this song became known to the public, had anything to do with its inclusion in the film, then bless you, too, Ashley! Mine is a better world with all of you people and this song in it. If you folks get a sense of adoration...well, you're right!...but fear not: I'm no stalker. Heck, I prob'ly couldn't even afford the gas! But this song's blessings are highly affordable. I suggest you buy it!

In the medieval tradition of the story-telling ballad, comes this, the second compilation by the group with the delightful name of The Legendary 10 Seconds. Their subject: The suddenly topical King Richard III (1483-1485), the last Plantagenet, whose earthly remains were only recently discovered in a Leicester, England car park. It may be the most exciting archeological find of our life times.

But you don't have to be an aficionado of that king (or even medieval music) to enjoy the infectious high spirits of this wonderful blend of pop/rock with the distinctive textures of old English folk songs. All pieces are original compositions, beautifully sung and performed with plenty of fine guitar- and keyboard-work. You'll hum the melodies and tap your toe to the beat, even as you listen to the complex lyrics and - just maybe - learn some unexpected 15th century history lessons. The band has done its homework, researching the period in order to tell each riveting Tale. Some are sad, others are cheery, but all are consistent with the time-honoured Art of the Ballad. Think old songs like "Mary Hamilton" or "Robin Hood and the Sheriff," and you will know how effective ballads were at informing their audiences back then...and now. For this was the way news of that time was disseminated. Whether by flickering candlelight at the royal court or by the roaring fire in some wayside inn, minstrels literally sang for their suppers, giving their listeners good value for their bread and brew.

It is a fact King Richard searched throughout his realm for the best singers and musicians. Foreign visitors praised his good taste in music. If he, indeed, came back to walk among us, I think he would be right pleased to have such a talented ensemble as 10 Seconds providing the latest news. And all this, done with such an engaging style and indomitable spirit, you'll want to listen, again and again.

Even a king lacked this advantage of our moderntechnology. Download - and enjoy!

After Note: I've been told The Legendary 10 Seconds donates profits to a UK Scoliosis Charity. We now know the king was no hunchback, but did have scoliosis. Every purchase helps somebody live a better life.

review_headline: An excellent choice for the casual fan
review_body: Growing up, my best friend was a Beach Boys fanatic. He played their music incessantly (influenced by his mom's love of their music), and for years it seemed as if a day didn't go by without him mentioning a tidbit of info about the band while playing their music. While I would listen and even sing along to the words I knew, in my mind I dismissed them as simple musicians who only sang about surfing. As he got older he drew in other musical influences; in doing so, I purposely steered clear of their music due to the overexposure in my childhood. Now, approaching the age of 40 and more open to various types of music, I noticed Amazon had put their Greatest Hits collection for a great price.  I bought the mp3, listened to every track, straight through without interruption, and I've realized that The Beach Boys were much more talented and creative than I had ever given them credit for. Songs like "Wouldn't it be Nice", "God Only Knows" and "Don't Worry Baby" have such phenomenal harmonies...this stage of their careers prove how they elevated their music from the basic "sun, sand, surf, and sports car" formula of their early days. Even the one track I wasn't familiar with, "That's Why God Made the Radio", surprised me. And while I'm not ready to run out and buy every Beach Boys album, this collection is a perfect representation of their best music.

review_headline: A purity that strives to organize sound along the lines of an ideal that is both religious, as well as, artistic...
review_body:
Even though I've been listening to classical music for over thirty years, I've actually only listened to very little music that was composed prior to the Baroque period. Indeed, except for Beethoven and some Bach, Vivaldi, Handel, Haydn and Mozart; the bulk of my listening pleasure has always been from the Romantic, Late-Romantic and Early Modern periods.

As of the past year or so, this had changed, as I became very interested in the music of Orlando Gibbons (1583-1625) who lived and worked about a full century before Bach. While I was looking for other composers who were contemporaries of Gibbons, I managed to obtain some useful recommendations on the Amazon's Classical Music \\"Discussion Board\\". Albeit, my current situation of helping to put adult children through college has me on a tight budget to the point where I can only purchase about one or two CDs per month.

In this regard, I was delighted to come across the \\"Big Choral Renaissance Box\\" which is actually a collection of over nine hours of Renaissance, as well as, Medieval choral music.

While I haven't yet listened to all of it as of yet, I'm particularly struck by the music of one Guillaume Dufay (1397-1474) who, according to my own bit of informal internet research, was a \\"Flemish\\" composer. Dufay's music seems to have a purity that strives to organize sound along the lines of an ideal that is both religious, as well as, artistic.

I also listened to Guillaume de Machaut (1300-1377), a Medieval composer whose music reaches for a heavenly ideal but retains a very raw edge of one who might have been a witness to the war and disease of Medieval times.

As to the rest of this collection, I've skimmed through much of it here and there and have found a lot that I want to explore in greater depth, with a more mindful approach that will allow me to get to know and evaluate each composer individually. Indeed, while it may seem at face value, that much of this music sounds \\"the same\\"; repeated and patient listening may reveal that the composers of the periods which came before Bach had much personality and creative genius.

While skimming through parts of this collection, I did find a couple glitches here and there; but as long you're paying ONE DOLLAR for the whole thing, what is there REALLY to complain about?

Once again, the \\"Bach Guild\\" has done it again, and I'd count this collection as one of many great download deals on Amazon.

People say that \\"you get what you pay for\\"...and others say \\"What can you buy for a dollar these days?\\"

review_headline: This is a great update and releases for the first time in one ...
review_body: This is a great update and releases for the first time in one compilation all three of Mary Macgregor's albums from 1976, 78 & 80.  All the tracks are mixed up, but all 30 tracks are there.  The only disappointment is that the final Ariola single of "Wedding Song (There Is Love)" and its B-side "Benjamin" was not included, as well as her Japan only tracks of Sayonara, Love Light and her very last RCA single.  If a full dig of tracks could have been done, Mary had a duet with another artist on his album (cannot recall at this writing), plus had a few tracks on Radio Shack's Realistic Records, one a Christmas duet with Mike Love of the Beach Boys of "Do You Hear What I Hear", and a guest appearance on another album doing an electronic pop version of the Archie's "Sugar Sugar".  These six tracks would have completed the set, all released prior to Mary's 1999 release of "Perfect Yellow House" as the Mary Macgregor Band.  Though the tracks sound like they are from vinyl, they are much better than other bootlegs issued on CD before.  It is also the only way to get all these great tracks in one place besides looking for the vinyl.  Highly recommend, especially for fans.

review_headline: The crowning achievement is that it raced to #2 on the Adult chart (then called Easy Listening). I am convinced it would have be
review_body: How important of a single for Jody Miller was "He's So Fine"?  Well, in summer of 1971, not only did it chart in the Top Five Country and Western survey, but it also crossed over to the Billboard Hot 100 where it climbed to 54. The crowning achievement is that it raced to #2 on the Adult chart (then called Easy Listening). I am convinced it would have been #1 there, had it not been held off by Carole King's reign at that spot with "It's Too Late." Still fresh sounding today, this song is a must have for any country or pop fan. You will love it. In fact, you will love Jody's entire "Complete Epic Hits" CD. Five stars

This album is not generally regarded as being among Johnny's finest albums, and if I were to rank his albums in order, I'll concede that there would be more of his albums ahead of this one than behind it, so if you only want some of Johnny's music, you'll probably give this a miss. All that said, I think there is plenty to like about this album.

The outstanding track is Cisco Clifton's fillin' station. It is an excellent story song about somebody who made a good living until a new road was constructed, which took away all the traffic.

Other tracks that I particularly like are Call Daddy from the mine (about a daughter worried about her father trapped after a pit collapse, possibly caused by an earthquake) and The whirl and the suck (about the hazards of navigating a river before a dam was built).

There are other interesting songs too, but I still maintain that this album is for committed fans of Johnny Cash rather than casual fans,

What serious Autechre fan can remain displeased with ANY of their releases, old or new? Because what may not make sense, from them, one day, will reveal itself as amazing another day. To hear Autechre progress in their "AUdio TECHnology REsearch" is a treat and a blessing in itself. But then, their individual tracks, albums, and EPs also stand alone as great works of art. I actually consider them contemporary classical music! For the reason that they explore, employ and merge sounds, without words, to create definite effects on the listener, as most of the best of traditional classical music from the past has done; they do not have "an agenda", lyrically or in terms of gimmicks or fashion; they just create and publish various blends of sound, employing melody, harmony, and (perhaps especially) rhythm. L-Event, unsurprisingly, didn't make much sense to me at first, but each time I listen to it (again, not surprisingly) it appeals to me more and more. (This is how Autechre usually effect me.) This is a brief, 20-something-minute EP, with only 4 tracks, but it's good!

review_headline: King Chip's debut album is dope
review_body:
I first heard of King Chip (Chip Tha Ripper) because I am a huge Kid Cudi fan and he was featured in quite a few of his songs. Fast forward to me going to a Cudi concert featuring his newly released album Satellite Flight at Barclay's Center. King Chip opened for him, and I didn't recognize any of his songs, but I was still enjoying them. One specifically stuck out to me, "BLK on BLK" and a few days after the greatest concert of my life I proceeded to look through my videos (I wish I enjoyed the music more rather than recording it) and I listened to BLK on BLK again and loved it. I then decided to look it up on youtube and found King Chip's mixtape, 44108. I gave it a quick listen through, but didn't really delve into it. Then a few weeks ago I was on a Cudi fansite and saw him promoting Chip's mixtape which was now going to be an album! (make a kid named cudi an album too please!) I had to wait a few weeks until release but I had no hesitation when it came to purchasing it. After listening to it a few times I absolutely loved it!

Cudi and Chip are my favorite duo in all of music, and I love how they're best friends (or Brothers ;) ....) I also love how King Chip is making his own name for himself. Keep making dope music guys.

review_body: One word AWESOME!

Hadn't listened to this album for a while so cued it up and got re-introduced to it all over again.
After over a quarter century ( ! ) it still is very good and as reviewer Jack so aptly states it is Robin's "Imaginative Transition" period.
I got this on vinyl and Compact Disc in 1988 and I feel it is very well recorded and mixed . The cast and crew is the same as on the previous years GNP Crescendo " Passion " album although there is not as much keyboard support on this one. It seems Atlantic must have bought the contract and album after it was completed ? The band was touring a lot and getting airplay at the time.
The drum sounds and vocals are particularly well recorded with Davey Pattison right up front in the middle and the soundstage is pretty wide. Teetering on a bit much echo in places, but still very good sounding .
The drums/bass sound a little "modern" on a couple of tracks but, heck...they were trying to get played on the radio in 1988 and sell records .
"Tear It Up" kicks and takes names, and why it didn't become a bigger hit is just plain not right.
I really like "Shattered" and it's cool to hear the maracas panning during the guitar solo, marching past you and in and out .
The last album recorded before he tuned down the guitar another half step from Eb with it's 3 flatted notes to D with the 2 sharp notes
Do yourself a favor and listen to this on a good setup, not a $99 CD Player or as an MP3 .
I used a Marantz CD player, Music Fidelity V-DAC , Little Dot II+ Headphone amp with NOS tubes and Audio Technica M-50 headphones and it sounds really good.
Not the best gear.... but decent entry level listening .
Music this good deserves at least that much to listen to.
Everyone plays their best here and sound great and the songs are good

review_headline: Pure Ska - Oreskaband just keeps getting better and better!
review_body:
"Carry On" is probably the most purely ska song Oreskaband have ever done. Even more so than some of the early material, which always carried a strong dose of 3rd wave crossover ska. The song is as catchy and infectious as anything they've ever done with verses sung in Japanese and chorus in English. Strong reggae influences abound, there are two sections of toasting and the band continue their increasing use of organ and keyboards alongside the horns.

I was a little worried that with their departure from Sony Japan production quality might suffer but the track is expertly recorded, mixed and produced and features a strong stereo separation that gives each instrument a distinct space and presence in the overall mix, a very important consideration given how much is going on in the track.

If you're a fan of "Dance Crazy" 1980 era ska or late 1960s Trojan style reggae you'll love this!

I know I've been long in awaiting this, and I can't believe I waited several days AFTER the release of Mr. Roach's newest work of art, \\"The Delicate Forever!\\" This album might very well be considered a whole new level of exploration for him in his on-going journey into the deeper realms of aural discovery! I for one have enjoyed the more recent releases of Mr. Roach, as he always strives to develop something special in each and every one of his works, but there is indeed a new and unique set of sound-scapes to be found here that have only been scratched upon the surface of what could potentially be blossomed.

However \\"The Delicate Forever\\" also takes one on a deeper, more enchanting journey into the vast mist-filled, delicate spaces of perception and thought meditation on the ultimate forever in ourselves, which I believe is mortality; the ever present dance of life and death, fate and destiny, good and evil, and all the other unseen driving forces behind life.

In final words, Mr. Roach has indeed entered a new doorway with \\"The Delicate Forever.\\" According to his website, much of this new discovery came from his re-mastering of \\"Structures From Silence.\\" With this being but the new beginning, I can only try to imagine what might come next! Five well-earned golden stars, as well as two thumbs way up, from me to Mr. Roach!

review_headline: All the studio albums from the original trio
review_body:
This is a set of America's WB studio albums, it does not include their final album for WB Live!, which was a recording of a live concert performance. This is also the complete set of albums with the original trio, Dewey Bunnell, Gerry Beckley and Dan Peek (Peek left the band after the release of Harbor). This is an excellent collection. All seven albums were hits and include several songs that were hits or received significant airplay on radio stations that played album cuts. Four of the albums (Holiday, Hearts, Hideaway, and Harbor) were produced by legendary Beatles producer Sir George Martin.

Their first album, America, was released in 1971, went to number 1 in the US and stayed there for 5 weeks and was certified Platinum by the RIAA. It included the number 1 hit A Horse With No Name and the top ten hit I Need You, as well as the album classics Sandman, Three Roses, and Riverside. The album was produced by British rock pioneer Ian Samwell. It is their most acoustic based album and is a folk rock classic.

Homecoming was released in late 1972 and was a top ten hit, also being certified Platinum. It includes the classic Ventura Highway and the hits Don't Cross The River and Only In Your Heart. Other songs that received airplay included To Each His Own, Cornwall Blank and California Revisited.

Hat Trick was released in 1973 and peaked at 28 on the Billboard album chart. It included the original version of Muskrat Love as well as the rocker Green Monkey which features Joe Walsh on lead guitar.

Holiday reached number 3 on the album charts in 1974 and was certified Gold. It includes two songs (Tin Man and Lonely People) that the made the top 5 on the Billboard singles chart which also hit number 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart. Baby It's Up To You, Hollywood, and Another Try also received significant airplay.

Hearts was another top 5 album that was certified Gold in 1975. It includes the number 1 single Sister Golden Hair and the hits Daisy Jane and Woman Tonight. Ol Virginia, Bell Tree, and People In The Valley were in the rotation of stations that played album tracks.

Hideaway just missed the top ten in 1976 and was certified Gold. It includes the hit Today's The Day, it stayed at number 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart for two weeks, and the minor hit Amber Cascades. Several album cuts received significant airplay including Jet Boy Blue, Letter, and Watership Down.

Harbor was the final album which featured all three original members and peaked at 21 on the album chart in 1977. While the album did not produce any hits, it includes several strong songs including God Of The Sun, Don't Cry Baby, and the rocker Hurricane.

This is a great collection and a must for any America fans. It is a great value.gle Sister Golden Hair and the hits Daisy Jane and Woman Tonight. Ol Virginia, Bell Tree, and People In The Valley were in the rotation of stations that played album tracks.

product_title: Beethoven: Symphony No. 7 in A Major, Op. 92
review_headline: The Finest Performance of Beethoven's Symphonic Dithyramb
review_body: Heretofore, my favorite recording of Beethoven's 7th was a little known and regarded CD by Barry Wordsworth and the Royal Philharmonic.  That recording is notable for the unrestrained, if a little rough, playing by the RPO.  What makes the recording so desirable is the wild and joyous performance, what I believe Beethoven intended the music convey.  But this recording by the young Guido Cantelli has supplanted the Wordsworth in my estimation.  The energy and drive of the symphony never falter throughout and the orchestra's playing is impeccable.  Guido Cantelli may have been Toscanini's protege but, in every regard, Cantelli surpasses Toscanini in his conducting of Beethoven.  And this performance also surpasses those of the two Kleibers, Karajan, Furtwangler, and even George Szell.  What is evident in this recording is that Cantelli was headed to be the premier conductor of the 20th century, tragically taken from us when he was but 36 years old.

review_headline: THE LAST GREAT Fania All Stars recording and a 1980’s Salsa MASTERPIECE with some eccentric tunes!!! SIMPLY AWESOME!!! GET IT!
review_body:
This HIGHLY INSPIRED 1981 Fania-All-Stars recording is an ABSOLUTELY BRILLIANT album that features a unique, original and one of a kind stylish sound that sometimes feels psychedelic and melodramatic with some massively complex and elaborated “orchestral” arrangements.
The usual TIGHT and INTENSE rhythm that we associate the All-Stars with is also featured here with a wide diversity of tunes and again, a different singer to sing each song. There is also a GREAT balance between the singer and the orchestra involvement for a 1980’s Salsa recording. In other words, it’s not just another boring singer oriented album with the band stepping back and taking second stage like in so many other homogenous 1980’s Salsa albums.
Also worth mentioning is the album’s front cover. By looking properly at it, one could indeed be led to think that it’s a “humorous joke” reflecting on the state of cocaine in the general musical scene...

1.Semílla de Amór begins with a slow and unusual melodramatic jazzy intro with strings and Flugelhorn Trumpet playing by Juancíto Torres before turning into a lyrically passionate tune fantasising about the process of falling in love, passion and having a baby all in a very emotional way.
Héctor Lavoe as always does a GREAT job on lead vocals and the tune features some SUPERB orchestral arrangements and some fine jazzy Trumpet soloing by Juancíto Torres.
A THRILLING tune!...

2.Dime Qué Te Pasa, written and sung by the GREAT Adalberto Santiago is a BRILLIANT Afro Puerto-Rican Bomba tune.
Adalberto gives a macho feel of “over confident Latin Lover” and “Doctor of love” to the tune that works out really well. The tune also features some nice street “barrio” type of drum interventions and some GREAT horn arrangements and Trumpet soloing by Luis ‘Períco’ Ortíz towards the end.
This is a HIGHLY SUCCESSFUL tune that DOES NOT sound romantic/cheesy/gooey AT ALL and
that Adalberto really made his!
DEFINITELY a house favourite at home!

3.Voy A Vivir Para Siempre (I will live forever), written and sung by Willie Colón is another eccentric song about extreme egocentrism ranting about how people love him, how he’s the best, how they’ll remember him forever, how he’ll reach the sky and etc!...
I find this song hilarious and really funny when I think about it and I just wonder whether there’s not a certain link between this song and Cocaine...
Otherwise, I feel the swing of the tune is a bit too often interrupted by the “funny” passages where Willie rants about himself but in between, you also have very substantial musical passages with the choruses coming in, Pacheco doing some nice Flute work and some GREAT horn arrangements.
At the end, a WINNER tune!...

4.Nina is a WONDERFUL re-make of this song Cheo already recorded in 1963 with the Joe Cuba Sextet on ‘Vagabundeando’.
Of particular note, other than the high quality swing and intensity of this tune is the very inspired vocal performance by Cheo really ‘at home’ and the classy rhythmic jazzy part with Louie Ramírez soloing on Vibraphones followed by the AMAZING horn arrangements!
A BELTER tune that (in my opinion) has surpassed musically in every way the very different version that Joe Cuba recorded in 1963.

5.Bilóngo, the Latin classic written by Guillermo Rodríguez Fiffe is another VERY FINE version of this tune featuring an ABSOLUTELY FINE Ismael Rivera on vocals contrarily to what I read some others have said.
The tune is distinguished by a HIGHLY INSPIRED Bongo solo by Roberto Roena, AMAZING musical arrangements and some FINE Trumpet soloing by ‘Períco’ again!
A KILLER tune and another favourite at home!

6.Mi So Den Boso, with Celia on vocals singing in Papiamento language is a rather unusual, but VERY CATCHY tune featuring a quick call and response thing betweenthe choruses and Celia, and a nice fairly fast tempo pace which to me seems reminiscent of the Dominican Meréngue rhythm but which I somehow cannot quite place or pinpoint.
Anyway, there’s a set of horn arrangements towards the end which I think could have been better and more creative, but otherwise it’s definitely an interesting and different tune which I find HIGHLY ENJOYABLE and FUN!

7.El Caminante, with Ismael Miranda on vocals does take us back to the more typical 1980’s style of Salsa sound with the usual and big important emphasis on the singer, a LONG first part to the tune and some slightly monotonous rhythm and musicality.
The 2nd part is another story as it comes to life with Miranda boosting it up and saving it along with some complex orchestral arrangements and a welcomed Piano solo by Papo Lucca.
Overall, a tune good enough not to be skipped.

9.Rosa En El Fango, with Pete ‘El Conde’ Rodríguez really finishes the album IN BEAUTY!
It features a rhythmic Cuatro-guitar solo by the late Yomo Toro and further classy complex orchestral
arrangements.
I also think Pete did a GREAT job on this tune which (I think) isn’t quite as much in his style as some of the Charangas he used to sing in the 1960’s or the Cuban Conjunto style of music he was known for with Pacheco, in his own albums or on Menéame La Cuna

The last thing I would like you to think about this recording is that the ONLY reason to get it is because it features one of the last appearances by ‘El Sonero Mayor’ Ismael Rivera! Quality is ALL OVER THE PLACE here and that’s just a highly valuable point of view for the COLLECTOR, but not for Buyers or listeners!
This is THE REAL Fania-All-Stars comeback after some VERY MEDIOCRE albums and also the good predecessor ‘Commitment’ from 1980.

review_headline: Music that speaks to your soul
review_body:
This is probably my favorite song by Aradhna.

Once you move beyond the *shock* that an American has such an authentic Hindi accent, you begin to truly appreciate the music.

Aradhna's music is authentic - heart and soul. Their sound reflects the content of their songs. I'm not a 100% sure about this, but they are probably the first Christian Bhakti western fusion band. It is dangerous and uncharted territory and I'm sure many have tried and failed miserably at this. But Aradhna's music speaks (and sings!) for itself.

This song has a very special place for me, because Jesus' sermon on the mount, which contains the Beatitudes is my favorite part of scripture. And this song beautifully puts the Beatitudes to music in a truly unique way - in Indian Bhakti style. If you reach a point in your life where you feel so self-obsessed that it makes you sick, just sit down, drink some Darjeeling tea and listen to the smooth melodious sitar and guitar sounds put to rhythm by a softer tabla in this song. It will truly help you look outside yourself and see what God is doing in the world - among the poor and the meek of the world.

Buy this song. You won't regret it.

To me, there are few things more "personal" than a person's music preferences. So, I pick and choose various arrangements from artists I like. I am a jazz aficionado, but I do like some instrumentals.

Anyone who has ever loved, and lost.... this song, and Linda Ronstadt's utterly stunning voice, encapsulate, with crystalline perfection, the ache that grips the heart. This is a masterpiece.

This remaster, as K.J. Farmer has already noted, really opens up the song. It unveils the brilliance of the instrumentation, allowing it to mesh more perfectly with... that voice. Aaaah, that voice...

If you are unmoved by this song... seriously.... go in search of your soul....

review_headline: Jureesa McBride's CAN STILL MAKE IT reminds us of the strength we need to survive
review_body:
No matter where you live or what you try to do there will be situations you face that will challenge you and put you to the test.

In her single CAN STILL MAKE IT Jureesa McBride addresses some of these things (especially relationships), and let's the listener know that no matter where you can get through whatever comes your way.

"We were headed in different directions," she sings. "You tried to take it all for me. Now the only space for affection is with my daughters and my family." This shows that when things became rough she was able to turn to those who she knew would have her back. "Even birds that fly have broken wings," she sings. This reminds us that although a bird might be knocked down that don't stop. "When life knocks you down, you can get back up. You can make it through. I know you can... All you have to do is believe in yourself."

Knowing that you weren't built to break is the key to remembering that if you don't give up there will be other opportunities. All you have to do is believe.

review_body:
First, and to be honest and upfront - I know next to nothing about this guy, there's precious little online and the only work I've heard before, and then without knowing who was doing the sterling riffing, is with Shooter Jennings (who I recall also went space-wide with a cosmic concept album some time back...) - so it stands to reason that if you like Shooter you'll be fine here; but there's a whole lot more than country to be chomped through on this album -

The cover will either draw you in or drive you off - personally I love it - looks like Clyde's boy from \\"Any Which Way...\\", all growed up and flying the cosmos, taking out the trash and naming names - very, and way cool.

\\"Weightlessness\\" - sets the tone with acoustic guitar, a synth sounding something like an electric jews harp, and a voice that crackles somewhere between c.b. radio and Major Tom - not a bad start, but it all gets real good, real soon

\\"Time Flies\\" is awesome - proper seventies rock, a bit of Who's Next - that \\"I'm hitting middle age and am angsty\\" bite in both the music and lyrics, in amongst this, dare I say Kansas-like tune. It's also got a massive chorus and an organ/guitar midsection that kills - should be a single - top 10 easy - that is, in a proper world where this would be everywhere and I would be reviewer 700 and something.

\\"King Kong\\" - like Blue Oyster cult jamming with Faith no More - and as good as that sounds!

\\"Overlords...\\" - does go on a bit to be honest, but keeps the time/space theme going; and now I listen again, the vocals are good and gritty, and wouldn't be out of place on Baroness's last disk - it's also reminding me a bit Diamond Dogs era Bowie, which is never bad; and more Blue Oyster Cult - not my favourite track on the record to be fair, but still pretty out there on a country record - and country needs to get out there a whole heck more often.

\\"Rising\\" - much more like it for me - some Seger, and moreSeger is all that will save humanity in my humbly 100% accurate opinion - bit of \\"Her Strut\\" to the groove, bit of \\"Turn the Page\\" in it's DNA - some metal in it's riffs too. The lyrics are post-apocalyptic, kiss the sky and get out of here type of thing, in fact a nice twist because my rock-addled brain was expecting a road-dogs lament about hitting the open road - the whole \\"Freebird\\" rip; and it is that, except here the road goes on, literally forever - so good twist and a rockin' song.

\\"Brave New World\\" - good instrumental tune - think Daft Punk does Country.

\\"Lost In the Future\\" - grand eighties metal - who doesn't love this stuff - only wrong people, that's who - some Kansas again - plus Blue Oyster Cult - these guys should really meet... tour and record together and save humanity from dull rock and crap country - synthesise to survive brothers and sisters.

\\"Liz\\" - my favourite song here - starts like Baroness and countless other cosmic metal seventies rock addicts that are out there if you seek - and that is a recommendation by the way - but then the song is balanced by a sweet chorus that is still metallic, yet has a Flaming Lips quality - so a metallic countrydelica is what you get here - some moogy sounds (sorry not a musician!!!) underpin the whole and overall it's just a blast.

\\"Brainscan\\" Pink Floyd Darksidey, with slide guitar - makes sense in the context

\\"Star\\" - more Roger Waters in the lyrics, but with lovely finger picked backing and that organ/moog??? again - this is the most \\"cosmic\\" country song , in the Gene Clark of \\"No Other\\" sense.

\\"Death Machine\\" - like Neil Diamond singing a slowed down doom-metal ballad - just as awesome as that sounds.

\\"Checking Out\\" - Gene Clark again - and some Eagles in the chorus - a fitting end to a bizarre and truly wondrous \\"country\\" album. Maybe some Jimmy Webb in the scope and feel too.

This gets five stars for not being dull, for having a space monkey on the cover ( and come to think of it, there's a bit of Buck Dharma (via Planet of the Apes of course!!!) about that cover dude too); it gets the maximum for daring to show that songs that paint outside the lines of dumb genres need to be celebrated and played really, really loud over any system where the tired old and the lazy young still allow s*** to be bright enough to sing for their hearts - and any record that sounds like Leon Russell making a metal album has to be worth a listen - you might be disappointed if you buy this, it ain't perfect I'll admit, but it will keep your belief in crazy-assed bearded folk making big, cosmic music for no real reason, but that it sounds like a good idea at the time and that is a damned good thing.

So instead of reaching for Darkside the next time you want to bliss out on the big headphones (i know you got them if you like the look of this record), give this a spin and be good and glad there are still out there people out there making stuff like this.

review_headline: Such a timely blessing for us both!
review_body:
After purchasing an MP3 album on Amazon as a gift, I received a notification that I had £1 credit to spend. So I looked around for a track of 'Soaking music' that I could use during my prayer times. Seemingly by chance I landed on this track, which includes an amplified rendering of Psalm 91, which leads on into prophetic personal declarations of faith in God's unfailing protection and provision. This was just what I was looking for, so I downloaded it to my mobile and found it a great blessing personally.

A week or so later I played it to my wife one night, when she was suffering from a stomach upset and exhaustion. By the time she had finished listening, her sickness was almost gone. But, about a week after that she discovered a lump in her breast that turned out to be cancer. With no inkling of this, I had also ordered a copy of Sid Roth's book, 'Supernatural Healing,' as a gift for my wife just a week previously. - and the very first chapter was on Psalm 91; so we made this the basis our faith stand against this curse.

The surgeon, himself a Christian, told us after the operation that the outcome had been 'the best of the best.' Although the cancer had probably been there for 2 years, it was significantly smaller than the original scan had suggested, and there was no sign of any spread. It is even doubtful whether radiotherapy will be recommended.

review_headline: It's good, sort of a return to form, you already know
review_body:
It's easy to say this is a return to form album for Sabbath, but it would depend solely on what form it's a return to. Yes, it's heavier than anything Ozzy has recorded solo. Yes, it's probably heavier than the vast majority of the Sabbath albums, maybe dating even back to Volume IV. That's where the comparison stops and probably should. It does kind of feel like a continuation of where Sabbath left off in the mid-70s. Come on Ozzy/Sabbath fans, they dropped way off on those last few albums of the 70s, this one is better than those, but not better the original 4, maybe 5.

There are probably more authoritative Sabbath fans out there, but this is my experience with Sabbath. Heard them for the first time in the late 70s, early 80s, when I was maybe 5-7 years old. My older cousins listened to Sabbath and somehow, I ended up on the porch, "in the circle" as they listened to Paranoid. I was hooked enough to buy all the Ozzy-fronted Sabbath albums on cd, in the late 80s. Then I saw these other Sabbath albums, "Heaven or Hell", "Mob Rules", "Born Again", "Seventh Star" and "The Eternal Idol". I've told in my review of the re-released, "Rules of Hell" that Dio is my favorite of the Sabbath singers and I think it hurt my view of the Ozzy fronted-Sabbath.

Even so, I did still buy the Black Box when it came out with the remasters of the Ozzy-era albums and do listen to it quite a bit. Which is why I can at least be a little critical of this 13 album. It has some really great songs on it like God is Dead, End of the Beginning and Loner, but after those 3 album openers it falls into the feeling, "Lets just keep playing these songs with new lyrics". That's not to say they did that, but the album does start to become redundant. My wife, who is not a heavy metal fan, really liked the first 3 songs, but soon said, "Did the album start over?"

On a positive note, I was lucky enough to see one of the shows live, with 5 of my older cousins who first introduced me to Sabbath, one of them is in his 50s and the live show was just great. That's probably stopping me from giving this album a 3 star. It's a good album if you're a Sabbath fan. Other people who are new to the band would be better off trying out any of the first 4-5 albums, if you like Ozzy that is. Otherwise, I could sit here and make an argument for Dio and Hughes both sounding better with Sabbath than Ozzy has or if you don't want me to say "better", I'll say "more consistent". For the most part I enjoyed the whole vibe of this compilation. It's pretty infectious quality IDM, with the main emphasis on beats and the intricate manipulation of rhythms.
Stand out tracks are from Jeff Pils (which sounds very Plaid-like), Sonar Base, Sky Tucker, and Quinoline Yellow. These artists include enough melodic activity and/or enough changes in the manipulations of the beats to produce the most solid tracks.
Surprisingly the biggest disappointment were the 2 tracks from Adapta and Uexkull, which are the 2 brothers that made up Bitstream. The weird thing is that most Bitstream tracks I've heard would be the top tracks on this compilation, but somehow these guys never fine tuned their skills on their own. Each of their tracks are very basic, repetitive, and have no real hooks to warrant the already short time frames.
This leads me to the constructive criticism of this compilation/genre in general. No doubt all these guys are pretty adept at sound design and programming mean beats. They certainly know how to milk cool effects too. What I found is that after the main "wow" factor of the groove kicking in, many of the tracks didn't develop in a musical way, all the progression was just further manipulation of the same exact beat/bass line that started 4 minutes earlier.
I do love electronic music that gets my head bobbing, but I also notice when not enough is being added. Maybe I have spoiled myself with listening to too much Plaid and Kettel.
Overall this a a solid compilation. If you want to hear a much better set of this type of music with a better flow i highly recommend the compilation by Andrea Parker called "Nobodys Perfect 2". I have not heard any set better that that, and it includes Bitstream at their prime.

review_headline: Completely off the wall...in a good way.
review_body: Closure in Moscow seems to grow in leaps and bounds between releases.  Their first EP (released in 2008), was a slightly prog-y post-hardcore album.  Their LP (2009), combined that style with a heavy Mars Volta influence.  After five long years, they've grown much further away from their roots than I ever imagined.  Pink Lemonade is a fusion of classic rock, funk, dance, psychadelic rock, disco, post-hardcore, and a bit of jazz.  Just everything possible, it seems.  And it somehow works.  Every song is quite distinct.  It's an extremely ambitious album.  And extremely well produced.  I don't know who worked on it, but it's heavily effected, full of analog and tape warmth and fuzz, sonically unique.  Another amazing thing, there's no auto-tune or quantization.  As in, they didn't hack the thing up on a computer to make it sound perfect.  Yet it doesn't sound sloppy or half-assed.  I'd bet few bands could pull that off in 2014.  If you search around, there are some live studio performances, and both band and singer can nail their parts.  Very talented.  For the tracks, Pink Lemonade, Neoprene Byzantine, and Church of the Technochrist are the most familiar sounding for CiM's style.  But all of them have quite a bit of head-bobbing rhythms.  Brahmatron and Happy Days would almost sound at home on a classic rock station.  If Seeds of Gold ever gets on indie rock radio, it's going to blow up.  Beckon Fire is awesome as well, love the detuned vocals.  Dinosaur Boss Battle and the last track are both crazy in a good way.  My only criticism would be that the album overreaches a bit too far in places.  The first track doesn't really need to be there.  The closing minutes of Pink Lemonade are a weird drag early on in the album.  Sometimes the lyrics are just so weird that you cringe.  But I'd rather see bands push themselves so far that they seem strange than play it safe.  So a well-deserved four stars in my eyes.  I can only hope they tour the US because this album seems like it would be an absolute blast live.  EDIT: Bumped this one to 5 stars close to a year later.  I listened to this so much last summer, that even though there were a few oddball tracks I mostly skipped, the high points were so incredibly high that it ended up in my top five albums of the year.  Brilliant is how I'd describe it.

Faith Evans is one of a handful of artists whose career exists in an almost paradoxical state. Few people can deny Faith’s vocal and songwriting talents, however her albums tend to get overlooked. Ironically, whereas much of Faith’s fame derives from her early work, 2005’s “The First Lady” marks her best-selling album to date. Despite the sales, it appears to be an album that was simultaneously successful and in some ways ignored. Much of Faith’s fame is linked to earlier efforts, including classics such as “Soon As I Get Home” and more upbeat tracks such as “Love Like This.” Unfortunately, some of the attention she received, at least initially, was also due to her personal life. As the widow of the Notorious B.I.G., it was especially important for Faith to establish herself as an artist in her own right and distance herself from her past. “The First Lady” came after a four-year hiatus that included the departure from Bad Boy Records as well as an arrest for drug possession. Whenever an artist has such a long break between albums, there is always the risk that fans will move on to the next new artist. 2005 was a particularly crowded year for R&B albums, however Faith seemed to accumulated enough of a loyal fanbase to ensure that her release gained some momentum. Once again, she releases a strong album that deserves more attention than it received.

The album begins with “Goin’ Out,” in which Faith sings about going out with her friends after having problems with her partner. It’s a nice track and a decent album opener, but suffers mostly from the extremely repetitive chorus. Faith’s vocals sound good, and the verses are written well enough. Even Pusha T’s rap verse and the brief opening lines by Pharrell are decent. Upbeat tracks often suffer from cloying, repetitive choruses, and this one is no exception. It is by no means a bad song, but Faith has done this style so much better in the past. Lead single “Again” directly addresses some of the issues that led to Faith’s break between albums. As one of the more personal songs the album has to offer, it gives listeners a window into Faith’s life and experiences. The track even takes on a more optimistic approach, with Faith recognizing that she made mistakes and stating that she would go through it all again because it’s shaped who she is. “I Don’t Need It” is an early album highlight, with a style that suits Faith’s voice perfectly. It is also a track that takes on a fairly typical theme in a relatively unique way, with Faith singing about wanting more time with her partner. The bridge in particular is strong. Although the lyrics are a little on the simple side, they suit the intent of the song well and Faith’s delivery keeps it from becoming repetitive.

“Stop N Go” has Faith questioning how far to let a relationship go with a man who may be a player. This track makes strong use of basketball metaphors, which some listeners may not like, however they work surprisingly well to reflect the situation. Faith sounds great on the verses, however she is overshadowed by the background singers on the chorus. Once again, the bridge is one of the strongest parts. This track is definitely one of the most surprising that the album has to offer, as it is much more impressive than it looks on paper. Second single “Mesmerized” is a fan favourite, largely due to the homage it pays to the classic soul style. It is a track that can take some getting used to, since it initially seems so different stylistically from the rest of the album and even the majority of Faith’s career. However, it is a style that fits her voice and allows her ample room to showcase her vocal talents. “Tru Love,” the album’s third and final single, is much closer to what one would expect from Faith, and it stands out as an album highlight. Produced by Jermaine Dupri and Bryan Michael Cox, the track was considered reminiscent of Usher’s “Burn” and even garnered some comparisons to Mariah’s “We Belong Together” (also produced by Dupri) released the same year. These comparisons may have somewhat hindered the track’s success, since audiences are often quick to assume that artists are attempting to copy other’s hits. However, this is one of the more stripped-down tracks that the album has to offer, which gives Faith’s voice room to shine. Her straightforward and sincere delivery are what really make the track, since it is clear that Faith genuinely means what she is singing. This is easily one of the strongest tracks the album has to offer, but also one that unfortunately gets overlooked due to its similarities to others.

“Jealous” is a mediocre track where Faith sings about her possessiveness over her partner. The production on this song is a little too busy, almost to the point of being distracting. The lyrics are again on the repetitive side in the chorus, although the verses and especially the bridge are strong. It is a decent album track, but far from the best that this album has to offer. “Ever Wonder” is inexplicably considered one of the album’s weaker tracks, with much of this attributed to guest artist Mario Winans’ vocal limitations. While it’s true he does not have the most powerful voice, he is perfectly capable of holding his own on this track. It is a simple, catchy track that probably would have been quite radio-friendly if it had been released at the time. It is one of the more memorable tracks on the album and it is difficult to see why so many people dislike it. “Catching Feelings” is a romantic, somewhat unconventional ballad. The style of this track is quite unusual and it can take some getting used to. However, by the end of the track, the style has already grown enough to be enjoyable. Faith’s vocals on this track are excellent, as she sings about a younger man who needs to grow up before they could become anything serious. In asense, this is one of the riskier tracks on the album due to its style, but for the most part it works.

“Get Over You” is a decent mid-tempo, and one of the most relatable tracks on the album. Although there is nothing wrong with this track per se, there is nothing that really stands out about it either. It ultimately ends up remaining a solid filler track, but one that is quickly forgotten soon after it is over. “Until You Came” fares somewhat better due to its stronger lyrics. Even Faith’s delivery on this track seems much more passionate, which helps keep the song from faltering. Faith’s spoken-word verse toward the end of the track helps to keep it from becoming too repetitive. It is still far from the best on the album, but it once again makes an enjoyable listen. The biggest problem this track has is that it is almost a full minute too long, with nothing to show for it other than repetitions of the chorus leading to a brief instrumental segment. “Lucky Day” is an oddly placed upbeat track that may have fared better earlier on the album. It is a surprisingly strong dance song that showcases Faith’s versatility to pull off different styles, but it seems out of place so late in the album. Nonetheless, it is one of the strong tracks that the album has to offer and serves as a reminder of Faith’s talents with more upbeat material. The album ends off with “Hope”, a Twista track from the Coach Carter soundtrack featuring Faith. Although listeners have very split opinions about the inclusion of this track, it is still one of the album’s highlights. It is rare for a track to be truly inspirational without being too forceful with its message. It is somewhat odd for Faith to be a guest artist on her own album, but her role in this track is dominant enough that it is acceptable. It is definitely one of the rare motivational songs that truly achieves its purpose.

Overall Mark: 4/5

With her fourth album, Faith continues to build on her legacy as a talented artist who deserves much more recognition than she receives. Further cementing the paradoxical nature of her career, this album saw Faith attempting to branch out to work with a wider variety of producers, with mixed results. Branching out often brings artists into collaboration with writers who bring out their best, however in Faith’s case it seemed that she was best left on her own to write. Although Faith still had a hand in the majority of the tracks here, the songwriting was not quite as strong as fans may be used to. Faith was almost single-handedly responsible for writing and producing her first two albums, which are a testament to her skills as a songwriter. While the lyrics themselves are still quite strong, this album seems to have a stronger tendency toward choruses that are repeated far too many times. Despite this, the album as a whole is quite strong, and is one of the rare albums where the first half actually fares better than the second. There is not a single truly bad song to be found here, but the tracks on the second half tend to lack the same kind of impact to make them truly memorable. Nonetheless, Faith once again delivers a strong album that is likely to please fans

The songs match the bleak and listless tone of the game itself, and they flow together very well. There's a hint of the old-time bars and back alleys of the 20's and 30's mixed in. The songs hold their own, even while not in context of the story, and are a great listen. I bought this sound track before I played the game, and I thought it was fantastic.
The songs themselves are moody and depressing, with a small number of casual, slower tempo melodies that even out the music. The guitars go well with the synthesized sounds, and the drums have a jumpy rhythm that bounces about, or is more lax and sedating, depending on the track.
Most of the music is heard in the background of the game itself, but there are a few that have added vocals. While the mood is heavy, melancholy, and generally sad, Ashley Barrett lends her voice and makes some of the songs truly stand out.
Everyone's musical preferences differ, but I personally recommend this to anyone and everyone who likes the dreary tune that floats through the album.
Good work, Darren Korb!
