This is a stunning example of how business corrupts and betrays art. Columbia Records recorded this in 1960, with one of the most solidly established pop singing stars of WW 2 and into the 1960s, backed by another gold-edged musical security in Johnny Mandel, who wrote the arrangements and led the band. The third big fail-safe was to put together a band so solid and filled with well-deserved celebrities that even if the singer hadn't shown up you'd have a great recording. The players were the stars of the Duke Ellington orchestra -- Johnny Hodges on alto sax, Ben Webster on tenor sax, trumpeter and sometime violinist Ray Nance, the incomparable baritone saxist Harry Carney, the warm sound of trombonist Lawrence Brown -- combined with some of the finest West Coast players, guys who made a steady living in the movie studios but also on recordings and California gigs: Conte Candoli and Don Fagerquist trumpets, Jimmy Rowles piano, Russ Freeman (Chet Baker's musical director) on celeste, Mel Lewis and Shelly Manne sharing drum duties. Of course, in music nothing is guaranteed, although it's unlikely to nearly impossible that these people would make a weak record. And they made a terrific record, in fact. Jo Stafford is just a great singer and she was in her prime. Big Ben's and Jeep's obbligatoes and solos, however brief, are worth the price of the ticket, and there is plenty, plenty of other gems throughout, not least of which are Mandel's swinging arrangements and voicings.
But Columbia essentially dumped the project. They hardly advertised it and, as far as I can tell, never offered it on their very popular record club. One could say that Stafford was a victim of the rise of rock, but she was poised to survive (as Sinatra and Tony Bennett and others did) and Columbia didn't help. She and her husband, bandleader/arranger Paul Weston, formed their own label, Corinthian, and in 1977 reissued this treasure. Now it's available once more on cd and download.Stick it in your device, or in the cd player of your car and you will be listening for weeks.

product_title: Unexpected Songs of Joy, and Celebrations of Music Stars
review_body:
I heard about Matt on an episode of TLDR, a podcast offshoot of On the Media. The TLDR reporter asks Matt to sing a song for his step-mom's birthday, and Matt obliges after taking just a few seconds to whip up some lyrics. At the time that I heard the podcast, my wife's birthday was about 2 weeks away, so I emailed and asked if he'd be up for writing one for her. I didn't expect to hear back, but about a week later, he emailed me a terrific song, and never asked for a dime. When I asked how I could pay him, he wrote that I didn't have to--that he enjoyed doing it--but if I really wanted to, he said that I could buy some of his music off itunes or amazon, which I'm finally getting around to doing now.

Matt, if you're reading this, you have my sincere thanks. And if you're not Matt and you're reading this, I encourage you to buy some of his music. You'll be supporting one of the kindest people I've ever traded emails with.

review_headline: Review by Lynn René Bayley (Fanfare Magazine for July-August 2014 edition)
review_body:
BEETHOVEN Piano Sonata No. 23, “Appassionata.” CHOPIN Fantaisie in f. Piano Sonata No. 3 Sophia Agranovich (pn) ROMÉO 7303 (73:46)

Sometimes it’s interesting to compare and contrast pianists with different approaches to music, and this was the case for me. I came to Sophia Agranovich’s recital of Beethoven and Chopin (titled Passion and Fantasy) after listening to Jerome Lowenthal’s collection of such modern composers as Rochberg, Chicara, and Rorem, and the contrast was not just in the material being performed but very much so in their approach to piano playing. Lowenthal, a pupil of William Kapell and Alfred Cortot, is all about touch and nuance; despite a superb technique, he takes time to investigate, you might say, the spaces between the notes. Agranovich, on the other hand, is a Russian (Ukrainian) pianist, and thus by training and instinct a musician of direct gifts. Trained by Anna Stolarevich, Alexander Edelmann, and (at Juilliard) the great Russian émigré Nadia Reisenberg, her métier is geared more towards music as architecture: a stylistically direct approach, albeit with fascinating and telling moments of rubato, an evolving sense of both mood and structure as two sides of the same coin, and a smoldering sense of passion in her playing. In short, she is a tigress of the keyboard, yet one who knows just how much to attack and when to pull back. She is a sort of cross between György Cziffra and Dinu Lipatti, a tigress who is also a poet.
Listening to the first movement of her playing of the “Appassionata” Sonata, one hears a number of moments when Agranovich pulls back from her forward thrust to inject rubato, moments of sensitivity, even complete stops when the music and the mood call for them. More interestingly, she allows only a few seconds’ silence between the end of the first movement and the start of the second. Since we know that the last movement is played after the second without a break, this gives the whole sonata a feeling of unbridled momentum. She can, then, both shoot the moon and pull back on the reins in a way that keeps the listener fully engaged in her music making. It is musical brinksmanship of an extraordinarily high order.
Since Agranovich studied with Reisenberg, an outstanding Chopin pianist, I was particularly interested in hearing her performances of the Polish composer’s music. Yes, there is some of the Reisenberg “touch” in her playing, but her sense of time—her specific way of phrasing and use of rubato—differ in many small details from the way Reisenberg played. Yet it is certainly valid and interesting Chopin, a shade more delicate on balance than her Beethoven, yet without sacrificing her keen feeling for the musical line. Still, Agranovich’s Chopin has much more in common with the post-modern approach of Ian Hobson than with Reisenberg.
In the Sonata No. 3, I was able to compare Agranovich with not only Reisenberg but with Lipatti, Cortot, Cherkassky, and Cliburn—certainly a clutch of outstanding pianists to drawn on. Agranovich does not really resemble any of them but comes closest to Lipatti, who also brought out the structure of the music he played. Yet I found her approach more poetic in places than his, pulling back a bit more on the phrases to allow moments to linger in the mind.
Agranovich is an interesting pianist. I certainly look forward to her future releases.

Lynn René Bayley

review_headline: Continuing Creative Music out of Chicago
review_body:
This is the seventh album by Rob Mazurek and Chad Taylor as the Chicago Underground Duo, although they have collaborated with other musicians on albums as the Chicago Underground Trio, Quartet, and Orchestra. The Duo put on a great live show and I saw them at a small club in Chicago back in the ‘90s. Mazurek and Taylor have also collaborated with other Thrill Jockey bands and musicians, such as Isotope 217, The Sea and Cake, and Tortoise. The Chicago Underground Duo are solidly an experimental, avant-garde jazz group, but at times there are influences of some of these other projects, such as the melodic vibraphone-like sound on “Yaa Yaa Kole,” which also sounds a bit like Isotope 217. Or some of the more electronic-influenced sounds that are reminiscent of Tortoise or Isotope.

This is a diverse album and is not an easy listen, although there are some great songs on the album. Personally I tend to like the more melodic songs like “Yaa Yaa Kole,” or the loopy sound, with poppy drums, and catchy horn of “Boss.” “Kabuki” is interesting, sometimes catchy, sometimes repetitive, sometimes a little irritating, reminding me of The Residents. Missing is the nice, long song or songs that are typically on a Chicago Underground album, like the twelve minute “Blue Sparks From Her and the Scent of Lightning,” from Synesthesia, or the nine minute, “Two Concepts for the Storage of Light,” from Axis and Alignment. The longest song on Locus is “Blink Out,” at 5:44.The album ends with “Dante,” which does have a tense, claustrophobic feel, filled with struggle and plodding, as Dante’s journey through Hell and Purgatory were in The Divine Comedy, and it ends with a brief, beautiful expansiveness, like the sun shining through the clouds, or Dante’s illumination.

It is a beautiful, catchy, challenging and dissonant album. Definitely experimental jazz and experiments are often risky and don’t always pay off, even when creative, but it is great when it all comes together.ut it is great when it all comes together.

review_headline: Let's Try Out This Exquisite But Unusual Hit
review_body:
Fresh off the success of his extravagant live 2-CD set Progression: The Art Of
The Trio, Volume 5 (2001) and his “99/00” Millennium World Tour, Brad Mehldau
decided to take on a harrowing bright note in 2002 with this next CD. So with his
trio placed in a small ensemble setting, Largo would find the jazz piano master in
a challenging atmospheric recording took on a contemporary and hybrid acoustic
artistry blended together, which is done on a slightly low-key manner with upbeat
results. Beginning on a crystal-clear note on When It Rains, this exuberant track
set proceed on other memorable tracks like You’re Vibing Me, Dusty McNuggett,
Franklin Avenue and the Latin-tinged Alvarado, as well as successful versions of
other classic standards, like The Beatles’ Dear Prudence, Radiohead’s Paranoid
Android, the theme song from Free Willy and Antonio Carlos Jobim’s Wave, just
until ending nicely on the solo piano tune I Do. But what is even intriguing about
Largo is that it even has a dash of electronica-driven effects just alongside some
of the funky beat and acoustic background (as evident on several tacks, such as
Dropjes and Sabbath), which adds to the CD’s well-deserved success, although
there is never a flawed moment. Now here is another special classic from Brad
Mehldau that deserves equal recognition and ranks as one of his finest albums.

review_headline: Great songs on here for the most part
review_body:
I have to say it's taken me a little while to warm up to Pepper. But now that I have, I love all their albums except for the one I haven't gotten yet, which is their 2013 eponymous release. I'll describe a few of my favorites below when it comes to individual tracks. I would say this album is on par with what they have done in the past, or maybe just a little worse, but no big deal.

Songs I really liked include:

Rent: A really catchy song about paying rent and how you can never catch up to all your bills.
No Control: This is one of their best songs of all-time. This was the first Pepper song I'd ever heard back in 2008 or so, but it took me a few years to get through Sublime, Matisyahu, LBDA, and Dirty Heads before I started listening to Pepper.
Lost in America: A song about getting lost in America, touring everywhere, going here, there, etc. Catchy.
Nice Time: One of my favorites on the CD. Very nice, fun, catchy, balanced song...really worth a listen.
Crazy Love: A slower song about being with someone you know could only be trouble, but still enjoying yourself and getting all caught up in it.
Old Time Problem: Another GREAT song with a female singer as well. Lots of energy and great chorus.
Wanted: A little bit whiny, but still is a good song. Something to do with a breakup...but has a lot of emotion in it.
Zicky's Song: This song I didn't listen to until recently, and now I think it's one of the best songs on the track. A little bit slower than some other songs, but has a somber tone to it. Just an excellent song to close out the album.

Very nice album, especially for Pepper fans, or even fans of similar music. I'm a huge Sublime fan and I think Pepper is a great band. I'm not going to compare them to other bands in terms of where they rank in ska-punk-reggae band circles, but they are very good on their own merit. They are \\"key.\\" 311 is not key.

review_headline: ~Paul Taylor is still On The Horn.~
review_body: Ever since his opening act, his initial release On The Horn 19 years ago (WOW!), I have followed the smooth jazz of Paul Taylor and it is so very good that he continues to enjoy longevity in an arena that sees one CD release artists unfortunately go the way of the dinosaur. I often wonder what the process is like for an artist, trying to keep the creativity fresh & update; always aiming to produce the right mix of ingredients to keep their fanbase strong and hopefully growing, while never sounding like any of their contemporaries, both past and present. With Spur Of The Moment, Mr. Taylor gives us a mid-tempo melody that gives you a rhythmic head bop that flows into steady hand claps, all fitting together like pieces of a puzzle. For the first time in his career, he utilizes one producer, Dino Esposito, to cover the fullness of Tenacity, the most appropriate title that defines why he is still making the smooth jazz that we continue to enjoy. Keep doin' ya thang, Paul; we are most definitely listening. ~K.I.S.S~

The best ever recorded performance, full-throated in the chorus, elegantly shaped in the orchestra, was Michael Tilson Thomas and Boston when MTT was in his twenties; only ever available on LP, Deutsche Grammophon should absolutely bring this (with its fine 'Sacre' companion) to re-release on CD.

review_headline: Haven't you heard of Jonah Kue?
review_body:
If you're like me, probably not. Apparently, Jonah has been flying under the radar for some time, releasing his music for free on the internet. Harvest Redux is (obviously) a departure from this trend, but it is worth every penny; and probably a fair amount more. The album is a musical journey from one song into the next, so I'd highly recommend purchasing the album as a whole. That being said, there are definitely AAA quality singles that stand on their own. Usually, when I purchase an album, a particular song (maybe two) will get stuck in my head and stick with me throughout the day. With Harvest Redux, that number is SIX. That's right, for the past several days I've been humming and singing along to: Sleepless, The Beat, Chardonnay, Belong, Colors and Smooth.

Off the top of my head, I cannot think of another album that sounds quite like Harvest Redux. Jonah's silky smooth voice is impossibly both soothing and invigorating at the same time; and several songs feature accompanying artists, which compliment Jonah quite well. His lyrical style is hard to categorize. I'd have to describe it as a sort of blend between alternative pop and smooth jazz. This is all set to an, often bass heavy, atmospheric electronic track. "Sleepless" and "Belong", in particular, are like worlds unto themselves. They absolutely suck you in to this overbearingly desolate, monumental place. It is like standing on the edge and peering into the void.

Harvest Redux is an experience unlike any other. I'll be singing it's praises for some time to come.

review_headline: Angelic performance but poor sound reproduction
review_body:
It's like listening to the 78 rpm records on a cheap mid-20th century player - in fact it takes me right back. As a result excellent string players sound tinny, there is relatively little separation in the orchestral layers and somehow at times the ensemble, both choral and orchestral, sounds ragged, even cacophonous. I doubt this performance was actually ragged; I think it is just an effect of the old, poorer recording. Instead of the ambiance sounding spacious as it should in a hall with good acoustics, the sound is muffled, closed in.

I figure this must be a revival of the old 1950 studio recording.

The overture starts right out at breakneck speed - how do they move their bows that fast?! The solo voices are to die for. The musicians' intonation is right on. The superb musical direction is obviously that of the legendary von Karajan. And Mozart - the genius of Mozart! For people who value historic performance, this will doubtless have value, most particularly for those who want to study or just enjoy the vocal performances of Erich Kunz, Irmgard Seefried and Elisabeth Schwartzkopf. It happens that those do not suffer much in the recording process. But if you enjoy and are used to the sonic results of today's superior recording techniques, you may find, overall, listening to this offering a bit trying... although I find the mind does get used to it remarkably quickly.

review_headline: Skip the CD versions. Get this album on 2xLP black vinyl.
review_body: It's getting harder and harder to find this album in its original version. Rhino just reissued it as a digital release and the remastering in the clips sounds great but it's the later version of the album, which replaces Professional Widow with its remix. It was a hit, yes, I remember but that was in 1996. No one's who's interested in this album now wants this commercially butchered version of it. Most versions also feature the single remix of Talula rather than the original album version, which was only briefly available on CD. What you might not know, however, is that this album was only ever issued on vinyl once, with the original track listing and the mastering, by the legendary Bob Ludwig, who mastered Tori's first three solo albums sounds amazing. Not to mention, this album is the first of many Tori Amos albums specifically designed to be heard on vinyl. Each side (it's a double album) starts with a short interlude song, the most famous of which is Mr. Zebra. If you do decide to get this album on vinyl, I highly recommend tracking down the black vinyl, which is actually more of a rarity than the attractive but sonically inferior clear vinyl release. I have heard both and the difference in sound quality is astounding. The black vinyl version of this album sounds better than any other format and features the original track listing. It is absolutely how Tori Amos and Bob Ludwig intended this album to be heard and it is an amazing album.

review_headline: Not your typical Def Lep sound....
review_body:
Okay, first, this is NOT new Def Leppard album. It was released in 1996. The "Deluxe Issue" is a new release of old material featuring different mixes of the original songs on "Slang". Having said that, is it any good? It's different. There are no songs on this record that blatantly sound like they could have been on "Hysteria". That is not to say there's no good material here. In fact, there are many songs that fans will find appetizing from the departure from Lep's signature sound. This is due in part to the absence of Jeff "Mutt" Lange, who had produced Lep's previous albums.
With this release, you get thirty (!) songs. While about half of them are remixes, they are some ear-worthy riffs here. If you can listen to this without the "Adrenalize" or "Hysteria" framework in your mind, you'll likely find some tunes you actually love
Happy listening!

Wakolda, known in English-speaking countries as The German Doctor, is an Argentine film directed by Lucía Puenzo, based on her own novel. Set in 1960, the film stars Àlex Brendemühl as the doctor, scientist and Nazi war criminal Josef Mengele, and depicts the time he spent in exile in South America following the end of World War II. Having adopted a new identity, Mengele moves into a Patagonian hotel run by German-speaking Eva and her husband Enzo. Unaware of his identity, Eva and Enzo welcome the hesitant romance that begins to develop between their daughter Lilith (Florencia Bado) and the handsome, charming foreigner; however, having won the family’s trust, Mengele finds himself renewing his interest in the human genetic research that cemented his terrible reputation during the war.

The score for Wakolda is by two veterans of the Argentine film music industry, composers Andrés Goldstein and Daniel Tarrab; the pair previously gained some international exposure following their scores for the 2004 film La Puta y la Ballena and the 2007 film XXY, but this score could really enhance their reputations internationally, if enough people have the opportunity to hear it.

The score is fairly small and intimate, written for a chamber orchestra augmented by percussion, electric cello and various electric and acoustic guitars, giving it a feeling that is somehow classical and modern simultaneously. There is also a slightly “off” feeling to much of the music, somehow insinuating that, despite appearances on the surface, things are not quite as innocent as they seem to be. A cue like “Just a Game”, for example, has an expressive acoustic guitar melody that is quite lovely, but the string sustains bubbling underneath give off a slight sense of unease. The same sort of feeling filters through the subsequent “The Journey”, where the orchestra is augmented by brushed snares and a moody, hooting duduk clarinet – again, attractive, but with a subtly anxious undercurrent.

The duduk becomes a much more prevalent timbre as the score goes on, almost acting as a leitmotif for Mengele’s twisted mind and sinister intentions. Its use in cues such as “Blood and Honor”, “Dolls Factory” and “The Persecution” allows the score to embrace the darkness of Mengele’s looming presence fully. Similarly, the regular return to the core thematic ideas and instrumental choices – guitar and percussion on top of the small string orchestra – in cues such as “Nazi’s Bunker” and “The End” allows the score to maintain its personal identity in a way that is very pleasing. One further standout cue is “The Hunt Has Begun”, a more strident and forceful piece featuring a more prominent piano element, which acts as one of the score’s few moments of straightforward action. Parts of this action style return in the vibrant “End Credits” piece, ending the score on a pleasing classical note.

The only drawback to the score is the careless placement of several period songs – “Rain Song”, “Lady Sunshine Und Mister Moon”, “Wumba Tumba Schokoladeneisverkäufer” and “Let’s Dance” among them – which almost ruin the carefully constructed mood Goldstein and Tarrab create with their score. It’s so jarring to go from the low-key tension of “In the Mountain” to a piece of old-fashioned upbeat dance music, and these cues need to be programmed out of the listening experience so as not to break the mysterious spell the score otherwise creates.

Parts of Wakolda remind me of something Mychael Danna might write for one of his ‘disturbing urban drama’ scores, The Ice Storm or Felicia’s Journey or something like that, where the public sheen of normality and respectability hides something much more emotionally monstrous behind the curtains and under the beds. It’s a difficult notion to convey musically, and the fact that Goldstein and Tarrab have succeeded here is testament to their talent.

review_headline: Victorians are somewhat unique/somewhat not, but what they pull off is EPIC
review_body:
Put simply, if you like Nightwish (lets say with Floor Jansen), Xandria's Neverworld's End album, and Within Temptation, then you should buy this album, no questions asked.

To elaborate, I see this album as a combo of the groups I mentioned above. I am actually on my first listen through of this album as I right this review, but I sense there are certain songs which will grow on me fast once I give this album a few more listens, and I will certainly do that. Its not often I stumble across a symphonic metal group which is literally right up my alley in the style that I am searching for, but this album hit the bulls eye.

Most of the songs are more on the fast paced side. This lady singer definately can do the "opera" voice, but she can sing in a 'non-opera' voice as well. She does this very well, and not only that, but the songs, the instrumentals, and the band playing the music is alive. It is not dull, nothing on this album is filler.

To be quite frank, the more I am listening to this, I would say this album is up there with Xandria's Neverworlds End album, and I consider that album to be really epic. I would rate this album higher than 5 stars if possible.

I urge everyone reading this review to buy this album to support this amazing group.

review_headline: People All Around the World Can Benefit From Erica Campbell's HELP
review_body:
We've all been there: felt as though our backs were against the wall and not able to see how we are going to be able to move forward.

For individuals of Faith we know that God is able to do all things, and when things are looking their worse that is when we need him the most. Sometimes we don't know what to say, but thankfully He gives us just what we need at the right time. HELP, the debut album from Mary Mary's Erica Campbell, offers us the words we need in such a time as this.

HELP offers not just words of encouragement but praise for all of us when it seems all hope is lost. I had a chance to talk with Erica during her promo tour about the lead single and the way it was affecting the lives of others. "It let's me know that what I'm singing about or talking about is needed right now," she told me during our phone interview. "I don't think it's ever inappropriate for anybody to call on help, especially the help of God... I feel honored to be used in that way, to sing a song that is reaching people, helping people, touching people."

For over a decade Erica and her sister Tina have been a blessing to others, sharing their gift of ministry through song with the world. In HELP Erica is able to show that being a Christian doesn't make you immune from life's trouble, but it does give you help. "I choose to live for God, and I do it proudly," she told me.

The first single that many of us heard from the upcoming album was A LITTLE MORE JESUS. Since then we have been anxious to see what Erica would have in store for us next, and when the single HELP was released it proved to be everything we expected and more. Featuring Hip Hop artist Lecrae the single touches on many areas of our life that we might struggle with. I asked Erica if she went into the single knowing she was going to be that transparent about her own life. "Not necessarily," she said. "I thought I was just writing a song, and then 2013 happened with all it's fury...And all you can really say is help."

No matter who you are there comes a time when you have to surrender, knowing you can't go any further on your own. That is what Erica sings about, and it is that message that resonates through every verse of the single.

Other stand-outs on the album are LOOKING LIKE which through faith speaks that "I'm going to make it through this" and the single NOBODY ELSE which reminds us that He (God) did it for us when nobody else could.2013 happened with all it's fury...And all you can really say is help."

If any album would be considered as the \\"Soundtrack of the 1980s,\\" it would be this one. Track after track, these classics pack a wallop like few others. Not only were the hooks strong and the songs powerful, but, how could listeners also not instantly think of the accompanying music videos? Gender, race, religion, sexuality and other social mores took center stage in Madonna's one-woman assault on entertainment and culture. Not only did she she get us to enjoy the pure bliss of her pop, but she also showed that pop music could also penetrate the mind. With her music, videos and stage shows, she got us to ponder, think and debate- and \\"The Immaculate Collection\\" summed up pop culture rather nicely for the 1983-1990 era. She also was thinking of the moment, making over the tracks for the times (and giving them a timeless quality); only the hardcore contingency will notice the subtle differences (the only true remixes come in the form of \\"Like a Prayer\\" and \\"Express Yourself,\\" which maintain the integrity of the original recordings). The then-new tracks, \\"Justify My Love\\" and \\"Rescue Me,\\" close the collection just fine (with \\"Justify\\" adding to her cultural goldmine), but it's the 15 classics that make this an essential purchase. So, sit back and enjoy the tour-de-force that comes with this era-defining collection of pop at its finest.

This song, like the whole Speed of Darkness album, is decent enough. It's just not the Flogging Molly that we're used to. On past albums, Flogging Molly told stories that cut to the core of the human experience. While the stories were King's own, the themes were relatable to people of any nationality, any class, any generation.This album, in trying to be political and current, lost a lot of that. The album stacks up competitively against other recent left-leaning working-class punk acts' albums (think of the Street Dogs), but it doesn't have the timeless, universal power that Flogging Molly brought to Swagger, Drunken Lullabies, Within a Mile of Home and (perhaps to a lesser extent) Float.

I guess that, as decades pass, bands have to evolve with the lives of their members. This was a respectable effort at that evolution, but I hope that FM tries a different approach on future work.

So if you like 60s R&B with exciting, stripped-down heartfelt music and vocals, "Breakout" is a great choice. It was Mitch Ryder's band's second album (the first, "Take a Ride," is also excellent), and it contains the endlessly covered hit, "Devil with a Blue Dress/Good Golly Miss Molly," one of the greatest of the mid-60s rockers. But this album is far from a one-hit wonder. It includes the band's excellent version of "Little Latin Lupe Lu," and nice versions of Marvin Gaye's "Stubborn Kind of Fellow" and Wilson Pickett's "In the Midnight Hour."

But my favorites are the ones that create a kind of frantic party atmosphere that was for me Mitch's signature sound and his raw, powerful vocals. The title tune is a great example. This is one of the best and singularly interesting recordings of the symphonies I've heard in a very long time. The most stunning aspect of this recording is the thing that makes this the most quintessentially Beethovenian recording of these works I've ever heard - the sense of unflagging maximum effort one gets when listening. All of the things that make Beethoven so difficult to play - sudden dynamic changes, the need to sustain long lines and even single notes well past a performer's comfort zone, a relentless rhythmic pulse - not to mention the difficulties inherent in just executing the notes correctly, the Orpheus players handle with a wild-eyed zeal, virtuosic ease and incredible enthusiasm. My wife and I both kept saying over and over that we could have been there for these live performances (even more incredible when one realizes this) and as we were listening in the car at the time I found myself speeding. So, don't listen to this while driving, but do find a place for this recording on your iPod next to the ones by Kleiber, Gardiner, Furtwangler and all of the other great recordings you might have. You'll be hard pressed to find much more enjoyment for 8.99 anywhere.

I have all three Best Coast albums (The Only Place and Crazy for You being the others) and I agree with the other reviewers that Fade Away is the band's best album yet. Best Coast's first album, Crazy for You, was eclectic and upbeat, but the low-fi production distracted a bit from the music. The Only Place was well-produced but had a lot of ballads which made the album kind of homogenous, though it had its gems.

Fade Away, by contrast, is the best of both worlds--there's enough of their original, garage-bandy sound to stay true to their vision, but there's also clean production that makes the riffs sound just that much better and Cosentino's vocals even more spot-on. The songs on this album are upbeat and energetic, the kind of songs that made me fall for Best Coast in the first place. "Fade Away" and "Baby I'm Crying" are the two ballads, and they're just enough to provide a mellow counterpoint to the rest of the album which is melodic, fast-tempo surf-pop. Lyrically, I also think this album shows a lot of growth--in particular, "I Don't Know How" really illustrated Cosentino's raw, unadorned lyrical prowess.

Overall, I loved this album, and the fact that the title song, "Fade Away", got some well-deserved airplay on television as well. Best Coast is one of those bands like She and Him that have a very specific sound and niche--their consistency is their strength-- so if you're looking for a huge departure from their earlier work, you won't find it here. But if, like me, you're a fan hungry for more of their classic, California sound, you'll love these new songs.

Channel 3 were a most unlikely band : they did not fit neatly into either the Long Beach hardcore scene nor that of Huntington Beach.

Their city, Cerritos, at the junction of 2 major freeways, the scene in 1987 of a horrific mid air collision between an Aeromexico DC-9 and a small private plane that devastated a neighborhood with massive falling debris.

The main guys, Kimm Gardener and Mike Magrann were both "A" students who went on to take degrees at nearby Long Beach State University. Posh Boy signed them as replacements for the departed (for Frontier records) T.S.O.L.; in those heady days of early 1981, it was as though there was gold just lying in the street waiting to be picked up. Indeed, CH 3 were signed on the basis of that most improbable medium, the demo cassette, handed to me by Cathy Conway who had obtained it from one of the band's female admirers.

The re-recorded demos formed the basis for their first 12" e.p. which followed closely on the heels of the T.S.O.L. 12" with similar high contrast black and white artwork by Kevin J. Walker. So where did Channel 3 fit in? In England, of all places; 1982 saw the release there of the I Got A Gun 7" on the Oi dominated No Future Label. The single hit the indie charts running and Channel 3 had made their mark in hardcore history.

This along with Living In Darkness were probably the recordings most influenced by Robbie Fields' production values. Kimm and Mike were still willing to listen at this stage of their relationship with Posh Boy and one of the results of their going along with the production team was the L.A. radio hit "You Make Me Feel Cheap" with a female vocal part co-written in the studio by Robbie Fields himself. That the lady singing was d.j. Rodney Bingenheimer's then girlfriend, Maria Montoya, did not hurt the record's chances for success.

Channel 3 records were not only licensed to No Future for the U.K., but also were some of the first recordimgs to appear on the Roadrunner label out of Holland.

In the year 2002, a game called "Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem" made its debut on the Gamecube. It's been among my favorite games ever since and holds an unassailable place in my heart.
One of the things that made it so perfect to me was the soundtrack, which is absolutely stellar. To my knowledge it's never been released for sale but was given as a bonus to Nintendo Power subscribers way back in the day. The thing that seemed to be missing from it, though, was the chant from the beginning of Anthony's chapter. It was played in very small part on the track entitled "The Penitent", but that didn't satisfy me.

When Soundhound first arrived on my phone, one of the first orders of business was to try and identify that haunting refrain, but to no avail.
I tried again and again, with weeks and then months between attempts. I listened to samples of every Gregorian chant I could find online, listening for just that one.

Finally, a light shone in my (eternal) darkness: Soundhound picked something up! Dare I hope? Could this really be it? I gave it a listen---the very thing!
Eleven years of searching have finally reached an end.

review_headline: Why can we not buy a copy of the original?
review_body: I, and my fellow Marines heard, "I'm a man" a thousand times a week in my Marine Corps (the P and S are silent) barracks in 1970.  We had over a hundred men in that open unit and I never heard one man complain that they were tired of hearing it.  We had only vinyl then and it took me years of tapes and disks to appreciate the records I once complained about.  For some reason, the MP3 just did not evoke the feelings I experienced in the barracks in my first year as a Marine.  Of course, I was only 19 years old then but, in my mind today, no less the Marine and ready to go at any time my country calls for me again.  I only wish that I took better care of my own copy, purchased a year later.  Now, after reading up on the issue, I find that the only way I could get a non remastered copy would be to buy the record from someone who DID take care of their own copy.  I am thankful I live under capitalism - even with all the socialist arrows shot into it - because I feel the optimism that it naturally brings with it gives one hope that they too might be able to find their own copy of, "I'm a man" as well as possibly measuring up to that level of testosterone - even back in the 1970's. I doubt greatly that even in the US, the average man cannot hope to attain the level of testosterone of the greatest generation - even in the women in the 1940's.  Anyway, I think that Steve Winwood still has the best version of "I'm a man" available to the average person today.  I sure liked the original one from CTA though.  It sure brought out the feeling of greatness and possibility that today's "music" falls far short of.

review_headline: He was what he was.  Christian with blues roots.
review_body:
After being blinded in childhood by a hateful stepmother, Willie Johnson grew up to be a powerful advocate for the Christian faith. Almost all of his music is explicitly Christian, but his guitar playing was strictly slide guitar blues.
His voice as heard on this album varied widely, from a mellow crooning tone to an almost painfully harsh, grating, gravelly sound. I don't know whether this was an evolution over time or a day-to-day variation. At its most gravelly his singing was almost hard to listen to.
Willie Johnson wrote or made early influential recordings of songs that would become blues standards. Among those on this album you will find \\"You're Gonna Need Somebody on your Bond,\\" \\"Mother's Children,\\" (commonly known as Motherless Children) and \\"Nobody's Fault but Mine.\\"
Blind Willie Johnson was what he was: a very creative, but uneven, preaching bluesman.

review_headline: But only if you want to hear Fröst play the "Kegelstatt" Trio
review_body:
I purchased this CD principally because I wondered why Fröst would want to re-record Mozart's great Clarinet concerto so soon after having just released such a wonderful performance of it only a couple of years ago. - Well, I still don't understand it.

Now if you're curious about Mozart's \\"Kegelstatt\\" Trio and maybe you'd like to hear Fröst, Andsnes,and Tamestit play it, fine. But why couple it with yet another go at the famous K.622 Concerto when the previous recording was paired with the great Clarinet Quintet K.581? Here,the \\"Kegelstatt\\" is hardly as felicitous a coupling.

On top of that, the earlier recording is more beautifully played by Fröst and the Amsterdam Sinfonietta lends wonderful support. It is also a wonderful SACD recording as well, and frankly a better buy.

review_headline: Glenn Lewis' Closer Show What True Love Is
review_body:
Like much of the world I was introduced to the song "Closer" by Glenn Lewis through the hit show on VH1 LOVE AND HIP HOP. On a show with so much drama you could see why a song like this is fitting.

Through the words we are able to see that Glenn is talking about not just getting closer physically but in every aspect of their lives. "Girl come closer," he sings, "and I'm never gonna let you go. I'll make you mine for life darling. I'm gonna love you so the whole world knows."

Definitely a song that can help in the healing of a relationship, Glenn shows why he's one of those go-to artist when you are looking for the right words to say. "Don't let your fear get in the way," he says. "Don't let anything come between us but opportunity and space." These are words you would say to someone you have a true connection with, and that is why they mean so much.

Once again Glenn Lewis uses his gift to show what true love is. CLOSER is another musical masterpiece.

review_headline: One of the great song-writers of our time
review_body:
It never fails to amaze me how little recognition this guy gets. He's had only a couple of hits in what must be 45 years, though others, like Joke Cocker, Judy Collins and Aaron Neville have had hit covers of his songs.

This one's about the devastating effect a huge storm has on a small Louisiana community, and the relative indifference the rest of the country:

'President Coolidge come down here in a railroad train,
'With a little fat man with a notepad in his hand.
'President say, "little fat man ain't it a shame,
'What the river has done to this poor cracker's lane?'"

What great song writing--simple, direct and so eloquently phrased.

review_headline: This one put them over the top
review_body:
I came across this 2009 remaster on a promo the Stones put out back then, it's the first song on the promo disc and was the last song on "Sticky Fingers." For some reason listening to this made me think that while the Stones never overtook the Beatles (nobody did), they sure as heck outlasted them and ultimately were the better true band (vs. artistic enterprise, which the Beatles became, quite spectacularly, after they stopped touring). No longer chasing the Beatles, or copying them as oftimes accuse, the Stones upped their game and kept it up, and this song is as good an example of the musical excellence they displayed on the five albums between "Beggar's Banquet" and "Exile on Main Street."

I have no problem with the sound of this remaster (or most of the ones I've heard, reviewed elsewhere on amazon.com). I am not an audiophile, and I listen mostly in my care. So far, of the bunch I've heard from the 2009 remasters, "Beast of Burden" stands out.

Don't get me wrong, I love the likes of DKM too, even though they shout more than sing, but Blaggards make even Flogging Molly sound off key, which they often truly are, but compared to many of their contemporaries, they are some of the best singing in the genre.  I will add that I still prefer Young Dubliners' Rocky Road To Dublin, and nobody can touch DKM's Fields Of Athenry, but both are well represented here and Drunken Sailor kicks some serious tail!  If you like these other artists, you will no doubt love Blaggards!

This is just amazing! I don't understand the negative reviews. No, this isn't a polished recording of perfectly mixed songs. This is a recording of a group of young musicians and singers getting together for the holidays and singing old favorites; some gospel, some rock, some country. Quite a few of the songs are complete, but others only contain a verse or two because the boys forget the rest. Even so, the boys are all having fun playing, singing and chatting about music. It just so happens the boys are Elvis Presley, Jerry Lee Lewis, Carl Perkins, and Johnny Cash at the very start of their careers, before any were kings and legends, but all full of incredible talent.

I agree with the reviewer who said that listening to Elvis do a "cover" of Jackie Wilson's cover of Elvis's own "Don't be Cruel" is worth the price of the entire CD, but I also LOVE the gospel tunes they sing, usually with Elvis in the lead and Jerry Lee Lewis doing the back-up vocals. Old-time Southern Gospel as it's best. I am not old, Southern, or Christian and I love that stuff!

Johnny Cash fans should be warned that it's very hard to hear him on most songs, either because he wasn't there for some of them or because the open mic didn't pick him up. But Elvis is loud and clear on most songs, and Jerry Lee Lewis also plays a large role. Carl Perkins doesn't sing much but his guitar playing is clear and terrific.

What a remarkable piece of rock 'n roll history!

product_title: Mahler: Symphony No. 4 in G Major
review_body: A thoughtful, personal interpretation with nothing bizarre about it, yet not like any other I've ever heard, and I've heard 80 or 90 Mahler Fourths. Certain phrases are slowed down and/or hushed ever so slightly to make a contrast with the previous or the next, yet nothing is stretched or jerked around too much: it is all very musical. The quality of the interpretation and of the playing and of the recording all add up to a new experience of the symphony -- I'm hearing details I've never heard before. If you love this piece as much as I do (and I once mortgaged my house to lease Horenstein's from EMI so I could put it out on CD) you need to hear this one. The soprano is fine, in my opinion, more listenable than most; like Fischer, a personality worth getting to know.

review_headline: the Lehto & Wright album I've been waiting for
review_body: This is the Lehto & Wright album I've been waiting for, for years. I've always appreciated the manner in which they integrate traditional with contemporary and acoustic with electric. And most of their acoustic material is performed impeccably but the rocker in me longed for a full album's worth of music performed by two of today's most gifted electric bassists (John Wright) and guitarists (Steve Lehto). Sure there are folk passages here. It's in their blood and can't be avoided nor should it. Their proficiency on acoustic instruments adds color, depth and dynamics to an album predominently emphasizing their rock talents. When listening to NOVEMBER I am reminded of giants like Steve Howe, Chris Squire, Martin Barre, John Wetton, Richard Thompson and others. This is riveting progressive rock played in the classic sense as few others performing today can. The opening track 'The Humors of Tuaimgreine/Rakish Paddy/The Cllahan Stomp' along with 'Tom Joad' display a side of Lehto that heretofore hasn't been heard on record; It's the opinion, especially in prog circles, that Robert Fripp's and Steve Hackett's guitar "shredding" is unsurpassed but after listening to excerpts from those 2 tracks, I'd add Steve Lehto to that short list. Gentler tracks like 'Redemption Song" and 'Shenandoah' allow for a breather after some truly breathtaking playing. An amazing album. For fans of Tull, Crimson, Genesis (w/Gabriel).

review_headline: A joyous, brilliant explosion of harmonies and sounds

I got this album on a whim about a week ago, after buying San Fermin (which is also amazing, and features the vocals of the two women of Lucius) and hitting repeat on "Sonsick" about a million times. Now I cannot stop listening to Lucius (and San Fermin).

This is upbeat, joyful pop (indie? alternative? whatever, it's good) music minus the saccharine and vapid lyrics. Highlights for me are "Turn it Around", "Tempest", and "Don't Just Sit There", lively standouts that almost demand listeners dance and sing along, and "Go Home", a haunting, heart-wrenching ballad. But in all of the songs - even if the lyrics are biting or bleak - you can just hear how much these musicians enjoy what they are doing, and the feeling is somehow contagious. There's not a bad track on this album.

I recommend looking up live Lucius performances on youtube (Tiny Desk Concert is a good start) to get a better idea than what Amazon has up for samples. But really, just get this album.

I probably will end up sorting these songs under the \\"Electronic\\" genre and they might feel pretty lonely in my iTunes library since Electronic music isn't really my thing but when it comes down to it, genres really don't matter. These are two quality songs that I recommend you purchase especially if you enjoy listening to the vocals of Cedric Bixler-Zavala.

If you're interested in another project featuring Cedric Bixler-Zavala that you might not have heard of, check out the self-titled album by Anywhere. Just bought this to replace my long lost copy after seeing the Paisley Underground reunion show last week, featuring The Three O'Clock, Dream Syndicate, Rain Parade and Bangs! So I had to hear it again, and again...

(The Paisley Underground, for those not familiar, was an alternate music scene in the mid-early eighties that was kind of a sub-genre of the garagepunk revival that was happening at the time. In LA it included the above mentioned bands, plus The Unclaimed, Thee Fourgiven, and others, in San Diego bands like the Crawdaddies and Tell-Tale Hearts, the east coast produced the Chesterfield Kings, The Fuzztones, The Fleshtones and the Lyres. And so many more. Each of these bands had their own takes and interpretations of the music and styles of the original sixties garage rock bands, but all were united by their love of the genre. See and hear Rhino's Children of Nuggets boxed set or The Knights of Fuzz dvd for more!)

review_body:
I truly love this album, as well as "A Passion Play." I want to hear the remix Steve Wilson has done for both albums, but my understanding is, his mixes are in 5.1 surround only!! I thought that he had produced a 2-channel stereo remix for both albums. The only equipment I have is a hybrid Blu-Ray and HD player, purchased back when the war was on between Blu-Ray and High Def DVD's. Blu-Ray films came in the blue box. HD films came in the red box. That player cost me $900 when I purchased it! (I just knew that I wanted and needed the best and the most recent technology to watch and listen to films, back then). ANYWAY, can someone please tell me the best alternatives for purchasing TAAB, with a remastered original "two track" AND a remixed Steve Wilson two-track (NOT a 5.1 recording) of the master tapes?? I suspect that if I were to purchase one of these issues, it simply wouldn't play on my existing Blu-Ray/High-Def player, and I would end up paying serious money for something that would be nothing but silence over my headphones and speakers. Corporations CANNOT keep fudging the playback technology of their proprietary releases upon non-audiophiles who don't have the existing equipment! They should NOT assume that everyone has the most up-to-date equipment and can enjoy it at their leisure, in a no-matter-what forum....
Now, can anyone help me on re-buying this incredible album in CD format?? With all 8 pages of the St.Cleve Chronicle liner notes, with a remastered original recording and a remixed stereo format, courtesy of Steve Wilson? Or am I simply "SOL?"

review_headline: Many rare tracks and one an Elmo Hope fan would want
review_body:
Too often these compilations are rehashes of other compilations. In this case, though, there is surprisingly little overlap between this collection of tracks and a value-priced six album set titled [[ASIN:B0085Z5AWU Six Classic Albums]].

You can listen to the sound samples to get an idea of the sound quality, which is - frankly - a but spotty in places. However, overall, the quality is listenable.

Another thing that mars most of these compilations is the lack of documentation. I have tracked that down and am providing it below. For some reason the tracks are scattered all over the place. I can live with that because there are some albums and tracks here that I do not own. Here is what you get:

Tracks 1, 7, 8, 9, 15, 17, 20, 24, 35 and 36 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000000Z6L Meditations]] that recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on July 28, 1955. Hope is backed by John Ore on bass and Willie Jones on drums.

Tracks 2 through 5, 13, 14, and 25 through 27 are from an out of print album recorded for Blue Note titled Elmo Hope - New Faces-New Sounds. This album was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on June 18, 1953 with Hope backed by Percy Heath on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.

Tracks 6, 11, 19, 21, 22, 30, 31 and 34 are the album titled [[ASIN:B0035RW05I Elmo Hope Trio (Digitally Remastered)]] that was recorded at Radio Recorders in Los Angeles on February 8, 1959. This album was recorded for both the HiFi and Contemporary labels with Hope backed by Jimmy Bond on bass and Frank Butler on drums.

Track 10 is from an album titled [[ASIN:B000050SKZ So Nice]] that was recorded in Recorded in Los Angeles, 1958. Hope leads a rhythm section comprised of Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Frank Butler on drums backing a front line comprised of Stu Williamson and Rolf Ericson on trumpet and Harold Land on tenor sax.

Tracks 12, 16, 18 and 29 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000000Z8K Homecoming]] that was recorded for Riverside at the Bell Sound Studios in NYC on June 29, 1961. Hope is backed by Percy Heath on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.

Tracks 23 and 28 were recorded in NYC on August 19, 1963 for Audio Fidelity. The title of the obscure album is Elmo Hope Ensemble - Sounds From Rikers Island and features Lawrence Jackson on trumpet, Freddie Douglas on alto and soprano saxophones, and John Gilmore on tenor sax. Hope leads the rhythm section with Ronnie Boykins on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.

32 and 33 are from an out-of-print album titled Here's Hope. This album was recorded in NYC in 1961 for the celebrity label and has Hope backed by Paul Chambers on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.itled [[ASIN:B000000Z8K Homecoming]] that was recorded for Riverside at the Bell Sound Studios in NYC on June 29, 1961. review_headline: Distinctive, but if you only want one recording of this, look elsewhere.
review_body:
I'll be honest: I haven't found a favorite recording of this amazing piece yet.

So, while I don't have a "perfect" version to recommend, I can say a few specific things about this recording that might help you determine whether you want to own it.

Yes: it is very distinctive. Perhaps unique. There is no mistaking this for some other recording.

The recording itself, however, is muddy, and the recording volume is pretty low. For pure audio pleasure, a lot has been lost in this one. It's kind of like listening to your neighbor listen to the requiem, if you have really, really thin walls. Ok, not quite that bad, but definitely not good.

The performance is... I've been hunting for the right word. I'm going to go with "ponderous." Yes, it's slow. But not just slow, it is technically deliberate. Intellectually, this is an interesting and appropriate choice. It is a requiem, and the seriousness and somberness of the occasion is very well captured in the performance. If you are accustomed to more vivacious renditions, this is off-putting at first, and then it grows on you as purposeful choice made about the music.

But it returns to off-putting after a while. A requiem is a somber occasion, but it is not just about death, it is about the life that has been lived, and the choices that go into this performance do not feel at all right or appropriate when considering Mozart's life.

Additionally, there are some technical choices that true scholars of serious composition will probably find rivetting, but which -- to this casual listener -- detracted more than they added.

None of this speaks a single word against the skill of the performers or conductor. Within the constraints of what seems to be intended here, this is a magnificent job. For those who want to study the music, or who want multiple recordings in different styles, this particular version is well worth owning.

But ifyou want just one recording of Mozart's Requiem, and you want to lose yourself in the rapturous beauty of the piece, I am afraid this is not the one I would recommend. When I find the one I recommend, I will.. recommend it.

review_headline: Sparkling Chapter From A Landmark Live Event
review_body: For those who heard the highly praised Since We Met from 1976, you had come         to realize that it was part of The Bill Evans Trio’s S.R.O. live club date they gave at         The Village Vanguard in 1974, and was later be released in 1981 to equal success.         With Re: Person I Knew, you can hear the other half of the live event from this time         honoured club date that Evans gives his first live trio performance there since 1961         (as captured in Sunday At The Village Vanguard and Waltz For Debby) where they         deeply impressed the music press and jazz fans alike. Serving up the delightful live         track set that begins with the title track, this half of the landmark event conclude on          other crystal clear acoustic piano takes the trio showcase very well several original         compositions, like Sugar Plum, T.T.T. (Twelve Tone Tune), and 34 Skidoo, as well         several standards, like Alfie and All The Things You Are, which he performs with a         slight keyboard Midas touch and high octane skill.  Although bassist Eddie Gomez         and drummer Marty Morrell never does erode the memories of the early trio sound         of bassist Scot LaFaro and drummer Paul Motian, the music speaks with as much         eloquence that The Bill Evans Trio could muster up with elaborate style.  So if you         want to hear the live event in it’s own complete format, make sure you get both Re:         Person I Knew and the highly lauded Since We Met together in their own complete         formats with time-honoured results.

review_headline: Another great buy from Bach Guild...with a few glitches
review_body:
Here is a very nice selection of Viennese waltzes and other dance music by the Strauss family and some of the other Viennese masters. At 99 cents its a no brainer to grab it, but let me list a few pros and cons.

Pros:
1. Here we have 81 tracks of good music for just over 1 penny per track.
2. You get a nice mix of familiar masterpieces and less well-known but appealing compositions.
3. Waltzes are just plain fun.
4. The fourth of the \\"Six Contredanses\\" by Beethoven (track 18) features a tune that later played a starring role in the finale of Beethoven's 3rd Symphony (Eroica). It's startling to hear this melody emerging from a stream of engaging but unfamiliar dances by this great composer. Beethoven deployed in this theme in what turned out to be the pivotal work in his middle and heroic period. In the process, he transformed and exalted the theme while retaining the same melodic outline.

Cons
1. This is really sort of a Pro-and-Con: There are two conductors in the set, Anton Paulik and Willie Boskovsky. The latter leads his ensemble brilliantly, and all of his performances have that true Viennese lilt. Of course, Boskovsky later went on to fame and fortune as one of the prime interpreters of the Viennese waltz tradition. Paulik's performance are more middle-of-the-road. Not bad, but not really inspired, either. And since Paulik generally conducts the famous works of Johann Strauss, Jr.--Boskovsky gets very little of the Waltz King--we miss out on really primo performances of the best loved works in the canon. In some ways, the most appealing dimension of this set is the intro it offers to those lesser known works.
2. There are, as often happens in these Bach Guild sets, some mislabelling issues. I this case it occurs through the duplication of track names: tracks 10, 17, 20, 58, and 64 all inaccurately duplicate the names of the previous tracks. But the music is different and the correct track names can be found here on the Bach Guild's own website: [...] Since Bach Guild has the correct data, the problem may be on amazon.com end, but it would be nicer to customers if they didn't have to do research to get accurate labeling of their tracks.

So a somewhat mixed bag, but as usual a nice offering from Bach Guild at a great price.

review_headline: Glorious progressive neoclassical symphonic instrumental shred
review_body:
Tiluland, for me is the greatest music discovery in the past several years. The progressive neoclassical symphonic musicianship is plain stunning. The intro track Prologue, in the best tradition of Symphony X, clearly tells you right away what kind of treat you are in for. The glorious, melodic, liquid speed, interwoven guitar and keyboard shred will make you want to consume the entire album in one breath.

The album is purely instrumental and easily, tastefully, flows like one big homogeneous musical message. I have never ever felt so much emotion from one instrumental album. The joy in the guy's chanting at the very end of the last composition and on top of the beautiful symphonic album finale feels so natural and appropriate ... he is happy, happy, euphoric, ... and the album fades at the full speed. Gorgeous, is an understatement ... I want more, man, when is the next Tiluland album coming out :-) ?

Lovers of music by Vinnie Moore, Tony Macalpine, Malmsteen's instrumentals, Symphony X, as well as Nightwish (for the richness of the symphonic part) will be delighted. And, oh yes, the sonic quality of the music mix and recording!? ... few, very few albums can compete. To get a CD format of Tiluland is a very good idea, too.

I started listening to Elvis back in the summer of 1977, before entering college.  From that very first album, I was a huge fan.  Elvis is one of those artists whose Aim is True, in the sense that he seems to be honest and true to himself.  David Bowie, Van Morrison, John Lennon, Sting, and Frank Sinatra are/were those kinds of artists.  They weren't afraid to re-invent themselves from time to time, often pursuing sounds radically different from what they'd previously produced.  I admire that kind of courage and integrity.  I've not liked everything that Elvis has recorded but I've always respected his efforts.  I'd read a number of reviews of 'Wise Up Ghost' that rated the album highly yet still expressed disappointment.  It made me hesitate to purchase the CD.  But then I thought, "Hell, this is Elvis!  You love Elvis."  I'm pleased to say that I love this CD.  It challenges my ear in places, but good music should do that.  It should give you some sameness, some familiarity so that you're not totally anxious.  But, it should also provide some unfamiliarity, to take you to new acoustic territory.  I enjoyed this new journey with Elvis and I'm grateful for being introduced to The Roots.  Elvis has previously helped me to appreciate Anne Sofie Von Otter, the Brodsky Quartet, and Allen Toussaint.  I'm eager to see where Elvis takes me next.  I trust him.

Caterpillars – The Other Side (Independent)
Dallas band, Caterpillars are creating a considerable buzz with their new “The Other Side” LP. Indeed, various publications have commended it, including the much respected AbsolutePunk site, which described the record as “one of the most exciting albums of 2013”. That’s high praise indeed, though it only takes a few spins of “The Other Side” to understand the sentiments. Their take on contemporary alternative rock is emotionally mature with heavy emphasis placed on melodic progression. The result is exhilarating and rewarding, and singer-songwriter Christopher Robinson fully understands the balance between passion and control.

He’s ably supported by the other members of the band, Drew Black, Carson Brooks and Ben Love, and between them they move between intense, angular riffs and dreamy, contemplative passages. It’s always involving and accessible, and songs like opener “Winter Haiku” and “Light in This Room” delicately bridge the different aspects of their music, while building to euphoric conclusions. The tumultuous “Rebirth” stumbles gloriously, repeatedly pulling itself together for further assaults on various summits, and the title track displays a gentleness that tugs at the heartstrings. The quartet brings the album to a close with “The Foundation”, a fiery, desperate paean to dashed hopes, and quite possibly the best song to be found on the collection.

As with the legend associated with their hometown of Phoenix, Arizona; Throw Logic is a band reborn in September of 2012 from the ashes of other successful regional acts. Great music has laid the foundation but the true test of a rock act is their ability to duplicate that success live and in front of a rapidly increasing and loyal fan base. Countless performances all over the country with some of the best in the business; including Saving Abel, Hoobastank, Taproot, Karnivool, Red Line Chemistry and Burn Halo have allowed Throw Logic to hone their craft and present a visually stimulating live show topped with raw energy that leaves fans craving for what’s next.

What’s next is their debut single and video “Counterfeit”; out right now; followed by their first EP; “Breaking December” coming in July of 2013 and supported by a live audio assault headed across the U.S. later this summer. product_title: Mario Lanza: The 50th Anniversary Collection - 40 Tracks!
review_headline: Exceelent Collection for the World's Greatest Tenor and Singer
review_body:
[[ASIN:1470062917 A Kid From Philadelphia,: Mario Lanza: The Voice of the Poets]]

It is hard not to be a fan of Mario Lanza. Once someone hears his voice,they fall in love with this enormous talent. This collection represents him well.

Mario Lanza was the most versatile tenor who ever walked on a stage. He could sing opera like the greatest tenors of all time. He was a master at \\"crossing over\\" from lyric opera to popular singing. As a result, he was a top recording artist and concert performer. In the \\"Great Caruso\\" he also showed he could be a global movie sensation. The movie about the amazing Neapolitan tenor actually was about Mario Lanza. It turned the Great Caruso into the Great Lanza. He exhibited all of his splendid qualities.

His movies and recordings inspired me to write my recent book about Mario Lanza: \\"A Kid from Philadelphia, Mario Lanza, the Voice of the Poets.\\" It is not a biography. There have been several excellent bios about him. This is a book from a fan. It exhibits his qualities, talents, passion and love for his art. I wanted it to be a \\"page turner\\" that would be impossible to put down while listening to the magnificent voice of Mario Lanza. Listen to these recordings while you read the book. It will be an experience.

Anyone who loves Lanza the movie star, the tenor, the popular singer and the human being, who did so much in such a short time, will love this selection.

review_headline: Yea to the singing, nay to the download
review_body:
This is a split decision for hte 21st century -- a marvelously performed work of art delivered on an atrocious download. Peter Anders was a wonderful German tenor from the prewar era known mostly for opera but also a fabulous lieder singer. He is among those that died early in their prime, going at age 46 in 1954 the result of an auto accident.

His signing in Schubert's Ganymed, a song about love and passion from Goethe's poem, is passionate beyond compare. His high notes in the romantic arches are wonderful -- full, clear and without distortion. Unfortunately, the download has robbed this music of almost all the lower tones and bass, making it a caricature of what Anders was singing. It's one of the worst examples of a download I've heard.

MP3s are fine for people that don't care about sound quality and those that only care about putting hundreds of songs into a little handheld player. However, for those of us that crave reproduction that mimics what something actually sounded like when it was recorded, the MP3 can be a great disappointment. If you don't know, the file is compressed (the reason so many songs fit into a little player) because the sound technology discards a bunch of the musical signal.

I know people that tell me you can't hear the difference. One listen to this download and anyone will be able to tell the difference. This download is atrocious even when the singer is above criticism.

Christopher Drake has been the star of the DC Universe Animated Original Movie composers since the beginning. Starting with his intricately layered, rich and epic all digital score to the 2009 DCUAOM \\"Wonder Woman,\\" Drake has exhibited the composing, orchestrating and music editing talents of the best in Hollywood's new generation of film composers, including John Debney, Harry-Gregson Williams, Tyler Bates, Christophe Beck, John Powell, Marco Beltrami, and Michael Giacchino.

Drake's score to \\"Batman: The Dark Knight Returns, Part 1\\" is another original, powerful achievement in his catalog of visionary scores for DCUAOM films. It is his greatest soundtrack since \\"Wonder Woman.\\"

Drake's score for \\"Batman: The Dark Knight Returns, Part 1\\" is a complex combination music genres, all intentionally interwoven amongst and dominated by eighties synth and electronic scoring techniques. While Drake introduces the sound of live instruments, it's the pulse and feel of an eighties synth score that dominates his work here - and for good reason.

Like film director Jay Oliva and screenwriter Bob Goodman, Drake must have first immersed himself in the film's source material, Frank Miller's classic graphic novel \\"Batman: The Dark Knight Returns.\\" Drake must have discovered that Miller channeled the tone of `electronic, synth, industrial and post-Punk' music pouring primarily out of England during the early and mid-eighties as a `visual pallet' in creating the Mutants, the Mutant Leader, Bruno, and sequences such as the battle at the Dump, the Pipe and Wayne's pursuit and battle with Bruno while in disguise as a homeless woman. The strongest evidence Drake found for the influence of this genre of mid-eighties music on Miller was his reinterpretation of the Joker.

Daringly, from a mystifying influence, Miller reintroduced the Joker as a flamboyant, arguably metro/homo-sexual toned psychotic killer, whose line of admiration for Batman becomes brilliantly blurred by a potential `romantic' obsession with The Dark Knight. This new characterization and look for the Joker, both verbal and visual, echoes the music of eighties post-Punk, industrial bands such as Bauhaus, the Cult, the Cure, Dead or Alive, Echo and the Bunnymen, the Eurythmics, Flamming Lips, Human League, Joy Division, Ministry, Modern English, New Order, OMD, Sisters of Mercy, the Smiths, Soft Cell, Sonic Youth, Split Ends, Talk Talk and Ultravox.

It seems Drake then went back and studied at the most influential composers of the eighties who worked solely in electronic and synthesizer score production. Listening to Drake's score for \\"The Dark Knight Returns, Part 1\\" reveals echoes of the best techniques John Carpenter, Vangelis, Giorgio Moroder, Wendy Carlos, and Brad Fidel developed in their work of the late seventies and first half of the eighties. He also seems to have taken time to focus on the work of Jerry Goldsmith, particularly his classic score to `Star Trek: The Motion Picture.' Goldsmith was the master of incorporating electronic and digital effects into full orchestra scores so well that the `artificial' playback seemed as organic as the human performance.

\\"Batman: The Dark Knight Returns, Vol. 1\\" is an electronic based score, rooted in the traditions of the eighties, with real instrument samples utilized to give the score its own shape and identity as a modern work. The best summation of his achievement comes early, with the album's first track, \\"Gotham City, 1986.\\"

A low, rumbling synth note evokes the terror of John Carpenter's greatest scores - a harbinger of the story to come. A higher synth note is introduced, nearly evoking a choir. Percussion accents the continuing higher note as a brief electronic guitar blast introduces additional, more complex electronic background tones. These closer emulate a human choir. Strings are added, yet they contain a clear electronic distortion - indicating they are not true `instrument' samples. A distant `chime' is then heard, a true instrument sample. A beat of percussion is followed by a new `wavering' electronic tone. The chimes are then reintroduced, followed by a brass movement made up of true `instrument' samples. Deeper single percussion beats are spaced out as the chimes and brass begin to evoke Vangelis' classic score to `Blade Runner.' Drake then dismantles the whole `feeling,' distorting the sound, dropping everything out, and ending on an ominous, hopeless dominant note.

In just one minute and thirty seconds, Drake musically sets the tone for both the film and his score. Drake will be echoing, at times emulating, the electronic music of the early to mid-eighties in establishing the 1986 setting of both Frank Miller's classic book, and Jay Oliva's film adaptation.

The story arc of \\"Batman: The Dark Knight Returns, Part 1\\" is self-contained within both Bruce Wayne's experiences and Gotham City's heightened instability at the hands of the Mutants. Director Jay Oliva chose to follow Frank Miller's first 2 books of his 4 part series with a high level of fidelity. 'Batman: The Dark Knight Returns, Part 1' is intensely focused on the re-awakening of the Batman within Bruce Wayne, the birth of a new Robin in Carrie Kelly, Batman's initial defeat at the hands of the Mutant leader, followed by his redemptive victory and the emergence of the 'Sons of Batman.'

To maintain the film's high level of raw emotional intensity as delivered by the actors, and propel the never-ending, highly cinematic action set pieces director Jay Oliva delivers, Christopher Drake made the wise stylistic choice to score most of \\"Part 1\\" with eighties-styled pulsing, electronic synth notes, heavy percussion, electronic guitar rifts, and other nods to a bygone era of film scoring.

Even in quieter, tender moments such as the tracks \\"Carrie Kelly...robin\\" and \\"Robin's Legacy,\\" Drake's choice to score \\"Part I\\" in the vein of the great electronic composers of the eighties firmly roots Jay Oliva's film in the year he chose to set it in, 1986. This was the year Miller's book was released, and it is laced with political commentary directly related to the politics and social issues of the time. It was a daring move on the part of DCUAOM, Executive Producer Bruce Timm, Director Jay Oliva and Writer Bob Goodman to directly adapt Miller's book and retain most of Miller's mid-eighties political and social commentary. Christopher Drake's carefully constructed synth score, evoking the music of that period, brings Miller's world to life just as effectively as Oliva's direction, Goodman's script and the actor's performances.

There's so much `in sync' with Drake's musical interpretation of Frank Miller's graphic novel, I'd recommend the next time you sit down to read Miller's classic book, you put on Christopher Drake's score to accompany your reading. Drake's soundtrack to \\"Batman: The Dark Knight Returns, Part 1\\" isn't just the score to Jay Oliva's film, it's the true score to Frank Miller's original graphic novel. That is, perhaps, the highest praise anyone can give the soundtrack to a film based upon a pre-existing book or graphic novel. That the composer's score brings the original book to life just as much as the film based upon it has.

My Ransomed Soul is a metalcore band from Maryland, USA that formed in 2007. They released their debut EP in 2009 when Brendan Frey (vocals) was still a young teenager and the band line-up had not yet gelled. They followed up with their `Hourglass' EP (2010) and `Perceptions' EP (2011), before settling into a more stable line-up for their full-length album `The Chains That Bind Us' (2012). After extensive touring, they signed to Red Cord Records for their second full-length album `Falsehoods' (2013). My Ransomed Soul is not afraid to state that they are a Christian band made up of all Christian members.

After a brief introductory track, they launch into `Call For Arms'. At first I thought this was going to be another cliché ridden track about `the scene', but its nothing of the sort. In the UK, there has been much denigration of the Christian faith, so that it is seen as a secular or post-christian society. So I can appreciate their concern over the decline in Christianity in America with a marked rise in indifference, rejection or hostility towards religion. Brendan screams \\"How can we trust when all systems fail? / We must stand united / To fight the fight, so truth will prevail / or we will fall divided.\\"

They follow a similar theme in `Selfish Distance' (featuring Ricky Armellino from This Or The Apocalypse). They state \\"Apathy is going to be the death of our society. We get so caught up in our own lives that we forget that we are not the center of the universe. We tend to ignore the needs of our fellow man more often than not. The thing we need to realize is that each individual can make a difference in the life of another. We have the power to extend love in ways that could change lives around the world. The question is, why don't we? We can't allow society to accept this as normal.\\"

`Deceptions' has a solid stomp with jagged riffs throughout, whilst also featuring clean guitar sections, before grinding to a halt. `Vices' and `Amalgamate' follow in a similar vein. So when the instrumental `Revelations' opens with understated rhythms, its melodic influence makes a natural break before the next outpouring of `Dystopia'. \\"We will stand our ground, instead of being bound / Open your eyes, find truth all around / Use the tools at hands; this will be our stand\\". They move up-tempo in `Regression' with its technical guitar and time changes bound together by excellent drumming. And `Transcendence' throws down one last challenge \\"We focus on what we can see; we always struggle to believe / Our trust lies in nothingness, as our souls start to digress / We stand in disbelief, where is our faith?\\"

The band seems to have found a secure foothold and has produced a solid release. review_headline: Compilation of extras from the OLR catalog
review_body:
One Less Reason is one of those bands that have a large following but yet aren't a huge national act. It's unfortunate because Cris Brown is more talented than almost every other contemporary artist out there.

Some artists write a good song here and there and sing a nice song and play their instruments just fine. Cris has written so many mind-blowing, heart-felt songs I cease to be amazed every time a new OLR offering is released. I feel that a trait of an outstanding songwriter is one that can create a song that pulls the listener right into it. The trick is that even though the listener doesn't necessarily directly relate with the words, the writer/singer pulls you in and makes you feel all the emotion that went into the song. That is exactly what Cris has done time and time again.

This compilation of full-band and acoustic live tracks, extra studio cuts and previously unreleased material is a must for any current OLR fan. It is also useful as a starting point to spread the music of OLR to more people. There are music fans out there that need to hear songs like A Day To Be Alone, Ghost, The Distance, etc.

All that being said about this release, if you haven't already you should check out their back catalog and explore what OLR has to offer.
