review_headline: Suffers from the Same Issues as "Four Parks, One World", Tenfold...
review_body:
I was really hoping my complaints about the previous release had been heard by Disney. Alas, I was blinded by hope. This release suffers from the same issues as the previous release, \\"Four Parks, One World\\" and while it's clear they attempted to try and remedy the issue, the issues that still exist are far to powerful to allow me to overlook them and give it the \\"okay\\" this time. I just don't like it.

The main reason behind this... call it childish, but it's because they didn't release that one track I had be dying for on the disc. That is an updated mix of Grim Grinning Ghosts from the Haunted Mansion. In 2007, the ride was give a massive refurbishment that saw the installation of may improvements to the ride's soundtrack and sound system. One of the more notable additions was the re-recording of several vocal tracks used in the ride's musical graveyard finale. The new vocal tracks sound far less dated, and add a great deal of quality to the overall soundscape of the scene. All the performances sound much more lively and involved. But alas, we are present with the same old mix that we have been getting since official park albums became a thing back in the 1990's and 2000's. The vocals are the pre-2007, dated versions. Not only are the vocal tracks not the ones used at Walt Disney World, but even the key of the Foyer Organ music is off! All the little details really do matter! I do not have room for another one of these 'same old' mixes in my collection!

** Randy Thorton, please hear me out! Release a single on amazon of \\"Grim Grinning Ghosts: The Re-Haunting\\", with the new vocal tracks (similar to the \\"999 Happy Haunts\\" track off the Haunted Mansion album from 2009) It would be a dream come true! Isn't Disney all about making dreams come true? Plus, I guarantee you it will sell. I know plenty of others who are just dying to own a copy of the new vocals! Jaylis – Precious As The Diamonds (Independent)
Jaylis is the name given to Sandra Loerincik Barrat’s latest musical project, instigated when she picked up a guitar and began to write songs – around the time her second child was born. Collaborating with arranger Raphael Noir, Jaylis has fashioned a collection that’s full of joy and positivity, and wrapped up in memories of childhood. In her own words, she describes “Precious As The Diamonds” the result of “what life can bring to you if you smile at it”, and that simple sentiment is reflected throughout the album’s dozen tracks.

With regard to sound and style, the Lausanne native delivers her material with an indie-folk whimsy, which is utterly appealing. Names like Kate Bush, Tori Amos and Norah Jones come to mind, and she’s never scared of incorporating non-traditional elements – from the country-rock rhythm of the title track to the spaghetti western atmospherics of “Break”. Both songs provide standout moments in the collection, though they’re hardly alone.

Opening cut “Flowers” is a perfect scene-setter. Jaylis’ vocal is sweet and assured, and her musicians (and Noir’s arrangement) build the song beautifully, filling the gaps, but leaving it uncluttered. “USA” is a perfect three-minute pop song. It’s catchy and infectious, and deserves huge radio attention, and the ethereal “Ghost” plays with vivid imagery, and musically, it resides in the wastelands of a broken heart. It’s moving and touching, and quite lovely.

So What, is the story ? This is a tale of a Young woman Living overseas, and returning to her flat in an evening. Being in an a foreign land all the sounds around her seem unnatural and foreign,. her heart accelerates which each new sound, wondering straining to hear and make out the things she hears, the wind chasing at her back , a storm coming ?, she turns to check ,.strange insects, vibrations in the ground from the subway trains and trams , night falling , light rains, whispers , shadows,. and her mind starts t imagine around this snakes in tall grass by the roadside , winds returning, circling her as she walks like dragons or spirits.

She stops, closes her eyes and to settle herself thinks back on a welcoming place, she remembers her home,. in her minds eye she returns there seeing the morning sun shine through the window, the sweet tinkle of her Mother;s voice and the scent of fresh flowers. She remembers sitting on the lawn her toes in the grass feeling the soft mound ans she turns pages in a book lazily. Remembering being served hot jasmine tea in an afternoon ands relaxing with sewing in, out over and under , in , out , over and under the never ending path of the needles through cloth. Then the scent of cooking, of family at the table and the chatter and laughter around the table. She feels warm , Love happiness and calm.

As the scene unfolds in her mind she steady's her pace and a smile breaks on her lips,. she is on her way home. The unknown sounds and world around her fall into the background .

I love the way this song ends with the slam of her door and in the vibration you can hear all the night noises that were nipping at her heels shudder. It is a classic case of the light driving away the dark .

review_headline: A Funky, Haunting Dance Tune that talks about...
review_body:
Based upon a haunting flute, a rhythm guitar, and staccato bass hits from a synth of sorts, we have a funky dance tune - and a very haunting song full of lyrical imagery.

At the New Moon Born Review, I had made a comparison between Jana and Sting. Jana also has a very similar lyrical style with Tony Banks of Genesis (circa 1980's). The difference is Jana expresses her feelings through lyrical imagery whereas Tony Banks expressed I don't know what.

For this reason, I also wonder if "Out the Window" is an intro to "From A TightRope" as a form of rock musical imagery (out the window onto a tightrope). If so, I wish there was a better flow between the songs.

From A TightRope seems to capture a gloom and doom feeling about the world wherein the "tightrope" is the straight line you have to walk. But that line is "wavering, suspended in mid-air," so you're constantly in danger of falling into that gloom and doom world. That's my interpretation. Someone try to do better.

"Never Fall" at New Moon Born Seems to be the healing antithesis of "From A TightRope." The laid back, relaxed Reggae Rhythm tells me I'm right. Thanks, Jana. You have flooded my mind with your intense lyrical and musical imagery!

Triple 6 Mafia always "repped" Memphis. Their earlier work referenced a lot of local places, people, and things, making it difficult for people not from the area to get into. They were also quite dark, delving into areas most rap music did not. Unlike other rap acts, Triple 6 Mafia is heavily influenced by heavy metal, punk rock, and other types of music rap and the black community in general rarely explore.

This album maintains a lot of that darkness and metal influence in the music but not necessarily the lyrics, making it more palatable to the mainstream without compromising their style (which they dubbed "crunk" - the style they pioneered). This song in particular is more straightforward "gangsta rap" and just rocks HARD.

review_headline: Far From Their Best, This Is Still A Five-Star Record!
review_body:
Talking Heads - True Stories (1986)

Probably the Heads' most highly underrated album, TRUE STORIES nonetheless comes up a winner in my book. As a fan of David Byrne's voice as well as the band itself, I much prefer these versions to the ones Byrne intended to release, the versions that appeared in his movie of the same title. The pop songs dazzle and the slower, dreamier numbers are some of the best you'll ever hear from this band. TRUE STORIES is a smorgasbord of styles, every one of them successfully realized with a top-notch song. Listening to this album again in order to write this review was a sheer delight.

Breakdown!

\\"Love For Sale\\" - is a straight-up, hooky rock song and a swipe at the sexploitation typically seen in ads. The video is one of the most clever and entertaining in their catalog. *****+

\\"Puzzlin' Evidence\\" - has sort of a Gospel thing going for it and a great groove, real energetic. Love the choir! ****

\\"Hey Now\\" - sounds kinda like a dorky kids' song but it's actually quite good. ****1/2

\\"Papa Legba\\" - featuring Caribbean rhythms, this is one of the best tracks. *****+

\\"Wild Wild Life\\" - a smash hit and deservedly so, thanks in part to the cool video from the movie featuring wild karaoke singers. One of their most fun songs. *****+

\\"Radio Head\\" - The song that gave Radiohead their name is a winner, full of energy and Zydeco flavor. *****

\\"Dream Operator\\" - is a tranquil, dreamy wonder, another candidate for best song. *****+

\\"People Like Us\\" - This is my least favorite track, pretty much a full-on country number. It's very good, just not really my thing. ***1/2

\\"City of Dreams\\" - A moving tribute to Native Americans, this is the song that actually gets my vote for best track. A must for Talking Heads fans. *****+

bonus tracks -

\\"Wild Wild Life\\" (extended mix) - worthy! *****

\\"Papa Legba\\" (Pops Staples vocal) - Some people including David Byrne prefer this version to the Heads' one. I prefer the Heads. ****

\\"Radio Head\\" (Tito Larriva vocal) - another track from the film. Interesting, but again I'd rather hear the Heads. What can I say? I'm a fan!Staples vocal) - Some people including David Byrne prefer this version to the Heads' one. I prefer the Heads. ****

product_title: Game of Thrones (Music from the HBO® Series) Season 3
review_headline: The Score Hits New Emotional Strides In Season 3 That Really Make It An Immersive Experience
review_body:
It's hard to find someone who hasn't seen Game Of Thrones and it's definitely one of the most popular shows on television right now. Fans of the books and show alike were treated to a stunning third season that finally saw some raw emotion pumped into what can be a slow show at times. I admit, I had to truck through the first two seasons struggling to connect to these characters. The show took a dialogue-heavy approach that left little room for score to work dramatically, and I'm a person who needs score in whatever I'm watching. Other than the fantastic main title theme the show never had \\"musical moments\\". Everything changed in season 3 as the show really took off. Season 3 of Game Of Thrones is not only the series' best music but it's also some of the best work from Ramin Djawadi.

The stakes have been raised a lot in terms of what characters have to lose, and when that happens it allows the music to support the story more. Djawadi had always successfully established a unique fantasy sound grounded in realism. I mean the music sounds like it's capturing a time period in history, and that's amazing. Ramin has effectively established a time period that doesn't exist and he did it through music. That makes it timeless. This season saw characters breaking apart more into their own separate journeys. This gave room for focus and the music rose to that calling. The motifs are so strong in this album and Ramin was even able to build superb dramatic tension and suspense. Everything was sonically superb. The music also references the main title theme a lot more than in the past two seasons, and the strength of that theme is something to behold. I found the music to take on a new sense of elegance as well since we saw a lot more romance. The barbaric violence was saved for the end of the season and that allowed the music to resonate stronger through the characters. The bursts of action found throughout the season were also expertly scored as Djawadi brought in some great percussion. Then there is the \\"epic\\" scope of the series that really found new light in season 3. The closing moments of the season were scored by the track \\"Mhysa\\" which is a beautifully grand variation of the title theme with a chorus. It really was a great moment for the character of Daenerys. All in all this was a stunningly superb season musically. The show finally showed it's true colors in my opinion. The amount of characters and material is so incredibly dense that finally Ramin's music was utilized in a way to help digest it. I felt for the characters, I cared what happened and at times the score gave me chills.

If Season 3 of Game Of Thrones is a sign of things to come then I can't wait for what Ramin brings to the table for the rest of the series. I really hope the producers, writers and directors decide to use his music more like they did here in Season 3. The first two seasons didn't allow much in terms of dramatic scoring, but if they keep up this sort of structure I think great television moments will continually be had. Ramin Djawadi is one of the great talents working today and he continually proves it be it a blockbuster like Pacific Rim or a rich fantasy epic like Game Of Thrones.me great percussion. product_title: Dirt Road Gospels: In the Beginning
review_headline: These boys just blew me away!
review_body:
[[ASIN:B00G70DZGS Dirt Road Gospels: In the Beginning]]

I just picked up this album on a whim when I saw it next to Hank III & the price was right.

Not what I was expecting at all, but man what songwriting. The songs have some real depth to them. Most of them remind me of a story or something these boys have actually experienced, otherwise I don't see how you would come up with some of the songs they've got.

The production has a certain grittyness to it but it kind of adds to the feel of the album. I suspect these boys operated on a limited budget with it being their 1st album but they hit a homerun here. Maybe someone will put a little money behind them at some point.

Another cool thing is every song sounds different so you don't get bored with the songs. One song may sound like southern rock, the next song old-school outlaw country, then a heavier sounding tune, then another Waylon style song, then one that is straight up rock. I get pretty bored when I pop in an album & every song sounds like the last one.

Hopefully these guys have some follow up releases, consider me a new fan.

It's safe. It will make a splash after Break the Spell bottomed out only selling half a million copies (compared with his debut which sold 7M worldwide.) So blatantly we see it is no longer about the music and only about the $$. Sure we can sugar coat things and profess how profound the lyrics of this album are, but they mean nothing if the music is drab and uninteresting.

Add Daughtry to the ever growing list of rock-sellouts (Linkin Park, AAR, even Maroon 5 to an extent) that had too much fame in the mid-2000s and now are producing poppy garbage. Every single one of these bands have debuted a new style of album and turned their backs on TRUE rock fans. I previewed each song in full length to see if it was worth buying and frankly... wait til it goes on $5 sale if you want it.

review_headline: Stands On It's Own - Not Just A Preparation For Later Work
review_body:
The only reason that I got this album is because I'm already a fan of Regina's later, commercially-released work. So I came to it prepared to be charitable, to view it as an attempt by a promising amateur to explore American music - i.e. to learn the box, so that she could later break out of that box with her own style. No charity was needed. Although she must have \\"learned the box\\" somewhere and sometime, by the time she made this album she had it down pat, and was already breaking out at the corners.

This is a brilliant collection, very different from all of her others, but still entirely her own. Some of these songs explore unpleasant aspects of human nature. Some, mostly on the blue side, are about love. Some, and these are the ones that can get you teary-eyed, are about ordinary folks caught in not necessarily terrible, but life-wasting situations that they don't know how to escape. Regina doesn't offer easy answers, and yet, her trademark quirkiness often shines a smile through the tears.

I don't know how she does it, but on the occasions that she adds some lighthearted word play, or image, or quirk of intonation to a heartbreaking story, it never comes across as insensitive or mocking. It's like a ray of sun from behind the clouds, sometimes hinting that there are things to celebrate even in a dark hour, at other times hinting that \\"yes, there is something more to life than what you've seen so far.\\" With these songs, Regina again strikes gold.

review_headline: This Man Has His Emotions On His Sleeve!
review_body:
So much of R&B in the last 10-20 years been focused on man-hating anthems sung by women & sex-me-sex-you-up themes sung by men ... so many of which have been totally devoid of any genuinely worthwhile emotional or lyrical content! It's a rare pleasure for me to hear a song where a man really puts his emotions out there in a song! What man can't relate to this song??? What man can't relate to going through changes with his woman when she's STILL bringing up stuff that happened last week, last month, last year, 5-10 years ago ... refusing to move on and let their love grow! The classic masters of R&B always had a begging-I'm-sorry-pleading type of song in their repertoire and Shaliek may very well become one of those venerated masters one day.

As a song, \\"THE PAST\\" will certainly hold it's own in playlist of classic aching-hearts songs like: \\"ON BENDED KNEE\\" (Boyz II Men) ... \\"NEVER KEEPING SECRETS (Babyface) ... \\"MAYBE I DESERVE\\" & \\"PLEASE DON'T GO (Tank) ... \\"LET'S WORK IT OUT\\" (Lattimore) ... \\"I CAN'T SLEEP\\" (R. Kelly) ... \\"BECAUSE I LOVE YOU\\" (Lenny Williams)

As an R&B vocalist, Shaliek brings to mind Ginuwine when you first hear him! I swore up and down this was a new Ginuwine song, but I don't recall Ginuwine ever getting anywhere near this emotional until his hit 2009 hit \\"LAST CHANCE\\". And while Ginuwine has spent most of his career as a sex-symbol R&B crooner, Shaliek has very obvious potential to be an excellent heart-on-your-sleeve balladeer with an R. Kelly-type raw edge, yet with the pleading earnestness of Babyface and the smooth elegance of a street-wise Peabo Bryson!

I certainly hope Shaliek won't be a one-hit wonder; never to be heard from again after this song! Even if he does, I know a lot of men everywhere will get a lot of mileage from playing this excellently rendered song ... each every time their woman starts yanking their chain about \\"THE PAST\\"!!!

The title of the review is not intended as a put-down towards the album. My first observation is that if you don't like remix albums, you obviously shouldn't buy this. You would think this is obvious, but it feels like every remix album ends up getting some bad reviews just because its a remix album. In this case I think you're getting exactly what you would expect. Like previous Puscifer remix albums you get enough originality in the tracks throughout the album that you don't feel like you're re-purchasing the same CD again.

The overall mood is not quite the same 80's synth-pop vibe as their Donkey Punch the Night, but there are some hints here and there. Given the direction that it took as an album, All Remixed Up feels like a reasonable next direction for Puscifer's ever-evolving style. The songs range in style from some experimental (perhaps Radiohead-esque?) to bass/drum driven (The Green Valley (Stolen Babies) has a great, chunky bass line), to relaxing and cathartic (Oceans (Zac Rae)). I could see some of the more experimental tracks turning some off (some pretty in-your-face stereo panning and a couple of the more repetitive samples come to mind), but all things considered I'm not displeased with my purchase.

All Re-Mixed Up is a great companion album to Conditions of My Parole. I hope that Maynard and Co. keep them coming into the future.

review_headline: An adventure that mixes styles, time, and a constant battle between simplicity and complexity.
review_body:
This album is a great continuation of Omar Rodriquez Lopez's great guitar work while opening new ears to the light coos and battle cries of Teri Gender Bender. The drummer, Deantoni, was on the last Mar's Volta album and is solid. The bass player ,Nicci, is solid as well.
The album starts off preparing the listener for what they are about to experience.
Eli starts as the album will end. Nice steady tempos with an overall building to the end.
Worthless builds on the lyrical complexity while experiencing everything that is great about Omar's playing. On the surface the music is simple enough to keep the less musically trained person interested but also has a depth that is constantly contradicting the simplicity. Great melodies between Teri and Omar along with solid rhythms.
Dig Right In Me starts to get a little more spastic guitar followed by a great wall of sound. At times this song is almost funk but the dominant femininity that Teri brings backs it off.
The Eye Fell In Love begins with this sound of peril. Than it kicks into a delicate groove which is somewhat sappy but also sweet. The bass and drums help to keep this one grounded.
I Cry for You is stressful in a good way.The vocals really match the lyrics which is unusual these days. This song has some great dynamic moments.
Morning Sickness. You might ask yourself, "Is this the theme song from Portlandia?" Its not but it has that great light sound to it. The listener thinks they are listening to this happy walking groove than all of a sudden you think you are in a Noctournaquat. Great dynamics and diversity in the sounds chosen for this song. Great grooves as well.
Torn Maps channels the 80's in a good and fun way. Keeping with the strength of the musicians Teri kind of does her thing in this song channeling every 80's heroine in every melody and harmony. Than an excellent solo busts in.
Turtle Neck is next up. Some times this seems hard to listen to because it is a flighty almost uninvolved groove and than 3:00 kicks in. Its straight up rock building. Takes a few listens before it becomes as great as the rest of the album.
Always on the Run never disappoints. It has the attraction that many of the song on System of the Down's Hypnotize had with strong melodies, of course. That comparison may also be because Omar sounds like Milikian when he sings. Everything is solid on this song.
Red is a masterful song. Great keyboard work to match the rest of the band.
Mother, Father, Set Us Free channels western guitar riffs and Geddy Lee. If you close your eyes you might imagine that Teri is actually Geddy Lee on the top of a butte in Mexico while gun fighters below are having a battle. Strong sounds from all the group but a great way to end the record. Lyrically it also has great building the way people internalize things. Genius. Than it breaks and builds to the end giving an amazing cap to a great album.

Overall, this album is exceptional and will give the fans of all previous groups of the members something to crave. The enigma that was the simplicity constantly battling the complexity shined through and truly gave this album something special.

Soft Kill joins a growing faction of bands mining the darker and more doom-laden regions of early 80s post punk and goth. As soon as the drums on the excellent opener \\"From This Point On\\" kick in, one can immediately detect a strong strain of the Wake's first album, Harmony, what with the stiff, pounding, tom-heavy drumming; prominent, driving bass; pulsating analog-sounding synths; and treble-y, thorny-yet-sometimes-kind-of-pretty guitar melodies, all with a crisp production that would make Martin Hannett proud. The only difference is in Soft Kill vocalist Tobias Grave's singing, which, unlike the softer and more tentative voice of the Wake's Caesar, is deep, bellowing, and commanding, and when combined with the monochromatic music, alternately recalls the guy from Red Lorry Yellow Lorry, the guy from Clan of Xymox, and the guy from Music For Pleasure.

Several songs, like the aforementioned \\"From This Point On\\", as well as \\"Death In The Family\\" and \\"Within This Mess\\", are quite good, striking an effective balance between brooding melancholy, energized immediacy, and catchy melodies. The arrangements and production sound as if all that time between the early 80s and now never happened.

The only real problem is that whereas bands like the Wake kept things interesting by employing a wider variety of rhythms, tempos, and sonic textures, Soft Kill's music gets a bit repetitive and samey over the course of the album. Also, Soft Kill and many of their post punk adoring contemporaries may want to take note of the emphasis their forefathers put on melody. Bands like Joy Division, Sad Lovers and Giants, Magazine, etc..., were well aware of the importance of an engaging melody or hook, however simple it might have been. Some of Soft Kill's songs demonstrate a pretty good grasp of this, but in the end not enough of them do to sustain this listener's interest over the entire album.

Soft Kill is definitely a band to keep an eye on, even though the same issues reassert themselves on their 2013 follow up, Circle Of Trees. (And what's with all these bands with 'soft' in their name? We've already got the Soft Boys, Soft Cell, Soft Moon, Soft Metals, etc. Can we please think of some other adjectives?)

review_body:

The "B-section" between statements of the theme is very busy, and has no recognizable single melody. Thankfully, it ends quickly. Itzhak Perlman's violin antics were pure Borscht Belt schtick, and, although amusing at first, were, in the end, just overdone, and were rapidly becoming tedious when, just in time, the song ended.
I'm an occasional party entertainer (VERY occasional), and I'm not sorry I downloaded this, because the main theme really is quite lovely. But you can't use the whole song. Perhaps a few bars of it could be a lead-in to a medly of Jewish songs.

review_headline: Exciting and original works for electric guitar quartet
review_body:
As an existing review here indicates, this is not an easy album to listen to, but it is nevertheless an extremely rewarding one, if you are interested in original and challenging music. Brilliantly played by Dither, with a mixture of precision and laid-back directness, it contains works of contrasting styles by 5 young American composers.

Lainie Fefferman's opener, Tongue of Thorns, is a throbbing Branca-esque art-rock drone, with shades of David Lang, concluding with a thrillingly screaming solo. Jascha Narveson's Vectors sounds like a micro-tonal gamelan with pitch-bend wheel, and ends with something that sounds like a kind of baying of electronic hounds. Joshue Lopes's Pantagruel is a more conventionally thru-composed piece, but as a member of the quartet, he is able to make excellent use of the sound potential of the electric guitars. Erik K M Clark's exPAT apparently involves the four players being prevented from hearing each other, leading to a somewhat cacophonous result, perhaps the least successful track on the album, but one which builds up an incredible head of steam nonetheless.

The disc concludes with Lisa R Coons's excellent 4-movement work Cross Sections, the first movement of which, Entropion, is a noisy mix of jangly lines, quasi-minimalist sections, and crashing dissonant chords. Subsequent movements offer abstract noises with a wide variety of effects and processing, gut-wrenching extended siren-like glissandi, intricately chaotic contrapuntal textures and more meditative sections, which come more to the fore as the piece progresses. Overall the 24-minute piece is immensely absorbing and intriguing, seeming to exist within its own sound world and compositional logic, certainly a work of considerable originality.

Overall the album is to be hugely recommended.

review_headline: A Fun Introduction To the Chieftains
review_body: This is certainly one of the most fun introductions to Celtic Music especially if you are already a fan of alternative or progressive folk music. Even after a 3rd and 4th listen through, I still found myself tapping my foot along to the beat of The Punch Brothers rendition of \\"The Frost is All Over\\" or The Decembrists version of \\"When the Ship Comes In\\". Since the \\"Voice of Ages\\" comprises multiple artists, it would be helpful to get the liner notes if downloading the mp3 album, however most of the artists in the compilation have such distinctive styles it is very hard to confuse them. Purists might object to the fact that, in many ways, The Chieftains unique approach to Irish traditional music is over-shadowed by the very distinctive personalities of the bands covering the songs. In this sense the album might not be an ideal tribute album. But even with this caveat, it still remains an utterly accessible album with tunes that will have you humming along to Celtic tunes well after the last track has finished.

product_title: A Hunt in the Balck Forest
review_headline: A very silly piece of music of great nostalgic value to me
review_body:
If you lived in the greater Hartford, CT area anytime in the 60s or 70s, then you probably listened to The Bob Steele Show on WTIC AM radio in the mornings. This was his sign-on music every weekday morning at 6:00; I can't count the number of times I awoke to it. A number of years later I managed to locate an old Victor 78rpm recording of it (which I since have lost in a fire). Imagine my surprise when I came across it as an MP3 download!

There is no way you can really call this \\"good\\" music; it's a cheesy novelty piece from beginning to end (cuckoo clock, bird calls, hunting horns, gallopping horses, barking dogs, etc)- but for me it carries a huge nostalgic value, and if you have fond memories of the Bob Steele show - or if you just enjoy collecting musical oddities, you owe it to yourself to add this to your collection.

review_headline: Slightly Experimental but on Par with Previous Albums
review_body:
A few years ago I saw Sara in Chapel Hill performing with Greg Laswell. I realized there that Sara was simply just the real deal. She has both a magnetic joy onstage as well as the actual vocal talent to make her live performances sound as good as if not better than her studio albums. Something I've always found really special about her music though, is how accessible yet a little left of mainstream it tends to be. Its equal parts catchy and heartfelt--yet I never feel like she's trying too hard.

This album builds upon that by incorporating some new elements like jazz and electronic into her special brand of aware piano driven pop music. While listening to the exquisite ballad \\"Manhattan\\", I could see a dark smoky jazz club from the 1940s with Sara lying across a piano, crooning about a lost love to a hushed audience. Another more upbeat jazz influenced album standout, \\"Little Black Dress\\" sees the appearance of Sara's older sister doing Motown inspired pitch perfect background vocals which just mesh perfectly with Sara's voice. \\"Satellite Call\\" on the other hand, with its slight reverb and haunting melody makes me feel like I'm somehow underneath the Northern Lights just staring up at the stars lit up in swirling colors.

\\"I Choose You\\" starts with a subtle stringed bass line and understated vocals, yet builds into a very sweet and honest love song. It's the type of song that you could see being used in one of those lip synched marriage proposal extravaganzas on YouTube. Overall, this album probably is a bit more upbeat--not so much in tone (as many of the songs sound like breakup songs), but musically than her past two albums. \\"Eden\\" especially embraces this driving electronic sound. In the hands of a lesser talented vocalist, I don't think it would have worked and would have stuck out like a sore thumb. But Sara's smooth and melodic voice is the glue that pulls the range of musical genres together into a package that just feels right. Highly recommend listening through a few times before making up your mind about this album (it's streaming on iTunes), as I found myself being nonchalant about a few songs the first time I heard them--but then going back and just losing myself in them.

Longtime fans of Sara will not be disappointed with this album. She managed to push herself musically and keep things interesting, while retaining everything that makes her art special. It has poetic quiet moments, bombastic inspiring anthems (\\"Brave\\" was co-written with Jack Antonoff of FUN.) and above all a determination to embrace life to the fullest and well, be brave. Excellent pop that does more than entertain--it speaks for a generation.

***For anyone looking for new similar artists, I recently saw piano pop singer/songwriter Jillette Johnson in concert, and she positively blew my mind. review_headline: A Classic Blues Album Done His Way!
review_body: The blues may have played an important role in The Guitar God's development and          rise to international fame, Eric Clapton was eligible to take some time to record a blues          album from start to finish in late 1993.   For years, fans and admirers had waited for an          all-blues album from Clapton, and this CD have managed to re-create the ambience of          the Post-WWII electric blues era just right down to the bottomless thump of the rhythm          section. With the CD's ambience well-handled by Clapton's three dogs- Sock, Billy and          Treacle, From The Cradle, released in 1994, showcases a superb form of blues guitar          artistry which he performed with great success and sheer gusto, to which he take on a          stirring set of blues tracks that includes Blues Before Sunrise (also a hit for Stevie Ray          Vaughan), Third Degree, Reconsider Baby, Five Long Years, How Long Blues, Driftin'          (also not to be confused this early Herbie Hancock hard bop classic), Blues Leave Me          Alone, Someday After A While and Five Long Years, while it feature a series of classic          blues songs composed by Muddy Waters, Charles Brown, Elmore James, Willie Dixon,          Freddy King, Leroy Carr, just among others.  Officially billed as his official blues album,          the award-winning From The Cradle managed to recreate the ambience of Post-WW II          electric blues right down to the bottomless thump of the rhythm section and even serve          as another important milestone in his proud highly prolific recording career and \\"for his          contribution to the blues\\", which helped make this one both another blues masterpiece          and a well-fitted fixture for The Guitar God that truly rank as one of his finest and most          beloved albums in his rich groundbreaking legacy.

review_headline: Doesn't Fit His Style, but good theology
review_body:
Just because this is Christian Hip Hop doesn't mean I can't be honest in a review.

Let me say this.

I like all types of Christian rap. Even the types most people hate. I love Stephen the Levite, Shai Linne, S.O, and Timothy Brindle. I also love Lecrae, Thi'sl, Flame, etc. I love all types of Christian rap. So I think I'm unbiased enough to say this.

I just don't think this fits his style in any way. He was SO GOOD at his genre of music. He made hood music about where he came from. It fit his voice so perfectly. His voice, his hooks, everything he really did in his hood music went together.

But this album, and even "Growing Pains", seems to be an attempt to make a "hood rapper" into the next Shai Linne.

The bottom line for me, this album doesn't fit the style of music he is most gifted in. That doesn't mean it's horrible music. I just know he has such a higher gift in another sub genre of Christian rap.

Regardless J'son has great theology in the album and I'm sure you will leave the album feeling edified if you listen to it.

I'll give it a 4 just for the message, hoping that others can hear it, but I had to keep it real for my CHH fans out there.

This piece is totally unlike anything else Weather Report had ever done. The band was known for a Jazz-Rock Fusion sound that was very distinct and edgy. Jungle Book is a delicate blend of instruments, sounds and distant voices that never quite come together to create a big melody, but which instead remain continually elusive and distant, an impression of a faraway place in a distant time. They built on an earlier EP release - that contained the track "Beat Box" (an early hip-hop hit) -  to create an eclectic sound based on noises, vocals and music samples often processed through the famous Fairlight CMI. While that description sounds like it could be a train-wreck in the making, what was actually produced was a creative and energetic record (with a few lighter, softer moments) that somehow takes a giant mix of sounds and noises and cohesively pulls them together. It's not a record for everyone, but for those who are interested in something a bit different, this record pays of quite nicely.

Call the genre whatever you want (art-rock, post-rock, experimental, ambient, downright tasty), Iceland's Sigur Rós is one of the best bands of the current generation. Big claim, I know, but Kveikur only solidifies the band's stature as one of the genre's best. If you like Sigur Rós, go ahead and pick this record up.

In past years, Sigur Ros has been criticized for having a \\"formula\\". If you're a fan of the band, you probably have some idea of what this formula is: soft, atmospheric music, swelling chord changes, and a gigantic build up that leaves the song on a massive crescendo. Perhaps the band has been aware of their critics. Since 2008's Með Suð í Eyrum Við Spilum Endalaust, the band has retreated from their past \\"slow-burn to explosive finale\\" tendencies. Their 2008 record found the band attempting to write more conventional pop songs (well, what would be pop for Sigur Ros, I suppose), and 2012's Valtari was an exercise in decrescendos. Valtari (a record I love), was created around music starting somewhat big and working its way down - the album even ends on a 3-song streak in which each proceeding song is a bit softer and a bit more minimalist than the last. For this reason, coupled with the loss of multi-instrumentalist Kjartan Sveinsson, I was prepared for a minimalist exercise with Kveikur.

Earlier in the year, the band released \\"Brennisteinn\\" as their single to promote Kveikur. This feels a bit misleading (not dishonest though) - the single doesn't really represent what the album sounds like, but rather, it indicates that Sigur Ros is still tooling around with their sound. To put another way, the rest of Kveikur doesn't sound like \\"Brennisteinn\\" - instead, it seems to be an assurance that we aren't getting another Valtari, or another ( ), or another Von. Because this song leads the album, it starts Kveikur off with a near-industrial crunch. At almost 8-minutes, it's one of the most unexpected turns for the band.

Similarly, second-released single \\"Ísjaki\\" isn't as representative either. Ísjaki is busy in ways that most of Kveikur isn't, and Jonsi's vocals constantly keep the melody moving along. But these two singles together tell the story of Kveikuer perfectly - many of the moments on Kveikur are characterized by poppy melodies thrown against a jagged backdrop. The title track for example has Jonsi singing incredibly catchy vocals over distorted electronics. These moments give the album's cover (a boy holding an old gas mask over his face) some context. Other tracks like \\"Yfirborð\\" and \\"Stormur\\" try to strike a similar balance, with Jonsi staying squarely in the spotlight this time around, rather than letting the music play on without him like we've seen in past releases.

The band continues toying with its sound, so there is plenty of new things to hear here though. Musically, this record feels like a mix between Með Suð í Eyrum Við Spilum Endalaust and Valtari - these songs are perhaps a bit more straight-forward than the Sigur Rós we are used to, but every song is loaded with a healthy dose of atmosphere. By the time the closer \\"Var\\" comes around, it feels like we can finally rest. It's a quiet, ambient track that gives listeners a chance to reflect - so much of Kveikur is loaded with business, it feels somewhat relieving to have this moment before circling around back to \\"Brennisteinn.\\"

If you haven't liked anything you've heard by Sigur Rós so far, you probably won't find much on Kveikur to change your mind. For fans of the band though, this album is a must-hear. Don't let the lead track \\"Brennisteinn\\" scare you away - there's plenty here of the band you know and love, but there's also plenty that you've never heard from them before. This might be my favorite of their's since 2005's Takk...

Notable tracks to download/sample: \\"Ísjaki\\", \\"Yfirborð\\", and \\"Kveikur\\"

Some music is great but has become famous for other reasons, like \\"I Put a Spell On You\\" from Screamin' Jay Hawkins, which gained notoriety mainly after it featured prominently in the film \\"Stranger Than Paradise\\". And there is a ton of other great blues here.

We could all quibble with the selections. For example: Only one Robert Johnson track? And where's Leadbelly?

But the bottom line is this is a fine set and a fine bargain. Warmly recommended.

review_headline: What was I missing all these years.
review_body:
I'm extremely late to the Threshold party. Honestly, I never paid much attention to this band other than knowing that they were a prog-metal band based out of England. But in my fervent searching and exploring of different bands, I ended up getting reeled in and hooked by the song "Ashes" from their album March of Progress, and subsequently gave that said album LOTS of play. What I liked about Threshold's approach was that instead of going the show-off wanky approach that a lot of so-called progressive bands take, they went the route of careful arrangement of all facets of the music, and in the end crafted an album of wonderfully catchy-yet deceptively complex, deep songs.

I remembered hearing "Slipstream" a long time ago and it didn't have the same impact. But, I decided to go back and give this album a try, and I like this one as much if not more so than March of Progress. All of the elements that I fell for on MoP are present, plus the additional edge of their previous singer, the late Andrew "Mac" MacDermott.

If you're new to the Threshold party like me, here's what to expect...a ridiculously tight rhythm section, uplifiting guitar and key solos, tremendous vocal performances, and world-class song arrangement. Another thing that I'm noticing both on this as well as on March of Progress is how these guys incorporate influence (intentional or subconsciously, it's all there) from the UK...you'll hear Queen, Pink Floyd, and even Duran Duran (listen to the rhythm section word of DD; Threshold is very similar in a lot of ways) in addition to some Maiden and Priest influence.

From here, I haven't started digging in just yet but I will likely be exploring this band's extensive back catalog soon and if anyone has recommendations on where to go next with Threshold albums, let me know!

review_headline: Quite simply...the most beautiful music ever written...in the history of the world!
review_body:
Pop fans conditioned to hear hard noise sounds who are either unfamiliar with or unable to appreciate innocence in art can't comprehend the ethereal status of this breathtakingly poignant music. The play of notes is set to such an emotionally romantic pitch that you almost get the impression it was sent down from heavens above somehow.

Since the movie soundtrack is lush with a famous Rachmaninoff Concerto inspired by Paganini, Barry's love theme gets confused with it. But this the audio centerpiece of the movie whether derivative or not is in and of itself a sublime virtuoso composition. Lots of great classical music pales in comparison to this peerless and divine master work.

It bears a similarity to more orchestral tracks used in films scored by John Barry like King Kong and Raise The Titanic. But these notes are what you want to hear on your way to the next world. And I'd even go so far as to say that the most beautiful music ever written was indeed by the late British film music composer from York, England.

instrumentals that are done with such striking artistry. Headed by an electrifying track
set that begin with the show-stopping opening track Tree Frog, the big band ensemble
heats up with other classic hits like Blues For Alfy as it feature an upbeat high-rocking
flute solo from the big band ensemble, as well as Something To Live For, Flirt, Ticker,
Swee-Pea, Too Close For Comfort, The Git and the title track, in which Basie handles
with care and well in balance. Once again they released another great masterpiece,
one that is performed with unique charisma and timeless brilliance, even though there
is certainly never a dull moment, you will find this tour de force recording a daring and
uptempo listening experience that is truly satisfying in some ways. So I would like to
highly recommend that you check out this big band masterpiece and then include it in
your MP3 system, because in Basie's making of the album `he told us so'.

review_headline: By far my favorite VAC album.
review_body:
I have an enormous amount of respect for Velvet Acid Christ, and I own quite a bit of their work. However, I have been far from consistently impressed with his music -- it can be very hit or miss for me. This album, however, is excellent. It has the driving, dance beats that I love in my industrial, as well as the haunting atmospheric darkness that is integral to VAC's style. Seriously, just listen to the first song on the album, \\"Evoke.\\" If that doesn't do it for you, then ignore this review altogether, because I clearly am not speaking for your tastes. \\"Bend the Sky\\" is another hypnotic masterpiece that I never get tired of listening to.
Initially, I wasn't in any hurry to buy another VAC album. But because of the recommendation of a good friend, and by attending a concert on their latest tour wherein he played a few of the best songs on the album, I did end up buying it. And I am very, very pleased. I am also happy to see a long-time presence in the industrial music genre still managing to put out great music -- despite the fact that he's bat-$hit insane. (Seriously, I've never been to a weirder concert - he was great, but so bizarrely insane.)
In other words, BUY THIS. IT IS GREAT.

Hussy Hicks - The London Sessions (Funk Fauna)
Hussy Hicks - Julz Parker and Leesa Gentz - a progressive folk duo from the Australian East Coast, got together in 2006, and were busy from the off, gigging, recording and releasing their music. Indeed, they debuted on plastic in 2008 with their \\"Life Plays Out\\" album, and have issued new recordings, on various formats, every year since. Their prolific output suggests they're enjoying what they do, and that certainly comes across on their 2013 offering, \\"The London Sessions\\". The pair - Parker plays guitar, and Gentz sings - throw themselves into the music, and their enthusiasm and joie de vivre is palpable. The sound is completed by a rhythm section that understands its obligations, and they swing like few folk groups do.

Not that they're purists by any means. Taking inspiration from various genres, including jazz, soul, old country and blues, the different combinations they employ keeps their music fresh, without sacrificing their trademark sound. That's defined by Parker's expressive musicianship - she's played with a variety of acclaimed guitarists from Tommy Emmanuel to Lulo Reinhardt - and Gentz's distinctive and versatile vocals.

Standout performances come thick and fast. Opening cut, \\"Armageddon (Outta Here)\\" arrives on blues-rock guitar lick, and Gentz is soon in on the act. It's a cracking start, and brings to mind Little Feat, Bonnie Raitt and the best of `70s FM radio. \\"Breaking It All Down\\" serves up a little social commentary, though it's observational rather than preachy, and not forgetting my current fave, the rootsy, old-fashioned \\"Empty Room\\", which would probably be hailed a classic had it originated in Austin rather than Australia.

review_headline: Kanye raps over Year Zero - with mixed results
review_body:
10 seconds into the album, I immediately thought \\"is this a NIN song?\\" which for hip-hop, is definitely different and made me very excited. The dark synths that create the soundscape for the 1st half of Yeezus remind me a lot of \\"Year Zero\\" - but with more of the minimalists feel of 808s and Heartbreak. (Seriously - go listen to \\"Survivalism\\" by NIN and tell me you don't hear the similarities to \\"On Sight\\")

That said, I'm a bit torn on this album after several listens. I think how YOU will feel about it will be based on what you WANTED to hear from a new Kanye album. If you are looking for hit singles and slamming beats, you will be very disappointed. The song structures are random, almost no drums, and I don't think there is a single chorus on the entire album. Thats a huge departure from his last album (Dark Fantasy), which was pretty much the exact opposite. The whole album is VERY experimental. Its not bad, but it definitely lacks mainstream appeal. This is an \\"artists\\" album at its truest form.

Given what Kanye has accomplished thus far in his career, I guess it makes sense for him to try something like this. In the perspective of his entire collection, this album is cool, but I don't think I'd want to hear him release another album like this anytime soon. He could have taken the dark synths and rapped over it with normal song structures, and it still would have been totally different than anything in hip-hop. Instead, he put out a disc that is probably going to be a little too far \\"out there\\" for most people. Of course all the \\"critics\\" will praise it so they can appear elite to the average person who \\"doesn't get it.\\"

Only time will tell if this album is truly groundbreaking, or just random/different for its own sake. The answer is probably somewhere in the middle.

Featuring some of the most glam-inspired cover art of its day, their second album was (like its predecessor) actually a potpourri of styles ranging from gritty RNB and sparkling pop to hard charging boogie rock. Astute axe handler RICK DERRINGER, who'd produced and played on the debut, proved a more than ample replacement for the departed RONNIE MONTROSE. Another secret weapon was multi-instrumentalist/blue eyed soul belter DAN HARTMAN, who wrote and sang lead on many of the best tracks including the rockin' warning sign RIVER'S RISIN'(which just nicked the Top 40) and the smooth SUNDOWN. Sax wailin' band leader EDGAR WINTER weighed in with jazzy, laid back vocals on EASY STREET, the polar opposite of the speaker-distorting screamer ANIMAL, a creature-feature cousin to his chart topping jam FRANKENSTEIN. Criminally ignored by early seventies radio, the underrated SHOCK TREATMENT is probably the best early seventies album that many folks never got to hear.

review_headline: Jen Chapin's Reckoning Authentic and Inspiring
review_body: In her latest release Reckoning, Jen's honest introspection is woven into a beautiful musical tapestry that projects both outward and inward. Understanding her role as both caring mother, loving wife, and concerned citizen, Jen's lyrics and music touch the hearts and souls of all of us -- allowing us to see more deeply into the humanity of those that struggle to feed their families, pay their bills, or make a living wage. Yet, she also admits to the long slow road toward a true democratic justice that seems to get side-tracked and detoured in the mire and mud of mindless polarities. She revels in both the joys and challenges of parenting, and in the day-to-day agony and ecstasy that defines the best of what a good marriage really means. Hearing all of this in the framework of a highly talented backup band blended with Jen's beautiful vocals will make for a CD experience that you will treasure over and over again, and will lead you to consider what you are being called to go, and do, and be.

Drummer Lenny White may be a little bit below the radar for some, but he has a pretty wide ranging discography, moving from several albums as a leader to stints with Return to Forever and a famous sideman gig on Miles Davis' epochal Bitches Brew. Surprisingly, the music here was recorded 15+ years ago, and didn't see the light of day until musicians began pestering him to release it. It was a wise move, the band has Mark Ledford on trumpet, Bennie Maupin on saxophones, Foley and Victor Bailey on bass, Patrice Rushen and Donald Blackman on keyboards is hot and very tight making strong jazz fusion that transcends the limitations of that sub-genre. Opening and closing with alternate takes of "Whew, What a Dream!" demonstrates what makes this group memorable. Having two bassists makes for a powerful groove, allowing one to keep the beat with the other sols and accompanies the music. Same thing with keyboards, especially on the alternate take where one solos on piano, while the other keyboardist frames the music with subtle synthesizer. "East St. Louis" is an epic track, coming on over twenty minutes in length. Building slowly from a subtle bass and drums groove, Lepford drops in for a well paced solo, before Bennie Maupin kicks in, and there is a feature for unaccompanied piano. "Pic Pocket" takes a jaunty angle, with electric piano shading coloring the song, while White provides a rhythmic kick from the rear. On the track "Dark," the synth keyboards provides a foundation for saxophone and trumpet to shimmer, before White drops the hammer and the music blasts off. Maupin now tears open on his horn, peeling off hot layers of music while the band before a powerful bass solo backed with thundering drums sends the music into outer space. This album worked very well, and fans of fusion or R and B tinged jazz should definitely take note, the combination of funk, jazz and fusion make a potent mixture.

review_headline: SYNTHESIZER-MASTER AND PIANIST STEPHEN SAVAGE OPENS THE DOOR TO THE FUTURE
review_body:
Keyboardist Stephen Savage has taught classical music for more than three decades and has served on the faculties of both the prestigious Berklee College of Music and the New England Conservatory of Music, but when it came time to compose and record original compositions for his first album, Future Memory, he went in a different direction and created synthesizer-based space music.

\\"I love classical music, but I am energized by the possibilities of space music,\\" says Savage. \\"I especially enjoy how it allows me to subtly incorporate elements of ambient-new age, avant-garde jazz, modern-classical and electronica.\\"

Savage's musical influences range from Pink Floyd to the modern classical music of 20th Century composers such as Bartok, Charles Ives, Elliott Carter, Varese, Stockhausen, Stravinsky and Copland; jazz starting with Parker, Coltrane and Monk, and moving through Hancock, Corea, Tyner, John McLaughlin, Weather Report and Pat Metheny; and the very avant-garde cutting-edge music of artists such as John Cage, Steve Reich and Pierre Boulez.

Five of the tunes of Future Memory include drums or percussion to add the rhythm element to the music, but most of the other pieces are space-ambient in tone, texture and style with a more floating presence as the tunes progress. While synthesizer is the predominant instrument, listeners also will hear piano, guitar, chimes and other familiar instrumentation. This album signals the emergence of a strong new voice in the realm of synthesizer music.

product_title: The Man Who Sold The World
review_headline: He Gave A Challenging And Startling Performance
review_body:
By the time David Bowie successfully entered the 1970’s as confident as ever,
he had already established himself as a singer-songwriter known for his folk-rock
stylings, stylish artistry, mystical storytelling, preppie musicianship, and relentless
personality. Though it did never contain any chart-topping singles, The Man Who
Sold The World, released in 1970, did serve as the beginning of his classic period
where he started working with fellow session guitarist Mark Ronson and producer
Tony Visconti, as he developed a tightly twisted heavy form of guitar rock done to
a radical tone that gnarled upon each listen. Beginning with the crackling opener
The Width Of A Circle, the poetic action concludes with its rapid pace with All The
Madmen, Black Country Rock, Savior Machine, The Supermen and the title track.
What could be best described as a stark denunciation of tyranny and the far-right,
The Man Who Sold The World is a fascinating view of mankind’s dark side, which
ranks as one of his best and most challenging masterworks as it still rings out just
as clear and relevant as ever, which the fuzzy base razor-thin guitars and Bowie’s
voice meld with his band’s relentless attack. (Oh yes, Virgin Records may want to
check on the unreleased track Lightning Frightening that first appeared on a 1990
CD re-issue, which gave it the finishing touch the first time around).

review_headline: 8.75 albums plus half the Christmas album
review_body:
Downloaded this tonight and haven't gotten through it all yet but I think I've sorted out exactly what is in this collection and from which albums the tracks come. This should help if you've already got a few June Christy CDs and want to compare. These 100 tracks include all of the following albums - not including the bonus tracks issued in the CD era:

Something Cool (1954)
Duet (1955)
Fair and Warmer (1957)
Gone For the Day (1957)
June's Got Rhythm (1958)
The Song Is June! (1958)
Ballads for Night People (1959)
Off-Beat (1960)

It also includes:
This Time of Year (1961) - 5 of the 10 tracks from [[ASIN:B002RLIRPA June's Christmas album]]
Big Band Specials (1962) - 9 of the 12 tracks from [[ASIN:B00000HYBT the reissued version]]

What tracks are missing from [[ASIN:B00000HYBT Big Band Specials]]? June's vocal version of Benny Goodman's [[ASIN:B000TDF6K2 Goodbye]] and Duke Ellington's [[ASIN:B000TEIPC2 It Don't Mean A Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing)]], probably because a version of the latter is on the album \\"June's Got Rhythm\\". One bonus track is included, \\"Time Was (Duerme)\\"; one is left off, \\"Until (The Mole)\\",

One bonus track from \\"Duet\\" with Stan Kenton is left off, [[ASIN:B000TR33JO Prelude To A Kiss]], probably because a version is included on \\"Big Band Specials\\". One bonus track from \\"Duet\\" is included, \\"Thanks For You\\".

The sound quality is fine on my laptop; listen to the samples and judge for yourself. (Update: I'm hearing notable clicks and pops on \\"Do Nothing Til You Hear From Me\\"). Sound levels are consistent throughout, unlike other generous Amazon mp3 collections of pre-1960s material. The only faults I would find with this collection are

1) the seriously cheesy artwork that looks like it took five minutes to slap together, using a photo taken long after the era in which these classics were recorded, and

2) because the songs were shuffled around, pacing is messed up. The collection hits stretches where song after song have the same melancholy ambiance. It might have been advisable to just leave off the few songs from the Christmas album, include all of the songs from the other albums present, and run them in sequential order.

Still, given the generosity of this collection for this price, these are trivialities. Maybe this label will put out a second set comprising the other half of June Christy's 1953-1965 catalog.

Update: After listening to this collection in full it occurs to me what the problem is with track sequencing. June made several concept albums and those tracks create a mood in the context of albums like \\"Duet\\" or \\"Ballads For Night People\\". But taken out of that context and dumped into a bin and randomly scrambled with songs from six other albums you lose the power and feel of those albums. You'll gain much more of an appreciation for June's artistry by listening to the albums sequenced as nature intended. One option would be to look up the original albums here on Amazon and create playlists putting this collection's tracks in album sequence. Another option would be to shell out an extra ten bucks, get [[ASIN:B008NC2DIY the eight albums on CD]] which should present each album in sequence. I have to admit the photo design does little to entice- which is probably why I didn't listen to samples right away. The music within, though, is truly divine.

But to decide to use BOTH their catalogs- well, that just means even more great songs get left behind. But what IS chosen- is rendered with imagination, respect, the highest level of talent, and a whole lot of grace and polish. I don't think I have heard ANY performer (outside Mr. Coward himself) deliver his patter songs with such excitement. I would dare say \\"I've Been to a Marvelous Party\\" rivals the recordings of the master himself. \\"Just One of Those Things\\" is another standout track.... An absolutely breathtaking arrangement sung perfectly. It's albums like this that makes one long for volumes 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6......
There are a few verses to songs I haven't heard before- including a man's verse for \\"Mad About the Boy\\" which had me laughing the first 10 times or so I listened to it...
If you are a fan of these writers, or cabaret performances, I don't see how you will not love this recording.

product_title: Epic Score - Epic Drama Vol. 1 Intros & Underscores - ES013
review_headline: The single best album from Epic Score
review_body:
Epic Score makes music that is licensed in movie trailers and advertisements. Sometimes it's more rock-style music, other times it's very orchestral. But the one constant about their music is that it's always good. They are well-known for their \\"Epic Action & Adventure\\" and \\"Pounding Percussion\\" album series, but this album is actually my personal favorite of everything they've done.

While many of the albums from Epic Score are full of loud and thrilling action cues, \\"Epic Drama Vol. 1\\" is their best album because it slows down and lets you breathe. Don't worry, there is plenty of tension here - but there's also a lot more pure emotion mixed into the music as well. They also use vocals in a very effective way.

Track 14, titled \\"Can't Change My Past\\", is the best piece on the album. But the whole album is worth a listen.
Here are a few of my other favorite tracks: (6) I Have a Story; (9) Taking the Fall; and (12) Mysterious Letter

One of the standout notes of the album is the guitar work of John 5 (previously featured on Marilyn Manson records, as well as Rob Halford of Judas Priest's 2WO) - he plays some very diverse styles over the course of the album, but you can hear in the way his builds up his riffs that he's having a lot of fun making this album. All in All, one of Rob Zombie's better recordings and, much like "Educated Horses" was, this album has a distinct feeling of being a Zombie album but it also stands apart from the expected sound of both volumes of "HellBilly Deluxe" and "the Sinister Urge".

review_headline: Can wait to the the whole album!
review_body: I'm very  mixed on this one.  In some ways I actually was hoping to hate this song.  While I've been dying to hear the new Sabbath, I'm also very disappointed and ticked off about the way the band treated and handled the Bill Ward situation.  To call this a Black Sabbath "Reunion" is criminal without Bill Ward.  What made the original Sabbath so special was those 4 guys.  Without Bill Ward, 25% of the magic is missing.  That's a pretty big chunk.  On top of that, NOBODY plays drums like Bill Ward.  Period.  Without his drumming, Sabbath doesn't have the feel and style that made them so unique.  However, the bottom line is that I have to admit that I really like it.  Does it live up to the masterpieces that were the first 3 Sabbath albums?  Not even close.  But it's definitely better than anything off "Never Say Die" or "Technical Ecstasy".  It's moody like a lot of the early Sabbath songs and has a great Tony Iommi riff that I would put right up against many of the old classic songs.  If you're expecting this to live up to the impossible to match levels of those first 3 Sabbath albums, then stop right now.  But if you keep an open mind and give it a chance, it's far better than just about any of the new metal that's out there these days and it does stay pretty true to the Sabbath style and sound.  I think it's great and I'm planning on picking up the CD when it comes out now.

When it comes to the underground you have bands that are SO far underground that even the majority of underground fans aren't even aware of them.
Which brings us to Dead Silence from Minsk...
From where???
Minsk is right in between Russia and Poland if that helps.
I was originally introduced to DS via Youtube when their video popped up when I was watching something else.
So what's so special about these guys?
If you like Symphonic Death Metal then you may like these guys.

The group has since relocated to the US and has signed with Artery and released their \\"Symphony of Hope\\" album.
First off the symphonic elements are amazing.
The vocals alternate between clean, harsh and core shouts.
The core shouts are something I hope they do away with...I'm just not a fan of the tough guy shouting sorry. Thankfully the core shouting is at a minimum.
The majority is death vox with clean vocals
There really isn't much in the way of breakdowns either.
I guess all vocals were done by four different guys...not sure who but the group is recruiting a vocalist now.
The songs are mature, constructed well and very catchy.
I see big things for this group in the future as long as the label promotes them properly and puts them on some good tours.
They're simply too talented not to have a huge following.
The production is crisp and clear allowing for every instrument to come through clearly.
The piano and symphonic elements are what really set this band apart.
The album opens with the instrumental \\"My Nightmares Turned Into Reality\\" and simply doesn't let up.
One of the major problems with core bands and the term core barely applies here at all but a lot of the songs tend to bleed together.
Not here...every song has a unique identity and just about every song on the album could be a single.

Brutal.
Beautiful.
I dare say...somewhat radio friendly (?)
It has some elements especially the layered clean vocals that could be considered commercial.
I have no problem with that as long as it's done with integrity and it is here.
All in all this group deserves a fair listen.
One of my 2013 stand outs for sure.
Give it a shot if you like symphonic death metal that isn't afraid to step outside the usual boundaries.
I wish DS all the success in the world.
They're too talented to go unnoticed.

Pop Evil hails from just across Lake Michigan from where I am from, however I had never heard of this band until [[ASIN:B002708QHA 100 In A 55]] went national and got some big air play in my area. I really like a majority of War Of Angels, which battled their self-titled album for best songs. This album makes a great addition to the collection thus far and in many ways is a continuation of the sound off War of Angels as their second release from eOne. Time to hit it:

Onyx is a great mix of style and sound from Pop Evil and to this point is probably their most 'adventurous' album, if that is the correct word, in terms of breaking the classic rock style of hard songs and ballads. The lead single Trenches which has been getting major airplay is a rewarding mix of pop style beat with the hard rocking riffs and guitars of a classic Pop Evil rock sound. Directly following is Torn to Pieces which is the best of the slower songs on the album with a great backing of minor keys and harmonizing.

However some of the steam built over the first 5 songs decreases in the meat of the album, bottoming out at Sick Sense which is the albums worst song, and far too pop-influenced. Luckily, things rebound quickly with Fly Away and finish off great with the head banging Flawed.

-Conclusion: Fans of War of Angels style ballads won't find a Monster You Made or Purple hiding here in between the hard rocking tracks, but the balance of the hard rock and harmonized slow songs makes a complete balance and a solid album.

-Standout Tracks: Deal With the Devil, Trenches, Torn to Pieces, Flawed
