review_headline: Progressive funk to keep you grooving 'til the day is done!
review_body:
The Fritz have put together a fantastic piece of work, \\"Prehistoric Stomp.\\" Hailing originally from Jacksonville, FL, around the time this album was released they moved to the hip music center of Asheville, NC (considering Asheville is home to Moog inventor Bob Moog, I'd say it was a good choice). Since then, the band has continued to hone their skills and develop their style - which is signature, to say the least. Frontman Jamar Woods plays keyboards, including MiniMoog synthesizer and a Korg Workstation. His sound could be comparable to that of Keith Emerson, Chick Corea, even Rick Wakeman; except with bright youth and focused funk-attitude. Guitarist Jamie Hendrickson's sound is reminiscent of Trey Anastasio of Phish and his guitar melodies are comparable to Camel's front man Andrew Latimer. Now, the man who really runs with a tight groove: Jake O' Conner. Reminiscent of Jaco Pastorious, Stanley Clarke, Victor Wooten, he plays clean, accurate, tight lines, and holds groove firmly with drummer Michael Tillis and percussionist Mike Evans. Tillis provides strong backbone with his fierce rhythmic \\"stomp,\\" if you will; he is on the nuggets. Evans makes fun and challenging rhythmic interplay with Tillis, and is especially enjoyable on stage.

The band's forthcoming \\"Bootstrap\\" album will be guaranteed to blow minds and even make their awesome debut seem like nothing in comparison. I saw them live in Beaufort, NC earlier this year, and they played a majority of new material. They've released a single in advance called \\"Sounds. Habits. Blame.\\" and its b-side, \\"Sawbones\\" (a personal favorite of mine.)

Overall: imagine funk, jazz, progressive rock, fusion, soul, MiniMoog solos, and Jimi Hendrix-esque vocals, all combined into one package. This is the Fritz.

product_title: A Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols
review_headline: Unique, hard-to-find Christmas gems finally in digital release!!
review_body:
I have been waiting for this old, classic recording for DECADES. I grew up listening to the tape and finally it is available digitally. What do I love so much about it?
1. First track \\"Once in Royal David's City\\" is sung half a step higher than all the other recordings of this traditional opening track. The higher key renders it sweeter and more piercing. Before this digital release, I figured our tape player played songs high and I'd loved the song in the \\"wrong\\" key. I resigned myself to the less enjoyable versions in the apparent \\"real\\" key - G major. But now, here it is, the version I love, higher and sweeter (in Ab major). Bliss!
2. The remarkably creative \\"Invitatory\\", from the Christmas Oratorio (actually a lovely tone poem of Luke's gospel) is another gem for which I have vainly searched. A baritone sings the narrator's part (\\"And there were shepherds in the same country abiding in the fields...\\") and a boy soprano voices the angel. I still get chills when the baritone sings, \\"And the Angel said unto them...\\" and the piercing high voice sings, \\"Fear not...\\" Only after the heavenly message is delivered does the Oratorio's roaring, full-choir praise of God, \\"Break forth oh beauteous heavn'ly morn...\\" get sung, suggesting the countless angels singing and praising God before the astonished shepherds.
The rest of the albums is almost exactly as I remember it. I admit, the sound is a bit iffy, but that is ALSO how I remember it. If nothing else, buy tracks 1 and 3. (I love 5, 11, and 15 too...)
I am a bit confused as to Mr. Michnay's complaints in the other review. This seems to be a faithful reproduction of the tape I knew and loved. While the last few tracks are unfamiliar to me, I suspect they were omitted from the tape b/c, back in 80's, they couldn't fit everything on those limited magnetic reels. Secondly, I wonder if he is expecting a different version from this one. Don't most \\"lessons and carols\\" have a fair amount of leeway in terms of what readings and carols they include? I certainly understand the frustration of hearing a beloved Christmas album played differently (see my above review!), so perhaps HIS beloved version is available among the intimidating corpus of King's Choir Christmas albums...or not yet released.
I genuinely wish him luck in his search. For me and for my family, this album a is gorgeous Christmas surprise, the end of a long nostalgic search.

The title doesn't really make sense. It's a Wu-Tang Clan and D-Block (Lox) collaboration; Ghostface and Sheek are the prime members for this set; but the Wu Block moniker implies a Clan takeover. The title doesn't linguistically represent both groups, in other words. It seems to favor Wu-Tang Clan over D-Block because the \\"Wu\\" is semantically equivalent to the \\"D\\", not the \\"Block\\". If you take out the \\"D\\", it can be anybody's \\"Block\\", depending on whose name you put before it, just as it could be anybody's \\"Clan\\". If it were D Clan, the problem would go the opposite way.

Not that I'd expect either group to consider proper English. This is rap music for uneducated street thugs; the type of \\"n*gg*s\\" who rob and shoot people when they aren't selling drugs to them. The first song, as it goes, is a collection of Crack Spot Stories. It's also one of the best because it's one of the few that isn't dampered by a tawdry hook. Stick-Up Kids, inspired by a tired Fat Boys catchphrase, and Been Robbed, which limits its verse space to just four bars, are particularly annoying. The only commendable chorus, in fact, is the one provided by guest singer Erykah Badu.

Sheek has become the best rapper of The Lox though. \\"My high school teachers, they said I wouldn't be nothing; sitting on the bleachers,\\" he says, \\"Now I'm sitting in a Phantom, trying to figure-out the features.\\" Jadakiss and Styles provide guest verses for comparison's sake. Other Clan members, and Cappadonna, are also featured. I would've liked to hear a verse from Rza, but Ghostface holds it down. He and Sheek Louch actually make a dynamic duo. When Method Man finishes their story about a shady \\"bitch\\" named Stella, he only distracts from their chemistry.

product_title: David: Les Brises D'Orient / Les Minarets
review_body: Late at night, after the working day is done, dinner has been served and the football game has ended, some people like to kick back with a good book to help them enjoy the rest of the night before bed. During the day, when given the chance, I bombard my ears with symphonic music, especially symphonies and poems by romantic composers like Liszt, Myaskovsky, Brahms, Beethoven, Raff, Saint-Saens and the occasional Atterberg. At night, partly because I'm pensive, and partly because I don't want to disturb the neighbors, I gravitate to my all piano program. This usually means sonatas by Beethoven, Haydn, and Czerny and piano pieces by Chopin, Liszt, Busoni, and Schubert with the occasional Scriabin thrown in for good measure. I had the chance to audition David's Les Brises d'Orient recently and I was extremely pleased. When I listen to it I hear shades of Chopin, Field and Alkan. Not a note seems out of place. Daniel Blumenthal's fleet-fingered performance is warming and gentle to the ear. The recording is superb. The crispness of the strings, the dynamism from ppp to fff, and the rhythms and tempi of his interpretations are nothing less than stunning. All of the works, firmly entrenched in the romantic vein, wouldn't sound out of place next to the works by, say, Mendelssohn, Schumann or Rachmaninov. And that is a good thing.

review_headline: Where did this girl come from?
review_body:
The first most people heard of Cher Lloyd's 'Sticks & Stones' was the first US single 'Want U Back' - a fairly annoying song, but catchy nonetheless. It also has a lot more clever lyricism than you will find on many 'break up' songs, incorporating a satirical nature and a type of self-influence when the singer tries to tell herself that she's not jealous, but clearly the guy didn't think this through. This type of clever lyricism was the first thing that stood out to me about Cher Lloyd.

Swagger Jagger is one of my favorite songs of the year, and I'm sad it didn't get more radio play in the US. This song is simply incredible - catchy, danceable, and Cher Lloyd demonstrates just how versatile she is - great rapper with an excellent singing voice.

Oath rounds the album out and is a perfectly welcome new BFF song for the teenage girl

When asked to explain Cher Lloyd, I usually compare her to Ke$ha, only with less glitter and more talent - an actual singing voice and an actual rapping voice, and the stage presence to hold her own with the big girls. Cher Lloyd is a welcome addition to the girl pop-music culture and stands alongside Karmin as one of my favorite new rap/pop combination efforts of the year. I'm very excited to see what Cher Lloyd brings us in the future - this girl has got some serious skills!

When I listened to Diamonds for Eyes' album, The Era of Our Ways, I can't help but hear the story of my life in it. Obviously the album wasn't written about me, but you can tell the measure of a great album by how well it relates to you. That's not always the requirement, but in this case you can tell the songs are deeply personal and each one feels deeply personal to me.

The lead singer has a sound that reminds me of Johnny Cash, though he doesn't sound like him, more like Cash may have inspired him. The lead singer is uniquely his own voice, which is great because it doesn't sound like the overplayed stuff on the radio. And definitely no auto-tune.

I love this record and I'm looking forward to purchasing their next album, Catacomb Fires.

What a treat ... that is if you're already been riding the backroads with Ryan Bingham and his band of alternative country gunslingers. If not, then you still have the pleasure of discovering he and his music for the first time, though for those of us who've been on the road so long we no longer know north from south, or east from west, Lost Highway, for their 10th year anniversary have been releasing some of their back catalog in revised and exciting formats. In this case, the sensational Mescalito can now be yours in a gatefold, on two platters of 180 clear vinyl, delivering Ryan's weathered voice and rambling songs with a much warmer analog presentation to delight your ears and eyes. There are some things that are just better on record, and this outing is one of them. Spin it, drop the needle and try and tell me I'm wrong ...

His songs have a brilliant country feel, yet are heavily laced with blues, and a slight taste of Mexico ... creating a traditional sound, nodding to his influences, all the while creating his own original sound. Ryan has a close association with The Black Crows and The Drive By Truckers, but don't go thinking for one moment that his music is derived from either of these groups, he's an artist who stands his ground, and owns every square foot of it. His vocals and lyrics are placed front and center, with the guitar, pedal steel and mandolin evoking themes of loneliness, and the tall tales of an old man sitting on his front porch with crystal clear eye.

review_headline: One of the best instrumental seasonal albums ever
review_body: Growing up, I didn't like much of the music my parents had, but I loved George Winston.  December was one of my favorite albums then, and it has remained so.  Winston's artistry and joy shine through in every song, with a beautiful balance of quiet/contemplative and joyful celebration.  His own compositions blend with arrangements of familiar seasonal (winter/Christmas) favorites to produce an album with wonderful flow and cohesion.  Whether you only have time for one song, or you can sit and listen to the whole thing, you will not be disappointed.  Use it to create a beautiful holiday ambiance, or sit and immerse yourself in its intricate pacings and rhythms.  Either way, it shines, and should be considered as a must have for the season, especially if you love solo piano.  I have always been impressed with the fullness of sound that Winston can create as a solo pianist, and will listen to this album over and over and over each winter season.  So very glad to finally replace my old and no longer functional cassette of this album with high quality digital version (MP3) from Amazon.  Thanks, Amazon, and thanks George Winston!

product_title: Remembering the Platters - Songs of My Father
review_body:
Franchesca Robi is the daughter of the late Paul Robi, who was the baritone voice of the legendary Platters from about 1955 to 1965. He was featured on all of the group's LP's on the Mercury label. In this album, Franchesca pays homage to this extraordinary group by doing modern versions of not only their biggest hits (like \\"Only You\\", \\"The Great Pretender\\" and \\"Smoke Gets In Your Eyes\\") but to some of their lesser known recordings (\\"Wish It Were Me\\", \\"The Mystery of You\\", \\"I Wish\\", et al).
She has a smooth, sometimes sultry voice and can even hold that big final note on \\"Smoke\\" and \\"My Prayer\\".
Some of the cuts have big orchestrations with full strings, others have a smaller combo background. It's all quite special if you have a love for this trailblazing group. And if you don't, you should.
It is curious, however, that in an album sub-titled \\"Songs Of My Father\\", she didn't do any songs her father sang lead on in all those Mercury albums. Paul, who had a rich baritone voice, was well represented on most of their LPs and was a fitting contrast to the soaring tenor sound of lead singer Tony Williams. But all of the songs in this collection were fronted by Tony in their original versions.
With the passing of bass singer Herb Reed, earlier this year, the five originals are now all gone. This gem of an album gives us a welcomed fresh spin on a group that is now vastly underrated and long plagued by talentless imitators.

The composition itself is interesting for a number of reasons.  First, there is the historical context: It was composed under Mussolini by the apolitical Respighi in the period between the two world wars.  Second, it combines technical features such as a recorded nightingale's song with the use of ancient instruments such as buccine.  Third, it has had significant influence on modern works such as Basil Poledouris's score for Conan the Barbarian.  But the recording here does not do justice to the dynamic range of the work, which runs the gamut from a low hum to a cacophonous roar.  It sounds like it was recorded with a very small number of microphones placed far away enough to capture the entire sound of the orchestra in each microphone, and the concert hall reverberation sounds canned.  There is no substitute for a live performance, and this recording doesn't get very close to that experience.

review_headline: A Classic That Still Sounds Fresh and New Today
review_body:
Being new to Irish Traditional Music and the tin whistle, I bought this to help inspire my own practice. Ms. Bergin's prowess of the instrument draws listeners to her and doesn't let them go. The tunes, most with Irish titles, stands the test of time. I believe her playing has as large an impact now as it did when it first came out in 1979, despite the number of masterful whistlers in print today. Ms. Bergin needs no accompaniment when she plays, so the other instruments are rarely noticed - you'll be focused to her.

I gave this five stars for the performance, but the sound quality has to be addressed. I don't think the digital age and dynamic playback of music was considered when the final audio mix was released. The original printing on tape or LP record probably helped compress the sound, but today's digital devices provide more range, even with the MP3 files that I bought. Sometimes the shrillness of the whistle, especially with higher pitched notes makes me turn down the volume. This isn't related to Ms. Bergin's performance. I just think the music should be remixed for the digital age.

If you want to listen to a master of Irish tunes, don't pass this up. Mary Bergin proves that the tin whistle is a serious musical instrument and not a toy for kids.

Perhaps I am still under the spell of meeting them, but if alternative rock band Three Days Grace's (who are super sweet in person, by the way) albums were Olympic medals, I would rank their newest, \\"Transit of Venus\\" ($10.99 on Amazon MP3), as a \\"silver\\" when compared to the \\"gold\\" that was \\"One-X\\" ($9.99 on Amazon MP3). \\"Transit of Venus\\" is a solid album, no doubt, but there is more filler here than on the nearly perfect \\"One-X\\". \\"Life Starts Now\\" ($6.99 on Amazon MP3) would be the bronze of the group, making the band's debut album ($9.99 on Amazon MP3) a runner-up. Let's be fair; the debut just needed more training.

Frontman Adam Gontier is back with his signature growl, while guitarist Barry Stock, bassist Brad Walst and drummer Neil Sanderson are here to deliver what you have come to expect: the same hard-hitting riffs, killer beats and signature hooks that have provided the band with the longevity they deserve. Why TDG is not featured more prominently on mainstream radio, I don't know, but this is not necessarily a negative. Airwaves tend to remain silent when it comes to music of superior quality.

\\"Chalk Outline\\", the first single off of \\"Transit of Venus\\", will play in your head for days, as will \\"Operate\\". \\"Happiness\\" is pretty solid, and I would have loved to have seen my face when \\"Give In to Me\\" came over the speakers. Not only was TDG paying homage to the legendary Michael Jackson, but they chose a lesser-known gem from his catalog (and one of my favorites) which fits their style perfectly. The sexy instrumentals are freshened up here (sans Slash, of course), and scorned, forlorn Gontier is a perfect match for these lyrics.

As for what I didn't like, \\"Anonymous\\" and \\"The High Road\\" bored me, while \\"Unbreakable Heart\\" was good, but not great. \\"Sign of the Times\\", the opening track, starts off in a different vein from what we're used to, but you'll find yourself saying, \\"ah, there it is\\" about thirty seconds in. All things considered, \\"Transit of Venus\\" is a solid album worthy of your hard-earned cash. It didn't hurt that a promised autograph in person came with the pre-order, and that said positive memory will always be linked to the purchase, but I'm happy to say that the CD did not become a coaster. A great experience and a great CD make Three Days Grace a band I will be even happier to support in the future.

It's been a long 10 years since Cody ChesnuTT released \\"The Headphone Masterpiece\\". For those of us who considered that a classic, this release will not disappoint. Cody is a true artist who makes music on his own terms and has no intention of following the mainstream. Fans should be aware, however, that a decade of life will change an artist's approach to making music.

It might catch fans off guard to hear Cody on properly recorded songs and with a band. The updated sound will grow on the listener fast though. Cody ChesnuTT's voice now sparkles like it never did before on a low-fi recording. Where the last album contained some rock influences, this one definitely has more of a soul feel to it. 10 years ago, one might encounter sporadic bouts of casual curses and humorous cockiness from Mr. ChesnuTT. Though he has grown out of this approach, his songwriting and vocals are still as genuine and potent as they've ever been. If anything, his talents and artistic intent are even more refined now.

On socially relevant songs like, \\"What Kind Of Cool?,\\" and \\"Everybody's Brother,\\" he reaches new heights in writing about the human condition. \\"Till I Met Thee\\" is the type of inspirational album opener that can only be the result of some intense soul searching. The blissful and romantic \\"Love Is More Than A Wedding Day\\" is a testament to how Cody's perspective of love has matured. The up-tempo \\"Where Is All The Money Going?\\" not only asks an important question in today's day and age, but the song is downright funky! It really showcases how the band adds to Cody's musical vision.

All in all, \\"Landing On A Hundred\\" is a triumphant modern soul record suitable for people of all ages. It showcases the growth and evolution of not only Cody ChesnuTT the musical genius, but also of Cody ChesnuTT the human being. It is most definitely worth the purchase.

product_title: Song of Simeon: a Christmas Journey
review_headline: `A light to enlighten the nations and the Glory of your people Israel'
review_body:
It may be only the end of October but thoughts of Christmas are circulating already and one of the first entries into the arena of Christmas celebration is this new recording by the Will Scruggs Jazz Fellowship. It is a very beautiful combination of jazz, folk, traditional, ancient and contemporary music that allows a fresh look at the Christmas story - outlined in the heading of this review as the line form the Song of Simeon from the Bible.

Will Scruggs was born in 1980 in Atlanta, GA, and grew up in Raleigh, NC. He has toured and recorded with Natalie Cole and has been featured as a special guest soloist with Dave Brubeck. He is a top call studio saxophonist in Atlanta, having recorded with the likes of Cee-Lo Green, the Wood Brothers, Dallas Austin, and Jermaine Dupri. He is also an accomplished bandleader, composer, and vocalist who has toured internationally to significant critical acclaim. When commenting on this new recording he stated, `The process of creating this music was an incredible journey for me, both musically and spiritually. The CD is an instrumental jazz suite in two parts, based on the message of the biblical Song of Simeon. The disc features all new arrangements and improvisations based of 11 ancient melodies that explore the mysterious side of Christmas.'

The result is a 2 part jazz suite that explores the deep, mysterious, and radical themes of the Christmas narrative using 11 ancient canticles, hymns, and folk melodies. Part I: The Glory -O Come, O Come, Emmanuel; The Annunciation; Song of Mary; God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen; Song of Simeon; Go Down, Moses. And Part II: The Light: Lo, How A Rose E'er Blooming; We Three Kings; T'Was In The Moon Of Wintertime; Ideo Gloria; Joy To The World. The Jazz sextet - Will Scruggs, soprano and tenor sax, Brian Hogans, piano,  Dan Baraszu, guitar, Tommy Sauter, bass,  Marlon Patton, drums , Kinah Boto Ayah, percussion,  with special guest Joe Gransden, trumpet, and is backed by an 8-piece horn ensemble -  Joe Grandsen, trumpet,  Ryan Whitehead, clarinet,  Brian Hogans, alto sax,  Norm Ficke, tenor sax,  Wes Funderburk, trombone,  Travis Cottle, trombone,  Lee Watts, bass trombone, and Will Scruggs, baritone sax: the result is a warmly beautiful musical sound quite unlike any ever heard.

Yes, the result is a celebration of Christmas, but the tone is a spiritual and almost timeless homage to the traditions of all peoples who come together at this time of year to go within as well as radiate the joy without. Grady Harp, October 12

review_headline: Buy Slova Czech, you'll be glad you did!
review_body: For those fond of traditional folk music of the Czech and Slovak regions, this is a fantastic album. The level of artistry in the performances is beyond top notch. The selections flow from one to the next in a way that keeps things interesting. The styles of the various ethnicities represented are quite authentic, and the arrangements take folk tunes well into the realm of art music. Most of the numbers are high energy and characterized by much virtuosic playing. There are some slower, more somber numbers. I particularly like the lullaby, Dobru noc ma mila. I'm a music teacher and am planning to teach it to my elementary music classes. I've taken to listen to it repeatedly as I can't get enough of it. When is the next album coming out! review_headline: Prophet says "Must Wear Headphones for Full Effect"
review_body: Of Menomena's trio (now duo), ex-band member Brent Knopf is/was the astral wonder mental man that put the ever-changing atmosphere's in their albums. He's now flown from that band and landed back on his perch at Ramona Falls. There he can explore his highly musical imagination in private and record his rambling visions.  As you may have already sampled from other media providing sites his songs, I must insist on purchasing the full HQ mp3 files by clicking the little button at the top right of this page to begin one of the most satisfying music purchases you'll ever make. Plus it's only fair to him. Afterward dig out or purchase a nice set of headphones (this a great place for that as well), launch your mp3 player and experience Brent's brain in it full musical capacity. Listening to his music through mere free standing speakers doesn't provide the experience he's intended for you. The instruments and sounds dance from ear to ear as a wonderful rhythmic common ground is centered and many times has you tapping your feet to it. My favorite song 'Brevony' is the perfect example of his music genius, the song is like floating broken pieces of instruments playing their sounds and somewhat together yet apart, the guitar intentionally forcing amplifier feedback, an almost out of place keyboard playing what seems like a piano teaching exercise, but just as one might think he's losing his mind he throws everything together and blasts with perfect rock rhythm and sound in 4/4 time that even the Foo Fighters could appreciate. It's only for a few seconds then the song ends. The pieces merged and became a solid which fulfilled my experience of the song like a nice desert. It's that suspense he creates that makes his songs so satisfying and genius. I really enjoy this album and with headphones I can see the big picture. That's really the only way one should experience Brent's music. Highly recommended

Hank Mobley is such a melodic, soulful, ceaselessly inventive and swinging player that I tend to listen to his recordings--under his own name as well those he made with Silver, Blakey, Lee Morgan, K.D., and Miles--more regularly than to the undeniably more innovative if not revolutionary Coltrane, whose recordings post-\\"Love Supreme\\"--or after McCoy and Elvin had left the quartet--can test the patience of Trane's most committed disciples.

The oft-repeated description of Mobley as the \\"middleweight champion of the tenor saxophone\\" is usually an occasion for Mobs' defenders to attack the apparent dissing of their hero. But if you can agree that sometimes it can be as gratifying to watch the punching and counter-punching of a Sugar Ray Robinson as the heavier punches of a Marciano, Liston, Frazier, Ali or Tyson, then the description can be seen as a positive. Hank himself initially resisted Miles' attempts to add him to the frontline of his quintet following the departure of Trane, protesting: \\"Miles, Coltrane was the Art Tatum of the tenor saxophone. That's not me!\\"

But Miles, of course, eventually had his way, and the results can be heard on the most unusual \\"Someday My Price Will Come\\", on which Miles appears to \\"blindside\\" Mobley by having Trane show up in the studio and follow Mobley with a \\"sheets of sound\\" solo that practically makes Mobley's prior solo sound rudimentary and reductive by comparison--especially to anyone unfamiliar with Mobley's approach: [[ASIN:B0015XWUHM Someday My Prince Will Come]]. Mobley could play solos that were disarmingly simple--but never \\"simplistic.\\" His game is not to \\"prove\\" anything, or to be \\"different\\" from his predecessors and peers, but to play the most inventive, heartfelt melodies on the chord progressions that were given him.

A validation of Mobley's approach can be heard on the recording that places him in the company of tenor saxophonists John Coltrane, Zoot Sims, and Al Cohn, especially his \\"clean-up\\" solo on Irving Berlin's \\"How Deep Is the Ocean.\\"[[ASIN:B005DIVEWW Tenor Conclave]]. But along with his own signature Blue Note date [[ASIN:B00000I8UI Soul Station]], Mobley submits some of his most poignant, soul-searching lyrical playing on \\"Bye Bye Blackbird\\" from [[ASIN:B00009KU7D In Person Friday Night at the Blackhawk, Complete, Vol. 1]]. Yet Miles is said to have stonewalled him, never offering any assurances to a player who resembled Coltrane in his willingness to open his heart to the public. Were the proverbial Time Machine to appear and offer an opportunity to return to hear in person any post-Bird musical group, my choice would be immediate: Miles' transitional group with Hank Mobley on tenor (I availed myself of ample opportunities to hear Coltrane as well as the other successors--George Coleman, Sonny Stitt (for a tour of France and Sweden), as well as Joe Henderson (who was never with Miles, to the best of my knowledge, but briefly upstaged Hank with his gritty, \\"different\\" approach), and of course Shorter (with Blakey, then Miles).

Mobley was something special--the player who comes to mind when I read James Baldwin's epiphanies about jazz and its exponents in his short story, \\"Sonny's Blues.\\" Sadly, there appears to be absolutely no footage of Mobley on video (I've been looking for years). \\"Newark 1953\\" is perhaps the closest the modern-day listener can come to Mobley in his formative years. It's true that he gets off some characteristically Mobley melodies, with numerous seamless insertions of familiar \\"quotations,\\" but Benny Green's trombone, though spirited and consistently \\"on,\\" tends to dominate the sonic canvas throughout (to a greater degree than when I heard Benny performing with Sonny Stitt in a Chicago south-side club). Hank apparently felt a need to defer to the extroverted, insistent horn of his senior, who comes off as the putative leader on this session.

There are other negatives--or at leastannoyances--about the session. I've heard many recordings from the '30s, '40s, and early '50s on which the bass was weak (in some cases, a refreshing change from the booming, floor-shaking, generic bass sounds I'm hearing on some present-day recordings and live sessions). On my copy of \\"Newark 1953\\" the bass isn't weak: it's absent! There's a leaden 4/4 pulse, but it sounds like the percussionist (hard to believe it's the redoubtable Charli Persip) is supplying the pulse with his bass drum--much like Gene Krupa in the late-'30s and early '40s.

In short, the bass player on my copy is a \\"no show.\\" And a warning to downloaders: if you elect to pay Amazon 99c for the \\"Announcement\\" (perhaps an opportunity to hear Hank Mobley actually speak--not as good as a video but better than nothing--save yourself the misspent 99c and subsequent disappointment. All you'll hear is some club owner or similar authoritative voice taking the microphone to warn some poor patron that his car will be towed if he doesn't move it. (Even though downloading is an automated process, you'd think that Amazon, iTunes, and the other providers would discover a way to prevent 19-second tracks of no interest--musical or otherwise--from being downloaded and put on the customer's tab.

I understand it's Walter Davis, Jr. on piano. I met him in Paris in 1958, when he was playing with Donald Byrd, who was studying with Nadia Boulanger by day and playing at Le Chat qui Peche at night. On this session, he sounds like hundreds of other pianists pounding out the same chords on the same tunes. By the time he joined the Jazz Messengers for a brief period, he had improved immensely, and in the 1970s Walter would contribute the most challenging, engaging, advanced compositions and arrangements to the Messengers' book of any composer-arranger in the group's history: [[ASIN:B00008G8H3 Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers]] (the preceding video of the Messengers at the Umbria Jazz Festival, which features Walter's compositions with the sole exception of a Mickey Tucker solo, is the most accessible--perhaps the only--example of his singular compositional genius),

In short, I'd recommend downloading no more than a couple of numbers from \\"Newark 1953.\\" There is far better early Mobley on a series of sessions he made for the tiny Transition label in Boston. The leaders are Blakey, Silver, Byrd and Doug Watkins--but the voice that is likely to stay with the listener because of the fluent, lyrical tenor sax solos on one track after the other is Hank Mobley's. product_title: The Garden of Love: Songs of William Blake
review_body:
Martha Redbone Roots Project - The Garden Of Love: Songs of William Blake (Blackfeet Productions)
Although \\"The Garden Of Love: Songs of William Blake\\" is Martha Redbone's third album, she considers it \\"a sonic rebirth and fuller flowering of her own rootsy ethos\\". It's easy to understand Redbone's thought process. William Blake was an 18th century visionary. An acclaimed poet and artist, an idealist, free thinker and republican, an advocate of free love and a scourge of organized religion. That's a heady mix for a man born in the 1750s, in pre-industrial London, and it's his words that Redbone has chosen to sing. No wonder they instill feelings of liberation and rebirth.

Upon listening to the album for the first time, it's fascinating to hear how contemporary it sounds. Blake may have written his poems over 200 years ago, but Redbone has placed them in a thoroughly modern Appalachian folk setting - if that's not an oxymoron. The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band's John McEuen produced the recordings, and he's done quite a job. The sound is splendid; warm, energized and inclusive, and Redbone is in fine voice; passionate and when the material requires it, sensitive and gentle. I'm sure it will be filed away under folk, but it's soulful and infused with gospel, and transcends simple genre classification.

They begin with the barnstorming title track, a shadowy, backwoods reading, which places the garden on the swampier side of the tracks. \\"On Anothers Sorrow\\" is equally intense, though the simple arrangement relies utterly on Redbone's outstanding vocals, and \\"A Dream\\" reflects its English roots until a flute and Seminole chants break the spell. It makes for a wonderful juxtaposition, and provides just one of many standout moments on this exceptional record.

review_headline: And I'm Lost In The Circle Again
review_body:
I have taken an interest in Joe Bonamassa since getting his album Driving Toward the Daylight earlier this year, and that led me to the \\"supergroup\\" that he is a part of - Black Country Communion - and their latest offering Afterglow. Listening to Afterglow is like stepping into a musical time machine back into the 70's and 80's calling to mind the likes of Led Zeppelin, Aerosmith, and ZZ Top. While Bonamassa was what drew me to BCC, it is clear to me that Glenn Hughes is the engine that makes the bad go. His vocals are a blend of Chris Cornell and David Lee Roth, but he also handles bass duties as well - and he acquits himself quite well on both accounts. The sound of Afterglow is various shades of blues infused hard rock. Bonamassa has a grooving guitar lick that runs under the verse on \\"This Is Your Time\\" while \\"Cry Freedom\\" is more of a blues shuffle. Both \\"Afterglow\\" and \\"Crawl\\" are driven blues rock songs that conjure Led Zeppelin. However the crown jewel of Afterglow is the seven minute haunting blues lament \\"The Circle\\". Hughes starts the song with a clear vocal delivery but he reaches his screeching intensity on the chorus \\"I'm in the middle of a dream. I just don't know what it means. I am at war with the fear. And I'm lost in the circle again.\\" If you liked the hard rock sounds of the 70's and 80's, Afterglow is a must have. I highly recommend it.

product_title: Portrait Bronislaw Gimpel (Violin Concertos & Violin Sonatas in recordings for RIAS Berlin, 1954-1957)
review_headline: Very Nice and Gracious Old World Violin Master Playing
review_body:
I had never heard of Bronislav Gimpel but in enjoying his beautiful violin playing, I found quiet but intense beauty. He was from \\" Lvov, Austria-Hungary, part of Polish Galicia (now Lviv, Ukraine), to a family of Jewish origin. Gimpel's older brother, Jakob Gimpel, was a noted concert pianist who also recorded music for motion pictures.\\"

\\"Bronislav Gimpel started piano and violin lessons with his father at the age of five. At the age of eight, he studied with Moritz Wolfstahl at the Lwów Conservatory. After 1922 he continued his studies with Robert Pollack at the Vienna Conservatory. At the age of fourteen, he played the Goldmark Concerto with the Vienna Philharmonic. A year later, an extended concert tour in Italy resulted in a succession of triumphs of historic proportion, with command performances before King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy and Pope Pius XI, and invitations to play on Paganini's famous Guarneri and to perform at the grave of the legendary virtuoso. Tours of South America and Europe followed. In 1930 he attended the Berlin Hochschule für Musik under the guidance of Prof. Carl Flesch. Thereafter he continued his solo career while holding the lead posts in Königsberg and Göteborg.\\"

\\"Gimpel immigrated to the United States in 1937. The outbreak of the War brought Gimpel to Los Angeles and to the concertmastership of the Los Angeles Philharmonic. After serving in the U.S. Army from 1942 to the end of the war, Gimpel resumed his solo career in Europe, where he was received, once again, with great acclaim. In 1963, he and Władysław Szpilman formed \\"The Warsaw Piano Quintet\\". His recording of Dvorak's Violin Concerto is considered one of the best interpretations of this concerto.

In 1967 Gimpel accepted a professorship at the University of Connecticut. From 1973 Gimpel was a Professor at the Royal Northern College of Music in Manchester, England. In this period of time he resumed his solo concert appearances in Europe, the United States and South America.
Gimpel died in Los Angeles\\". (History courtesy of Wikipedia)

Wkadyslaw Szpilman wrote a memoir of his survival in the Warsaw Jewish Ghetto and the Holocaust during Hitler's Occupation which was titled \\"The Pianist\\" which led to Roman Polanski's film of the same name. Whatever one may or may not think of Polanski personally, \\"The Pianist\\" was a
poignant, potent, and slicing film like Schindlers List. Can you imagine Gimpel and Szpilman alone on a stage in pre-war concert. Must have been
something else.

If you enjoy Gimpel's playing and that fine Old World sound, then also check out Michael Rabin

In retirement now, I finally have the time to pursue learning about and listening to classical and big band music. It has become a joy for me. When I was small; one side of my family was of Eastern European Jewish Heritage (Poland, Austria, and Bohemia) and I can remember some of their culture - music, food, humor, and stories and of course alot about Hitler and the Holocaust while the other side spoke alot about Pearl Harbor and the War in the Pacific and Big Bands. Add in the depression, and you have an early baby boomer's childhood years.

It's nice to go back and enjoy the music and memories as a reprieve from 2012 and the Obama vs Romney Melodrama as the Middle East continues it's centuries old effort to thwart the Infidels.

Hard to believe that it has been 30 years since George Michael and his days with Wham! had started. Through his highs and lows, he has honestly made some of the most distinctive music in the world that continues to get better with time and age. Something that very few and farther between artists have really learned from him. That is honestly because the songs are still as guilty pleasures in spirit and heart. He showed that in the 80's, ranking high with artists like Michael Jackson and Whitney Houston. But if there is one thing about George is that he is still here, and has made good choices with the way his music captures the heart. While he hasn't made anything new in the past several years, he still show no sign of his music getting old. While he has battled some vices, including being open for accepting that he is gay and a recent turnstyle against pneumonia, he did beat his odds well. Now that he is 30 years into the business, he has a lot to celebrate.

George Michael's 2008 release of Twenty-Five is a consistent reflection of his solo days and his days with his work with Wham!. The collection handles well by bringing in his biggest ballads, as well as his deepest standards that withstood the test of time. Every song has been remastered well, and include hits like Wake Me Up Before You Go Go, Faith, the driven covers like the intimate The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face, to the classic Don't Let The Sun Go Down On Me with Elton John and the overshadowed As with Mary J. Blige. Every song never gets old, but there are a few heavy snubs for the album. The biggest one is I Want Your Sex, as well as I Knew You Were Waiting For Me. While its video is here on this extended set, the song isn't standing alone as a download, as well as his rendition of Somebody To Love with the surviving members of Queen. There are though some songs that make up for that overshadowing like Father Figure, and a intimate contemporary duet of Heal The Pain with Paul McCartney. While there are videos of his classics here, it still could've been more for the songs to stand alone to make it even stronger.

Nevertheless, George Michael's Twenty-Five is still a strong collection of his big hits. If you are honestly new to George Michael, than this would be a good record to buy. While I do wish that it did have more from his days with Wham! like The Edge Of Heaven and Bad Boys to just name a few of there classic songs, still it stands up well. There are fewer artists that are out there right now that still stands out well from the 80's, that are with great music alone. George Michael is only one of a few of them. While he hasn't made anything new in awhile, his classics stand tall just like he has. \\"Don't You Think He Is Looking Older?,\\" as he sang at one point? Not really, he has gotten better with age.

review_headline: Great album for hip-hop and rock fans
review_body:
I'm a guy with a love for both 90's hip hop and 90's-present rock. It is damn hard to find an album that combines the best of both worlds, but this one did it. I can understand why that would make this a tough album to listen to for some people - anti-rap fans who heard What It's Like might be turned off by the more hip-hopish tracks like Get Down and Praise The Lord. Likewise, people who don't like rock probably won't dig tracks like Today and Hot To Death. And then there's the hybrid tracks like Ends that you have to be a fan of both rock and hip-hip to appreciate. I think if you can at least tolerate hip-hop and folk-rock you'll find this is a damn fine album. I've got 6 tracks on here rated 3/5 (good enough to listen to on repeat) or better: Ends, What It's Like, Get Down, Hot To Death, Praise The Lord, and Today.

Overall one of the best albums I've heard for fans whose musical taste drifts between hip-hop and rock. Well worth a listen.

He wears neo-tribal masks (like the one featured on the cover) any time he performs or is photographed. As for the track sounding like an early 90's club hit, this is probably true considering the UK garage genre started at that time. But what we are hearing here is a revivalist style, which has brought 2-step back into the forefront of the underground and mainstream electronic music scenes, much to the pleasure of LOVERS of funky bass lines and easy-to-dance-all-night-to 4x4 beats (like myself) or the chagrin of others (like the previous listener). I don't know how they did that, but the album may have the most physically powerful production sound I've ever heard.  Next you'll notice the musicianship and songwriting, which is incredibly interesting and diverse.  I have to say that the jazzy/bluesy piano on \\"All Aboard\\" gives my heart the melting feeling.  Then, the deepest layer IMO, is the lyrical quality and the uniqueness of Jon Williams as a singer.  The frustration of living in this weird world is perfectly captured in these words.  Again, \\"All Aboard\\" has to be my favorite.  I wish I knew what he was thinking about while writing each of these songs (some may be easier to discern than others), but to me it sounds like a lot of frustration with organized religion and the standards that are forced upon us as individuals...and maybe that's why I connect with this album so much.  Then again, maybe I'm just hearing what i want to hear.  Either way, this record is brilliant.  And they include their \\"Worst of Many Flaws\\" EP in the purchase, so just buy it! What a deal!

Independent artist Craig Smith has been writing and recording his own songs on and off for over 20 years. This is easily his most uncharacteristic release. Influenced in part by some of Steven Wilson's (of Porcupine Tree) solo efforts as well as the creations of Kraftwerk, this album started as a simple experiment with computer software designed to create music based on various loops. \\"Xplztq\\" may have been the first result of those experiments, and unfortunately the only even remotely weak track on an otherwise consistent program. \\"Usurper\\" is very Tangerine Dream-like, even if the artist has never been a fan. \\"Inelegance\\" is my personal favorite, built around a hauntingly perfect electric piano line (and as a result, sounding the least bit \\"electronic\\" of all the tracks contained here).

Modern methods of music sharing inundate us with below par creations from people around the world, which makes it very difficult to find the hidden gems out there that too few will hear. Smith's Electronic Music, Volume I is easily one of those gems. Give it a try and enjoy what we've been given, because recently Smith has suggested that he no longer intends to create Electronic Music, Volume II.

It's hard and pretty pointless to discuss whether this music is Jewish music or not, but they're definitely Jewish songs. All but one of the songs are in Hebrew, most of them incorporating scriptural or liturgical phrases. (The final track, \\"Echad\\", also has some English vocals in counterpoint.) The one song written in English, \\"Bring Gilad Home\\", now (thankfully!) an outdated plea for the release of Gilad Shalit, is the closest to a sad song on the album. Yet the underlying optimism in this song provides a good example of the joy and faith that Yerachmiel puts into his music and his singing. Many of the songs on the CD would (and probably do) keep wedding guests dancing. Indeed, tracks 2 and 7 provide original melodies or arrangements for the quintessential Jewish wedding lyric.
I've had the pleasure to experience Yerachmiel performing live. And although naturally nothing can capture the atmosphere of being there, I'm happy I own this CD. True to its title, \\"In The Hands of Heaven\\" ranges from being comforting to inspiring.

Umskiptar, the tenth full-length album by Burzum, Varg Vikernes' one man band, is nothing less than an atmospheric triumph. Vikernes sets the sixty-six stanzas of Voluspa, the opening poem of the Norse Poetic Edda, to the unmistakable soundscapes of Burzum. It works. Reading through English translations of Voluspa by Vikernes in his book Sorcery and Religion in Ancient Scandinavia, as well as a translation by Carolyne Larrington (Oxford World's Classics), the music and words complement each other power for power.

The music is pure Burzum, full of chainsaw guitars, repeated motifs in the songs, and full, epic sweep. Changes in dynamics, such as the solo piano in Alfadanz and the pounding drums that open the album, break things up without jarring the listener or detracting from the atmospheric spell that Vikernes weaves.

Vikernes' voice is no longer the pained, angry yowl of his youth; nevertheless, it is quite expressive and suits the mood of the music and words well. His voice takes on different roles. At times, he sounds like a grizzled chieftain relating the tale. In some places, he sounds like a poet. On Valgaldr, he sounds downright otherworldly.

Umskiptar is the fourth Burzum album to be released in just over two years. Vikernes maintains a standard of high quality. Umskiptar is to be savored from beginning to end; it is a rewarding experience. Recommended.

Old Crow Medicine Show's hiatus didn't last long: announcing the break around August 2011 only for it to be concluded by December 2011. The hiatus came with change though -- founding member Willie Watson and mandolist Cory Younts parted ways with the band, and founding member Chris Fuqua rejoined for recording. Even though the member lineup may have changed, the band's sound for CARRY ME BACK stayed largely the same (Willie is featured on many of these tracks).

Marked with stand-up bass, fiddles, mandolins, and acoustic guitars, Old Crow Medicine Show has a very old-timey sound. The band pulls the sound off well, pleasing both fans of folk and bluegrass. Opening and title track \\"Carry Me Back\\" is a brisk, bluegrass tune that is both a great way to start the album and good message-statement to the world. The album follows the pace set by this title track: CARRY ME BACK stays upbeat, and its brisk pace makes the album over before you even know it. That's not too say the album feels too brief (the album is 37:01) -- it just feels like a bunch of friends having a good time. When the band slows its pacing for a few songs, it's to good effect (\\"Genevieve\\" and \\"Ways of Man.\\") While the band feels somewhat anachronistic in the modern day, they do a good job sounding like authentic pre-World War II musicians.

CARRY ME BACK will please both newcomers to the band and longtime listeners. Fans of the folk-based sides of Mumford and Sons, Trampled by Turtles, and the Avett Brothers might enjoy what Old Crow Medicine Show has to offer. This album also marks a good place to start listening to the band -- even though the music is very niche, it's very accessible. However, if you weren't convinced by the band's past work, this album won't change your mind. Standout tracks to sample/download: \\"Carry Me Back,\\" \\"We Don't Grow Tobacco,\\" and \\"Genevieve.\\" Although past efforts might be a bit more consistent (like O.C.M.S.), CARRY ME BACK is a great entry to the band's discography.to the band's discography.

Never been shy about spreading word on an artist or album I dig. Big fan of Johnny Dowd. Word is he cut his 1st record at the tender age of 50. But one listen to his raw, gut-bucket debut, Wrong Side of Memphis & you know he's been making racket for a lifetime...With a life time to go...

The more polished Pictures of Life's Other Side, has long been a classic on my shelf. A mad gumbo of Hank Williams & Kurt Weill...Sam Shephard & Noir's Jim Thompson...Surf Rock & Captain Beefheart...Springsteen & Waits...David Lynch & Gabby Hayes armed with a chainsaw...

In short, an original...A \\"maverick\\"...

But there's something going on with his latest, No Regrets that kinda floored me. No one meets a grisly end, but there are plenty of ghosts. Every track is a different woman's name. The whole thing plays like a farewell glance in your little Black Book before jumping off the bridge. Or moving on...

But who knew stalking the ghosts of girlfriends past could be so Funky? So Rockin'?

High school sweethearts, blind dates, broken marriages & one night stands...\\"Betty\\" kicks things off like a twisted take on Waits' \\"Martha\\"...A drunken call to his old high school flame to finally get back his red leather high school jacket since their pledge of eternal love didn't quite work out. Heck she doesn't even have to mail it, he'll stop by.

\\"Sherry\\" may be the \\"bedroom missionary\\" and \\"Susan\\" the \\"stripper from Atlanta\\" but maybe the heart of it all can be found in \\"Billie\\":

\\"Days of envy/ days of greed
Come into my kitchen/ watch my vultures feed\\"...

\\"Billie's on a holiday/ all she had she gave..\\"

\\"The Day's new/ the Story's old\\"

That said, leave it to \\"Abigail\\" to lend bitter irony to the album title...

While Dowd's output's been labeled \\"Alt Country\\", truth is it can't be pinned down. Especially with this one. JJ Cale meets Beck? Beefheart duking it out with the Velvet Underground? W.C. Fields backed by a pissed off Booker T & The MG's? Throw in some twisted Lounge and a tortured sax solo that would make Ornette Coleman blush & ya sort of get the picture.

A warm and engaging performer, Tom Kell has a smooth, mellow voice that suits his brand of low-key, California country rock.  Unfortunately, on this album he just doesn't have the songs to put him in the same lofty pantheon as his 70's idols.  The tunes are bland and shapeless, without noteworthy lyrics or memorable melodies.  Kell's characteristic, polished, enjoyable sound is in place, but the songs just aren't interesting.  Clicking through the album, is less like a walk past the tall, regal palm trees of Santa Monica Boulevard and more like a stroll down a cookie cutter cul de sac in some nondescript section of the Valley.  Instead of a zinfandel; sliced cheese; sesame cracker; and chicken salad spread, Kell gives us Sprite, mushy white bread, and a baloney sandwich.  This disk is a notch down from Kell's previous albums.  Let's hope that Kell's muse returns for his next foray and someday he cuts that classic paean to LA that brings him the attention of a wider audience.

review_headline: An interesting step between Percect Pitch Black and White Silence
review_body:
Cave In is a unique band. My first listening experience with them was when Antenna came out back in 2003. I had no idea they were a metal outfit back in the late 90s. I just thought it was a solid rock album and never really looked into the band again until earlier this year. I bought Until Your Heart Stops (which was a little jarring for my ears after hearing Antenna first) and have been playing catch up ever since.

This is an interesting little EP. It consists of 4 tracks. Two are of the hardcore nature (\\"The Red Trail\\" especially and \\"Cayman Tongue\\") with heavy guitars and the screaming and whatnot and the other two (\\"Air Escapes\\" and \\"Retina Sees Rewind\\") have more of an upbeat punk feel to them. All 4 tracks are great. It's hard to pick a favorite. I would say \\"Cayman Tongue\\", but I find the weird, spacey interlude kind of annoying and I think it breaks up the flow of the song. If it would have been an actual instrumental break instead of a bunch of random noises and effects, it would have stood above the rest of the pack.

A strong EP for Cave In. I'd recommend it for anyone that likes Perfect Pitch Black and White Silence.

Yes, I'm a little late to the (tea) party -- it was only a few weeks ago that I finally got around to watching Tim Burton's "Alice in Wonderland."

What I thought of the movie is a story for another day, but something caught my attention as the end credits finally began to roll. That would be "Alice," a song by Avril Lavigne that she wrote just for the movie... and as much as I wanted to like it, the wailing vocals and generic lyrics meant that I spent most of the song wishing IT would fall down a hole.

Lyrically, the song is strangely generic. There's only one specific mention of anything "Alice in Wonderland"-related, and it flits by so fast that you barely notice it. In fact, it's hard to even tell if the mention of "Wonderland" was in there originally, or if Lavigne just took a typical teen angst song and replaced a single line.

Instead, the song is crammed with cliches like "I can't stop it now," "get back on my feet," "I'll survive," and "I'll take a stand until the end" -- almost nothing actually applies to Alice, despite the song supposedly being about her.

It's doubly tragic because it's such a BLAND song. Wonderland is a colorful, insane, terrifying place, and you would think that Lavigne's single would convey at least a little of that. It has no texture, no evocation, no descriptions that make anything pop in your imagination -- it just has a choppy list of complaints and observations ("Trippin' out/spinnin' around/I'm underground, I fell down/ Yeah, I fell down").

Also, the song is shrill. VERY shrill. Lavigne spends much of the song wailing and screaming "AAAAAYYAAAYYYYYYAYYYY, I'll get BYYYYYYYYY!/AAAAAYYAAAYYYYYYAYYYY, I'll SUR-VIIIIIIIIIVE!". It might have worked if she had sung it softly... but instead she tries to imitate Amy Lee. Trying to belt out the high notes highlights every vocal limitation and deficiency that Lavigne's voice has.

The best part of this whole mess is easily is the dark, heavy piano melody, which does convey a feeling of apprehensive dread. But sadly, even that is flawed -- whoever is playing the piano is thumping too hard on the keys, which robs it of any subtlety or delicacy.

The music is... tolerable. But the lyrics and vocals of "Alice" are a bland, screeching disaster that left me with blood pouring from my ears. Don't you try to stop me, I won't cry.Lavigne's voice has.

I've been a Scandal fan since BEST * SCANDAL (their major label debut), and I own all the import albums and even managed to see them live at Budokan (amazing show!). This, their second major label album and first of all-new material, is the perfect mix of \\"new\\" and \\"old\\" Scandal, and has a ton of great songs on it.

A lot of old-school Scandal fans like me think there's just something cool about these four Japanese high school girls playing hard rock music. Well, by Temptation Box they had \\"graduated\\" into the real world but they still stayed basically true to their roots. Their music and look reflects that on this album, although the compositions (written by others for them, as is the norm for female rock bands in Japan) had definitely become a bit poppier already than those on BEST * SCANDAL.

Still, the combination of these somewhat poppier compositions mixed with the raw appeal of their early years led to some of their classic live show staples like \\"Everybody Say Yeah!\\" and \\"Aitai\\", some cute new musical styles like \\"Shojo M\\" and \\"Namida no Regret\\" (their first ballad) while still allowing them to just flat-out rock on tracks like \\"Shunkan Sentimental\\". Their improved musicianship also shows through on this album on tracks like \\"Hi Hi Hi\\", where Tomomi shows off her Red Hot Chili Peppers-inspired slapping technique.

It's saying something that despite another all-original album in the meantime, when I saw them at Budokan in 2012, they opened with \\"Shunkan Sentimental\\" and \\"Everybody Say Yeah!\\" from Temptation Box.

Honestly, if you're new to Scandal and trying to decide which album to start with, it really should be this one. product_title: Beethoven: Piano Sonata, Op.111 / Schumann: Symphonic Etudes, Op.13; Toccata Op.7 / Chopin: Nocturne Op.55/2; Etudes Op.10 Nos.8 & 10, Op.25 No.6
review_body:
I bought this album primarily for Pogorelich's Op. 111: He has (or had) plenty of power; a lot of energy and volume where necessary, but you always feel there's a good deal in reserve. He also has a fantastic control over touch and dynamics. He uses the latter, especially, to good effect in this recording.

The first movement is given all the weight and attention it deserves, which is not always the case in other recordings. Very strong, very thought out, very precise. Maybe the precision goes a bit beyond the point where it impairs spontaneity, and maybe there's such a thing as too much clarity in this music. But it's hard to complain.

He does just about everything right in the second movement as well, starting off slower than many or most -- though it works well here. The fast \\"boogie-woogie\\" variation is played for all it's worth, without smearing the rhythm at any point (rare). After that, things proceed as usual, and the accuracy of the various trills, double trills, etc., is something to hear. Bravo!

Was not very familiar with the Schumann Symphonic Studies. Sounds like Robert was somewhat inspired by the Diabelli's, and he did a nice job of it. The Chopin pieces were more familiar. All are played with great control and a virtuosity that is always at the service of the musical conception.

The piano and recording are second to none. Easy five stars. Be sure to buy the re-issue, as the original lacks the Chopin.

review_headline: an original Broadway cast recording that will never be outdated
review_body:
One listen to this original Broadway cast recording of My Fair Lady and you'll know why this music still sells. These recordings, here as MP3 files for download, sound fresh, clear and crisp. There is no background noise! Moreover, the songs by Lerner and Loewe are brilliantly composed and the lyrics are clever, witty and poignant.

The track set opens with the overture to the musical stage play and then goes right into the first song entitled \\"Why Can't the English?\\" \\"Why Can't the English\\" fleshes out Rex Harrison's character's (Henry Higgins) lament that too many British people don't speak English well. The melody is catchy and the lyrics are funny at times, too.

The lesser educated British have their say in the next number, \\"Wouldn't It Be Loverly.\\" In this song, sung by Julie Andrews as Eliza Doolittle with male backup singers and a chorus of whistlers, demonstrates how these persons really do want to lead a much more sophisticated life with more luxuries.

Other great songs include the rousing \\"Get Me To The Church On Time\\" sung by the memorable Stanley Holloway with backup; the beautiful love ballad \\"On The Street Where You Live\\" performed by John Michael King; \\"I Could Have Danced All Night\\" which is performed flawlessly by Julie Andrews who belts out those incredibly high notes; and \\"The Rain In Spain\\" delivered by Julie Andrews, Rex Harrison and Robert Coote with a chorus. Excellent!

One especially amusing song is entitled \\"A Hymn to Him\\" performed mostly by Rex Harrison with some assistance from Robert Coote. The violins at the beginning of this number are beautiful in the musical arrangement.

\\"I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face\\" couldn't have been performed any better than what we get here from Rex Harrison. The violins play so sweetly and then the orchestra fleshes out the ending music flawlessly--so don't be surprised if you get the urge to download all these MP3 files and play them over and over again.

The musical arrangements are carefully planned and executed throughout; only Lerner and Loewe were capable of producing such a fine score to go with this stage play. Rex Harrison (mostly) sings his songs while in the London production Rex mixed singing and actual talking during his key musical numbers.

We even get 2 bonus tracks: There is commentary from Rex Harrison, Julie Andrews, Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe.

The music and lyrics to the original Broadway cast recording of My Fair Lady are superb. Even today, more than 5 decades later, the soundtrack still sells well; My Fair Lady will remain a classic musical. May you enjoy this soundtrack as much as I did!n.

review_headline: Another offbeat song from Peggy Lee
review_body:
Sometimes wrongly credited to Nina Simone, Willard Robison wrote this cynically humorous song about the end of a marriage. He was a bandleader from Missouri, performing in the late 1920's and early 30's. No one else wrote songs like Willard Robison. He came to be more famous for another of his songs about broken love and a lost marriage. His \\"A Cottage for Sale\\" was recorded by a who's who of the music world, with basically the same theme of a broken marriage. When she sings the lyric, Peggy Lee captures the humor as well as the sorrow in the lyric. I'm leaving you, Don't look for me and Don't smoke in bed.

Corrected update: Well, it's not hard to understand why there is so much confusion about who wrote this song. While Robison came up with the original idea for the music and lyric of the song, according to Peggy Lee in an interview with Mark Steyn and claims on her tribute website, Robison was unable to finish the song so she and Dave Barbour had to finish the lyric and orchestrate the music. She gave sole writing credit to Robison out of the goodness of her heart. This is the original version of the song and the best in my opinion.

Christophe Willem has a terrific voice, and his song writing skills transcend the genre.  \\"Starlite\\" is a high energy song that flaunts dance music influences from the 70s through the 00's.  \\"Cool\\", perhaps the album's highlight with its pounding synth bass and \\"ooh-ooh-ooh\\" chorus, is the coolest pop song you've never heard.  Romantic themes vibrate throughout the album.  Christophe sings mostly in French, but some songs mix both English and French lyrics, which makes you realize just how cool it would be to be bilingual!

I have to admit that sometimes it's hard to write about music. Not only is it difficult to put the right words that have concrete meaning to something that exists in an abstract and tangible way, but I often run out of adjectives to describe particular sounds, attempting not to stay repetitive in my observations. There is only so much I can say about \\"ambient\\" and \\"drone\\" and \\"noise\\" and \\"experimental\\". Often, after re-reading my write ups from years ago, words like \\"lush\\", \\"somber\\", and \\"textured\\", begin to lose all of their meaning, drowning in sounds which swallow the void. Thankfully there is always the music itself, which does a much better job at convincing the listener of its value. The only thing that's left for me to do is to guide you towards the source. Here... listen to this...

Attilio Novellino produces experimental soundscapes, that drone out the noise in lush ambient textures. The somber tones are enriched with distortion and swell beyond the horizon until they recede like dark waters after the storm. Elements of white noise are also present throughout the frequency rich pads, which swirl in the ocean of motionless layers. Exploring the boundaries between melody, dissonance and noise, Novellino incorporates electronics, guitar, piano and field recordings to build up the foundation of his atmospheric work.

Through Glass is only a second full length release for the Italian \\"soundartist\\", Attilio Novellino. His debut album, Anonymous Said (Inglorious Ocean, 2009) was recorded under a curious moniker, Un Vortice Di Bassa Pressione (tr. A Vortex Of Low Pressure). The production on Through Glass is very mature, rich, and clean (even though noise is the predominant element in the composition). This music will absolutely appeal to fans of Tim Hecker, Fennesz, Stephan Mathieu, Ben Frost and Lawrence English. This is another win for Alexandr Vatagin`s Valeot Records which continues to steadily release quality material and satisfy my cravings...gs...

product_title: Schuricht - Brahms: Tragic Overture - Reger: Variations & Fugue on a Theme of J.A. Hiller - Beethoven: Grosse Fuge
review_headline: Two veterans in old age recall the ethos of  German romanticism that nurtured them
review_body:
Here's an unusual, and not very marketable, pairing of two conductors. The Brahms Tragic Over. and Max Reger's Hiller Variations - one of the few orchestral pieces that this post-Brahmsian conservative once survived by - are conducted by Carl Shcuricht from a January, 1964 concert with the London Sym.; the aged Schuricht was 84 at the time. The orchestration of Beethoven's Grosse Fuge is under Adrian Boult with the Philhamronia (briefly rechristened the New Philharmonia) in August, 1968, when he was 79. So it's two old masters giving their late thoughts on the Austro-German tradition. With all due respect, one wonders sadly if anyone is really interested?

Schuricht belongs in a class of thoroughly assured German traditionalists like Joseph Keilberth (who unfortunately did not survive past sixty), not to be classed among the greats but capable of very fine performances. This Tragic Over. isn't remarkable but is so confident and echt-Brahmsian that one would be hard-pressed to find its equal today. There's not enough drive or intensity to make it truly memorable, however. Better is the Reger (he was Schuricht's teacher), a work rarely played today that is reminiscent in its high spirits of the youthful Brahms's two Serenades, not a bad recommendation. An astute online reviewer points to a resemblance with Weinberger's 'Schwanda the Bagpiper,' once a staple of classical pops concerts. There are eleven variations with a big (9 min.!) fugue to cap the proceedings, and Schuricht so believes in this music that he imparts a good deal of vibrancy to it. A score that could come off as more Teutonic than jolly is quite rollicking, even if the overlong fugue almost deflates the souffle.

The fugal form is the rationale, no doubt, for including the Grosse fuge, but I've never really bought the various orchestral transcriptions, because this grueling finale to Beethoven's Quartet Op. 133 is so demanding that four string players are hard-pressed to keep it sounding coherent, in tune, and even playable. It is one of Beethoven's most peculiar and in its way awe-inspiring creations. Perhaps for reasons of scale his titanic conception needs to break the bounds of chamber music, yet hearing an entire string orchestra attempt the nearly impossible has its own hazards. the issue is moot given that Boult's reading comes in remote Albert Hall sound that is also muffled. Bernstein's DG reading is more intense, yet in a way Boult's relatively relaxed, no-pressure approach is easier to absorb - if only it sounded better.

As a memento of a lost age of conducting this odd CD is welcome. I enjoyed every performance, especially the Reger.ounding coherent, in tune, and even playable. review_headline: Smart and mellow, a great debut album
review_body: I loved this album!  It's very smart, mellow, comfortable, romantic and lovely to listen to.  \\"Nighthawks\\" sets the tone, a quest for something indefinable...love? peace? solace? reaching for something that is never obtainable, the ever-searching human condition perhaps.  The most beautiful song is \\"Skin,\\" a love song we all wish was about us.  There's irony, intellectual honesty, and a strong country flavor in \\"Sleepless 'Til Dawn.\\"  Musical tributes to traditional genres and styles in \\"Stuck Blues\\" and \\"Streets of Temptation\\" are varied and fun to hear. It's hard to categorize this album, because its influences are eclectic with a Dylan influence certainly, but there's lots more than that. In short, an excellent debut album from a very talented singer/songwriter.  I can't wait to hear more from Michael Weiskopf.  But meanwhile, I'll be listening happily to INSOMNIA.  BRAVO!

Overall, ZBB sticks to the formula which has made them successful the past few years with tight harmonies and super polished sound...But they continue to push the concept of what defines them and it works just as well this time around. Great summer addition to your playlist.

As a side note, I'm constantly amazed how Amazon can offer new releases at such affordable prices. Kudos to them for providing an alternative we all can afford.

product_title: Otmar Binder Trio feat. BJ Cole & Christian Dozzler - Boogie Woogie Turnaround
review_headline: The Flavors of Yesterday Served  Up Hot!
review_body:
Boogie-Woogie is more than just a strange name it is an American Icon. Get ready for time travel! Otmar Binder, an Austrian piano player who served as accompanist for many singers and actors, holds on to memories of his favorite music from childhood - boogie-woogie - and here joins with BJ Cole and Christian Dozzler who form the Otto Binder Trio. This album is completely devoted to boogie-woogie music and it not only stirs memories on another time, it also stirs the soul.
For those who are unfamiliar with the history of boogie-woogie, the following is offered to instruct: `Boogie-woogie is a style of piano-based blues that became popular in the late 1930s and early 1940s, but originated much earlier, and was extended from piano, to three pianos at once, guitar, big band, and country and western music, and even gospel. While the blues traditionally depicts a variety of emotions, boogie-woogie is mainly associated with dancing. The lyrics of one of the earliest hits, \\"Pinetop's Boogie Woogie\\", consist entirely of instructions to dancers:

`Now, when I tell you to hold yourself, don't you move a peg. And when I tell you to get it, I want you to Boogie Woogie!'

Boogie-Woogie is characterized by a regular bass figure, in the left hand. The bass figure is transposed according to the chord changes. The earliest documented inquiries into the geographical origin of boogie-woogie occurred in the late 1930s when oral histories from the oldest living Americans of both African and European descent, revealed a broad consensus that boogie-woogie piano was first played in Texas in the early 1870s. Additional citations place the origins of boogie-woogie in the Piney Woods of northeast Texas. \\"The first Negroes who played what is called boogie-woogie, or house-rent music, and attracted attention in city slums where other Negroes held jam sessions, were from Texas. And all the Old-time Texans, black or white, are agreed that boogie piano players were first heard in the lumber and turpentine camps, where nobody was at home at all. The style dates from the early 1870s.\\"

Now, history lesson complete, settle back and be dazzled by the artistry displayed by these phenomenal musicians. There are 17 tracks, variously penned by Binder, Cole and Dozzler and there isn't a weak track among them. Hearing the piano played in this manner brings a new appreciation to the technical skills this music form demands. This is a classy recording with some of history's greatest proponents of a style of music that, thanks to them, will never be forgotten.
