review_headline: The Obstruent Unification of One's Pursuit to Our Shadow Self.
review_body: Ms Black's follow up song to \\"my moment\\" is intriguing in many more ways than her preceding musical prowess. Lets break it down shall we.  When you talk, I listen, I like that  When you listen, I smile and I like that  Why you lookin', lookin' at me just like that?  I like that  I like that  This would be a disposition of the unconscious battle with an undeveloped psychoanalytic archetype screaming to get out. The representative of \\"that wholeness which the introspective philosophy of all times has characterized with an inexhaustible variety of symbols, names and concepts\\". As far as Jungian Psychology goes \\"the archetype is the introspectively recognizable form of a priori psychic orderliness\\". Of course she likes it, it reinforces the conscious mind while suppressing the shadow self. She claim's to be \\"listening\\" when in fact she ignoring the true self. Ms. Black of course realizes this is part of the journey and embraces the conscious mind in order to truly understand the unconscious.  There's a crime scene on the dance floor  Ring the alarm  Police tape on the front door  And you are  Well now we see her regrets and thoughts as she believes them to be a crime. While the crime is a metaphor it is great one for the journey she is taking. The alarm has been rung, the crime is in evidence due to the use of the \\"police tape\\". Here lies the regrets of undeveloped recognition unconscious mind. The first part of the journey is to accept the true self; not the ego but truth that lies within the unconscious, thus the use of the lyric \\"are you there?\\".   Tabula rasa is the epistemological theory that individuals are born without built-in mental content and that their knowledge comes from experience and perception. Mrs Black has recognized the shallowness of this theory; one's personality, social emotional behavior and intelligence are not begun as a blank slate but there are some forms of genetic predispositions with in the conscious and unconscious. Much like Plato's Theory of Recollection explains that we possess some non-empirical knowledge (e.g. The Form of Equality) at birth our environment can shape our ego and unconscious thoughts but it would be crime to only accept the nurture vs nature side of psychological development as so many of done throughout history.  A person of interest  A person of interest  Can't say I'm love yet, but certainly impressed  You are a person of interest  A person of interest  Can't say that it's love yet, but somebody's obsessed  Here Ms. Black has realized the fault many human beings collide with into whilst seeking a partner. One can be impressed by their partner but it usually due to their own lack of knowledge of true self. They are using the other person to fill the void and shortcomings they have within the unconscious this can then lead to an obsession with the partner. Only knowing thy true self will break this obsession thus becomes the journey to Enantiodromia, \\"Everything arises in this way, opposites from their opposites.\\"  When we're dancing real close, think I like ya  But when the lights go down low, I can't find ya  Now, I can't get you outta my mind, yeah  It's a crime, yeah  This is the most powerful verse within the song it self. As she approaches assimilation with the shadow self she finds, as the majority of people do, that the closer you get to the merger with shadow self the more difficult it becomes to truly find a it, a paradoxical psychiatric trick our mind plays within itself. The crime lives within this void as to not recognize will effectively end in one's own demise and ultimately psychosis.   There's a chalk line on the dance floor  In the shape of my heart  Crime scene tape on the front door  And you are  The chalk line represents the paradoxical problem of the shadow. The dance floor of course represents the eloquent movement one has when following the road to the destination of the true self. The line is drawn; however, Ms Black ingeniously describes it as a heart.Love thyself. Only then can one truly find a journey that is meaningful with regards to relationships with others.  Can't deny, implicated  In the mayhem, in my mind  What has got me so frustrated  You should be mine, you should be mine  Ms Black now can't deny the importance of the merger with the shadow self. Our whole life we fight against it only to lose every time. By fully embracing it makes assimilation possible. Every descent is followed by an ascent and it is only then that one can lose the capitulation of the fight with the shadow self. Here Ms. Black has reflected upon need of another individual to find individuation and sees the answer has been lying within the whole time. The 'you' she is referring to in this aspect is a fantastic use of metaphorical language and irony.   Ms. Black you've done it again and continue to warn us of our psychological processes involve a life time of learning. As many Jungians have described it - 'acknowledgement of the shadow must be a continuous process throughout one's life and 'the later stages of shadow integration' will continue to take place - the grim 'process of washing one's dirty linen in private'        Now begins her journey.

I read somewhere that Nancy Kaye's new album, \\In The Light\\", had been motivated by a love of David Bowie. There's certainly a hint of the Thin White Duke's vocal style to be heard, though perhaps it's his talent for reinvention that has most inspired the recording. Kaye launched her music career as `Rosey', and quickly signed to Island/Def Jam. Her 2002 debut \\"Dirty Child,' earned her the title \\"The Lovechild of Robert Plant and Rickie Lee Jones\\" by Entertainment Weekly and other reviewers were universally positive. She featured on the Bridget Jones' Diary soundtrack, toured with Melissa Etheridge and Morcheeba, and released a jazz album in 2008 called \\"Luckiest Girl\\".

In 2009 she released Lal Meri, named after her band, and founded the Creek Kin music collective, which brings us back to \\"In The Light\\". Released in February 2012, its mix of psychedelic folk and soulful pop sounds utterly contemporary, though obviously informed by pre-glam Bowie, and female singers such as Zoe Pollock and Grace Slick. It works so well because Kaye is adept at mixing those old-school influences with modern techniques. For example, take the scattergun percussion of \\"Still\\", the big pop production of \\"Dream Journal\\" or the head-down beats of \\"Time\\". Best of all, the haunting \\"Keep Falling\\" and the CSN referencing \\"Cut My Hair\\" - you don't get to hear acid banjo everyday.

review_body:
Ike Moriz - Still EP (Mosquito Records London)
Ike Moriz' latest release is a five-track EP comprising of the title track, taken from his \\"Breathing Dreams\\" album, a new song called \\"Angie Blue\\", together with German versions of those two songs, and another of \\"Not About You\\", also originally on the \\"Breathing Dreams\\" LP. The South African singer-songwriter is no stranger to performances in languages other than English, having previously sung and recorded in Spanish and French, though these songs mark his debut in German.

\\"Still\\" was one of the standout tracks from the fore mentioned long-player, so makes an ideal single. Its lilting rhythm and punchy chorus seem tailor made for grown-up AOR radio. The extremely catchy \\"Angie Blue\\", with its glammy sunshine vibe and sing-a-long lyrics, equals it. Again, radio surely beckons. Of the German versions, it's difficult to single any track out - I don't speak or understand the language. I can say that Moriz' approach is chock-full of confidence and vocally he nails them, in much the same way he usually does.

My only complaint is that it's over so soon.

Favorite tracks are P8 - Fragments or POS - Gravity. Andrew Bayer is a audio genius and this compilation will introduce you to his sound.

The Dirty South remix at the end of the second disc is kind of out of place...it's a rather poppy selection that does not match up well with the sound of the rest of the compilation. Minor gripe though because it's just one track.

Also, if you're into this kind of progressive sound there are several great free podcast out there to check out such as Jaytech Music, Silk Royal Showcase, Adam Beyer's DRUMCODE, and of course Above & Beyond Trance Around the World.

product_title: Staring Down the Path of Sound
review_body:
I was fortunate to have the opportunity to watch and listen to this album take shape over the past year. The end result is absolutely brilliant and well worth the wait! The album comes out strong with the single, Fall and its infectious guitar riffs and potent vocals. The album continues to develop into a story that seems to reflect cautious optimism through an overall narrative of struggle and confusion. Background vocals by former Messenger's member Lauren Faye complement the dreamy soundscape created by Kolbeck's guitar and Sobel's deep, soulful voice, particularly on the second half of the album. The addition of keys on this record adds another layer to key tracks, particularly Illuminate and Thaynara, giving the album a well-developed feel compared to some of the band's earlier work.

This is a record that is truly best absorbed as a single experience, with enough time and space to allow the music to permeate into the listener's heart. After experiencing the creation in its entirety a couple of times, key songs for cranking up the volume include Fall, Low, Resurrect Me, Anyone But You, and Bang Your Hands. For quieter, yet equally powerful experiences, take the time to experience Blue Always, Alvea, and Everything You Want It To Be in a quiet setting or with headphones on. The latter is destined for a movie soundtrack for sure. It's only a matter of time.

My review reprinted from [...] - October 27, 2011    Releasing the CD for full streaming and digital download purchase through their Bandcamp site at the same time that they officially announced it, XP8 gave this reviewer slightly more than 24 hours to listen to it and formulate a review... I needed about 10 minutes to know that I was listening to something special. And by the end, I had only one thought... this is amazing. I don't say that easily about an entire CD. A track here and there, yes, but this entire CD held my attention from beginning to end... and then over and over. A friend asked me \\"Who does it sound like?\\" and I could not think of any answer except \\"No one you are hearing on the floors right now... but you will be hearing a lot of bands who sound like XP8 from now on.\\" This CD is a game changer. With a nod to the great bands of the EBM and early futurepop years, it evokes a nostalgia while still looking ahead.    With the opening track, \\"Bullet Hole\\", you know that this band has hit its stride as a dance floor powerhouse. As the computer voice says \\"XP8 Two Thousand and Eleven\\", it's their year. This song will be played for years to come and it will pack the floors every time. The track that follows \\"Burning Down\\" is my personal favorite. It is also the track that has been chosen to have a video made for it by the same guys who did the video for \\"The Art of Revenge\\" a few years back. I can't wait to see what they come up with for this track! The beat does not let up for the next two tracks, \\"Fragility\\" which has a driving beat from the start and a different tone to the lyrics, and \\"Wake Up!\\", a track that has what could have been a floor-clearing nearly 40 second break in the middle, but the underbeat and the vocals make it an interesting, intensity building interlude that should not send the crowd looking for a drink!    \\"Trip\\" has a guest vocalist, Stewart Who?, a legend in the hard house scene. He and Wayne G recorded the track \\"Twisted\\" which went 5x platinum at the end of the 90s. XP8s remix of that track helped bring about the collaboration on this track. The lyrics are funny, cutting and timely and display a departure from the cliché lyrics that have been the norm in the industrial scene. This track has samples in it and it makes you realize how few samples have been used in the previous songs. Many bands have come to rely on movie samples to make the songs interesting, and the end result has been uninteresting music coupled with cliché samples. That is not the case with this song, and it has the potential to be a crossover hit into the house scene.    \\"Decadence\\" is another track dying to be played on a club sound system and of all the new material has the most re-mix potential. This is not to say there is anything wrong with the original track, but I can hear many opportunities in it for re-interpretation, harder, ethereal, trance, it could go in many directions. \\"The Wound That Won't Heal\\" completes the set of 7 new tracks on this CD and is haunting and very different. Although I am unsure of how it would play on a dance floor it provides a change of atmosphere to the CD that can be lacking on a lot of dance oriented releases. But X = 10 as any good Roman would know (and Marco is certainly a good Roman!) so the CD is rounded out with 3 brand new remixes of their biggest club hits to date.    Aesthetic Perfection (who have their own eagerly awaited release on the horizon) does the honors on \\"Muv Your Dolly\\" and I am sure we will see the return of this classic track to the clubs via this remix. My favorite new remix is \\"The Art of Revenge\\" reworked by Autodafeh (those Swedes know their electronic music...) a very catchy and danceable remix of a song that has always been a standout for any XP8 fan. And probably one of the most well-known tracks gets re-imagined by Vanity Police (Tom Napack), it is definitely a departure from the remixes and the original, but still delivers a dance floor punch. These remixes are surprisingly minimal and that serves to prove that a club hit does not need to be loaded with sounds to work.    This entire CD was mastered by Kolje Trelle, of Soman. He is an expert and it shows in the perfectly balanced sound of this CD. I think \\"balanced\\" is a good word to sum up this entire CD... a blend of old and new, that leaves you wanting more, but also extremely satisfied with what you have heard. If this is the result of a Decade of Decadence, may the party continue for another 10 years.

The 77s output has gotten more and more sparse over the years and one can't help but feel it is because of a lack of ideas.  Mike Roe admitted to a long period of writers block and drummer Bruce Spencer has had massive influence on both the best 77s and Roe solo music since he joined the band.  In all of his side projects, Roe mostly plays other people's songs, albeit with skill and flare.  His solo projects have become noodley acoustic guitar singer/song writer affairs that start sounding samey real quick.  And the last 77s album (delivered 7 years after their previous proper album) was 10 cover songs with just one original track tacked on the end.    Which makes the couple of EPs they put out (EP and Direct) real treats.  Therein, the 7s are able to muster up just enough inspiration to make short, solid offerings of excellent quality.  On 2002's Direct, The boys whip out a handful of mid-tempo indie rock numbers that create an enjoyable and coherent musical statement.  Even when there is an edgy guitar riff, as in the opening rocker \\"Born on Separate Days,\\" there is a mellow moodiness that pervades the album. \\"Perfect\\" starts slow and builds up on buried acoustic guitar strumming and wah-wah leads, lifting up Roe's pleading ad libs.  \\"Dig My Heels\\" is an album highlight - a skilled acoustic rock track that would fit in perfectly between Mellancamp and Petty on your local classic rock station.  \\"Lifeline\\" is a pleasant love song with long instrumental passages, but the album ends with the fantastic \\"Take Your Mind Off It.\\"  After a clever false start, it gets going with a smooth countrified groove and sing song vocals.  There are several passages of wonderful Mike Roe lead guitar and it ends the undertaking with that same mellow indie rock feeling that permeates the album.      The only misstep on this EP is the inclusion of the Solo Roe sounding \\"Rosebud.\\"  While better than much of his latter day solo tracks, it's out of place here and throws off the momentum.  Thankfully it is a short, slight song that usually ends before the need to skip to the next track.    This EP is proof that when The 77's can get enough original ideas together, the result is some amazing guitar driven rock.  The thoughtful arrangement and accomplished instrumental interplay give each song a unique character.  That Direct also has a distinct personality as a whole, is further proof that the talent and vision are there, even if it takes a lot of work.      For fans of the 77's, this a must have.  Also recommended for anyone who likes rock, indie rock or talented musicianship.

review_headline: One of the best releases of 2011
review_body: Georgia's late songwriting hero Vic Chesnutt made a lot of friends in the Twin Cities music scene early in his career, going back to his debut at the Uptown Bar when Soul Asylum's Danny Murphy introduced him by brazenly telling the crowd to \\"shut up and listen.\\" Right up to the end, Chesnutt had a large contingent of fans among our songwriters-over-singers-loving scene. That much is proven by the impressive turnout for the much buzzed-about compilation featuring Vic Chesnutt classics performed by Dan Wilson, Haley Bonar, Trampled by Turtles' Dave Simonett, Charlie Parr, Ben Weaver, Wendy Lewis, JoAnna James, Alpha Consumer, Luke Redfield and more. Dave Simonett kicks off the album with \\"Gravity of the Situation,\\" a had-me-at-hello type of introduction.     One of the compilation's highlights, \\"Soft Picasso\\" is performed by Minnesota native and Grammy Award winning singer songwriter and producer, Dan Wilson. Dan is best known for his work with his band Semisonic and for his collaborations with artists including Adele, The Dixie Chicks, Weezer, Mike Doughty and others. On Vic Chesnutt and \\"Soft Picasso\\": \\"I first learned about Vic Chesnutt from a friend of mine, a rabid fan. My knowledge of VC's music was limited to hearing \\"West of Rome\\" at various parties in the early nineties. But my friend patiently indoctrinated me into a broader awareness of his brilliance. I chose to record \\"Soft Picasso\\" because that same friend told me that it would suit my voice best, and he was right. I knew I couldn't match the world-weary cynicism of VC's version so I decided to go all the way in the other direction, in my direction. It's such a funny song; I hope I've done it justice.\\"    Rock the Cause will donate proceeds from the album and release show to Lifeworks Services to directly benefit innovative programs for people with disabilities. Proceeds will also benefit Sweet Relief to provide financial assistance to all types of career musicians who are struggling to make ends meet while facing illness, disability, or age-related problems. For more information, visit [...]    About Rock the Cause    Rock the Cause is a Minnesota Based 501(c)3. Our mission is to create a new generation of stewardship for other non-profit causes. We do this by combining the power of music, community and social media in a way that today's generation will find engaging.

\\"I'm Not Perfect\\" is actually a PERFECT way to start a much-needed conversation with me, myself, and I.  Amy Alley's debut cd is flooded with complex lyrical content and skillfully crafted guitar work.  Clearly conflicted with internal struggles relating to topics such as love, relationships, sexual orientation, religion, and identity, Amy lets it all fly loose as the tracks unfold.  It's raw and it's REAL.  We all benefit from such a lesson in self discovery.  What I love most about this gifted songwriter is her ability to encourage us all to examine ourselves and FEEL the feelings, and then use this knowledge to connect to ourselves in deeper, more meaningful ways.  She accomplishes this in multiple ways.  Whether it's through the tender, unassuming melodic tracks such as 'Butterfly' and 'Scared,' or through the obtrusive, in-your-face tracks like 'Think of Me/Fill the Hole' and 'I'm Not Perfect,' and even the spoken word tracks, particularly 'Anyway,\\" the end result is the same = everyone has struggles in life, and it's time we start to tune into our core gut and deal with the heavy stuff and manage it successfully.  As a music lover, I really appreciate the rather large spectrum of stylistic choices heard throughout the cd, and the genius way Amy gives parody a new meaning in the world of music. product_title: The Klemperer Legacy: Mahler Symphony No. 2
review_headline: disclaimer: I haven't heard the MP3 download - just the CD
review_body:
Just based on my own copy on CD, I'm in the camp of those of have given this five stars. Of course the playing isn't always immaculate. But neither is it sloppy enough to inhibit enjoyment, assuming that you can accept Klemperer's 'interpretation' at face vale. And almost as if to compensate for any imperfections, it's in really good stereo sound. It also boasts the incomparable Janet Baker, captured here in great voice (as usual).

The biggest 'shocker' to Klemp's interpretation is his slower-than-normal tempo for the scherzo (nearly 12 minutes in duration). I like it because it has a jaunty quality that also brings out the more subtle sense of irony that's behind this movement (listen to its original incarnation in \\"Des Knaben Wunderhorn\\"). It's taken a tad slower here than it is even on Klemp's more famous studio version. But frankly, Klemperer has spoiled me for all those who take the scherzo at a much faster clip (Gergiev is a good example). At the other end of the spectrum, Klemperer clocks in well less than 21 minutes for the first movement.

This was the hallmark of Klemperer's interpretation with the \\"Resurrection\\" symphony: a generally fast and dramatic first movement, followed by a slower, more ironic sounding scherzo. But in this 1965 Munich performance, Klemp' also trims a full minute off the finale in comparison to his studio recording. Frankly, I think it's one of the more exciting performances of the finale in the symphony's long discography (and not just loud, which I also like - of course).

Just to try to put things in perspective, I'm often accused of being someone who discounts historical significance and only really likes great sound quality. To be fair to those who make that argument, I don't believe that there ever was a previous 'golden age' for Mahler symphonies. For me, that time is now (ever since Bernstein, Kubelik, Haitink and Abravenel, shall we say). But is this one case where I'm happy to make somethingof an exception. With Klemperer's 'live' Munich Mahler 2, you can have your cake and eat it too: a unique yet persuasive interpretation, coupled to good quality sound in full stereo (even if it lacks a spit polish shine at times). I prefer it to Klemperer's famous studio account for EMI, but can fully respect the opinion of those who don't. Regardless, for five bucks, you're not taking too much of a risk. Instead, you might end up agreeing with those who think it's a steal.

Attractions was released in 2007, and like Cynthia Sayer's other albums, it is a wonderful collection of impeccably performed tunes. The band on this album includes Joe Ascione on drums, Greg Cohen on bass, Sara Caswell on violin, Jim Fryer on trombone, Randy Sandke on trumpet Scott Robinson on clarinet and saxophones, Bucky Pizzarelli on guitar and of course Cynthia Sayer herself on banjo and vocals. Cynthia also wrote all the arrangements, and it's obvious from the way this music sounds that she has a rare gift for finding new ways of presenting material that in some cases could be said to be well worn. You would perhaps expect tunes like Over the Rainbow and You are my Sunshine to have been done almost to death by now, but in Cynthia Sayer's arrangements and this band's brilliant performances, even these old standards get a new lease on life.   The selection of songs is very varied to say the least, with material by Sidney Bechet, Hank Williams, Irving Berlin, Django Reinhardt amongst others. The biggest surprise perhaps in this sense is the closing selection, which is a beautifully performed solo banjo version of Franz Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2. Regardless of what material she performs, Cynthia plays with a fresh and contemporary feel, while still being very respectful of the tradition that the music came from.  As usual, Cynthia Sayer has chosen her band members with care, and while they all play superbly, the collaboration with the great and legendary guitarist Bucky Pizzarelli is particularly inspired. These two master musicians complement each other perfectly and the interplay between them is a joy to listen to.   Cynthia Sayer plays the banjo with great flair and exuberance, and her passion and enthusiasm both for her instrument and the music she plays are very obvious throughout this excellent album. Her sense of rhythm and timing is perfect and she drives her band along beautifully with her infections and swinging style of playing.   Cynthia Sayeris known not only as one of the world's foremost banjo players, but also as a very accomplished singer. Her vocal performances on Attractions are better than ever and she puts her own personal stamp on all of the songs she sings. It should also be mentioned that she wrote two of the selections on Attractions herself; an elegantly swinging instrumental called Banjo Tango and a quirky little story called The Gift, which has a great tune and lyrics that are both humorous and thoughtful.   Attractions is a delightful album with plenty of variety and very inspired playing from everybody. I must have listened to it dozens of times by now, but still find that the music is fresh and engaging. If you like honest, heartfelt and authentic music, you can do no better than exploring the wonderful musical universe of Cynthia Sayer. Attractions is a perfect place to start.

product_title: J Krishnamurti Lecture Series: Madras - January 3rd 1984 7:30am
review_headline: why we put questions at all
review_body: In this the first of a series of question and answer sessions in Madras, J. Krishnamurti begins by pointing out that it is worth asking why we put questions at all and goes on the say that to have any chance of finding the right answer one cannot have prejudices or convictions. With that in mind, he asks the audience not to expect him to provide all the answers, but rather to investigate the questions together. In exploring the questions we find that the answer is there - not outside the question. In response to the very first question, J. Krishnamurti asks another, deeper, question: `Why do we have ideals at all?' and then goes on to look into the nature of crisises and how we face them. We need to have the freedom to look at the problem, not merely its resolution. ABOUT J. KRISHNAMURTI Jiddu Krishnamurti (May 12, 1895-February 17, 1986) was a world renowned writer and speaker on philosophical and spiritual subjects. His subject matter included: the purpose of meditation, human relationships, the nature of the mind, and how to enact positive change in global society. Krishnamurti was born into a Telugu Brahmin family in what was then colonial India. In early adolescence, he had a chance encounter with prominent occultist and high-ranking theosophist C.W. Leadbeater in the grounds of the Theosophical Society headquarters at Adyar in Madras (now Chennai). He was subsequently raised under the tutelage of Annie Besant and C.W. Leadbeater, leaders of the Society at the time, who believed him to be a \\"vehicle\\" for an expected World Teacher. As a young man, he disavowed this idea and dissolved the world-wide organization (the Order of the Star) established to support it. He claimed allegiance to no nationality, caste, religion, or philosophy, and spent the rest of his life traveling the world as an individual speaker, speaking to large and small groups, as well as with interested individuals. He authored a number of books, among them The First and Last Freedom, The Only Revolution, and Krishnamurti's Notebook. In addition, a large collection of his talks and discussions have been published. At age 90, he addressed the United Nations on the subject of peace and awareness, and was awarded the 1984 UN Peace Medal. His last public talk was in Madras, India, in January 1986, a month before his death at home in Ojai, California. His supporters, working through several non-profit foundations, oversee a number of independent schools centered on his views on education - in India, England and the United States - and continue to transcribe and distribute many of his thousands of talks, group and individual discussions, and other writings, publishing them in a variety of formats including print, audio, video and digital formats as well as online, in many languages.evolution, and Krishnamurti's Notebook. The Baltic Woodwind Quintet was founded by Karol Respondek and his Gdansk friend musicians in 1990. During its earliest years of activity, the ensemble reached an important position in cultural life of Gdansk, arousing interest of music critics, media and especially - the public. The ensemble participated in such chamber music competitions as in Illzach and Tours, France, and took part in periodical music events like Music at the Lazienki Park, Warsaw, Per Cameram Ad Ecclesiam, The Days of Young Composers of Gdansk, The Dominican Concerts, as well as in chamber and organ music festivals in Warsaw, Kamien Pomorski, Kolobrzeg and Slupsk.    The Baltic Woodwind Quintet gave concerts at such estimable places as Paac Wilanowski in Warsaw, Palac Dzialynskich in Poznan, Zamek Dzialynskich in Kórnik, Zamek in Krokowa, Schloss Elmau, Bavaria, Marienlyst, Dennmark and Polish Consulate in Strassebourg, France. The ensemble performs regularly on stage of the Polish Baltic Philharmony in Gdansk and takes part in a summer concert series \\"Music in the Monuments of Gdansk\\". The repertoire of the Baltic Woodwind Quintet consists of pieces composed genuinely for a wind quintet (flute, oboe, clarinet, horn and basoon), although its major part comprises arrangements of polish and world music literature made by Karol Respondek. Among them one can find Seasons by Tschaikovsky, Kinderszenen by Schumann, Petite Suite and L'apres-midi d'un Faun by Debussy, The Firedance by de Falla, Ravel's Pavane or the Peer Gynt suite by Grieg.    The musicians of The Baltic Woodwind Quintet are:    AGNIESZKA RESPONDEK - flute  MARIETTA STEFANIAK - oboe  KAROL RESPONDEK - clarinet  EWA NACZK JANKOWSKA - bassoon  ZBIGNIEW KALICINSKI - horn

product_title: Transformers: Dark of the Moon - The Score
review_body: After hearing the first two scores to the Transformers films, I have been waiting for this score for a long time. Jablonsky takes a darker, more emotional style of music to this darker, more serious film. The darker tracks include Battle, Dark Side of the Moon, and Shockwave's Revenge. These tracks have drums, brass, and strings rapidly moving to create fast-paced action and dark tones. The more emotional pieces include Sentinel Prime, No Prisoners, Only Trophies (which is a piano solo through half of the song), and The Fight Will Be Your Own. The more emotional music has a very sad feel to it because of the slow moving strings and piano. This score is my favorite of the Transformers scores so far because of its use of the whole orchestra, a choir, solos of cellos, pianos, drums, etc. and the new themes that Jablonsky created. This score is Jablonsky's best so far. The best songs on the disc are The Fight Will Be Your Own, Our Final Hope, and Battle. This score was worth the wait and definitely worth buying. Thank You, Jablonsky, for another wonderful score that combines beauty with action.

When I saw that Annie Lennox had come out with a (gulp!) Christmas album, and it was called \\"A Christmas Cornucopia,\\" my first reaction was . . . what?! Annie Lennox is one of my all-time favorite artists, and she takes her time between albums, to put it mildly, so why did this new collection have to be of Christmas songs?

Three things that made me take the plunge and buy this album: 1.) Annie Lennox was born on Christmas. If that isn't a great excuse for gravitating towards a Christmas album, I don't know what is. 2.) Last year, Tori Amos came out with a brilliant holiday/winter season cd. So it is possible that this could be good. And 3.) It's Annie Lennox! I couldn't resist.

Well, Annie Lennox is a legend for a reason. She overcame my skepticism and put out a really fantastic collection of songs. However, I must say I don't like her use of auto-tune on God Rest Ye Merry Gentlemen one bit. It's a terrible nod to the current horrible trend and detracts greatly from the other outstanding vocal performances she delivers, both as the lead vocalist and as her own choir of backing vocals.

The production and arrangements on the album are excellent, and Lennox sounds as good as ever. Of course, it's an album that will only get listened to during the holiday season, but that time comes around every year, and this is better than any of the drivel you hear in department stores and supermarkets in November and December.

review_headline: It's not his best, BUT, it is still better than anything else!!!
review_body: Ok,    So this album is not as consistently brilliant es Un Dia Normal or La Vida Es Un Ratico. But it's still Juanes, and an inconsistent Juanes album is still better than anything else out there.    The 1st single should have been \\"Quimera\\" which is a great uptempo song where Juanes talks about the problems in the world including earthquakes in chile and the missing women of Juarez. In this current times of issues i think it would have been the perfect time to release this as a single as the song is essentially a song for change.     The best song on the album though goes to \\"La Razon\\". Is one of the most beautiful love songs Juanes has ever written. A simple acoustic guitar, acordeon, and base line... I mean if it's not my new favourite Juanes love song then it's in my top 3. That song should have been the 2nd single...     Then there are other great moments like \\"Amigo\\", \\"Esta Noche\\", 'Y No Regresas\\" and what i believe should have be the 3rd single \\"La Soledad\\" which moves between a slow verse and mid tempo chorus.    The record company is clearly choosing the singles off the album because \\"Yerbatero\\" is a terrible song... and then 3rd single \\"Regalito is not much better\\". 2nd single \\"Y No Regresas\\" should not have been a single either but is a good song. In fact, it's the more uptempo songs where Juanes has terribly failed. Normally you'd get a few great uptempo songs in a Juanes album, but this time around they are terrible with the exception of \\"Quimera\\".     The album is still brilliant because of its slower tempo songs. 6 out of twelve songs are still among the best i've heard since the last Juanes album.    Like I said, even inconsistent Juanes is better than just about anything else out there.

The hard core types on the [[ASIN:B003KNDMUY Dweezil Zappa]] World website and any number of others will disown me for this: I love this tune. It's simple, easy, accessible, and after the intro fades in, hooks you from the very first bar.

It's the music that makes this song, and not the lyrics or vocals (which are nice, but too perfect, too smooth, too commercial--they could be anyone who can do a 4+ voice harmony). It's a studio factory product, most definitely, with heavy synth, but that's overshadowed--positively--by the deep but not intrusive bass, the simple beat at just the right pace, and a unique rhythm track with just a little funky keyboard. The verses are simple, moving out smartly and building quietly just to break right back down with that three-note drop at the end, which keeps the song fresh and moving smoothly. And then you get that simple harmonica solo, just the right touch for the feel and spirit of the song; a guitar or horn in there would not have been right.

My only wish is that there would be a 12-minute jam mix of this tune, with no vocals and more solos.

Bottom line: I'm not Spice Girls fan, but I love this song. This tune is a triumph of pop creation and production, radio-ready and accessible to all, bam, right now. It hooked me the first time I heard it, and it's still in my music player to this day.

review_headline: No One Comes Close to Steve Morse
review_body: Several other reviewers have mentioned the quality of Steve Morse's composition as what sets him apart from other guitarists. While I wouldn't disagree with that, I would say that the quality of his composition sets him apart from almost all other musicians - period.    Almost all of Morse's compositions would sound just fine re-arranged for a symphony orchestra. Even some of his most technically brilliant guitar solos would transfer quite well - if you could find orchestral players who are actually that adept.    As a guitarist, Steve Morse is so versatile that I'm pretty sure he scares guitarists who have made a particular type of music their life's work - and who are at the top of the pile in their genre - so much that they figure he could take their gig any time he wants. Rock? No problem. Country? He can chicken-pick better than anybody. Classical? His classical guitar compositions put many composers who have made that instrument the entire basis of their musical career(s) to shame. And then there's the pure \\"Morseiana\\" that defies categorization.    There are only a few instrumental virtuosi who combine such technical skill with such compositional talent. Chick Corea comes to mind, and not a lot of others.    I had the pleasure of meeting Steve briefly at a concert my band played at several years ago. There were several other 80's giant bands there and Steve was playing with Deep Purple. The other guitarists for the other bands showed up in their tour buses, with their aging groupies, their bodyguards, their multiple guitar techs and multiple racks of guitars. Not very friendly, from what I could tell.    Steve Morse showed up in a taxicab carrying the guitar he'd made himself when he was at the University of Miami, and a luthier-made copy of the same guitar. He took them into the small break room where all of us non-stars were hanging out and began setting them up himself. Very friendly; very down-to-earth, and in possession of about 100 times more talent than all of the other players in the 5 other bands on the gig that day - put together.    Good guy, GREAT guitarist, fine composer. What else could anyone ask for?

I grew up in rural West Texas, where pretty well the best weekend evenings are spent in small dancehalls and at the dances at local festivals. The bands at such events can really be pretty varied. Sometimes, a really good cover band or a really solid band at the beginning of their career is hired, though it's pretty often just a group of locals who get together on weekends to play. Anyway, with all of those bands, and at all of those dances, there's a common moment, when the instantly recognizable violin hook begins and the crowd absolutely floods the dance floor. That's pretty much the central ritual, I think, of all those Texas dances. The band, no matter who they are, must be able to play \\"Amarillo By Morning,\\" and everyone must dance to it. Goodness, I even remember that from prom, when the types of music and tastes varied widely, but everyone, even the people who hated country music, danced to \\"Amarillo by Morning.\\"

So, obviously, it's a great song. It's got that beautiful violin hood that soars over the well-sung and pretty melody. The words are classic country--both melancholy and touched by the romanticism of pursuing the cowboy/rodeo dream. There's no wonder that it's as popular as it's long been. It's absolutely the quintessential country song, the one (among many very good ones) for which George Strait will always be most remembered.

review_headline: Amazing find out of left field
review_body: I have to echo some other reviewers, who have said this album is the best thing they've heard in years. It certainly is right up there.     This album caught me completely off guard. My first listen it was intriguing, quirky, I wasn't sure I liked it but was certain I wanted to hear it again. Listen after listen, I just loved it more and more and more and more. I listen to a lot of music and most of it has a shelf life of one ore two spins. I kept coming back for more of this. This album is so, so unique, it's hard to explain, but I'll try.    Twin Shadow (which is really one guy) seems to use 80's new wave as a base of operations, but this guy is in his own zone, and the music has a timeless quality. The songwriting is phenomenal, each song so solid and sturdy in its basic construction. Beats, hooks, choruses, melody, is all there in abundance. The songs are extremely tuneful and catchy. They are also exceptionally well arranged, making repeated listens very rewarding, and it is as good a \\"headphone\\" album as it is a party album, driving album, housework album...its appeal is really universal. And on top of everything else, the lyrics are really poignant (\\"I Can't wait for summer, I can't wait for June, when all the ghosts are quiet, when everything is new\\"), and the guy really has a great, tuneful, soulful, pitch perfect voice.    I love this music. Love it. This may sound like hyperbole, and maybe it is, but it really is that good of an album. You are depriving yourself if you don't at least try \\"I Can't Wait\\", \\"tether beat\\", or \\"castles in the snow\\". Redefining traditional musical formulas and blowing away the typical four piece alternative bands is just another day in the talented, vast world of Aron Lyrd. A complete one man show, Lyrd pulls off a variety of musical styles while single-handedly writing and recording everything from guitar to percussion to vocals. While the quality would suffer for many using this approach, he manages to build a full, dynamic sound which is demanding the attention of thousands across the world.    With millions of plays and numerous fans on his MySpace page, Lyrd's songs are catching fire at the speed of light, garnering the interest of critics, magazines, and websites. He was selected by the illustrious Alec Promotions as a featured artist, and successfully received airplay on Indie 104 iRadio in Los Angeles, California. His brilliant alternative rock jams are drawing comparisons to Matchbox 20, Oasis, The Killers, and David Bowie, while fans feverishly spin his infectious songs over and over.    A story of true inspiration, the singer songwriter is no stranger to adversity. After contracting transverse myelitis in 2004, which causes swelling in the spine, and suffering a stroke from a blood clot, Lyrd was paralyzed. Through ironclad determination and arduous work, he regained the use of his arm, and started writing poetry, which eventually led to music. Fast forward to 2010, and Lyrd has rapidly become a dramatic force in the alternative rock scene.    Lyrd already has five albums under his belt, including Dark Metallic Mist by the Moonlight, which received an outpouring of positive reviews from fans and critics. With 50 songs available for purchase in his iTunes store, there literally is something for nearly every music lover who's searching for the next breakout artist.    \\"The song starts off with a very intriguing intro. The vocals sound warm and very radio friendly. The lyrics are not bad either. The main hook is very effective (and memorable) in guiding the song throughto the end. I think this song has a very high chance of radio success. Great job!,\\" said DJ Riff Raff of Raleigh, North Carolina on the catchy track, \\"Just Wasting Time.\\"    Lyrd has multiple songs available for streaming on his MySpace page, and all of his records are available for digital purchase through iTunes. Experience what thousands already have, and bear witness to a single man who produces enough sound for a full blown orchestra.

It's been WAY too long since we've gotten a new David Cook song. It was worth waiting for!

Nothing about David Cook ever disappoints, and this first single from his 6/28 to be released album, \\"This Loud Morning\\", is no exception. First and foremost, David's incredible vocals are front and center. He has a way of singing the words as if he's singing directly to you. I almost feel like he's saying his goodbyes to me, and in such a nice way. I can't think of another singer who touches my heart like David Cook.

The only problem with this song, is that I can't stop singing it in my head. No matter how hard I try to get back to real life and concentrate, I keep hearing, \\"I didn't want to lose you...this is the last goodbye.\\" The beat is infectious - can't help but tap my toes. I think the term is \\"earworm\\", and it definitely fits this song.

The lyrics are poetry. Reading them, even without the music, is a treat. My favorite phrase, \\"a broken piece of art put on display\\". Lyrics like this are not the typical fare on the radio today. How does he do it? He and Ryan Tedder created a pop/rock song with a great beat, that has poetry for lyrics.

The music is also fantastic. His use of instruments is one of my favorite things about David Cook songs. I can't wait to see what David, and his band Neal Tiemann, Andy Skip, Monty Anderson and Kyle Peek do with this song in person. The record rocks, so imagine how it will rock out on stage.

In short - The Last Goodbye is everything I expected from David Cook and more. As a singer, a musician, a songwriter, a producer, and a human being, there is no one like him. I look forward to hearing this not only on my own ipod, but on the radio for quite some time to come. I hope he has lots of room for more platinum on his wall.

Yoga:  A Guided Session is a very basic hour long yoga class.  It opens with a five minute centering practice and closes with a five minute relaxation session.  In between, there's perhaps 15 minutes of postures interlaced with 35 minutes of endless explanation.  The instructor assumes the listener has no previous yoga experience and describes in great detail what you will be doing, and then explains it all again as you do it.  The posture flow isn't very well choreographed and the posture sequences often don't flow well from one to the next.  Postures include Lion, Cobra, Forward Bend, Cat-Dog, spinal twist, and leg lifts.  The pace is glacially slow.    I consider myself a beginning yoga student but I found this too basic for my needs.  It was worth trying for the price but I don't think it will hold up to repeated listening.

product_title: Feeling Wartime - From the Diary Of Monica Stella Heymann
review_headline: Wartime from a young girl's viewpoint
review_body: There are numerous books about World War II. This is the spoken diary of a 15-year old Berlin girl giving you the war from a very personal viewpoint. It focuses mainly on the years 1940/41 talking about air raids, shelters, food rationing and curfew turning her daily routine upside down. It's the little things she remembers, which is very touching. But above all, there is the constant fear of increasing danger for her being Jewish. In spite of all the trouble, she never seems to lose her sense of humour and her use of strong language ('Goering that swine' !!) plus the German accent of the speaker raises a smile! Worth listening.    Monica Stella Heymann and her mother were among the lucky ones who escaped a cruel fate being able to legally leave their 'Heimatland' last-minute. Others didn't, and her diary ends with a list of those who perished, family and friends, which left me with deep emotions.

product_title: The Tree Of Life (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
review_headline: Thoughtful and moving work -- but the transfer to MP3 is flawed
review_body: This is an amazingly reflective score from Desplat -- at times sonorous and deep, at others somewhat edgy. It all follows the director's request to have the music \\"flow like a river\\" throughout the film. For those complaining about the omission of the classical pieces heard in the film, anyone with a brain knows why: rights problems. It's possible there may be another album featuring that music, but most likely not from the same orchestras and conductors as heard in the film. The best idea would be to simply get a listing of the pieces used and find them elsewhere here on Amazon or other services. Shouldn't be that hard to do.    I have downloaded dozens of albums from the Amazon MP3 store without a hitch ... until this one. BEWARE: the transfer from original to MP3 was not done accurately, and \\"dropouts\\" abound throughout the tracks, especially the last one \\"Skies.\\" It almost sounds like tape dropouts, if you remember what those were like. Of course they are not, but they are disconcerting all the same. I've filed a complaint with the appropriate Amazon customer service department; we'll see how that goes.    In the meantime, if this appeals to you it might be a better idea to just get the CD and be done with it.

Playing guitar, harmonica and piano, Oscher tells the deep blues story on every cut, and the music has a certain something that you can't put your finger on, but you know is missing from most modern blues CDs. My favorites are his unique bass harp version of \\"'Round Midnight\\" and the striking \\"Ida Mae\\" with it's killer guitar sound that has overtones I guarantee you've never heard before. But every cut on this CD is a gem, including Oscher's hilarious reminiscence about a personal encounter with the great Little Walter. I understand this CD was just nominated for a 2011 Blues Music Award. It is surely a strong contender to win.

I had the good fortune to study with John McGuire at Columbia U. in 2001. When I first heard John's music, I was a die hard atonalist and  hostile to minimalism. John's music forced me to confront music that glimmered on its surface and was rigorously and logically structured underneath; music that is stationary from one perspective and thoroughly developmental from another. It demonstrated to me that rigorous craftsmanship can under-gird immediately gratifying ear candy.     Pulse Music III illustrates this attention to both the immediate moment and the overall narrative. Any individual moment glistens with pulsing streams of fractal consonance, but it's the long-term harmonic motion that sustains interest over its 24 minutes. The chord changes are paced perfectly and create a sense of both surprise and release. The imagination and rigor behind this feat speak to a talent that deserves greater recognition in the States.

The story of Simple Acoustic Trio goes back to the beginning of `90s. Still being students of the Music High School S.A.Trio. made their debut in 1991. They won the third prize at the Polish jazz contest-Jazz Juniors '91. In the same year, a sixteen-year old band leader - Marcin Wasilewski won the fourth prize at the International Jazz Pianist festival in Kalisz, Poland. Two years later the band won the first prize at the 7th International Festival of Jazz Bands \\"Chorus `93\\" during Jazzin' Sorgues Festival in France. In 1996 the band participated in two jazz competitions. In Getxo, Spain, the band won the first prize and Marcin Wasilewski was chosen the best soloist of the festival. In the same year the band became a prizewinner of the Leverkusen Jazz Festival, and again Marcin Wasilewski was considered the best soloist.
So far the S.A.T., formed by Marcin Wasilewski - piano, Slawomir Kurkiewicz - double-bass and Michal Miskiewicz - drums, has recorded four CDs. The first one called \\"Komeda\\" (Gowi Records) released in February 1995 was inspired by a successful live performance dedicated to Krzysztof Komeda during the Jazz Jamboree'94. \\"Up-dated\\" version of this album re-titled \\"Lullaby for Rosemary's\\" was released on Not Not in 2001. \\"When will the blues leave\\" (Polonia Records) is the title of the second release from December 1995. \\"Live in Getxo\\" (Hillargi Records) was recorded during Getxo Jazz Festival 1996. In October 1999, the band performed at \\"Jazz All Fil De L'oise\\" festival in France, and the fallowing month recorded their fourth CD \\"Habanera\\" (Not Two). The fall of 2001 brought the release of \\"Lyrics\\". The album came from co-operation between Polish saxophonist Henryk Miskiewicz and Simple Acoustic Trio, and was awarded the most prestigious prize in Polish phonographic industry \\"Fryderyk\\" 2001 for the best jazz album of the year. In the meantime S.A.T. was voted the best acoustic band by the readers of a polish magazine \\"Jazz Forum\\". In 2007 S.A.T. released its first album titled \\"Trio\\" for ECM.
Individually and as a group the members of S.A.T. have performed with prominent international jazz stars such as Jan Garbarek, Manu Katche, Louis Sclavis, Dino Saluzzi, Palle Danielsson, Jon Christensen, Bernt Rosengren, Arthur Blythe, Joe Lovano, John Surman, Bobo Stenson, Anders Jormin, Gianluigi Trovesi and also have worked with Tomasz Szukalski, Piotr Wojtasik, Michal Urbaniak, Janusz Muniak, Zbigniew Namyslowski. Since 1994 the musicians of Simple Acoustic Trio have worked with Tomasz Stanko as members of Stanko quartet. This co-operation became a springboard for their artistic and commercial success; Tomasz Stanko Quartet has made a great deal of tours all over the world.
Stanko argues that \\"In the entire history of Polish jazz, we've never had a band like this one. I'm surprised by these musicians every day. They just keep getting better and better.\\" But the pianist, bassist and drummer are much more than Stanko's `backing band'.
The trio is very much a group, and as Don Heckman observed, reviewing them with Stanko for the Los Angeles Times, \\"Their years together have resulted in an ensemble with an utterly symbiotic creative flow, solos darting through collective passages as the music streamed fluidly from one selection into another. Kurkiewicz and Miskiewicz play with a fertile combination of swing and subtlety...Wasilewski's piano soloing displayed a coalescing talent, a potentially emerging jazz star in his own right.\\"ased its first album titled \\"Trio\\" for ECM. review_headline: The Best of the Newer Live Releases
review_body: I've been listening to a lot of DMB's live releases for a number of years now, and I definitely have my list of favorites.  However, I was not very impressed with the last non-live trax release (\\"Live in New York City\\").  I just didn't feel the energy that is so noticeable in other live recordings.  That is why I didn't have high hopes for this release.  But I was VERY wrong.  The most noticeable improvement is Jeff Coffin's saxophone work.  It is absolutely fantastic, and even parallels Leroi's work at times.  The music has a much more rock-like sound than it had before, but it really works.  This makes me feel that DMB has pulled out of it's confused post-Stand Up years into a new mature, dignified, and modern sound.  I never though I would say this, but it's a change that I like!  Overall, this is by far my favorite live release in years.  Saying that I am very impressed is an understatement.  I'm sure this will get pushed under the rug as just another live release to most people, but it is so much more.  Also, this album has a great mixture of both old and new tracks, and they finally seem to blend together.  The Big Whisky tracks sound much more polished than they sounded on \\"Europe 2009\\".  Just as a pointer, some other concerts I would recommend are Folsom Field, Weekend on the Rocks, Central Park (of course), and Live Trax Volumes 2, 13, and especially 14.  And now, Wrigley Field is on my list too!!    As a side note, the version of #41 found on this album is one of the best that I have heard in a very long time.

review_headline: Exploring the Haydn Masses -- Nos. 8 and 10
review_body:
The more I listen to Haydn, the more I am moved by the power, depth, and scope of his genius. A recent eight CD box set of the complete Haydn masses on Naxos.[[ASIN:B002IVRBBU Haydn: Complete Masses [Box Set]]] has helped me come to appreciate this relatively unfamilar part of his output. The set features period performances by the Trinity Choir and the REBEL Baroque Orchestra of the famed Trinity Church of Wall Street conducted by J. Owen Burdick and Jane Glover. These are uniformly excellent readings played and sung with verve, passion, and enthusiasm. The recorded sound is full and lively.

This CD, no. 4 in the compilation, is available individually or as part of the set. It includes two temporally widely-spaced masses, one familar, the other far less so, conducted by J. Owen Burdick. The less familiar work, composed in 1782, is the \\"Mariazeller\\" mass, sometimes called the \\"Missa Cellensis\\", even though an earlier Haydn mass initially composed around 1766 also bears that name. [[ASIN:B0037TTQC4 Haydn: Cacilienmesse (Missa Cellenis)]] The Mariazeller mass is a work of about 34 minutes which is a transitional work between Haydn's earlier masses and his large-scale late works. It is religious music of lyricism and quiet power. Although this work includes two soprano, alto, tenor,and bass soloists, the most memorable parts of this work consists of rousing large-scale choruses, particularly in the opening sections of the \\"Gloria: and the \\"Credo\\". The choruses are based for the most part upon simple, inspiring melodies, but they include as well two fugual sections, the \\"Et vivam venturi\\" of the Credo and the concluding \\"Dona nobis pacem\\" section of the mass. Among the soloists, I continue to be impressed by bass Richard Lippold in his performance of \\"Et incarnatus est\\" from the Credo. The Mariazeller is a gorgeous, work in which Haydn realized his ambition to write learned, moving music that would at the same time be accessible to many people. The work is scored for strings together with oboe, bassoon, trumpet, tympani and organ. The recording dates from 2004.

The second and far better known work on this CD is the \\"Missa in tempore belli\\" composed in 1796, one of a series of six late Haydn masses. Composed after Haydn had completed his entire symphonic output, many listeners find a highly symphonic power in this late mass of about 37 minutes in duration, which was dramatically written in the midst of the turmoil that the French Revolution caused in Europe. The large orchestra for the mass includes strings, oboe, clarinet, bassoon, horn, trumpet, timpani, and organ. The martial beat of the tympani pervades this mass, giving it its nickname of \\"Pauken[tympani]mass\\".

Ths \\"Missa in tempore belli\\" is a work of contrasts which makes full use of both chorus and four soloists, frequently, juxtaposed against each other as in the opening Kyrie. Triumphal dramatic music is contrasted with much quieter, reflective sections, as between the \\"Et resurrexit\\" and the \\"Et vitam venturi\\" sections of the Credo. The Agnus Dei section of this mass consists of music of great peace and meditative beauty and it is succeeded by a large powerful concluding \\"Dona nobis pacem\\" in which choral sections alternate with ensemble writing for the four solo voices. The \\"Qui tollis\\" section of the Credo features further solos by bass Lippold accompanied by a thin obligato section in the middle strings. Burdick and his ensemble offer a full, rousing performance of inspired music.

Haydn's masses remain little-known treasures. This CD offers an outstanding introduction to Haydn's religious choral music.

Total time: 71:51

review_headline: HUGE sound, tight instruments, an absolute "joy"
review_body: Stumbled across a video for \\"Cradle\\", and was instantly hooked.  I noticed \\"The Big Roar\\" had some songs that were on their first EP, and figured a reproduced version would be superior.  I was right!  I've been listening to this album for days, and still have this music in my head.  How three people make this much noise is a wonderment; they have a fullness that few trios since Rush have been able to produce.  It will be interesting to see them pull this sound off on stage.    Off the bat, \\"The Everchanging Spectrum Of A Lie\\" is epic - the strange banging noises quickly evolve into a rollicking paced force of sound that doesn't relent for over 7 minutes.  Ritzy's vocal talent is amplified by the larger-than-life production that makes it sound like she is in a giant cavern - and the sweetness of her voice is balanced by the sheer assault of her guitar.  Not many women rock this hard and still retain a fragile, ethereal persona.    I found a number of the songs are infinitely replayable - Austere, Whirring, Cradle, and The Greatest Light Is the Greatest Shade will be in my \\"heavy rotation\\" playlist - but I also found Llaw = Wall to be a moody departure, with bassist Rhydian Dafydd performing a nice break in the vocals (while still pounding out serious basslines, often taking duties such as melody or counterpoint.)  One overlooked strength of this outfit - Matt Thomas' driving, relentless drums.    All in all, this is my favorite release of 2011 (as of early April) ... hope to catch them live later in the year, since I can't make it to any of their April U.S. shows.  Hear that, Ritzy?  Come to D.C.!    UPDATE: Saw them live at the Cat's Cradle in Carrboro, NC (Sept 2011) and got the opportunity to photograph the show from a few feet away. All three band members were pouring heart and soul into an 80 minute set that set the place on fire.  Loud is an understatement; the description \\"wall of sound\\" is quite suitable.  The mix was still clean, crisp, and coherent, more sothan the album. Ritzy and Ryhdian both use massive pedal effect sets like third or fourth instruments, and Matt's drums are relentless.  If you can catch them on their next tour, do not miss.  Check out some shots from the show at:  [...]

The story of Steve Forbert's contractual dispute with Nemporer Records / CBS is relatively well known.  Forbert had released four albums. After critical praise for his initial release -- Alive on Arrival -- and a top-forty hit single on his second release --  Jackrabbit Slim, his third and fourth releases had seen diminishing returns.  In 1983, in an effort to broaden his sound beyond that of the Greenwich Village singer-songwriter, Forbert enlisted the help of mainstream producer Neil Geraldo (Pat Benatar) to record an album that more fully reflected his rural Southern roots; an album that not only showed the influence of Bob Dylan but also paid homage to the sounds of the Everly Brothers, Elvis and Sun Studios.  Unfortunately, when Nemporer heard the resultant recordings they were disappointed.  Instead of another \\"Romeo's Tune\\" these recordings showed Steve moving deliberately away from the pop charts.  The record company's response was to cut its losses and shelve the recordings.  Forbert and the company would wind up in litigation; he would not release another studio album until 1988's Streets of This Town.  Except for the track \\"Samson & Delilah's Beauty Shop\\" which was included in the \\"best of\\" collection What Kind of Guy?, the tracks from the \\"lost\\" album remained locked away until 2010.    Twenty-eight years later, these recordings -- now released as Down in Flames -- no longer seem such a radical shift.  With the benefit of hindsight, Forbert's efforts to meld elements of folk, country, rock-a-billy, and rock `n' roll fall comfortably within the Americana genre.  Several of the songs (\\"Lay Down Your Weary Tune Again\\" and \\"His Was The Sound\\") were subsequently re-recorded and released on later albums.  Indeed, the overall sound of Down in Flames is in keeping with Forbert's post-Nemporer/CBS career.     If you are looking for an introduction to Steve Forbert, this may not be the place to begin.  A better starting place might be one of the collections: WhatKind of Guy? or Rock While I Can Rock or his latest release: The Time and The Place.  On the other hand, Down in Flames should be a welcome addition to those who know and appreciate Steve's music.  It is not a misunderstood lost masterpiece.  Rather, Down in Flames is a snapshot of a songwriter/musician struggling against the narrow catogorization which existed in the music industry almost 30 years ago.    PS:  a multi-disc version of Down In Flames containing bonus material is available directly from Steve Forbert's web-site.

Every piece of music on this album reflects top notch talent.  There are reminders of the darker prior successes of Killer and Love it to Death, interwoven seemlessly with the brighter, complex compositions that will lead to Billion Dollar Babies.  The West Side Story theme really gives it a special flavor that just makes it irresistable.  If you've never seriously listened to Alice Cooper, this is one of the best places to start. But, of the four, School's Out is the crowning achievement.

review_headline: My Star, Your Star, Everyone's Star
review_body:
Let's start with the obvious. If this album had physically come out in 2009, \\"You Make Me Beautiful\\" would have been at the top of my Best Songs of the Year list. . . but that just means it'll top 2010's list. Despite previous faves like \\"Ocean,\\" \\"Walk Away,\\" and \\"Underneath Your Sky,\\" this song is most likely my new Marina favorite.

The first word that comes to my mind when I hear \\"Thursday Song\\" is \\"wistful.\\" I know there's a story to the title, but I don't remember it. \\"I won't turn my back on you\\" makes it basically a song about trust, and with its languid acoustic guitar and occasional mournful keyboard, it's a song to play for your friends rather than hear it on the radio. . . unless there's a channel for that on satellite, probably in the 1000s.

\\"Blue For You\\" is very similar to the previous song from a musical standpoint, and it surprises me these two are back-to-back. Though this one does have drums. The lyrics are more lovelorn than wistful this time, not a typical Marina trope, but a fun change nevertheless.

In tone, at least at the beginning, \\"My Star\\" reminds me of the ghost story from the previous album, but kicks up with drums and a Wurlitzer-type keyboard and occasional, barely there, strings. \\"When the sun goes down, I'll be there if you fall\\" makes me think the lyrics are similar to Thursday Song, but there's more urgency, almost a desperation, to the pleas. Again, it's not typical Marina, not her usual introspective thinking, like the next one, but that's certainly not bad.

This is the third version of \\"Killing My Dream\\" on Marina's CDs, though in all fairness one was live. I used the word mournful earlier, but that would better describe the original version. Considering the topic, and you get the idea from the title, this almost sounds poppy in comparison, with a sparse albeit kinda jazzy electric guitar. It's kinda jarring if you've heard it so many times before as I have, but if you haven't. . . it's new to you, as the TV networks try to sell ya to watch their repeats.

\\"Don't Cry\\" is yet another slow ballad, similar musically and even lyrically, but mostly in feeling. (Yes, I know it's a cover, but there's still a reason why it was chosen for the album.) It forms a nice little trilogy with Thursday Song and Blue For You, if you can imagine Marina singing all three to the same person. Not being much of a Guns n Roses fan, I think it's easy enough to say I like Marina's voice better. . .

\\"Unbalanced\\" is one of my favorites live, because it looks like Marina's having so much fun--she gets to really rock out (instead of just \\"soft-rock\\" out). The Wurlitzer-like effect that Shannon Hurley does in concert is not present here, though, which I think is too bad for those of us who have heard it so often, but otherwise it's nice to have this, even if it's really not that different than the live version on her previous CD (except for the lack of a momentary pause before \\"So unbalanced\\"). And I hope I'm not one of those \\"friends\\" who is more screwed up than she is!

\\"Weight of the World\\" brings us back to Marina's signature soft-rock. I don't remember if this is the one she says is Beatles-inspired, but it sure sounds like it could be. She does some things with her voice I don't remember hearing before, and I definitely like the stop when she sings \\"Stop!\\" This is just so perfect quintessential Marina that I can't think of much else to say.

As Marina fans know, she includes a traditional Russian song on every album, like \\"Babushka\\" on the last one. This time we get \\"Tonkaya Ryabina,\\" incredibly haunting because she does it a cappella. I first heard this at the Pasadena library where she sat on the lip of the stage and somehow managed to sound so amazingly beautiful and creep me out at the same time. (Plus I got a great shot of her getting up after that, in those thigh-high black boots!)

review_headline: KING's TONIC establish a Rock Monarchy!
review_body: The king is dead - long live King's Tonic  The bustling German rock regents of King's Tonic are ready to give another audience in 2010. And with their new record \\"Rock Monarchy\\" the foursome won't even try to accept any compromises.     Far away from short-lived trends King's Tonic stick to the traditional basic principles of good punk rock music. Snotty, aggressive and a lot of sense for melody. However, for the first time the band got a brand new arrow in its quiver: \\"Rock Monarchy\\" is a split CD - the German variation of three songs plus another German bonus track are aboard and so it is up to the listener to choose which variation he downloads or whether he puts the English or the German version Monarchie des Rock\\" in his shelf.   A Rock Monarchy, an empire of words, a rebel's symphony  The reason for this new step is obvious: during the last years King's Tonic toured all around the globe, and with loads of concerts throughout Europe, South-East Asia, Russia or the USA the band realized: everybody over there was keen on punk rock music with German lyrics. During the last US tour in April 2010 the boys consequently decided to record and publish alternative variations of the new songs.  Being driven by music the quartet manifests its credo in their song Renaissance: all of this is \\"quite normal when you're addicted: to music, the soundtrack of our rock'n roll lifestyle!\\"

Upon completion of your first full listen of the album don't expect to be anything other than fatigued. The mental exhaustion i speak of however is far from a bad thing, nor will it stop you from wanting to immediately give the album another spin. And then another one. And another one. No. This mental fatigue comes from the albums ability to shred all of your preconceptions of what dark music and black metal is capable of, and it's really infectious. On \\"Paracletus\\" Deathspell Omega have manged to find the perfect balance between absolute twisted musical insanity and well crafted, beautifully dark melodies, which are presented through densely layered guitar work that literally leave you wondering how they came up with such genius ideas. This album is not only masterfully composed, but it's heavily progressive, and challenges some of the most atmospheric metal albums i've ever heard for the top spot.

From the opening dissonant guitar riff of \\"Epiklesis\\" all the way to the very last minute of the almost doomy and desperate melodies of \\"Apokatastasis Panton\\" this album never lets up. The songs transition into one another so flawlessly that if one were not looking at the tracks changing you'd never know it was a new song. This gives the album a very dense and epic feel to it, and although it's 42 minutes long the album is so good and commands so much attention that you'll never stop to think about the minutes going by. The only sign you'll find that time has passed when you are through with it will be the ringing remaining in your ears, as you will have had the irresistible urge to turn the volume up to immerse yourself more fully in the wall of sound that they create.

\\"Paracletus\\" is an album drenched with technical mastery, compositional precision filled with as many haunting melodies as there are terrifying dissonances, bass work that stands out as perfection in and of itself, impeccable time signature changes, stunning production, and vocal work that really tops off the smothering atmosphere that this monster of an album creates. What you won't find in this album is instant gratification. It's true that even just one listen of the album will prove that it is a force to be reckoned with, however, i've listened to it many times through now and it's still slowly coming together and revealing itself to me gradually. But every music lover knows that those are the albums that are the most gratifying in the end, and are the ones that will stick with you most over time.

If you like progressive black metal, if you like metal at all period and are up for the challenge, do yourself a huge favor; turn off the lights and give this a good listen. When I'm feeling anxious I just put on this track and by the end I'm breathing easy again. I was originally going to remove the beginning where he briefly tells you how to breathe, since I normally find that part boring, but his voice is so soothing it really helps set the mood.    There's some light music in the background, which isn't distracting but nice when he takes brief pauses. With Civilian, Wye Oak has mastered the art of creating songs that swell and progress to peaks of ultimate complexity. Many of the tracks begin with the spotlight placed squarely on Jenn's smooth, subtle, yet powerfully sultry vocals, only to have the mood tempered by distorted guitar riffs and resonating percussion. Although the general feel of the music is one of melancholy, the mesmerizing lyrics and diaphonous undertones keep the album from becoming too dark and burdensome. Heavy topics are approached with a sort of cautious intensity that carefully toes the line between drawing listeners in and pushing them over the edge.

The group has been tossed into the indie/lo-fi category--one that is overflowing with aesthetically similar musicians who ultimately have little in common, aside from their affinity for creating probing and consequential music. In a genre where anything goes, Wye Oak has responded by developing an entirely novel offering--from the introductory track's opening note to the album's final fade, there is nothing contrived or derivative to be found. Comparisons can be drawn to several of the band's contemporaries, from Rogue Wave to Pavement, but fans expecting a rehashed version of such artists' respective albums are in for an unanticipated treat.

Because Civilian is much more polished and produced than it's predecessors, it is more accessible. That being said, the band has stayed their direction, and their material has maintained the nuances and intricacies that brought them to the attention of so many discerning listeners. This album is a rarity, in that it will delight loyal fans and newcomers alike. The lyrical genius, gorgeous vocals, and singular instrumental arrangements make Civilian more than an experience of passive listening, but, as alluded to on the album's cover art, one more akin to musical immersion.

Alot of these have been used in movies and television for....ever. Like others have noted, the \\"dark\\" theme works on a good portion of this collection, but alot of it could be stuck anywhere...theme-wise.
