review_headline: For fans of Iron Maiden, Dream Theater and Queensryche!!!
review_body: I've been looking forward to hearing this album for over a year now and was wondering if it would ever get released? But here it is. If you like 80's heavy metal by the likes of Iron Maiden, Judas Priest the more progressive Queensryche tinged with a modern prog edge of the likes of Dream Theater and kamelot you are certain to be a fan of this album. Heavy, melodic, layered and with great vocals. I'm going to review each song track by track.     Opening track Head has one of the best intros of a song I've ever heard. Reminding me a lot of Dream Theater. A heavy melodic rock song which has the hooks to get you singing along. 8/10.     Sons of Bukowski. For me the best song on the album. Once gain the intro reminds me a lot of Dream Theater before erupting into a driving fast metaller. 9/10.     Absolution. Another rocker with a big hooking chorus. 7/10.     The Beating of Black Wings. This one sounds like it's come straight out of the 80's NWBHM. 7/10.     Ghost Ballet. The albums 1st ballad. Starts like it's gonna be a rocker before goin to a piano led ballad and gets heavier as the song goes on. Paul Kettley gets to show of the range of his voice on this one. 7/10.     Milovani. I really dont like this song. Heavy and well played but for me the lyrics just let it down. Don't let that put you off the rest of the album though. 4/10.     Oberon. Back to form with this tune. Yet another rocker with hooks with some female voices to help it along, which has become a fashion for many good rock bands to experiment with over recent years. 8/10.     Catch me. This one is more of a mid tempo rock song. Reminds me a lot of Bon Jovi at their best. I really like this one. 9/10.     Havels Hurricane - Another meodic heavy track mixed with pianos to give it a progressive sound with an excellent guitar solo from Nick Dunne. This really is great stuff. 8/0.     Words That Kill - Back in 1986 Queensryche released a song called 'The Killing Words'. I believe this song is heavily influenced by that track, despite it sounding very different, lyrically it has simularities. One of the best tracks on the album. 8.5/10.     Arual - The opening strings to this song definetely sound like Queensryche. The influence is there to be heard. A short instrumental. 7/10.     Bad Dreams - For the 3rd track on the trot I'm going to compare this one with Queensryche. This time their song 'Somone Else' from the 'Promised Land Album'. A piano ballad with some great vocals. 8.5/10.     Rise up (and fuel theflame) - A fast paced metal track which sounds like it has come straight out of the 1980's. 6/10.     Overall I'd give this album 7/10 with the inclusion of Milovani. Without this track I would have given the album 8/10. Well worth exploring for any hard rock or metal fan. Recommended.

review_headline: Fresh, Invigorating Musical Poetry Invokes Neruda, Donne, Kerouac
review_body:
Somewhere between songs and spoken word lands the Kevin Max/Adrian Belew project \\"Raven Songs 101\\". I struggled in considering how to describe this, since it hits several categories musically, stylistically and lyrically. Somehow, it ties together.

Gutsy, and not perfect, it goes to places avoiding genres, and shows that experimentation in music is a long way from dead. Not every allusion or symbol is clear, but there is a visceral challenge developed here worthy of exploration.

There is no point comparing this to dc Talk's work, as it is similar only in that Max brings the same genuine pursuit of God and art. Otherwise, there are only glimpses of hip-hop and pop rock. It does not contradict dc Talk's core message, but puts an entirely different voice and angle to it.

Listeners expecting Jack Kerouac will find something akin in the midst of something being extraordinarily different. The music written not just played behind the piece, but as an integral part. With Kerouac, jazz provided texture and tone. With Max/Belew, it is essentially unified with the lyrics. Unlike a song, the lyrics are not sung so much as they are presented as a variety of instruments.

The poetry is a cross between free verse modernism and Pablo Neruda, with a strong current of metaphysical poet John Donne in its realist-sensual-faith driven descriptions.

Like Kerouac, Max finds internal vowel rhymes, and with those, a natural cadence, as in the eponymously named cut: \\"I was spurned and churned, nocturnal immersions in the baptism of your love.\\"

Spoken word poetry is often associated today with memoirists like Maya Angelou, but those listeners will be disappointed. Max's poetry deals heavily with self introspectively, as in the pulse-beat metronymic, rhythmic 'Raising Cain':

I seize the light and draw it down,
and I cover it up with a blanket of foam
I break the bond that held us.
I curse the ground and live in caves.
I speak to the dead in the silence of shame.
I break the back that made us.
I drive the nails and draw the sword.
I do this even though I know the word.

This is a confession of brokenness and willingness, as opposed to a declaration of defiance or victory.

The music itself reminds me of the Art of Noise, Bjork, and even some industrial techno and punk. Some club beats, ambient guitar, Africanesque-jazz drums line the songs in a moody, yet understated expression.

Vocal layers add to the intrigue, as does some interesting mixing of stereo (especially in 'River'). Culturally and artistically relevant, Max shows a broad knowledge of the world outside of Nashville. Max does not deny he is part of the greater musical world, referring diversely to Frank Sinatra, Gene Simmons, Elvis, Nina Simone, the Sex Pistols and others in the hypnotic 'Black Leather and a Microphone.'

In the song titled 'Untitled', Max turns on the effects and his voice comes out like a Doctor Who Dalek. It is reminiscent of the Rolling Stones 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with lines like, \\"I saw the Gestapo alive with desire,\\" and \\"I saw old Judas hung from the gallows.\\" Unfortunately, in the distortion, it hard to catch the full meaning of the piece. A lyric sheet would be a great tool, but, in downloading an mp3 instead of buying a CD with liner notes loses that.

'And You Tremble At His Feet' has a 1960s coffeehouse coolness to it, but with more depth and sophistication.

In the fog horn imbued 'One', he addresses cynicism as we see the frail humanity declaring Christ. \\"What you felt was a pinch of realism in a world of cheapened orthodox,\\" seems to call upon on the sensibility of Dietrich Bonhoeffer. He wants real faith which does not succumb to the lure of Man, but the grace of God.

\\"It's not the singer. It's the song... There is one valid opinion among the screeching, seething leeches,\\" implies that beyond all the marketing, church camps, falsity found in Christianity, there is still one truth, and one true voice. The truth is still the truth.

'Whalers Tails' is the most standard reading. Unfortunately, it is the least interesting and most cliché. The first two stanzas come across weakly as he sounds like he is reading a poem, rather than performing it. Moody Blues fans might find themselves remembering the mod-psychedelic poem 'Late Lament' spoken at the end of 'Nights in White Satin'. Max redeems 'Untitled' at the end, \\"I lay in bones in bunched up pieces, and I see the heavens in choked-up freedom.\\"

product_title: Something Real & Here, Here and Here
review_body: An Unbelievable Find    I seldom feel compelled to write reviews, and this is my first for an album. But after listening to this double album set regularly for 6 month and not getting tired of it, I felt it was time. The three qualities that make albums worth owning are Vocals, Lyrics and Music. Meg & Dia have them all.    1) Meg & Dia provide great female vocals across a range of songs that vary in tempo, mood and energy. Dia (the lead singer) has great control of her voice. She can provide serious rocking forcefulness on one verse and drop to a soft melodic voice in the next while keeping her tone and texture consistent. Layer that with Meg's vocals and there's a depth and power behind the lyrics that I have not found with most other artists.      2) The lyrics are well thought out and meaningful. The songs tell parts of stories, just a glimpse, just enough, but not the whole story. I guess that's so we (the listener) can fit the song into our lives. Also, very seldom do Meg & Dia write repetitive lyrics. And when they do as in, \\"Here, Here, and Here\\", it really does feel appropriate and not tiresome.     3) The music is varied but all within the Alt-Rock genre. Slow, fast, upbeat, serious, happy, and sad. It's all exactly what I want out of album - consistent but not repetitive. You can't sing one song with another's music. They are all different; matching the music to the mood of the lyrics and vice versa.    I realize an album is really good when I don't skip over songs. I know how good an artist is when I don't skip them during random play. I rarely skip over Meg & Dia songs in either case.

review_headline: Believe in Emerson Drive Wavers with New Disc
review_body:
Prime Cuts: Belongs to You, Your Last, That Kind of Beautiful

Trouble has been brewing on the horizon for this Canadian group since the lead single \\"Belongs to You\\" only meagrely scrapped into the Billboard Country Top 40. And things took on an ominous turn when Valory/Big Machine Records kept postponing the release date of this CD. Moreover, Emerson Drive's reputation took on a further nose dive when the rumor mills started churning with the sudden death of former guitarist Patrick Bourque. As for the future viability of the group, it certainly is not to be found on this new disc. Not that it lacked good songs, other than \\"Belongs to You,\\" there's nothing here than spells hit. Over the years, Emerson Drive like many country bands (such as Alabama, Rascal Flatts, Restless Heart and countless others) has straddled the fine line between rock and country. Business is as usual here with \\"Believe\\"--there's the usual anthemic pop rockers bolstered by the group's tight harmonies, the normal line-up of Nashville's top writers (e.g., Tom Shapiro, Rivers Rutherford, Luke Laird, Tim Nichols and Dave Berg), and the commercial sheen burnished by veteran producer Josh Leo and former Alabama member Teddy Gentry.

Though sadly ignored by country radio, the true gem of this CD is \\"Belongs to You.\\" A gorgeous power ballad, \\"Belongs to You\\" portrays love at its romantic best made even more beautiful with lead singer Brad Mates' soulful vocals. Romance gets reprised again with the acoustic sounding \\"Your Last.\\" Intricate, intimate and heart warming, \\"Your Last\\" is a vital piece that deserves wide circulation. Unfortunately, these are the only two ballads and the CD's equity would certainly be inflated with more of such love songs.

As for the propulsive numbers, \\"That Kind of Beautiful\\" is a hooky splash of sunshine: its positive lyrics and its engaging melody are what make this a future summer time favorite. Penned by Josh Leo and Shawn Colvin, title track \\"Believe\\" with its electronic vocal reverberations has mass appeal for crossover pop success. The rest of the album is not ropey, nevertheless, there's nothing revolutionary about these cuts. They cover the tried and tied themes canvassed by modern country, including the pretty average \\"That Was Us\\" - a throwback into the protagonist's rowdier days. While \\"I Love This Road\\" adds nothing new to the burgeoning canon of road songs a la Sawyer Brown's \\"Six Days on the Road\\" and Kenny Chesney's \\"The Road and the Radio.\\" Similarly, vamped-up rocker \\"Livin' It Up\\" recycles the over-used theme of living life to its max without much freshness.

In many ways \\"Believe\\" tries too hard to be affable to country radio that it becomes like the million other songs played on air now. These 10 tracks are by no means offensive, except that too many of them do not possess their own identity to be memorable. Nevertheless, the redemptive value resides in the ballads. Shame that radio didn't do \\"Belongs to You\\" justice. I was aware that Jefferson Airplane performed at Woodstock but until this Amazon.com MP3 Download became available I didn't know a live recording of \\"White Rabbit\\" performed by Jefferson Airplane at the Woodstock Fair in 1969 existed.    In my opinion this MP3 Download is only fair in sound quality but it is in Stereo (not Mono) and a good amount of Grace Slick's vocals are clear enough to hear.    Unless you can find a better copy of this recording elsewhere I recommend the purchase of this Amazon.com MP3 Download \\"White Rabbit (Live At The Woodstock Music & Art Fair, August 16, 1969)\\".    Note that this same track is available on the 2-CD set of [[ASIN:B0026BD2GA Jefferson Airplane: The Woodstock Experience]] from Amazon.com.

\\"State of rock\\" is the collaboration of \\"Frontline\\" members Robby Bodel (g), Hutch Bauer (b) and Rami Ali (d) with British singer Tony Mills (\\"Shy\\",\\"TNT\\"). From their conception in the early 90s \\"Frontline\\" were one of the few bands that managed to blend in perfect balance 80s AOR with Hard Rock while finding appropriate markets to sell (namely Japan). This new band/collaboration is named after the title of the first \\"Frontline\\" album, \\"State of Rock\\", by all means a very appropriate if not needed release as the last \\"Frontline\\" album dates back in 2006.

\\"State of Rock\\" has the \\"Frontline\\" trademark all over it so you can expect lengthy harmonics, thick guitars, thumping bass from a release that is built on melody. At the same time choosing Mills as their singer was a wise decision as his vocal style is very similar to that of original \\"Frontline\\" singer Stephan Kämmerer.

So is this as good as \\"Frontline\\"? Well truth be told, \\"State of Rock\\" might sound rather typical on first play and will probably require the listener's full attention in order to perfectly appreciate this release. On that count, the more time you invest on this album, the better it sounds! Having played the album through over four times, I have to say I am very satisfied with the material on offer; still as those familiar with the band will remember, with \\"Frontline\\" you were hooked on their songs immediately as they demonstrated that intensity and mature aggression which unfortunately is not to be found on this album.

Needless to say, all songs here are up to standards, including standouts \\"Black & Blue\\", \\"Heartless Dreamer\\", the titanic \\"Hanging in the Balance\\" plus the super melodic \\"Without my love\\". \\"State of Rock\\" does justice to the \\"Frontline\\" heritage; it might not have you tearing the walls with excitement; but it will give you the best blend of AOR with Hard Rock through its 10 tracks.

\\"All That I Am\\" is definitely a mood piece, filled with heartfelt declarations of love but in a dark atmosphere that only hints at hope. What I most appreciate is how each verse and chorus, both lyrically and musically, builds and subtly changes -- first adding drums, then backing vocals, then an explosion of music -- before coming back down to earth.

review_headline: A Voice as Beautiful as a Songbird
review_body: I've had the pleasure of hearing Jillian perform live and couldn't wait for her project to come out and it is finally here. All I can say it was worth the wait. I am always one to hope that the album will sound like the live performance but just enhanced a bit. It seems most singer-songwriter's projects end up sounding completely different once the producer gets ahold of it. The main instruments they have used to write the songs are all but lost in the production and other instruments have taken their place. Jillian made a wise decision in hiring a singer-songwriter himself, Chris August to help produce the album. Chris was able to add the necessary additional instrumentation and background vocals to truly enhance Jillian's sound yet still keeping the basics of her guitar and beautiful voice intact. All of these songs are great but I still think Songbird is one of the most beautiful songs I have ever heard. It is my prayer that the world will get to hear Jillian's music and that it will soothe their soul as they listen to this beautiful voice and this beautiful project.

I love how Mr. Sir starts this classic with the the intro song \\"Come Here Boy\\".... It tells the story about his origins, love, desire and addiction for Hip Hop.. Mr. Sir treats Hip Hop like she is his first love that has changed on him over the years... She(Hip Hop) has changed so much that Mr. Sir even contemplates leaving her for good, but she keeps calling him back saying \\"Come Here Boy! Brilliant! The song is so clever and haunting that I put it on the level of \\"Me and My Girlfriend\\" by Tu-Pac, and \\"I Used to Love HER\\" by Common!  I beleive Mr. Sir when he says that he swings for the fences on all of his songs in the track \\"I Am S.I.R.\\" I say this because all of the songs are excellent!  This is the first album in a long time that I could just turn on and listen all the way through without skipping a track!  The production value is incredible and extraordinary for a debut album! The featured artists on the album do an incredible job! From the hard hitting track \\"This is What You Get\\" featuring B-Royale, pretty voiced Kyra on \\"Moving On\\", and Pat-Man Jones blowing on \\"That Ain't the Truth\\" and \\"Just Admit it!\\"  Hononrable mention \\"Go Get It Girl\\" will have strip clubs on fire, and will make exotic dancers a lot of money! review_headline: Some of the Best Hip Hop out there.
review_body: I've been listening to Heath McNease for a few years now.  I randomly picked up his first album (The Heath McNease Club Meets Tonight) at Lifeway Christian Bookstores, and was instantly a fan.  I've been waiting for both of these albums for a long time, and the wait has been worth it.  Heath has a very unique sound, blending acoustic riffs with hip hop beats.  It's something I'm used to because of the first album, but also very vibrant and new.  I've listened to the entire album, and I'm enjoying it immensely.  If your a fan of either acoustic jams, or hip hop and a little bit of comedy, you've certainly scored a bulls-eye with this kid.  My favorites so far are Nerd Out, The Gun Show, and American Idle.  Grab this immediately, it deserves to be in your MP3 player.

review_headline: Great compilation album; add it to your Spanish Rock collection
review_body:
I first heard Hombres G when I was in elementary school in Panama. The song was Devuelveme a Mi Chica, which was funny, catchy, and just a great rock n' roll song. Most of their songs can be best described in that same way, whether you are talking about Venezia or Ataque de las Chicas Cocodrilos, these songs are not to be taken seriously. There are a few slow ones that are more serious and sentimental like Temblando, but really, the essence of Hombres G are the fun songs. Is this a required Spanish Rock album? For me it is because it was part of the bands that I heard growing up like Echymosis, Soda Stereo, Los Enanitos Verdes, etc. If it is for you too, this is a bargain for the number of songs you get.

The 1 star review is completely undeserved and it is obvious that the reviewer does not understand Spanish Rock. Songs don't have to be serious all the time and songs like Vitaminas by Soda Stereo, Florecita Rockera by Atercipelados, and Cerdo by Molotov are fun and it's ok that the secret to life is not within their lyrics. The most incomprehensible thing about that review is the fact that the band U2 even comes up. That right there should let you know that you should take that review with grain of salt.

If you like Spanish Rock, Hombres G is one of the classic bands that should be in your collection.

review_headline: My thoughts on "One - EP" by One Sonic Society
review_body: Contemporary Christian music, especially worship music, tends to have the habit of borrowing musical clichés and rehashing old ideas, but that doesn't necessarily mean that the music isn't respectable.  While the One EP by One Sonic Society isn't anything you've never heard before, the release boasts a very solid, developed sound.  This comes as little surprise given famed CCM producer Jason Ingram and former Delirious? members Stu G and Jon Thatcher round out the band's lineup.  Even so, the One EP offers a mature, cohesive sound that you might not expect form a debut release.    If you've ever been involved in contemporary style worship, the first thing you'll notice about \\"Our God Will Come\\" is that the intro sounds eerily similar to the main guitar riff in Tim Hughes' song \\"Happy Day\\".  Fortunately, the intro blends into the rest of the songs and isn't much a focal point.  Soft piano and subtle guitar work comprise the verses as the song wanders into a slightly more rocking chorus.  The bridge borrows the intensity of the chorus and transitions into a guitar-focused instrumental that, in turn, leads into an ending chorus.    If you're a Hillsong fan like myself, you might notice that \\"Forever Reign\\" is the single from the next Hillsong Live album, A Beautiful Exchange.  Jason Ingram of One Sonic Society co-wrote this song with Reuben Morgan of Hillsong, which is why you will see it on the One EP.  There isn't much difference between this version and the Hillsong version of \\"Forever Reign\\" that is currently on radio, other than the Hillsong version sounding very \\"live\\", as opposed to the very produced, studio sound of the One Sonic Society version.  This version also sports some super low bass frequencies that guitar/bass players and tone freaks (such as myself) will really dig.    \\"The Greatness Of Our God\\" features worshipful lyrics and a simple, sing-along melody.  Musically, it's very similar to the first two songs.  The next song, \\"Burn\\", starts at a very slow pace, but the heartfelt lyrics keep you in the moment: \\"Lord, write me into your great story. Lord, write me into your great song.  Take all I have, it's for Your glory - one day all else will be gone.\\"  The song continues to build through a bridge proclaiming, \\"Your name be glorified!\\" The song starts goes through another intense chorus before fading into a drumbeat that ends the song.    The last song, \\"Meet With Me\\", starts at a slow pace like the song before it.  The first half of the song is musically somber, while the lyrics convey a sincere, personal longing for God to meet with us.  As the first half of the song spirals down into almost silence, the second half comes into being with ambient guitar tones swelling in.  Then, with little warning, the song hits you with a MuteMath style barrage of bass and drum.  Ambient vocals and guitar filter through the sonic attack as the song ends almost as abruptly as it began.    The One EP is a strong and impressive debut release from One Sonic Society that features lyrical integrity painted over a mellow, indie-rock style soundscape.  I look forward to future releases from One Sonic Society with great anticipation.

Rock solid production, even if, okay I can't help it, I would maybe bring the drums up just a touch on most tracks :) Nice shimmering acoustic guitars especially, and refreshingly bare vocals instead of all that over-processed crap.    Very, very nice work. Some listeners who are introduced to the more popular albums of this band first are less likely to appreciate this album.  I am also a listener who first heard their mid-career albums, and I still love those, but Karelian Isthmus must be heard and judged on its own merits.  When you compare this album to a lot of the death metal made by a host of Norwegian bands (even bands making albums today), you'll realize that Amorphis had a better-layered sound.  There are bits of melodic guitar and keyboarding that are stacked very well with the heavy staccato of the guitar riffs.  You're not going to hear this as well if you're driving down the highway listening through your car stereo.  This album must be heard through headphones to be fully appreciated.  Every style of death metal vocals pleases a different taste, but these vocals are some of my favorite.  They are as excellent as the British vocalists of the best grind bands of the early 90's.  I love this album not for nostalgia--I only recently gave this one a chance. I listened to a lot of metal during the early nineties, but I missed this one somehow.  How lucky I am to have heard it at last.

Coloboma - Eternal Invisible Hospital -  Has a nice alien and ghostly feel to it.  There are no reference points or instrumentation documentation so the listener is left to their own devices.   This also has its own feel in that it isn't really comparable to anything contemporary that I've heard recently.  If I had to make a comparison, some of this would have fit nicely on the old four cassette compilation \\"Journey Into Pain\\" put out by Beast 666 Tapes out of Osaka Japan in 1989, which is a rather futile comparison as that release is just about impossible to find at this point.  Leaves question marks, which is a plus.  Not easy listening by any stretch of the imagination and danceable only under a bizarre influence.  I recommend buying the entire package rather than a track or two and I'm sure Coloboma intended it that way too.   I'll try my hand at a brief track by track synopsis and I'm sure I'm off the mark on several of them, but here goes:    1 - Arrival - Rich.  Sounds like a helicopter medivac arriving.  New patient to the trauma ward?  Nice capture of the intimidating sound of a large, nearby machine.    2 - Brass Keys I - Lots of feedback noises.  Has a watery feel to it.  Sounds like it was recorded in a large, open room.  Various indecipherable voices appear and meander.  Has a pensive feel throughout and is saturated with delay and reverb.  Kind of drips through the speakers.    3 - Cricket Happenings - Short and sweet.  Has cricket sounds and some backwards electronic processing.    4 - Stackings - More percussive than the previous tracks.  Seems to use field recordings of machines and has a female voice uttering a phrase throughout.   Sounds like it was recorded in a gymnasium.    5 - Serious Words -  Delayed voice and twangy, trebly, percussive guitar sounds.  Can't seem to decipher the words on first listen.  Words have meaning seems to be the main theme.    6 - Nipponic Yukonic Adventure - This one is harsh on the ears.  Lots of high pitched feedback sounds.  First time I heard this was in the enclosed space of my car and it was pretty distracting.  Gets into your head and rattles your brain a bit.  Has hectic sounds that seem like they emanate from a TV set viewing a horror movie as well as other media.   You will probably turn the volume down during playback of this track.  If you listen to this at loud volumes and often, you may develop hearing problems.  You can feel it in your teeth.      7 - Invisible Patient - My fave track on this release upon first listen.  Swirly loops with what sounds like a homeless man hollering out echoed pleas for a desired drink.      8 - Our Home - Poetic feel with vocals and words by Roy Moller and ringing sounds in the background.  Nicely annunciated  and ends with a drippy, watery feel to it.    9 - Sinkings - Another percussive type track.  Rattles and hisses drenched in reverb and delay.  Also has a pensive feel to it.  Builds up to a crescendo, then saunters off a bit and fades into the next track.    10- Eternal Waiting Room - Sounds like the title.  Voices and footsteps and the natural reverb sounds of the room it was recorded in with some backwards sampling.      11- MRI Confessional -  Deep vocal sounds echoing and resonating with minimal music box sounds and whispery blurts.    12 - Hypertension - Buzzing harmonics.   The most musical track on here.  Has structure and is non-linear unlike the preceding tracks as it repeats a theme that can be whistled along to.  Placed nicely before the last track as it gives a feel of some kind of resolution.    13 - Departure - The listener is transported back to the location before the arrival at the Eternal Invisible Hospital.  Effective and precise.

review_headline: This man is a comic witch-doctor, providing the best medicine in the world.
review_body: This man will weave his beautiful comical poetry through your ears and make you open up and laugh. His honest look at himself reveals someone most of us can relate to and fall in love with. It's a simple look at a man who just wanted to be an artist as a young man, and how indifferent the world was toward him because of it. Ultimately his childish innocence is beyond endearing and something I haven't seen in the comic scene since Maria Bamford. This is a brilliant CD and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone looking for some real laughs.
It is a good album.

There are three sides to Megadeth imo; songs like Holy Wars, Hook In Mouth and Tornado of Souls are are flat out perfect classic Megadeth rockers.  Others such as Train of Consequences, Symphony of Destruction and When are more \\"modern era\\" Megadeth classics. Finally tracks like The Scorpion, A Secret Place and Crush 'Em are somewhere in between.  All three of these categories have had strong hit and misses in their respective areas    Endgame fuses the best of both perfectly and is an instant Megadeth classic!!       The best way to describe Endgame is to take the whole journey of Megadeth's evolution and only filter the best of all aspects.  Combine all of this with a grandoise effort and flavor likened to Rust In Peace and you have the excellent new offering which is Endgame.    This is Megadeth's Rust in Peace 2009 and their return to excellence!!    Don't miss this one droogies!!!

review_headline: Like "Indestructible" performed by a Rancid cover band.....
review_body: I honestly don't get what happened to Rancid. \\"And Out Come the Wolves\\" was probably the best 3rd wave ska album and one of the best streetpunk albums of all time. Their albums before that (S/T, Let's Go) were equally excellent, too.     Then we get \\"Life Won't Wait\\", which wasn't particularly bad (it has some great songs) but it wasn't a punk album, which is what Rancid did best. Then, seemingly in response to criticisms that they weren't a punk band anymore, they release an absolutely dreadful and completely tuneless eponymous hardcore album in 2000 sans Hammond organ (and any sense of melody).    Then comes \\"Indestructible\\", which like \\"Life Won't Wait\\" wasn't bad and had some memorable tracks - but wasn't great either mainly because while Tim's marble mouthed warblings were fine (and in most cases, worked well) for punk music, but they don't work very well on rocksteady and reggae tracks. He can't sing, at all. It hurts the music on that album. Also, like \\"Life Won't Wait\\", but to a greater extent, at some point you have to get sick of rocksteady 1-4-5 progressions and the hammond. Some of the tracks were repetitive and not terribly original.     Then all of a sudden Rancid listened to The Clash's \\"Sandanistas\\" and their own \\"And Out Come the Wolves\\" one too many times and we received this abomination. There are borrowed riffs aplenty on this album. It's probably the least original Rancid album besides Rancid (2000). There's even the riff from Roots Radical in the intro of one of the songs. I spit out my coffee when I was driving when I heard that.     Insipid lyrics about losing faith in America are on about half the songs (Disconnected, Liberty and Freedom, Locomotive), insipid lyrics that were probably written the day of the song on others (\\"Up to No Good\\" is particularly terrible). This album's lyric sheet reads reads like generic hardcore from the Reagan/Dubya administration - so the whole thing feels a bit dated. How the folks who wrote \\"The Ballad of Jimmy and Johnny\\", \\"Dope Sick Girl\\" and \\"Rats in the Hallway\\", \\"Warsaw\\" and \\"Arrested in Shanghai\\" wrote the lyrics to this album defies all logic. Lulu's not that bad, if a tad morally sententious, but that's about it.    Oh, and then there's my biggest problem with the album - you can't hear the bass. Matt's a great basist (he's honestly one of the best rock bassists playing today) and you can't hear him. Considering he's generally playing the melody line and the guitars are playing rhythm, it's ridiculous to mix the guitars up so high in the mix. This album is mixed like a heavy metal album. Whoever mixed it (Gurewitz, I think) must've been out of his mind at the time. It makes an already monotonous album even more so when you can't hear the melody. Really, how interesting is a 1-4-5 otherwise?    The Rancid side projects like the Transplants and The Silencers are still worth a look, but I think this is the last album from the band I'm buying (I own all of them and I was looking forward to this one too). They honestly sound like they're phoning it in at this point. Nothing about the album is terrible and it sounds like \\"Indestructible\\" for the most part, but it's so consistently mediocre (lyrically, songwriting, mixing) that I felt like I was listening to the audio equivalent of a bad Xerox copy of \\"Indestructible\\".     If you're new to Rancid, buy \\"And out Come the Wolves\\" if you're interested in ska/punk and \\"Let's Go\\" or \\"Rancid\\" (1993) if you're interested in their streetpunk period. Those are 3 of the greatest albums I own. If you like their world music oriented phase, get \\"Life Won't Wait\\" or \\"Indestructible\\". Also consider checking out one of the Joe Strummer and the Mescaleros albums, and of course if you haven't already, the Clash.    This album is somthing I can really only suggest in good faith to Rancid completists.

review_headline: Not Demon Days but this is a Good  worth the purchase Album
review_body: Plastic Beach is a Good album.  It is a different album than Demon Days in that it's not as rock heavy.  This album is full of synths and harder pounding beats.  This album doesn't include an \\"O' Green World\\", my favorite Gorillaz song, but that's fine as there are many stand out songs.  I like that the rappers are respectful with no swears and they stay on Topic with the Album Theme which is well Water, Islands, Ships, etc.      My fav's:    \\"Welcome To Plastic Beach\\"  is a nice smooth jam that has Snoop Dogg who I was surprised and happy to hear.  The music has a nice sound all around form the Sythed \\"Oooohh just like that\\" to the Horns and Bass.    \\"White Flag\\" is a fun song.  It starts with a in my mind a World Beat sound, maybe Arabic sounding mixed with some drums from Brazil or something and then the beat changes and Bashy whom I've never heard of jumps in and starts rapping.  Sounds Good to me.    \\"Rhinestone Eyes\\" has 2D(Damon) sounding like I love him.  That kind of monotone sleepy voice.  Once again this song is Synth heavy which sounds great.     \\"Stylo\\" is a PERFECT song! Mos Def is my favorite rapper with a nice little verse that he repeats, 2D sounds great and Bobby Womack sounds Badass!  There isn't anything bad about this song.    \\"Super Fast Jellyfish\\" is another Fun song.  De La Soul for the Win!  Great versus and the beat is nice.  The chorus is really cool as well.  Great song!  \\"Don't Waste time...\\"    \\"Empire Ants\\" is more synth again.  Very Good sounding song here.  It starts slow and then about the middle 2D the instruments/sounds pick up a bit and Yukimi Nagano starts to sing.  She sound good.  This song is superb.  Really chill.    \\"Some Kind of Nature\\" is another song that I REALLY like.  Never heard of him but Lou Reed sounds great in this song.  I love the lyrics also.  \\"Some Kind of Nature, Some Kind of Soul, Some Kind of Mixture, Some Kind of Goal......\\".  2D is awesome again, you can hear more emotion from him in this one.  Good Songall around.  This is my, \\"Stuck in my head\\" song but in a great way.    \\"On Melancholy Hill\\" has 2D with that monotone voice against a nice sounding synth track that sounds like it was made for the theme of the album.  I don't know the name of the instrument but I've heard it before in island songs from maybe the late 80's early 90's.      \\"Broken\\" has an eerie slow sound to it with that Organ sound mixed with a shock of electricity.  It's a good song.    \\"Sweepstakes\\" is my favorite rapper again and it's a track that I was expecting to hear.  I thought Mos Def would only be on Stylo and didn't expect to see him again. Mos Def sounds good on this even more so when he does the sing songy part of the song. I love the drums in this one and it's cool when the band picks up.    \\"Plastic Beach\\", the title track and sounds good.  Not much to say here but I do like the track.    \\"Cloud of Unknowing\\" has Bobby Womack back this time he still sounds soulful like in \\"Stylo\\" but it's more toned down.  It has an eerie sound I'm going to have to go check out Bobby Womack.  I'm super impressed by him.      \\"Pirate Jet\\" is an interesting one.  I love the over powering synth in this one and the vocals if I had to visualize it kind sound like 2D is singing with a group of brainwashed Zombies and I love me some Zombies!    In Conclusion, buy it!  It doesn't have any filler material you see most albums these days.  While I do like Demon Days better I am happy with my purchase. With Demon Days it was a 1 time listen and I was hooked and with songs like \\"O' Green World\\", \\"Kids With Guns\\", \\"Feel Good Inc.\\", \\"Last Living Souls\\", \\"Dirty Harry\\", the epic \\"El Manana\\", \\"November has come\\" well damn the Majority of the disc it was super easy to love.  That's a hard disc to beat not only by Gorillaz but by anything/anyone and it's one I've been playing since I bought it day 1. With Plastic Beach it took me a twice over to catch the very essence of this one.  There are some tracks I will get stuck in my head and say \\"Ohh I feel like hearing that,\\" but it doesn't captivate me like Demon Days did.  It's a Solid album though with majority of the songs being good.  Who knows maybe after even more listens I may fall in love with it like I am with Demon Days.  Plastic Beach also left me wanting more.  I remember hearing back when Demon Days was out that it would just be a trilogy.  I sure hope not.  I want more Gorillaz!

review_headline: The last Rod Stewart album I bought
review_body:
Every artist that you ever really liked had that one album that first knocked you out. And given enough time, they had that one album that stopped your fandom in its tracks. \\"Smiler\\" was the latter for me.

Based on some obsequious review in either Creem or Hit Parader I added \\"Smiler\\" to my Rod Stewart collection. And on paper it sounded good. I was a big Elton John fan at the time so how could the Elton John/Bernie Taupin contribution \\"Let Me Be Your Car\\" not be a home run? (Sadly, it turned out to be a throwaway that even an Elton John fan couldn't excuse.)

No, \\"Smiler\\" wasn't destitute, it was merely substandard compared to the monster albums that Rod had delivered up to that point. The highlight? Rod can't go wrong with Sam Cooke. \\"Twisting the Night Away\\" was a hit from the \\"Never a Dull Moment\\" album, and the cover here of \\"Bring It On Home To Me\\" eclipses the Animals' rendition of that same standard. Rod makes it his own.

Two of the songs that clock in under two minutes are instrumental interludes, following the pattern set by Rod's classic album, \\"Every Picture Tells A Story\\". They're pleasant but they're less full-fledged tracks and more for freshening the palate prior to the next song. You could really consider this album to have 10 songs rather than 12.

Chuck Berry's \\"Sweet Little Rock and Roller\\" is right up Rod's alley but for some reason it's always been one of those tunes that would sound great live, and would be welcome on a box set, but perhaps if Rod had recorded this with the Faces it would sound less stiff.

As I listen to these samples 35 years later some of the songs sound better than I remember. \\"Farewell\\" and McCartney's \\"Mine For Me\\" in particular may have been overlooked gems, or perhaps songs that a callow teenager simply couldn't fully appreciate at the time. \\"Girl From the North Country\\" doesn't replace Dylan's original, but who could complain considering Rod's subsequent output?

On the whole \\"Smiler\\" seemed like an album phoned in by an artist on autopilot. He'd had a few big albums so he could afford to toss off a contractual obligation tide-me-over before delivering another big one. For me it was sufficiently disappointing that I never bought another Rod Stewart album. Then again, given Rod's output since this album, I'd be more than happy if he returned to even this standard. Sure beats covers of \\"Sometimes When We Touch\\", doesn't it?lbum phoned in by an artist on autopilot. The song by Curt Smith featuring Zoë Keating is a finely woven mix of modern and traditional instrumentation wth expressive and expansive compositional motifs. As the Rock genre reaches into the 21st Century seasoned listeners being introduced to a new song can often find it like reaching into a memory or a feeling established by some past time when music brought a new emotion to life. Within or outside the legacy of Tears For Fears, the open and sensitive listener will find several touches of the familiar mixed with the new in Curt Smith's \\"All Is Love\\".   If permitted to bring our suitcases of musical pasts as listeners with Curt Smith, we recognize a fine thoughtful moment distinct with self reflection opens in the lyrics, \\"Look what you've done...\\". The expression hangs with tones of regret in passing moment or past contrition. This familiar touchstone comes forward to remind the listener our childhoods are always with us. We react to the statement as though it were a question. Now as adults, many of us as parents, a reflexive \\"What have we done?\\" comes to mind and the suggestion to \\"look\\".   In understanding the beginning of Curt Smith within Tears For Fears, the question remain the same, how are making life better for another generation? What have we done when faced within the cycle of parent to child to the issue of the upbringing, the shaping of another life?    The introduction opens with delicate pensive vocals set against the cello of Zoë Keating and strikes a classical tone that never really dips into melancholy but rather a mild dissonant introspection and the glances of our human foibles. As the piece unfolds we find moments of questions that confront us, the renown reminders of humanity sewn into many songs either from Smith or Tears For Fears in whole. Then the piece reaches out with a warm chorus. A complex sting arrangement reaching back into the oeuvre of TFF as certain touches reminiscent of Lennon and McCartnery chord progressions have settledinto the world around us. Reminders of who has come before us as artists and musicians -a reverb from that past that continues to touch lives, ensconced here and other arrangements with respect and dignity of our origins of a collective musical consciousness.   \\"Love for everyone\\" becomes a lyrical theme that repeats not with romantic limitations but the wish for a world where the love from homes in harmony will also bring a world closer to harmony. A psychological motif clearly familiar from the earliest messages within the legacy of Tears For Fears brought forward in this piece by Smith.   The really unique thing about this piece for me is the way the electronics and signal processing tilt and sway with contrasting textures to the acoustical elements of the cello, piano and orchestral parts. The modern, the now is still given thought and attention for those of us listening for \\"pet sounds\\". The piece is beautifully arranged and a sense of time of this creation is somehow not lost in the track time itself. Clearly, the thoughtful moments over the span that this creation came to life arrive with a sense of attention to detail with the larger, longer questions of how to give a piece such as this a full, rich, yet buoyant and poignant emotional package are met.  I as a listener feel only a sense of chagrin that this single is not the seemingly the preview of a larger body of work treated in this same manner of artfulness. May an album be forthcoming. Regards and for one and all that had a hand in the making and especially the featured talent of Zoë Keating.

Accomplished and Ambitious?  You betcha!   Songs in English, Latin, Spanish and French, no less.  Fearless in depth and breadth of choices.  Orchestras, choirs, slow rhythms, fast tempos and in-between. At the core of every song, arising with rich, gorgeous clarity and crisp, sharp definition out of the surrounding music is David Archuleta's velvety, smoky tenor.    Every song speaks volumes.  My top songs (and they change priority every time I listen):    What Child Is This - Pure genius.  Genuine, flowing seemingly from the center of Mr. Archuleta's heart and faith.  \\"This, this, is Christ the King...Whom shepherds guard and angels sing.\\" Vulnerable.  Authentic.  Tender.  STUNNING. And then there are the vocals, the voice, the talent -- but those are secondary to the purity and beauty of the message he delivers.    Ave Maria - This prayer on the album is a rare and unexpected gift.  The Infinite.  God.  Jesus.  Holy Mary, Mother of God. Life.  Love.  To be among Angels.  His vocalization of  \\"Amen\\" is a tsunami of faith.  A live performance could level mountains, make angels faint and demon weep.     O Holy Night - Soaring into the heavens and beyond.  Massive love. The Universal One. That last verse is simply gorgeous: \\"Noel, Noel...O night, O night divine.  Noel, Noel, O night, O night divine.\\"       And, then, there is Pat-A-Pan. Mysterious. Edgy.  A march.  \\"Tu-re-lu-re-lu, pat-a-pat-a-pan.\\"  David's voice giving us the sound of the drum, pat-a-pan, and the fife (small flute), tu-re-lu-re-lu, that the shepherds played to celebrate the birth of Jesus.  I suspect reams will be written about this song, especially the last sixty seconds.    The ceiling of the Sistine Chapel flashes through my mind when I hear the magnificent vocals and melodic interpretations with this collection of songs.  These are songs that touch ones soul.

Brain Trust  After dropping its vocalist, local favorite Left Brain continue to exist as an instrumental metal trio, to the delight of its fan base.  -  By Sane Farias - Local iQ Magazine     Albuquerque band Left Brain is living, local proof that striking originality, flawless musical textures and a refusal to concede to conventional music approaches are not just illusory anecdotes of the epitomized act. For nearly five years, the group has remained of the city's most favored outfits and after recently parting ways with former-vocalist Tristin Rogers, Left Brain has chosen to stick to a fully instrumental approach, a risky but practical decision that will surely pay off.  \\"We have been 'vocal-less' for a good part of the year.\\" said guitarist John Allen in a recent interview with Local iQ.  \\"We decided to continue playing music (after splitting with Rogers), acting as an instrumental band, and that takes either stupidity or the drive to continue playing.  The audiences have taken well to it, so that's why we've continued to go forth with this album.\\"   After receiving so much praise from audiences, opting to maintain a \\"vocal-less\\" sound seems like the most logical idea. And at this point, their credible innovation shines.  Now, with the release of its third album, Solipsism, Left Brain takes a new philosophical, inner-self seeking approach, which prompts a story-like feel throughout each track.  The aim of the album, according to Allen, is a therapeutic, intense experience of life energies and, \\"a deep investigation of an inner emotional world.\\"     Although it is not easy to categorize Left brain into a specific assembly of genres, it does possess a number of elements that help describe the music.  When one thinks of modern metal, the notion of constant screaming seems to surface before anything else, but the progressively tangible work of Left Brain sparks a psychedelic feel complemented by a bi-polar mix of emotions.  \\"The songs on the album are often stories unfolding, situations arising - sometimes going from bad to worse - but not without the expression of some sort of resolution, catharsis or lesson learned.\\" Clifford said.      After several lineup changes, the current members of Left Brain include Allen, Bassist Michael \\"Dr. Thunda\\" Clifford and drummer Giann Rubio.  Together, they have solidified their place in the local music scene, having garnered two New Mexico Music Awards, numerous nominations and recognition in Weekly Alibi's Best of Burque 2007 - second place for \\"Best Metal Band\\" and third place for \\"Best New/Emerging Band.\\"    The trio plans to release and promote Solipsism in a way that will make it more accessible to everyone. Since the availability of music today is so convenient, and nearly anyone can obtain an album by purchasing it or not, Left brain has decided to ship different tracks around for promotion, even if the track only contains on instrument.     \\"An idea that we want to do is to actually get the individual tracks out there for people to grab, so you can download all the drum or bass tracks just by themselves.\\" Allen said.  \\"That will be a little more of an incentive for people to just share the music and see what it's like to hear it without all the different layers.\\"     Left Brain will release its album on March 27th at Launchpad, and continue to promote in any effective way necessary.      \\"We're going to produce a limited run of hard-copy CDs.\\" Clifford said. \\"And then, from there on, we're going to focus mainly on web page distribution.\\"     The word solipsism is defined as, \\"The belief that the only thing somebody can be sure of is that he or she exists.\\" This is a strong message that only devoted and talented musicians could produce without the use of lyrics.  The title of the album sums up a general idea of the type of music Left Brain has produced - something even French philosopher Rene' Descartes could be fond of.     According to Clifford, \\"One possible interpretation (of solipsism) is that you are truly alone in a world made of simply your own projections - yourself.\\"

One can certainly find faults in John Wayne's huge 1960 production of \\"The Alamo\\", but Dimitri Tiomkin's rousing score is one of the film's major assets. Whether bittersweet (\\"The Green Leaves Of Summer\\"), whimsical (\\"Here's To The Ladies\\"), inspiring (Davy Crockett's Speech about \\"Republic\\", narrated by Wayne, himself), or rousing (\\"Charge Of Santa Anna / Death Of Davy Crockett / The Final Assault\\"), Tiomkin's mastery of musically defining key moments onscreen has never been matched. The 'epic' film, by definition, requires a huge canvas, and \\"The Alamo\\" is monumental, visually; Tiomkin gives a musical grandeur to the movie, as well as providing a very necessary 'pace', essential for a long narrative.

\\"The Alamo (Soundtrack)\\" is classic in the very best sense of the word, with Tiomkin at the peak of his skills; if you love film music that can lift you, each time you listen to it, look no further!

review_headline: Refreshing New Sound by a New Young Artist
review_body: The collection of songs on this album are quite interesting. When I first heard them I immediately wondered what life events inspired the artist. When I visited the artist's web site I had my answers. After that, I developed a much greater appreciation for the themes. The tunes range from the light up beat I Walk for Two to the dark introspective Save My Soul. As a singer-songwriter Marcus Vaughn really grabbed my attention with each new tune. When you go to the various links on his web site you find out that he did all of this in his home studio and he did all the music, voices and production himself. Some of the backing sounds in this album are genius. What I really liked most about this album is simply that it is genuine. When you get done listening to it, you want to listen again because you know you heard something that you think you heard but you can't pinpoint where it was. This is true singer-songwriter stuff in its raw form. The sound stands up to all types of playback and I must admit, I was singing along on most songs after I had heard them a few times. I hear his musical influences. This is very refreshing music and I look forward to the next release.
The singer is not Bob Seger, and it's not a very good imitation.  Don't waste your money.

review_headline: Angsty radio pop, Stonesish blues and twangy Americana
review_body: Hollis Brown lead singer Mike Montali is hard to pin down. He sounds a bit like the Black Crowes' Chris Robinson, a bit like Neil Young, a bit like the Gin Blossoms' Robin Wilson, and a bit like Robert Plant. He's got the high edginess (and falsetto) with which they each create emotional tension, and though the band's guitar, bass, drums, organ and harmonica share a `70s rock `n' roll vibe with the Crowes, Zeppelin, and Blossoms, they add twangy blues and country roots that really belie their urban Queens upbringing. The album opens with the exuberant \\"Show Love\\" and follows with the roiling guitars and stinging lyrical rebuke of \\"Walk on Water.\\" The songs track through Stones-styled rock, ambling Americana, broken-hearted country twang, shuffling sing-a-longs and angsty pop. The group's melodic hooks will stick in your head for days, and Montali's voice is memorable, whether singing up-tempo rockers or slowing to surprise with the Stax-styled soul of \\"Don't Wanna Miss You.\\" One can only assume Hollis Brown polished these tunes in numerous live gigs, as their self-assurance in the studio translates to terrific passion and swagger on disc. [©2009 hyperbolium dot com]

I've always felt that the comparative lack of attention received by Dwike Mitchell and Willie Ruff, despite their travels to South America and Russia (they were apparently more foreign to American ears) and a book written about them by William Zinsser, was due to their academic affiliations and absence from sessions featuring major players (Willie's name would show up on some orchestra sessions as a French horn player, but that was about it). Despite owning three albums by them, I don't think I've ever met anyone who has heard of them let alone heard them.  So the discovery of this date with Dizzy Gillespie comes as a pleasant surprise.  Like most of the duo's recordings, it's no longer available in any sort of album format--analog or digital--but Amazon has thoughtfully preserved the tracks for downloading.  Diz is in excellent form, frequently recalling the pre-1960s dominating force that he had been, both as a trumpet player and a musical innovator.  Unfortunately, his early recording of Strayhorn's \\"Chelsea Bridge,\\" though a masterpiece, is not to be found among the downloadable tracks of that tune.  So it's availability here, even if with scaled-down instrumentation, is all the more heartening.

I write this with the full knowledge that my opinion will change after I hear the whole EP and also that I will be BUYING the EP pretty much immediately. Why? Because it's NIN related and I'm an idiot. Not that those two things are mutually exclusive, but you get my point.

I really dig triphop downbeat electronica stuff like Portishead and even Supreme Beings of Leisure kinda fits the genre, so this is a decent track. I guess my issue here is that this is Trent Reznor. First, any fan will tell you he just recycled a piano riff from \\"Right Where It Belongs\\" in the chorus of \\"A Drowning,\\" but more importantly, I really hoped that something \\"not NIN\\" by Reznor would sound..... not like NIN. This is so similar that it's impossible to NOT compare them, which in a way isn't really fair if he's trying for something different. But so far, he hasn't succeeded - it's not different enough. Now, if HTDA was an acoustic group that had solos played on the saw and Mariqueen did some throat singing...... okay, I probably wouldn't like it, but I'd at least applaud the effort to do something totally different. I'm not saying I don't or won't like HTDA, but it's (currently) not as good as Nine Inch Nails and I've not yet heard a reason that they shouldn't be compared.

Jan and Lorraine were good friends of mine from Detroit when the original ABC Records LP album (ABC-691) was recorded in 1969. review_headline: I never knew what the song was about
review_body:
\\"Touch My Hand\\" is the third single from David Archuleta's debut CD. The song is about a singer who falls in love with a girl in the audience: I see the sparkle of a million flashlights/ A wonderwall of stars/ But the one that's shining out so bright/ Is the one right where you are. He wants to keep singing so that the girl will stay: Can't let the music stop/ Can't let this feeling end/ Cause if I do it'll all be over/ I'll never see you again. The chorus features him reaching out to her: Trying to reach out to you/ Touch my hand/ Reach out as far as you can/ Only me, only you, and the band/ Trying to reach out to you/ Touch my hand. Whether or not he gets the girl is left to the imagination.

While the lyrics and teen-pop sound are hardly novel, the song is very catchy and upbeat; I'm sure it will sound good on the radio. Also, the piano intro is lovely, and David's vocals are strong. After \\"Crush\\" was such a hit (#2 in the U.S.), David faltered with his second single, \\"A Little Too Not over You.\\" That song sounded very radio-friendly, but didn't even make the Top 100, bubbling under the chart at #114. I'm not sure whether \\"Touch My Hand\\" will re-establish David on the radio; I would have selected another song from the CD, \\"My Hands,\\" as the next single. However, \\"Touch My Hand\\" is a good song, and hopefully David's appearance on the April 22nd episode American Idol will help.

Listening to Slugabed for the first time brings back the memories of hearing the complexity of Squarepusher or the insanity of Venetian Snares who, incidentally, released his sweet venom on Planet Mu as well. But the music of this 19 year old, Bath (UK) based producer, Greg Feldwick, is not the broken rhythms of breakcore or drill'n'bass. It is a slow-paced wobble through the square edged 8-bit world of two-dimensional cardboard trees and bass-growling monsters. At times comical and playful, at times nasty and evil, the sound of Slugabed doesn't commit to classification - instead it begs for a genre of its own. Going back to my mentioning of the complexity of sound with which I was struck upon the first listening of Feldwick's six-track EP, the thick layers of sound and fractured beats take the listeners' time to fully unwrap and appreciate. The sluggish rhythm trolls through an alley of bit-crushed chords, often changing direction of the syncopated step. Closer to the sound of Harmonic 313 then any other dub-step producer, the raw production re-wires the bleeps and lasers of arcade-boxes and turns them into dance tracks that skipped the 80s to time travel to 2010. And if you listen closely, you will hear that behind the sharp and distorted hard-panned sounds, hide the beautiful melodies, as sung from the land of The Uglydolls. Slugabed's debut 12\\", Gritsalt, appeared in May of 2009 on Ramp Recordings. That summer, he followed it with a split with Coco Bryce, titled MYOR 02 on a brand new Dutch MYOR label. Another 12\\", Superphreak, appeared on Stuffrecords. And finally, Slugabed got picked up by the beloved Planet Mu. Welcome. This is your new home. Now get comfortable and bring us a full-length.

review_headline: Dark Ambient music is not always "sleep-inducing".Ugh!
review_body:
To the 1 star reviewer: just because TFBS doesn't put you to sleep that doesn't mean the album sucks. Not everyone makes dark ambient music with the thought that it will relax the listener; in fact, I'd say that very few ambient artists do that. They want an active listener just as much as anyone else. The thing is that most people can't see the forest thru the trees when it comes to this type of music. There's a smorgasborg of entertaining sounds that fit well against the soundscapes here.And seriously? You're calling a DCK album \\"metal\\" music? Uh...suuure. And \\"goth\\"? Maybe if you plan on using it as Halloween music, but this ain't no Midnight Syndicate--not by a long shot.

Think of this album as \\"Tunnel\\" meets \\"Disembodied\\" with elements of \\"Monolith\\" and the black album. You might not be able to use it as a sleep aid, but there is a wealth of great adventure to be had on this musical score to a Death Cube K rampage.

Why do I still continue to listen to Depeche after having bought Construction Time Again back in 1983? Because I find even their failures interesting, and \\"Wrong\\" is certainly no failure. At first it felt like an up-tempo version of one of their dirges like Condemnation, but after repeated listens I found the tone really interesting: it's ostensibly one of their \\"oh-woe-is-me\\" songs like Walking in My Shoes, but with an angry snarl. How many bands would make their lead single for a new album an electronic Calvinistic hymn about never finding grace. It's not easy on the ears, but it is interesting.

Written by Gavin Williams In a secluded temple a young monk sits drawing self-portraits. A winter draft from under the door prompts h...im to pull his robe tighter. Drawing careful lines, lost in his method and to time, the monk can see he is using up his last piece of drawing charcoal. He searches the room for many minutes to find more but without success. Placing his only stool in front of a closet space, he stands upon it. He reaches toward the back of the top shelf to find two objects. One, a small tin of his sought after charcoal. The other is an old acoustic guitar. He returns with both objects to his place on the floor. After setting the charcoal aside he then turns his attention to the guitar. The instrument is well worn but through love and not misuse. The monk delicately begins to tune it and notices the simple etched inscription \\"SPRING\\" at the top. Although the sound from the guitar is nostalgic the tones breathe a new life. So begins Anitya... After absorbing a gentle introduction we are re-introduced to the voice of Tully Mackay-Tisbert, and become acquainted with our immediate surroundings: lofty homes surrounded by woodland with trees exhibiting signs reading \\"Kapu\\". Contrary to the title's meaning, \\"Kapu\\" is the singer's prevalent invitation to disregard warnings and stray to places others won't normally venture. These places, and sounds, are new to the listener, but also being freshly unearthed by the artist. There still remains an essence of familiarity in both music and voice. These are two solid branches of a nearby tree. One is extended for us to cling to as lyrics from the overcome singer suggest woe and truth. The other branch is pointing the way for us onto a new landscape. A volley of strums and harmonics accompany simple yet just lyrics in \\"Don't Ask Me To Stay\\". This song is pure Tully and is the first tree to have the initials \\"TMT\\" engraved into it to mark the start of the journey. From this point on there are two paths through the forest. The first one, hidden, leads a listener to embrace the conviction of the singer's intentions in the song. The second, and more visible, leaves them hastily swept up in awe of the guitar arrangement. Although able to be appreciative of the artist's work, the later will perhaps have greater difficulty navigating the remainder of the journey. To the listener's fortune the paths intertwine and converge. Continuing along the path it is evident that Tully has guided listener to a grass clearing with a single large and resilient tree. Out-stretched branches appear to extend once again to the listener but in actuality, the limbs are forced to hold up the weight of the World, though with a yearning to let go. \\"As A Tree I Give Up\\" is a song caked in rich dark soil allowing the artist and album to grow. The arrangement for Guitar also allows for the nurturing of two more organic companions. First is Drum, cast away from a depleted drum-circle; Drum has found a new intimate setting to develop. Second to arrive is Guitar's closest friend, Flute. Flute traces the steps taken by Guitar but still manages to find his own liberty. Also mentioned in this song is the artist's desire for the solace of a temple. It is quest that takes unsuspected turns throughout the album. Before venturing further, the listener is given the opportunity to rest after an eye-opening early portion to the travel. The artist, at this time, feels compelled to involuntarily play an impromptu song from whatever lies deep within him. Through \\"Web Stretch\\" it becomes clearer that the path Tully is on is no path at all, and the one we have been following with him may not exist either. It is wandering. The journey ahead and behind are in flux and so are we. For this moment though, the comfort lies in the grace of this candid themed interlude-like song. By the time of \\"The World Alive\\" Tully is beginning to wrestle with the notion of attachment. He leaves the tranquil setting of the clearing by the tree and delves into the nearest brush. The listener can still follow him from a distance but will only manage to see him scramble up a mountain. This song pulls at vines in the singer's core. After establishing there is no real path, the singer begins to roam to detach from dependency of others and even distance himself from the listener. His way is his own and this is to be respected. Still, the song delivers tactful strings and flute to accompany the wishfully fleeting singer. From far away the listener can see the singer alone atop a mountain. With space of his own, Tully can meditate. Through the title track \\"Anitya\\", Tully finds himself pondering the changes he can make for others and changes he has made on his journey. The haunting musical backdrop echoes the passing of seasons. In the extended instrumental outro the guitar from \\"Spring\\" has retuned accompanied by a summer flute, autumn pipa, and winter drums. Seasons turn into years as Tully observes and considers the steady transformations all around him from the mountain. To a slow rambling guitar, Tully makes his way back down the mountain. At its base is a gravel path upon which he encounters a solitary dog approaching from the opposite direction. In \\"Stray\\" Tully identifies with his new yet temporary canine friend. Further along he acknowledges a less distant listener by relaying his thoughts of his current predicament. The steady musical accompaniment acts as a clear path to aide the singer along. The melody remains subdued enough to be reminder that although the path is clear, it still has an unknown origin or resolution thus causing the Tully to continue on his journey. A cool evening approaches as Tully stops to notice a breach in the tree line exhibiting to him a not-so-distant oceanfront. A delicate progression of guitar and harmony sings out across the openness and suggests a reddening, passionate sky as the sun begins to set whilst reflecting in the water, a \\"Rarity\\". The idea of the beauty we discover in our lives becomes a sombre notion due to the realization that like everything else, these instances are impermanent. The singer makes a soulful attempt to hold on to illuminated instances of love, nature or just being. Knowing the truth about these rarities makes one hold on tight to savour before continuing on. A cloudy night has crept overhead down by the ocean. A drum strikes up a campfire and a sleepless artist reflects on the steps that have taken him to this point. A half-burnt stick by Tully's side becomes a drawing instrument for use on rocks and sand. \\"I'm Drawing Monks\\" allows Tully to robustly express his revelations of the journey to this point. His emotions flare with the embers of the fire. He strains to see the familiarity of himself as portrayed within the fire, the wet sand and the ocean. Fits of crescendo increasing the sense of dissatisfaction become somewhat reduced by a moderate spell pipa to balance the sensations. Clouds dissipate to reveal the moon and constellations above. A spring breeze brought in by the sweeping ocean replaces the fading heat from the remaining fire's glow. There is comfort in \\"Waiakea\\". Pleased, Tully finds the joy in playing his lute under the moon to indulge in recovered sounds of \\"Spring\\" and \\"Anitya. Tully sings to the listener with genuine contentment rather than contempt for the natural impermanence of life. He makes no attempt now to hold on to the night but lets it go with a resolution to enjoy its passing. Tully has found his hallowed ground, his temple. In retrospect he sees it everywhere and in all the advances he has made through the landscape. He accepts the Anitya in all and understands that change is inevitable and beautiful. ...In the sanctity of the temple, the young monk's hands begin to tire. Placing the guitar lovingly aside he then selects his charcoal. Drawing careful lines, the monk completes another self-portrait. For a moment he has humble air accomplishment before preparing a fresh piece of paperto start yet another interpretation of himself.

Caveat - I am not a heavy metal connoisseur (read, I don't much like it). It seems mostly angry, non-musical (very limited chords used, little to no melodic line or harmony, much the same throughout a track, generally angry violent attitudes expressed in a gravelly cookie-monster singing style); however, I shall try to describe these as objectively as I can so you can decide what you like. A few tracks are what I would call Rock Hard and/or Rock Metal (which I do like) and the rest what I call Metal Heavy (which I apply to songs which have the characteristics noted above). Is that Thrash Metal?

On this sampler, I found the production values generally very good - the singers could be clearly heard, and the separate instruments distinguished, even on the live tracks. Most lyrics were reasonably understandable. I shall tell you in stars what *I* rated them for my own library (which may be useful to you if you can gauge your taste against mine - oh and * means it's damaged, ** means that I don't want to hear it again...ever - though my son might be interested - maybe). Oh, and when I say 'melodic' I don't mean pop, I mean that it sounds as if one actually needs talent and is changing chords and choosing which strings to play to create different notes that a person could hum as a tune as opposed to sliding slightly up and down the frets while strumming all the strings as fast as possible.

1. Rock Metal - Has Metal Heavy sections interspersed with more melodic Rock Hard sections. Philosophical lyrics - What do you fear? Fear is your God. ****

2. Rock Metal - A great deal of cursing. Basic message, I hate your world so I'll burn it all down. The main melodic line at the beginning, I swear I have heard in several other metal-type songs (including at 3:05 of Track 4). Has some decent melodic guitar work half-way on. Mostly Metal Heavy. ***

3. Rock Metal - Another angry one. A lot of very fast guitar strumming with little variation in the melody or chords. A bit rough in the vocals, but not totally cookie monster. Mostly Metal Heavy. ***

4. Rock Hard - Self-affirming, look to yourself, you can solve it, message. Melodic guitar counterpoints against base line. Backing vocals harmonize. Fast rocker. ****

5. Rock Hard - Lyrics warn about social injustice. Good deal of melodic guitar work. Sung with emotional emphasis and moments of backing harmonizing. Medium speed. ****

6. Metal Heavy - Fast drums, guitar very repetitive of usually 4 very nearby chord groups, cookie monster lyrics, very angry. Could barely listen to this one all the way through. **

7. I don't know... Metal Rap? If this is a 'song'... um, well, nope. Might make a good alarm clock sound if you can't wake up. Certainly has energy. Band screaming Wake up & audience repeats, some instruments doing something noisy - ends very abruptly. **

8. Metal Heavy - Bass or guitar carries structure but not what I would call a melody. Lyrics sound like cookie monster with a very sore throat pretending to be a demon under a pile of dirty laundry. I didn't understand a word. Another very hard for me to listen to. But hey, many other people like this kind of thing. Medium beat. **

9. Rock Metal - Busy guitars, strong chords, some heavy 'strumming' with fast drumming. Several voices together almost harmonizing. A bit hard to understand the lyrics. Has a saxophone solo in the middle (and some synthesizer throughout). Didn't quite 'pull together' into a coherent whole for me. More like loud angry mood music? Lone singer later using cookie monster voice. ***

10. Can't Say - Strong bass opening riff joined by band and several unintelligible cookie monster voices. At 0:37, my download turned to the deep buzzing sound of heavy electronic interference and remained that way for the rest of the track. Don't know if my copy got messed up, or if this is some sort of very odd artistic statement (which is possible, as at the very end, for the last second, the sound changed to a brief, different sound in the right channel - maybe a guitar chord). In either case, the opening wasn't enough to encourage my to download it again. *

11. Alternative Folk - Totally and completely different from all the other tracks. Male & female harmonizing with an acoustic 'buzzy' steel string guitar. Pleasant melody, good voices, 'rough' guitar gives it a 'cafe' quality. **** However, this track has NO place in this collection (unless the sole qualification is metal strings on ones guitar). Did my download go nuts? Maybe?

It only took 35 years for guitarist Frank Jones to pool his musical knowledge and experience to record his own music, but if you look at those years as practice for IT'S ALL ABOUT ME, then his patience has paid off. Self taught to the music of artists such as the Ventures and Duane Eddy, instrumental music remains his passion and every note on the EP exudes that passion and hard-earned talent. \\"K.B.\\" is light-hearted and mellifluous, while \\"Strat-o-sphere\\" takes a more upbeat path and showcases Jones' technical prowess on his instrument. Elegant and picturesque, \\"Slo-cruise\\" will warm your heart. \\"Starways\\" is perfectly titled; it is bright and vivid and stands out for all the see (hear). It was quite a while in the making, but if you take some time to make it all about Frank Jones, you truly won't be disappointed. ~BETH LEWIS

I've loved U2 for a long time. My first guitar teacher was a child of U2's power years and knew every song they had recorded through Pop (which is a testament to how diehard he was) Consequently, I learned to play many of their great songs, and somewhere the guitar transcriptions of Joshua Tree are on a bookshelf in my basement. I write this to explain that this review is coming from a long time fan, not a hater. But I listened to this record streaming online and I will not be purchasing it. U2 has put together an album of lackluster songs that sound a lot like ones they wrote 20 years ago. The lyrics are uninspiring. Bono has smoked away his voice (which is particularly evident on the title track). The Edge doesn't do much with the guitar that's all that creative. The production seems to try to make U2 sound like most of the other commodity-based rock groups around these days instead of a timeless, even legendary band on par with the Beatles, the Stones and Radiohead. When All You Can't Leave Behind came out, it appeared that U2 might have been bouncing back to a steady stream of great records on par with Joshua Tree, Achtung Baby and Zooroopa. It has since proven to be one of the biggest musical psychs in recent history. Give this record a good hard listen and ask yourself \\"Will I still be listening to this with reverence in five years?\\" I did and determined it was mostly disposable. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have to weep and gnash my teeth while clutching my copy of Joshua Tree to my chest.

review_headline: Sexy Singer with a Wicked Wit
review_body: Lene Alexandra is a sort of Cinderella story, in many ways; discouraged in her pursuit of a singing career at an early stage, she became a model instead and only later befriended a co-star in a reality programme who owned his own music label. She worked for him for free, with the ultimate desire to make her own music.    Welcome to Sillycone Valley is the product of that dedication, and it's quite a gem. All of the songs are incredibly catchy and easy to dance to, with the lyrics being the greatest delight. Lene herself has quite a wicked wit, even self-deprecating at times (the prime example being the album's headliner 'My Boobs are Okay'), but always entertaining. The album is unabashedly silly -- it's in the title after all -- but the songs are all actually good and fun to listen to, which is really the most important thing in music.    There are several parts where the music tries new and different things, several tracks that aren't afraid to do something unique, and that makes the album more interesting: there's so much variety on Welcome to Sillycone Valley. It's especially noteworthy in that the album itself has a certain concept, a certain feel about it, but it doesn't limit itself to a certain sound or constrain itself within a particular sphere.    I unhesitantly recommend Welcome to Sillycone Valley, a delight from beginning to end. You'll find yourself humming each and every song after hearing it. It's rare to find such a completely enjoyable album, especially in this day and age, but for anyone who likes fun, catchy, danceable songs, Welcome to Sillycone Valley is a rare gem.
